Subject: [UFORL] List 'housekeeping rules'

Confirmation of the list 'housekeeping rules':

1. The UFO Research List [UFORL] mailing list, operated via
'Yahoo! Groups', is open to subscription from those who advocate
and adopt a consistent, scientific appraisal of purported 'UFO'
related evidence. The remit encompasses associated topics which
may be relevant, such as 'black projects', or 'ball lightning',
etc.

The list currently has over 130 subscribers.


2. Subscribers must provide their full name and agree that
periodically, confirmation of all subscribers' names [e-mail
addresses will not be disclosed] can be posted to the list for
the benefit of other members.

Details of new subscribers may also be announced separately.


3. The list archives are *PUBLIC* and the forum is *NOT* intended
to enable secure discussions, although due copyright applies to
any subscriber's contributions. Particular care should be taken
when posting material which may be copyrighted. A suggested
approach would be, 'if in doubt, leave it out'.


4. The UFORL 'home page' is located on the Internet at URL:

http://groups.yahoo.com/group/UFORL

This provides access to the public list postings, plus the
addresses for subscribe or unsubscribe requests.


5. The list address for mail is:

UFORL@yahoogroups.com

With some e-mail software, using 'reply' may not send a response
to the list, it will be sent ONLY to the address shown in the
'From' heading, which is the person who sent the mail.

It's recommended that the destination of your reply is therefore
checked before sending and should always be as above.
6. The standard mailing list code applies and messages should be
unformatted, in plain text and no more than 65 characters in
length.

If replying to mail, only the relevant section(s) should be
quoted, not the entire original message.


7. E-mail attachments, especially large graphics files, should
*NEVER* be sent to the list - please contact the list owner if
you wish to make such material available.


8. Postings should not be anonymous and the sender's name is
expected to be contained either in the heading or signature.


9. Strict 'Netiquette' rules apply and all postings are expected
to be cordial, ensuring the list is always a pleasant
environment.

For further information see:

http://www.pbs.org/uti/guide/netiquette.html


Any related problems or queries should be addressed to:

UFORL-owner@yahoogroups.com


James Easton,
List Owner.

Subject: [UFORL] Roswell Evidence

For convenience, the following background is taken from an old
'bulletin board' text file which summarised some of the, then,
'Roswell' evidence:

Melvin Brown's Daughter

[Sergeant Melvin Brown was a cook at Roswell AAF in 1947. One
day, he was called out to help guard material retrieved from the
Foster Ranch. His daughter Beverly was interviewed by Stanton
Friedman in 1989.]

When we were young, he used to tell us stories about things that
had happened to him when he was young. We got to know those
stories by heart and would all say together, "Here we go again."

Sometimes, but not too often, he used to say that he saw a man
from outer space. That used to make us all giggle like mad. He
said he had to stand guard duty outside a hangar where a crashed
flying saucer was stored, and that his commanding officer said,
"Come on, Brownie, let's have a look inside." But they didn't
see anything because it had all been packed up and [was] ready to
be flown out to Texas.

He also said that one day all available men were grabbed and that
they had to stand guard where a crashed disc had come down.
Everything was being loaded onto trucks, and he couldn't
understand why some of the trucks had ice or something in them.
He did not understand what they wanted to keep cold. Him and
another guy had to ride in the back of one of the trucks, and
although they were told that they could get into a lot of trouble
if they took in too much of what was happening, they had a quick
look under the covering and saw two dead bodies, alien bodies.

We really had to giggle at that bit. He said they were smaller
than a normal man, about four feet, and had much larger heads
than us, with slanted eyes, and that the bodies looked yellowish,
a bit Asian-looking. We did not believe him when we were kids,
but as I got older, I did kind of believe it. Once I asked him
if he was scared by them, and he said, "Hell no, they looked
nice, almost as though they would be friendly if they were
alive."
[END]


I understand Kevin Randle and Don Schmitt also published details
of their discussions with Melvin Brown's Daughter, Beverly Bean.
I spoke with Beverly in 1995 or 1996 concerning the 'alien
autopsy' footage [she was most concerned it was a hoax which
clearly didn't depict the 'creatures' which her late father
described].

That aside, there was an interview with, if I recall, both of Sgt
Brown's daughters and which featured in a video - possibly a UK
production for a TV documentary. I have a copy of this on tape
somewhere and will locate it as necessary.

The point being, in this video interview the daughters produced a
piece of paper which it's claimed their father cited as
containing important verification of his story. Without double-
checking I can't be certain, however, I believe it was allegedly
in his own hand-writing.

When the freeze frame was used, the paper clearly showed details
of a bank apparently based in Roswell, plus a bank account
number.

Although insinuated that money had been paid into the account as
an incentive to 'keep quiet' [or something along these lines],
there was no indication the family had ever pursued this matter.

Was that 'document' mentioned in previous interviews and if so,
what transpired when the evidence was presumably followed up by
case researchers?


James Easton.

Subject: [UFORL] The Portage County [Ravenna], Spaur-Neff Case

This isn't a case I knew well and last year an overview produced
several, obvious questions - see:

http://www.virtuallystrange.net/ufo/updates/2001/may/m25-
004.shtml

Most of the questions raised were never answered.

I've now come across some significant, historical case material
and it may not be well known this is online at:

http://members.evansville.net/slk/portagedoc.htm


For myself, it results in a number of new questions and a
different understanding of the entire case.

I note the 'UFO' was described over the police radio, by one of
the witnesses as a, "bright light with a rope or string attached
to it".

As I previously enquired: "Some of the object's reported
characteristics resemble a blimp. Nearby was Goodyear's Wingfoot
Lake Airship Base at Akron. Did anyone check to definitely rule
out any possibility that a Goodyear blimp might have been even
partly involved?"

Presumably the answer is no.


Also particularly interesting, when the full evidence has been
revealed, is the witness sketch, at:

http://members.evansville.net/slk/raven5a.gif

Patrolman Panzanella's drawing is quite different from the much
better known sketch by Dale Spaur (incorrectly 'Spauer'
throughout the web site):

http://members.evansville.net/slk/raven7.gif

There's a critical piece of evidence which accompanies this -
Weitzel's explanation of the numbered points which are indicated
on Spaur's drawing:
http://members.evansville.net/slk/raven6.htm
From: "James Easton" <voyager@ufoworld.co.uk>
Date: Sat, 5 Jan 2002 02:11:45 -0000
Subject: Re: [UFORL] The Portage County [Ravenna], Spaur-Neff Case

"The only thing, the only sound in the whole area was a hum....
like a transformer being loaded or an overloaded transformer when
it changes".

So recalled Deputy Sheriff Dale Spaur, when the Portage County
'UFO' was first encountered and flying at low altitude - "I'd say
about a hundred feet", reported Dr J. Allen Hynek in 'The UFO
Experience'.

Had the infinitely more advanced technology of those purported ET
visitors never quite got around to a noise reduction invention,
or is it merely yet another remarkable coincidence that the sound
of an airship's engines is commonly described as a 'hum'...

There are numerous, related confirmations by simply searching
online for 'airship' plus 'hum'.


Yet, what about the UFO's reported airspeed... over 100 mph,
allegedly.

An airship, at maximum, would seemingly only be capable of around
half that.

It's claimed that NICAP 'thoroughly investigated' this case.

Why then, was one conspicuous set of related anomalies never
evidently addressed, additional to an apparently blatant
oversight which failed to safeguard if the blimp-like sketches
and associated 'UFO' attributes might have a connection to next-
door's Goodyear, Wingfoot blimp base.

According to patrolman Frank Panzanalla's report, "The object was
in my sight from 5:20 A. M. to 6:15 A. M". This was from Conway,
Pennsylvania.

However, patrolman Wayne Houston states he heard 'UFO' reports on
radio and the presumed same object, travelling east, wasn't
sighted by himself in Columbiana, Ohio until 5:30 a.m.

Are Conway and Pennsylvania not somewhat further due east?

How then, could the UFO have reached there some ten minutes
before it arrived at Columbiana?
Also, if Panzanella had 'the object in my sight' until 6:15, how
to reconcile with Weitzel's NICAP report, that:

"At 5:55, Lisbon relayed the order to return to Portage. Spaur
said 'Turning around now.' But it was 6:15 until Spaur and Neff
got back (west) past Freedom [Pennsylvania - James]".

If Spaur and Neff headed back at 5:55, doesn't that confirm the
UFO was still visible to Panzanella, 'in my sight until 6:15',
for an amazing twenty minutes afterwards?

Spaur and Neff's 'official statement', in a letter to NICAP,
claims: "In Conway, Pa., Officer Frank Panzanella met us where we
stopped, and we stood with him watching the object as it hovered
and then rose, twice, in a rapid climb".

Although that letter doesn't clarify if this was Spaur and Neff's
final sighting, in 'The UFO Experience' Hynek declares so,
writing:

Thus there enters the fourth observer: Frank Panzanella, police
officer in Conway. His signed testimony reads:

[skipping the introduction, which essentially concurs (although
not precisely as Hynek omits some content) with that online copy
- James]

"The object then moved out towards Harmony Township approximately
a 1,000 feet high, then it stopped then went straight up real
fast to about 3,500 feet. I then called the base station told
the radio operator to notify the Pittsburgh airport. He asked me
if I was sick. I told him if I was sick so were the other 3
patrolmen".
[END]


Panzanalla's online copy statement continues:

"The operator got the airport on the line and told them what
happened, he told them to hold the line and in the meantime we
kept watching the object and at that time a passenger plane
passed to the left about 1,000 feet below the object. We relayed
the message to the operator and he relayed it to the airport.
The object continued to go upward until it got as small as a
ballpoint pen. Then we received a message to make a phone call.
We preceded to the Rochester Police Department and made the phone
call. Officer Parr talked to someone and then we returned to
Conway Police Department where I gave Officer Parr my name and
gas for his police car to return home.
The object was in my sight from 5:20 A. M. to 6:15 A. M."
[END]


Hynek's account of the 'same' statement then dramatically
differs:

"The object continued to go upward until it got as small as a
ballpoint pen. Relative to the moon, the object was quite distant
and to the left of the moon [Venus was to the right of the moon].
I could not see the moon from my position. The object was seen
between two antennas in the backyard across the street to the
west. We all four watched the object shoot straight up and
disappear".
[END]

Which version of Panzanalla's official testimony is Hynek now
quoting from?

It's certainly not the same one as, "The Documentation - Courtesy
of CUFOS".


Aside from that, if, "We all four watched the object shoot
straight up and disappear", how did NICAP's 'thorough
investigation', account for Panzanella still statedly observing
said 'UFO' twenty minutes later?

Did it 'disappear' s l o w l y...

Before we might attempt to comprehend and perhaps explain this
founding NICAP/Hynek 'UFO' case evidence... it would be helpful
if it all actually made documented sense in the first place and
some evidentially elementary anomalies had perhaps been resolved
at the outset.

A brief enquiry of the local, Goodyear airship office could also
have been invaluable, if not a prerequisite.


James Easton.

From: "James Easton" <voyager@ufoworld.co.uk>
Date: Sat, 5 Jan 2002 09:43:24 -0000
Subject: [UFORL] 'Mothman' - Into the Flame

Leprechauns are real.

Seriously.

I have on more than one 'Celtic legends' video the evidently
sincere testimony of several witnesses, assuredly sober at the
time.

It's alarming, if not disconcerting, that there are many eager,
demonstrably, effortlessly gullible believers - the devout
minority who will voluntarily fall for and defend anything which
implies ET or Leprechaun encounters are 'real', ideally being
kidnapped, or now 'abducted', by fairies/aliens.

Mothman, Mothballs... or perhaps complete and utter Moth
bollocks...

Jimmy Wallis was a day-to-day contributor to that legendary
1995/96 CompuServe 'MUFON UFO' forum, as was Theresa Carlson [who
definitely proved the 'alien autopsy' footage was a hoax], Bob
Shell [who perhaps definitely proved Ray Santilli could use you
as a doormat], Ray himself, Michael Hesemann, Bruce Maccabee and
many others.

Therein, Hesemann challenged myself re Ray Santilli's 'Roswell
alien autopsy tent footage':

"I saw the tent footage many times and just the speed of the
movements and also the sharpness of the images indicates it was
shot with a 16 mm camera and not with video. The only reason why
Ray doesn't like it is that it is so bloody dark (dimly lit) and
looks pathetically bad. I personally think it shows the being
when the medics try to remove its spacesuit. A tent in the desert
at night... with no electricity, that's why it is so dark. But
all these sceptics will say again: Look, they have something to
hide, looks, why is it so bad...".

Pardon those lambasted skeptics, that 'tent footage' was
subsequently proven to have been filmed in a Bedfordshire barn,
featuring the local butcher as a 'doctor' - only invited because
he could contribute 'chicken guts' which were "used as the
alien's innards"!

There's just no fooling Michael Hesemann, an icon of 'ufology'
and what it typically represents.
Meanwhile, re 'Mothman' and Keel... Jimmy Wallis revealed he was
an acquaintance of "the Amazing Randi back in the '70's" and how
"Keel was a friend" of Randi's at that time.

Having duly perused Jimmy's 1995 revelations, especially
concerning a certain publication which contained 'monster' claims
that were allegedly admitted to be "fabricated" [I quote] and
"for the money" [I quote]... best, on any legal advice, if I say
no more.

Maybe someone can ask Randi to comment about Keel's stories, or
does anyone have a current e-mail address for Michael Curta,
then, 'State Director of Colorado MUFON'? I believe his related
insight might be interesting.


I note from:

http://www.lorencoleman.com/mothman.html

The endorsement:

"After a lifetime of research, Loren Coleman has produced the
most complete overview of Mothman and its minions--the scariest
family of monsters on Earth." --John A. Keel, author of The
Mothman Prophecies".

I can only say this perhaps does not equate - outwith the
superficially ludicrous, even for ufology, 'outsized butterflies
up a tree' claims - with some other, earlier, evidence.

I wonder if, when Keel affirms, "the scariest family of monsters
on Earth", he is perchance still duly concerned about a
malevolence which even Gandalf might not endure, or...if he is
literally laughing at 'ufoology' all the way to the bank.


One arguable point concerning the Sony 'movie' web presentation,
at:

http://www.spe.sony.com/movies/mothman/

Some might say that 'ENTER SITE' should, with even a somewhat
elementary, factual appraisal, be boycotted by our union. Not so
much 'ENTER SITE' as, 'ENTER SH...

What's that.. we don't have a union... Maybe time to tackle
reasons why.
"For 3 years a dark apparition terrified a sleepy West Virginia
town. This is the true story of the Mothman that should be too
strange to be real".

Spooky. How/why did 'ufology' ever end up endorsing... ad
nauseaum... "The true story of the Mothman"... an alien, or
whatever, moth stuck up a tree?.

Did NICAP never solve even this case?

It's all a baffling, unfathomable mystery, for sure...


James Easton.

I have the article where Fogl (corrected spelling) admitted it was a
hoax. It was made from two plastic display bases that came with model
Starfighter airplanes. They were glued together bottom to bottom. The
appendages were made from the ubiquitous sprue trees that held the
parts for the models. The model was hung from a silk thread.

In the article, he states that BUFORA knew the truth for 3 years (before
the magazine article was published), but withheld the information.

Incidentally, the Fogl photo looks a lot like the drawing Frank Mannor
made after his sighting.

I will get the reference to the magazine article and post it.

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Tue, 8 Jan 2002 12:37:34 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] 'Socorro' Update

10 to 15 seconds. But if he was in a hurry, it might have seemed like
more. It would depend on how long the power was off too. After 2
minutes, the full 20 to 30 second warmup cycle would be needed.

The cathode of a tube is very small (1/2 to 1 inch long, less than
1/8 inch in diameter, and hollow. It would not retain heat very long.
The outer glass bulb, at a much lower temperature, retains heat
longer (long enough to hurt your fingers after several minutes)
because it has a larger mass. But because of its larger area,
it doesn't retain enough heat to make the cathode heat up quicker.

Remember that ALL of the heat produced by the filament passes
through the tiny cathode, and then through the much larger bulb.
Since the heat is concentrated at the cathode, but distributed over
the entire area of the bulb, the cathode gets much hotter than the
bulb.

Larry,

Interesting point.

We can only note Zamora's subsequent, 1967 revelation - I can't
see any previous mention that the radio wasn't initially working
when he reported back to base, after the object's departure.

I'm now reasonably certain that, as Zamora claimed in the 'Look'
magazine 'Flying Saucers' 1967 interview, he didn't ask for the
state police to send out Sergeant Chavez until this latter stage.

Indeed, it's actually confirmed in case documentation, within a
statement provided by FBI agent J. Arthur Byrnes, Jr. He wrote:

Special Agent J. Arthur Byrnes, Jr., Federal Bureau of
Investigation, stationed at Albuquerque, New Mexico, was at
Socorro, New Mexico, and at the State Police Office there on
business late afternoon of April 24, 1964.

At approximately 5:45 to 5:50 P.M., Nep Lopez, radio operator in
the Socorro County Sheriff's Office, located about thirty feet
down the hall from the State Police Office, came into the State
Police Office.

Nep Lopez advised Samuel Chavez, New Mexico State Police, that he
had just received a radio call from Officer Lonnie Zamora to come
to an area about one mile southwest of Socorro. The call was in
relation to some unknown object which "landed and has taken off."
{END OF EXTRACT]

The quote is from Byrnes and if it's all an accurate
recollection, must prove that Zamora did not request Chavez's
assistance until after the object had "taken off".


Ray Stanford produces a copy of this statement in 'Socorro
Saucer', yet doesn't seem to have realised the anomaly. It's
particularly striking in Stanford's case as he goes to great
lengths emphasising how Zamora requested Chavez's presence
immediately when Zamora had that first glimpse for "possibly two
seconds or so" and before he had his closer, albeit equally
brief, second observation.

Stanford claims that Zamora made the request following that first
glimpse because, even then, it was clear to Zamora, "he was
encountering something in which he had never believed, never
wanted to believe - or else which might be a force-landed
experimental vehicle from White Sands proving grounds, something
that maybe he should not be seeing".

Stanford further alleges Zamora confirmed this and that "Zamora
wanted one reliable witness, other than himself, just in case the
supposedly secret research vehicle might leave the site and he
would be left alone with the accusation of having been 'seeing
things'".

That's been a long accepted understanding, however, it's
apparently not so.

Aside from anything else, as previously noted, Zamora explained
in his official statement that when first observed for those two
seconds, "At the time, I didn't pay much attention to what it
was--I thought it was an accident".

Clearly, he did not consider otherwise, nor did have sufficient
time to.


Stanford then relies on his claims as the basis for Chavez
arriving just as the object had departed and how even then, it
was already 'out of sight'.

Again, this has in later years been accepted as de facto evidence
that the UFO had rocket-like capabilities.

Not so fast, Mr Stanford...
If Chavez wasn't in truth informed until a) after the object had
taken off; b) until Zamora returned to his car and c) the radio
started working again, plus Stanford mentions that Chavez was
delayed because he took a wrong turning...

That's now a somewhat different set of, evidently factual,
circumstances.

Tim,

This is the full statement, as published in 'Socorro Saucer':

Special Agent J. Arthur Byrnes, Jr., Federal Bureau of
Investigation, stationed at Albuquerque, New Mexico, was at
Socorro, New Mexico, and at the State Police Office there on
business late afternoon of April 24, 1964.

At approximately 5:45 to 5:50 P.M., Nep Lopez, radio operator in
the Socorro County Sheriff's Office, located about thirty feet
down the hall from the State Police Office, came into the State
Police Office.

Nep Lopez advised Samuel Chavez, New Mexico State Police, that he
had just received a radio call from Officer Lonnie Zamora to come
to an area about one mile southwest of Socorro. The call was in
relation to some unknown object which "landed and has taken off."
Agent Byrnes finished his work in the State Police Office at
Socorro at approximately 6:00 P. M., April 24, 1964, and there-
after proceeded to the site where Officer Zamora, Socorro County
Undersheriff James Luckie, Sergeant Samuel Chavez, and Officer
Ted Jordan, New Mexico State Police, were assembled.

It may be noted that it has been the observation of Agent Byrnes
that Officer Zamora, known intimately for approximately five
years, is well regarded as a sober, industrious, and
conscientious officer and not given to fantasy.

Officer Zamora was noted to be perfectly sober and somewhat
agitated over his experience.
Special Agent Byrnes noted four indentations in the rough ground
at the "site" of the object described by Officer Zamora. These
depressions appeared regular in shape, approximately sixteen by
six inches rectangular. Each depression seemed to have been made
by an object going into the earth at an angle from a center line.
Each depression was approximately two inches deep and pushed some
earth to the far side.

Inside the four depressions were three burned patches of clumps
of grass. Other clumps of grass in the same area appeared not to
be disturbed. One burned area was outside the four depressions.

There were three circular marks in the earth which were smooth,
approximately four inches in diameter and penetrated in the sandy
earth approximately one-eighth of an inch as if a jar lid had
gently been pushed into the sand.

No other person was noted in the area the night of April 24,
1964. No other objects were noted in the area possibly connected
with the incident related by Officer Zamora.

So far as could be noted, there were no houses or inhabited
dwellings in the area or in sight of the area.
[END]


On the separate question of whether Zamora's UFO was a hot-air
balloon, one reference cited before is an early, related
publication:

"Hot Air Balloons Race on Silent Winds"
'National Geographic' magazine, March 1966

It's a feature about the National Championships held in Reno,
Nevada during September 1965. Almost a year and a half after the
Socorro incident, there are still few hot-air balloons in the
entire US.

Whilst that 'National Geographic' article is no more than a rare,
contemporary [as such] snapshot, one photograph therein helpfully
illustrates the approximate perspective of any comparative 'close
encounter' Zamora might have experienced. Previously I only had a
photocopy of this, however, I've recently located and acquired a
copy of the original 1966 magazine.

An enhanced [400 per cent magnification], colour scan of that
image can now be seen, at:

http://www.ufoworld.co.uk/socorro/p8.jpg
Although for information only, the smaller, central all-white
balloon would surely be *roughly* equivalent, at best, to any
hot-air balloon Zamora observed.

It _is_ difficult to comprehend how Zamora could perceive a
similar hot-air balloon to be car-sized, even from distance.

Still, ufology is nothing if not the realm of the 'unbelievable'
- it's a quintessential background to proclaimed 'UFO reality'
which has supposedly fooled mainstream science/media for decades.

By comparison, Zamora possibly being deceived by an unfamiliar
sighting and anecdotal occurrence is inconsequential!

There are also of course precedents, for example, as reported by the
'Louisville Courier-Journal' on March 4, 1993:

Police Chopper Attacked By UFO In Kentucky!

"Two helicopter policemen patrolling the sky over Louisville KY.,
said they were fired on during a harrowing, two minute dogfight -
with a pear-shaped UFO.

The strange craft reportedly shot three fireballs during the
encounter that also was witnessed by two other officers who
monitored the situation from their positions on the ground below.

The cops involved have been tight-lipped, declining interview
requests, but official reports, which are a matter of public
record and available for any citizen to see, clearly suggest that
the airborne officers were lucky to have escaped with their
lives.

'I know what we saw and we were not hallucinating', Kenny Graham,
who was piloting the helicopter, said in his report. 'I was
afraid the UFO was going to collide with us', he continued, 'then
it turned at the last second and roared away at a speed I've
never seen before'. Graham, 39, an 11 year police veteran, and
Kenny Downs, 39, a five year police veteran who was operating the
chopper's spotlight, were on routine patrol when they saw what
looked like a fire off to their left. Downs instinctively aimed
his spotlight on the object which was shaped like a pear and
drifting back and forth like a balloon on a string. Without
warning, the object sped toward the helicopter and circled it
several times before zooming off in the opposite direction, Downs
said. Then the UFO turned and headed straight for the chopper,
shooting fireballs that by luck or design fizzled out before they
hit, according to Graham.

Afraid the UFO would ram the helicopter's tail rotor, Graham
pushed his speed to more than 100 m.p.h. Far from being outrun,
the UFO shot past the chopper, instantly climbing hundreds of
feet. It descended again momentarily, but when Graham steered
toward the craft for a closer look, it flew into the distance and
disappeared.

The amazing aerial manoeuvring of the UFO didn't go unnoticed on
the ground. Officer Mike Smith saw the object for about a minute.
He confirmed it fired three fireballs and disappeared. Officer
Joe Smolenski said he tried for more than minute to catch up to
the UFO in his patrol car. 'I've been looking for UFOs for 14
years and I guess this is the closest I've come to something I
can't explain', Smolenski said.

A lieutenant described the two helicopter officers as solid guys
and good cops.

Downs said: 'Kenny and I both go to church every week. After
this, I might start going twice a week'."
[END]

The Louisville Courier-Journal ran a follow-up on March 6th,
revealing this terrifying UFO, encountered and separately
observed by several 'trained Police witnesses' was a 'fire
balloon', composed of a "dry cleaning bag, balsa wood, and a
dozen birthday candles" - see:

http://www.ufoworld.co.uk/v16.txt


That evidenced and recalled, the emblem on aforementioned SEMCO
balloon photograph isn't dissimilar to what Zamora reportedly,
originally described in Spanish; "una 'V' invertido con tres
lineas debajo", which, according to Stanford, translates as, "an
inverted 'V' with three lines underneath".

Doubtless coincidence and this SEMCO balloon [these were being
built from 1961] doesn't have an inverted, red 'V' - although the
additional, right-hand side SEMCO balloon does display same logo
in red.

Trusting Gary Anthony won't mind, he concurrently notes elsewhere
that Gray Barker's 'Book Of Saucers' [Saucerian Press, 1965, p
72] "goes on to state on same page that Zamora was sure of only
something like a V in a phone interview".

I'm sure there's considerable leeway involved in relation to
Zamora's 'insignia', no matter what our 'UFO' was.
As previously discussed, one prime candidate for that theoretical
'Socorro' hot-air balloon is the 'Channel Champ', a Raven
Industries balloon which, on 13 April, 1963, had been flown
across the English Channel by Ed Yost and Don Piccard.

Yost effectively developed the hot-air balloon in 1960 and one
article notes, "Even his first-ever hot air balloon flight across
the English Channel was made at the request of his government
sponsor who was looking for to demonstrate the range and other
capabilities of the new hot air balloon".

The 'Channel Champ' was subsequently used in those 'classified',
1963/64 'Albuquerque flights' I disclosed the existence of - see:

http://www.ufoworld.co.uk/v07.txt

A photograph of that all-white balloon, which had an inscription
in red lettering, has been elusive. However, I have been able to
trace what happened to the balloon canopy. In true Fortean
tradition, it has returned to Albuquerque!

I understand that Ed Yost, who presumably kept it for posterity,
has donated this historic aviation relic to the planned 'Anderson
Abruzzo International Balloon Museum', in Albuquerque.

The "11.5 million dollar budget" museum is apparently scheduled
to open in October this year, during 2002's 'Kodak Albuquerque
International Balloon Fiesta'.

Will the Albuquerque balloon museum unwittingly be displaying a
legendary 'UFO', whilst the Roswell UFO museum exhibits the
aftermath of an indigenous, historic 1947 balloon-train
experiment...

Hopefully, some continuing developments, maybe in both instances,
will clarify those odds, long before October.

In an attempt to maybe tidy some of the 'loose ends', I had
submitted a FOIA request direct to Ramstein AFB, in Germany [a
response is long overdue].

One of the questions asked concerned details of contemporary
flights between Ramstein AFB and RAF Bentwaters/RAF Woodbridge
and their purpose.

This relates to claims that after the 'UFO incident', one or more
'special' flights occurred and 'something' was flown to Ramstein
AFB. Halt and Penniston have spoken about the 'unusual' and
unscheduled aircraft activity at this time.

The point being, there are a number of pieces in our proverbial
'Rendlesham UFO' puzzle which still don't fit.


We know that the enigmatic lights first pursued by Burroughs,
Cabansag and Penniston were not Orfordness lighthouse, although
that's what they eventually ended up chasing.

The source of their original 'UFO' remains unresolved. Were those
lights observed circa 0300 a.m. on 26 December perhaps "Christmas
lights" from one of the houses beyond Rendlesham forest at Capel
Green - Burroughs did confirm in the 'Strange But True' TV
documentary, "There were strange lights out in the forest. To me,
it almost looked like Christmas lights at first, a Christmas
display.".

Or, perhaps the origin was a farm tractor, similar to the
triangular-shaped 'UFO' encountered by Senior Airman Kenneth
Greene - see:

http://www.ufoworld.co.uk/v20.txt

As I revealed in a lengthy 'Rendlesham' article publish in
November 2001's 'Fortean Times', it was helpfully documented in
'Skycrash' [Jenny Randles, Brenda Butler and Dot Street] that
there was a tractor located at Capel Green. Could a tractor's cab
have been the 'transparent' object which Burroughs described. A
tractor with an array of night/field lights is certainly UFO-
like, especially when the tractor itself isn't distinguishable as
it moves around. I know this for sure because I've seen it!
However, it can only be speculation and all subject to new
evidence changing the perspective.

It will definitely require to be altered if some new evidence is
factually accurate.

A new witness testifies to what is perhaps the most significance
corroboration of 'trace evidence' yet uncovered.


This witness reportedly shared a room with one of the original
three 'UFO encounter' participants - Burroughs, Penniston and
Cabansag. I know which one and will explain further in due
course.

The striking claim is that, "...was my roommate in the barracks
and had slight radiation burns on his face and hands from being
in proximity to the object. He covered this up by wearing large
sweaters and associated winter clothing. I only noticed it by
accident being his roommate. He shared the details of having
received them that night in the forest while observing the
unknown object".

Additional background has been provided which does indicate this
is, at the least, a sincere recollection. Indeed, some of that
background relating to the participant is insightful and would
make sense of other 'loose ends'.

My first question must be - is it feasible that someone could
receive such radiation burns without suffering severely from
radiation sickness?

If the object was emitting radiation, wouldn't there have been
high levels still later that day? Wasn't the 'landing site'
checked for radiation by those who first investigated the
'landing marks'?

Comments duly welcome.

I see several glaring errors in the above article.:

- If the wind direction during the balloon's arrival matched the wind
direction when it left, the balloon would have been much closer
to the patrol car than 3/4 mile when it was first noticed. And the
car's roof might have hidden the aerostat from Zamora.

(Note: If APRO was involved with the report of the wind direction, then
it was 180 degrees off. Coral Lorenzen constantly made the error of
stating the wind direction as the direction the air was moving toward.
As a result of this, she complained about many identified balloons "It
could not have been a balloon, because it was headed directly into
the wind." She seems to have learned the truth about wind direction
sometime in 1965, because her reports after that have it correct.)

- The horizontal ellipse orientation exists only when the aerostat has
lost lift and is lying on the ground. As soon as the burner adds lift,
it resumes its vertical orientation. As it flew away, Zamora drew the
vertical orientation.

- Hall's "shiny silver" is wrong too. Zamora first thought it was an
overturned WHITE car. Later he said it was aluminum-white (like
the oxidized aluminum found on many fishing boats). White
aluminum is NOT shiny, but dull. A nylon aerostat would be a
similar color, especially if it was dirty (like the nylon sail of the
sailboat I used to own got after use).

- Speed estimates against the sky are impossible unless the
observer has correctly identified the object and thus knows its true
size. So the departure speed estimate of 120 mi/hr is dubious.

- Do we in fact know the object disappeared behind the mountain?
Or could it have dropped down in front of the mountain, lost to sight
because it matched the color of the mountain closely enough to
prevent visual tracking? I once saw an airplane disappear, because
it matched the color of the sky. It reappeared a few seconds later.

- The imprints remained visible after several months because
steps were taken to preserve them. But Brad Steiger reports that
when the site was visited several months later, the marks were
"much obliterated." The rocks around the marks in the photos
were placed there to prevent erosion of the evidence. They were
not there when the object landed.

- The Holloman AFB Balloon Control Center was responsible for
coordinating weather balloons for the purpose of forecasting
weather. Identifying UFOs was an incidental use of the information.
Sport ballooning information would not have been sent there.

- The Navy's hot air balloon program was still secret at the time
of the sighting, so Quintanilla could not have released the info
even if he had found out about it.

- Propellant residue????? What propellant residue?

Hot air balloon propellant residue is normally water vapor and
carbon dioxide, unless something goes wrong with the burner.
How do you test for these naturally occurring residues, distinctly
from their normal occurrences in plants and in the atmosphere?

Any residual unburnt propane would have long diffused into the
air before the investigators got there, as would any water vapor
and carbon dioxide. Even the carbon monoxide from a
misadjusted burner would have diffused or blown away.

@ What could conceivably have produced a "very bad sunburn" after
@ short exposure, yet not have caused any other _noticeable_ effects
@ on health:
@
@ - ultra-violet irradiation?

Yes. Ultraviolet light is what causes sunburn.

An electric arc can produce this kind of burn. Arc welders must
wear protective clothing to prevent such burns. Eye damage is
also common when bystanders watch an arc welder. If a power
line shorts to ground through a metal connection, it can produce
intense ultraviolet radiation as well as an intense visible cyan light.
Most clothing will stop this radiation.

A mercury vapor streetlamp with the outer filter envelope broken
will still work, and can produce enough UV to cause a sunburn at
night. So can an unfiltered halogen lamp, or one with the outer bulb
broken. Some overhead projectors were made in the 1970s with
unfiltered halogen bulbs.

Disinfecting lamps for doctors' offices and animal compounds
use UV in the form of a clear fluorescent tube. So do the lamps
used by rock hounds (mineral collectors) and EPROM erasers.
The lamps in doctors' offices or animal compounds are not
supposed to be turned on while the room is occupied.

A dying fluorescent lamp giving off brilliant blue flashes is also
emitting some UV.

Some advertizing fluorescent lamps give off UV to activate
special paints. Usually these are properly shielded, but
occasionally I come across a dope who puts up a sign without
understanding the danger.
Follow-spot carbon arc lights in theaters and arenas give off UV.

Skin cancer is more likely later in life after strong exposure to UV.

The Cash-Landrum symptoms are closer to those of UV damage
than to those of other forms of radiation.

@ - X-rays?

X-rays usually cause internal effects before they affect the skin,
because the skin is very transparent to X-rays.

An electric arc in a vacuum produces X-rays.

Some old television sets produce strong X-ray beams out of the
backs of their cabinets.

@ - toxic chemicals?

There are many gases and dusts that can affect exposed skin areas.

I will add some more:

Allergens - cause allergic reactions on skin contact.

Allergens - cause a rash after being eaten or inhaled. NOTE: the
rash is not limited to exposed skin in this case.

Visible light - if strong enough, it can cause a burn

Infrared - if strong enough, it can cause a burn which is very similar
to burns caused by hot objects or liquids.

LASER radiation - can cause burns.

Microwaves - can cause a burn by heating the affected area.

Hot water - if heated too hot, can cause burns in a shower or tub.
The victim can be unaware of this if the water heated up slowly.

Steam - Exposure to a sudden high pressure release of steam
can cause symptoms that appear later.

Alpha radiation - is usually stopped by the skin, and so causes
effects there. Stopped by clothing. Note that the radiation meter
they had could NOT detect alpha radiation. Very large dose
necessary.

Beta radiation - usually causes internal effects first. Large dose
necessary.
Gamma radiation - usually causes internal effects first. Cancer
shows up later in life.

Neutron radiation - causes internal effects first. Cancer shows up
later in life.

Proton radiation - causes internal effects first. Requires a cyclotron.

Hey, they had nuke bombs at the base!

spend a lot of time sitting down for a couple of days yet he did do his job.
It takes all kinds.

As for the tanning bed idea, I am not sure that such a thing was in vogue or
actually popular in 1980. I don't remember it but then I was never much of a
sun worshiping (even though I grew up in Florida).

Tim Printy

There is a two phase power line that goes through the clearing I believe
corresponds with the clearing mentioned by the various witnesses. On the
poles are aluminium inspection plates showing that inspections took place in
1987 and 1994. This does not prove the poles were there in 1980, but since
this is the power line to the Forestry Commission Offices in the forest, as
well as Capel Green and the Boast house, a line has probably been there for
many decades. Arcing lines or a transformer could possibly have been a
source of the lights seen at a distance, but this explanation requires the
arcing was not identified as such when they got closer, which seems
implausible. The arcing would have had to have stopped before they got close
enough to see it was from power lines. Also, the clearing (like the field in
front of the Boast house) is at a lower elevation than East Gate and any
lights at these locations (e.g. Christmas lights) could not have been
directly visible at East Gate owing to the drop in elevation at the eastern
edge of the forest. I suppose if the lights were extremely bright, light
scattered by mist or the air might have been visible at East Gate.

Of more interest to me is the possibility that some poles were replaced in
1980, and that hole drilling equipment could have been in the clearing then.
This is a possible source of the deep indentations that apparently were in
the clearing (not the same indentations as the shallow indentations in pine
needles investigated by Col Halt in amongst the trees).

Best regards

Robert McLean

On the question of when those 'lighthouse pursuit' revelations within
John Burroughs' early written statement became public knowledge, the
first source seems to be, 'Bentwaters: The Testimony of John Burroughs',
by J. Antonio Huneeus, published in 'Fate' magazine, [September 1993, pp
70-71].

Huneeus wrote:

"On the night of 25-26 Dec. [of 1980] at around 03:00 while on patrol
down at east gate myself and my partner saw lights coming from the woods
due east the gate. The lights were red and blue, the red one above the
blue one and they were flashing on and off." Thus begins the official
handwritten statement of USAF law enforcement airman John Burroughs,
concerning the events of the first night during the series of strange
UFO incidents in Rendlesham forest near the NATO air bases of Bentwaters
and Woodbridge in Suffolk, England, in late December of 1980.
[END OF EXTRACT]

Huneeus evidently had a copy of Burroughs original testimony at this
time. Where was that document acquired from?

He continues:

John Burroughs' testimony is of particular importance because he is
perhaps the only witness who participated in two of the close encounters
reported near Bentwaters. Burroughs was a 20 year-old law enforcement
airman who had served in the twin bases since March of 1979. We met him
a few years ago at a UFO Conference in Phoenix when he had just
separated from the USAF with the rank of Sergeant (he is still in the
Reserve) and saw him again during the filming of the famous Unsolved
Mysteries' Bentwaters segment in a Maryland wooded area, which he had
actually spearheaded.
[END OF EXTRACT]

Was a copy of the statement provided by Burroughs during these meetings?

So far as I'm aware, it was only Halt who retained and provided copies
of all the original statements and Burroughs recently told me, "As far
as the lighthouse goes the statements that everybody made such a big
deal about were first made available by Col Holt [sic] during the
filming of unsolved mys and if you stop and think about it nobody asked
us if we ever followed the lighthouse beam. What i mean by that is we
did follow a light not knowing what it was but we at no time did we feel
that it was the object we first saw. We had lost contact with the object
we first saw and wanted to see what the flasing light in the distance
was".
Incidentally, one of the first [second] things Burroughs asked was if I
knew where he could contact Jim Speiser, "The second thing is i need Jim
Speiser E-Mail address ive been out of the loop since strange but true
and i would like to find out about all of the change's that seemed to
have happened since 94".


The point being, it seems that, by 1993 - the 'Unsolved Mysteries'
feature was broadcast during September 1991 - Huneeus and presumably
some others were perhaps aware of all those original statements and
resultant, documented, two-mile 'UFO' chase of a lighthouse.

Irrespective of whether Orfordness lighthouse was, or was not, the
initial source of perceived, unfamiliar lights, if the aforementioned is
factual, that realisation had fundamental repercussions affecting
perceptions of both the inaugural 'UFO encounter' and Halt's subsequent,
celebrated sighting of a flashing 'UFO' light... which was later
recognised [yet never publicly mentioned] to be, "clear off to the
coast" (from his microcassette recording).

There's no debate; before September, 1993 [given due publishing
deadlines], Huneeus had access to Burroughs' original statement,
evidently in its entirety, and including an accompanying sketch of the
'lights', as his article then confirms:

Burroughs wrote in his official deposition regarding the events on the
first night that, "we crossed a small open field that lead into the
trees when the lights were coming from and as we were coming into the
trees there were strange noises, like a woman was screaming, also the
woods lit up and you could hear the farm animals making a lot of noise
and there was a lot of movement in the woods. All three of us hit the
ground and whatever it was started moving back towards the open field
and after a minute or two we got up and moved into the trees and the
lights moved out into the open field." We asked Burroughs to describe
the UFO with more detail and he responded that it looked like "a bank of
lights, differently colored lights that threw off an image of like a
craft. I never saw anything metallic or anything hard." Burroughs drew
also a sketch of the object in his official statement, which we are
reproducing here for the first time in the USA.

Yet the most interesting part of Burroughs' testimony is not the
presence of the lights, but rather his sensation of an altered state of
consciousness, something that could be described as a sensation of
liquid reality, which he experienced at the Rendlesham forest.
"Everything seemed like it was different when we were in that clearing,"
Burroughs said in our interview. "The sky didn't seem the same... it was
like a weird feeling, like everything seemed slower than you were
actually doing; and all of a sudden when the object was gone, everything
was like normal again." Nor can the UFO experience of Burroughs' and the
other two men be dismissed as something purely subjective triggered
perhaps by the Orford Ness lighthouse, a police car or other prosaic
phenomenon, as several skeptics have proposed.

[...]

[END OF EXTRACT]


This warrants a closer look.

Huneeus claims, "Burroughs wrote in his official deposition regarding
the events on the first night that, "we crossed a small open field that
lead into the trees when the lights were coming from and as we were
coming into the trees there were strange noises, like a woman was
screaming, also the woods lit up and you could hear the farm animals
making a lot of noise and there was a lot of movement in the woods. All
three of us hit the ground and whatever it was started moving back
towards the open field and after a minute or two we got up and moved
into the trees and the lights moved out into the open field."
[END OF EXTRACT]

It's absolutely verbatim from Burroughs' statement, except the last
section, where Huneeus contends, "after a minute or two we got up and
moved into the trees and the lights moved out into the open field".

Burroughs actually wrote, "after a min or 2 we got up and moved into the
open field".

That aside, most significantly, Burroughs then directly adds:

"We got up to a fence that separated the trees from the open field and
you could see the lights down by a farmers house. We climbed over the
fence and started heading towards the red and blue lights and they just
disappeared. Once we reached the farmer's house we could see a beacon
going around so we went towards it. We followed it for about 2 miles
before we could see it was coming from a lighthouse".

Conversely, Huneeus seems oblivious to this most critical evidence -
which is an abject refutation of assertions that Orfordness lighthouse
(or the nearby Shipwash lightship) was a familiar landmark.

Not only does Huneeus omit that next paragraph, he goes on to conclude,
"Nor can the UFO experience of Burroughs' and the other two men be
dismissed as something purely subjective triggered perhaps by the Orford
Ness lighthouse, a police car or other prosaic phenomenon, as several
skeptics have proposed".


Those pivotal witness statements I was clearly fortunate to come across
were, apparently, from the CAUS 'Rendlesham' files. I realised they had
to be published, despite a distinct lack of the approval repeatedly
requested - for that full background, see:

http://www.ufoworld.co.uk/v15.txt


Bottom line; during 1993, or earlier, Huneeus had acquired a copy of
Burroughs' statement and then reported its contents, minus the crucial
lighthouse involvement [maybe his copy, somehow, didn't contain that
paragraph], maintaining how any lighthouse connection was patently
absurd.

It highlights the question why case researchers - especially Jenny
Randles, who had endeavoured for many years to make some sense of
available evidence - were never, seemingly, made aware of such
exceptional, accessible (to some) material and... well, it just all
seems to ask a number of striking questions.

I'm sure Jenny, and others, concur.

Comments and observations are, naturally, welcome!

Explanations even more so.

plus the photograph was analysed.

I wonder if the negative was examined.

Mark Cashman's MUFON, Connecticut web site states:

Randy Etting, a resident of Newtown, was taking a walk outside
his home. A commercial airline pilot with over 30 years
experience, he always looked at the sky... he saw a number of
orange and red lights... approaching from the west... He... got
his binoculars and called his neighbors to come outside. The
object by this time was a great deal closer and seemed to be over
I-84, just east of Etting's home... the lights were shimmering
like distortion from engine heat, but he could hear no sound...
"As the UFO passed over I-84, cars in both the east and west
bound lanes began pulling over and stopping. The UFO displayed a
semi-circular pattern of very bright multicolored lights. Five
motorists reported that, as the object became visible, a number
of cars lost power and had to pull off the highway. A State
Police officer [who wishes to remain anonymous] sent to
investigate photographed the object. "... Dr. Bruce Maccabee...
[analysed the photo]. His findings indicate the object was huge,
perhaps over a thousand feet across, and that the lights showed a
definite pattern. He also indicated the lights seemed to have
been flashing very quickly in some sort of sequence, giving the
impression that some were out of focus while others were sharp."
[END]


Although Maccabee is correct about the lights flashing, he's just
slightly out with his reported calculation of the object's size.

As an intentional hoax, this photograph would be at least the
third example - The Trent photographs and Ed Walters' Gulf Breeze
portfolio come to mind - which Maccabee has proclaimed genuine.

The other two mentioned are of course, or 'were' so far as the
now explicable Trent images go, declared to be the 'real'
evidence of flying saucers.

Which is true.

An irony is that the lights depicted in this photograph are
entirely consistent with a saucer-shaped object, not a
'boomerang'.

I suppose someone must have thought it could pass for the latter,
and they were obviously correct, although I've always considered
the photograph had no obvious connection with a boomerang-shaped
source.

As we can now appreciate, our Waterbury flying saucer is either
travelling upside down, or was photographed from above!

An illustration of this can be seen at:

http://www.ufoworld.co.uk/ftp/upended.jpg

[...]

It does actually look much more 'convincing' the right way up! -
See:
http://www.ufoworld.co.uk/ftp/watrbry2.jpg
[END OF EXTRACT]


A comparison of light correlations between the Waterbury and
Nashville 'UFOs' is shown my web site, at:

http://www.ufoworld.co.uk/ftp/saucers2.jpg

A further confirmation of prominent features:

http://www.ufoworld.co.uk/ftp/saucers3.jpg

The Waterbury image has to be both rotated and 'mirrored' to make
due comparisons, however, there's a blatant clue why these 'UFO
photographs' originate from a common, infinitely more terrestrial
source.

Noting this on 'UFO Skeptics', I last wrote, "I'll leave the
[clue] details aside for now as I'm interested to see if anyone
maintains the Waterbury 'UFO' is genuine and how they rationalise
that".


Still no takers?

They are, after all, avowed by 'rense.com'/'MUFON Connecticut' to
be landmark, 'alien visitation' photographic snapshots, such
that, "Even the most skeptical remain unable to explain this
object".


Is that a fact...

I saw the FX network show "UFOs, the best evidence caught on
tape 2" last night. I found quite a few interesting points:

- A brilliant red object with patterns of light on it was videotaped at
an arts festival in Nevada in September of 2001. But the theme of
the festival was the light sculpture (hint hint).

- A video of a large UFO next to the World Trade Center taken in
October 1994 was obviously not seen by the cameraman, because
he continued to pan the camera along the New York skyline. The
audio on the tape also does not refer to a UFO, but sounds like a
sightseeing trip.

- Objects in a NASA film seen just after the tethered satellite
experiment that failed on 2/25/96 are obviously very tiny debris
close to the lens and out of focus. The chowderhead who analyzed
the film on the show compared the angular size to that of the tether
and concluded they were discs 3 miles in diameter.

- 5/29/93 Stuttgart Germany video of an oval object identified as a
lighted advertizing blimp.

- A video taken in Derby England on 3/13/95 looks like a TV set
seen through a window to me.

- A video taken at Silbury Hill England in August 98 looks
suspiciously like the Pleiades.

- A video taken in Quito Ecuador on 5/15/96 is obviously a fire
balloon slowly rotating as it flies over low. I have seen this before.

- A video taken on September '94 in Mexico looks like a
window of a house to me.

- A video "taken at Area 51" of an alien is obviously done with
puppetry with computer editing. And a Jacob's Ladder would
never be used in a real scientific investigation, since it's purpose
is to demonstrate that an electrical arc produces heat.

Was that alien really wearing a necktie?

- A 9/96 Israel video shows three circular UFOs taken at different
places on different days - it looks like 3 similar hotel signs to me.

- A video taken in Kibbutz Hatzol (spelled right?). COME ON! It's a
video of a naked woman taken through a tent camper window by a
teenager. The UFO story was probably made up to explain the tape
when his parents saw it.

There was also a show on the Mothman last night.

- The John Keel description of the UFOs he saw sounds just like
fire balloons to me.

- Then Keel tried to link the sightings to the fall of Silver Bridge.


On the local front, a friend told me this week that he had launched
fire balloons here in Bloomington in the early '70s.

Nash-Fortenberry is one of my top-ten unsolved cases.

Thoughts:

- Menzel suggested a searchlight playing on thin haze layers below
  the aircraft.

- Any meteoric activity would have to have been reflected, since the
objects passed beneath their plane (but remember that they were over
water). This does not account for the reversal of the UFOs' course
unless the plane made a sudden turn.

- Some kind of mirage effect (similar to the Newfoundland case in
the 1950s).

- Military jets with afterburners on (not likely). The area is full of
military bases (I visited two of them, and drove past 3 others).

- As I repeatedly reiterate, NOBODY can estimate size, speed,
distance, or altitude of an unknown object. (although in this case,
they had upper limits on distance and lower limits on altitude,
because they flew above the UFOs). So their speed report was
based upon a guess that they were the size of airplanes.

This case occurred just before the Washington National case.

The object is out of focus, while the people and background are
in focus. The object was not seen by the photographer and is
not the subject of the photo. The above facts show that it was
very small and close to the camera lens. Possible identities:

- A bird or insect "frozen in flight" by the camera

- Windblown debris

- A defect in the negative

- Dirt, or a tiny insect, on the negative when the picture was
taken

- light leak

- Developing error

- Small model suspended close to the lens

I have now received a copy of the originalnewspaper article.
Unfortunately it is a very poor copy and the photograph with it does not
reproduce very well. (It is a typical local paper shot of a housewife
kneeling down and holding a ruler against the crater in her garden,
although this is undistinguishable in the copy I have.)

The text is as follows:

CROYDON ADVERTISER
Friday January 28, 1972

Fragments of a large block of ice which smashed a deep crater two foot
deep [65 cm] in a Shirley garden on Sunday morning are still being
examined by scientists at Heathrow.

The ice fell about 9 a.m. on Sunday when 39 year old bank official Mr
Peter Wakeford and his wife were drinking their early morning tea in
bed.

"There was a whooshing sound and a loud thud" Mrs Wakeford told an
'Advertiser' reporter.

We thought something had fallen off the roof but when we looked into the
back garden we saw a crater and pieces of ice."

Police from New Addington took the ice in a plastic bag, and put it in a
deep freezer.

It was later collected by Department of Transport officials and taken to
laboratories.

It was a lucky escape for the Wakefords and their neighbours in Lime
Tree Grove for the ice, believed to have measured at least four feet
across, also dislodged two paving stones.
A Department of Trade spokesman said on Tuesday that officials believed
the ice had come from an aircraft. It was possible for ice, formed on
the plane's wings, to fall off, he said.

Another possibility was a leaking tap in the aircraft's plumbing system
which would cause a build up of ice in the low temperatures found at
high altitudes.

When the ice reached a certain weight it could have forced open a hatch
and the fallen.

"It was lucky the ice didn't fall on the roof," said Mrs wakeford. "And
I hate to think what would have happened if anyone had been hit by it."

A couple of interesting points therein.

It's stated that Zamora reported the object was "oval shaped,
similar to football, possibly twenty feet long". That's a

giving such precise details elsewhere of both the shape and size,
at closest proximity.

It still doesn't seem to make any sense how he could have
contemplated such an object, even from "eight hundred feet away",

Zamora was statedly wearing 'green sunglasses' at this time and
also when he initially viewed the 'flame', object and those two
crew members wearing what resembled 'white coveralls'.

How could he make these colour determinations through green
sunglasses?


That aside, a striking coincidence - never revealed in 'Socorro
Saucer' - is how a military exercise, code-named 'Cloud Gap', was
taking place and involved New Mexico.

As indicated in the latter teletype, I would expect no bearing to
Zamora's sighting and there can't be, if that pivotal 'hot-air
balloon freaked local lawman' anecdote, actually documented by
Larry Robinson, does relate to Zamora.

What though was operation 'Cloud Gap'?

According to the FAS web site:
"The hundreds of secret compartmented programs at the Pentagon
are each assigned a two word nickname and a classified codeword.
The names are selected and combined, more or less arbitrarily,
from lists of pre-approved words, giving rise to an oddly
suggestive form of Pentagon poetry.

William M. Arkin, the independent analyst and author, picked out
the names of 26 particularly resonant Pentagon programs --
DIAGONAL GLANCE, CHALK POINSETTIA, CREDIBLE WOLF -- for a feature
he wrote in last Sunday's New York Times Magazine.

Several of these terms have not appeared previously in the public
domain. Furthermore, in several cases Arkin has gone where no
uncleared person has gone before and has provided a thumbnail
description of the contents of the secret programs. Someone,
somewhere in the Pentagon, will be grinding his teeth at the
impudence. See:

http://www.nytimes.com/library/magazine/home/20001203mag-
lexicon.html

An additional layer of obscurity is attached to these names
because of the fact that over time they may be reused for other
secret programs.

For example, Arkin identifies CLOUD GAP as a "classified Air
Force program." In the 1960s, however, CLOUD GAP was a joint
program of the Department of Defense and the Arms Control and
Disarmament Agency "to test the feasibility of theoretical arms
control and disarmament measures." The earlier edition of CLOUD
GAP, now practically forgotten, culminated in a test to
demonstrate the verifiable destruction of nuclear warheads.
[END]


Bizarrely, the above has some relevance to a certain 'alien
autopsy'. According to what was supposedly the 'cameraman's
statement', that 'crash/retrieval' had been designated as
'Operation Anvil'. However, 'Operation Anvil' is a well-known
WWII, 1944, military campaign.

The resulting question [if only for the record], was whether a
code-name might be re-used.

With the assistance of an acquaintance in the US, who has vast
'intelligence community' expertise, it proved possible to cite
instances where a prominent code-name had indeed been duplicated.
However, there were few examples and it looks like 'CLOUD GAP'
can be added.

> What though was operation 'Cloud Gap'?


"In testimony to Congress in 1970, Herbert Scoville noted that fixed
land-based ICBMs 'require extensive launch-site construction in order to
provide the necessary hardening to make them resistant to blast from a
nuclear explosion. This construction requires many months and therefore
ample time is available to permit its detection' In addition, Scoville
noted that 'after ... submarines are launched they require many months
of fitting out, during all of which they are subject to observation.'

But two years earlier the intelligence community had argued that its
sensitive overhead systems could not be employed for monitoring
[arms-control treaty] compliance. The community had argued that use of
those systems for verification purposes would require the United States
to make its capabilities public to establish that it could verify
compliance. It was also argued that signing an agreement to be monitored
by intelligence systems would reveal the capabilities of those systems,
and that charges of violations would have to be backed up by revelation
of the data indicating such violations. Thus, on-site inspection and
other sources of information would be required. To explore the
possibility of verification without the use of reconnaissance
satellites, the Air Force conducted a study named CLOUD GAP."

- Jeffrey T Richelson, "America's Secret Eyes In Space: The US Keyhole
Spy Satellite Program" (Harper & Row, 1990)

(Richelson footnotes the source of this item as "private information")

The following account was recently received via my web site:

Dear Sir/Madam.

I have just watched an american programme featuring 'silent
falcons/triangular ufo's. It mentioned the UK phenonmena and
Belgium, but the crafts they mentioned were a lot bigger than the
one that I experienced.

My encounter was very close, personal with a smaller triangular
object. I would like to find out what it was and if anyone else
has experienced similar 'close' encounters.

I guess I am looking for reassurance for something which as kind
of spooked me over the last 21 years. It has always been a
confusion in my mind how such technologies could exist. If it was
a covert flight by some experimental craft programme I would it
would make me feel happier but the technologies I saw were so
advanced.

Date:
Late night 8th December 1980

Proximity:
It came down to us from behind the houses, glided sliently just
above us (below roof level and just above the street lamp)
approximately 4m above us? I can recall event in detail if you
are interested.

Location:
Sussex St, Norwich, Norfolk. We were playing on our roller skates
outside my house whilst my friends mother visited a neighbour.

No noise, white glow. Aluminum/mercury type of morphing material.
No depth but full of spot lights. Almost still, smooth silence,
calm travelling when above us about 1cm a second.

Time:
9-10:30pm.

Duration of its observation of us:
5 minutes at least (we were put into a kind of trance and lost
track of time). Approach, interaction (felt as if I was being
read/observed but craft too thin for anyone to be in. This sense
of connection was broken by bang of front door which seemed
extremely loud (it was my friends mother closing her front door
about 10 houses away). We then watched it morph and fligh off
over house, over city centre (upside down lights facing upwards
when flew low level over city around city hall clock and off in a
southerly direction.

I would like to talk to someone about what I saw. I would like to
find out how I can answer what happened that night. Who should I
talk to?

Hope to hear from you soon,

Kindest regards
Rachel
[END]


Anecdotal and unsubstantiated of course, however, an interesting
story in a number of respects.

If this purported incident occurred on 8th December 1980, it was
just over two weeks prior to those infamous, late December 1980,
'small, triangular UFO' events at RAF Bentwaters/Woodbridge. The
location is given as Norwich, which isn't that far from the
former bases.

I can't think of any obvious explanation for what is described. A
hang glider wouldn't be silent and hovering at an altitude of
'below roof level'! A kite with spotlights seems no less tenable.

There was another witness, albeit evidently both young, and I'll
pursue the possibility of obtaining an additional testimony, plus
confirmation of the object's size and characteristics.

Does anyone recognise a comparative 'UFO' report?

From: "rotsky" <rotsky@wanadoo.fr>
Date: Mon, 4 Feb 2002 10:33:29 +0100
Subject: RE: [UFORL] 'Triangular UFO' Report

This strikes me as precisely the kind of 'event' for which one should not
necessarily seek a literal or physical explanation and where the details -
such as the height, size and material - should be taken as approximate at
best. It is, after all, a 21 year-old childhood memory. The more I read
about UFO encounters the more I'm convinced that a clinical or forensic
style of approach - where reported details are taken almost as if they were
physical evidence in front of the investigator - is inherently flawed. If
there are any truths out there, they will be psychological truths, not
physical ones.

a+
Steve

From: James Easton <voyager@ufoworld.co.uk>

Thanks to all for the feedback.

I thought it might be an interesting exercise to highlight this
account in its 'raw' state. Some of those comments have been
helpful and suggested questions which could be insightful.

In addition to a number of related questions now asked of Rachel,
I also enquired if it's possible to provide a sketch of the
object.

It is, of course, hugely problematic when we're dealing with
twenty-year plus recollections of a then child. That's, alas, all
we presently have to work with.

Should we forthwith conclude this account will remain unresolved
and isn't worth following-up. Arguably yes, however, as it was
reportedly a lengthy 'close encounter' and as Rachel doesn't
attribute the origins as an alien spaceship - indeed noting that
the object was "too thin" for it to be piloted - there's an
outside chance of perhaps further understanding some overall
probabilities.

Surely Rachel's mother would have observed the object when she
came out of that nearby house. What about witnesses from passing
cars during the stated, approximate five minutes which elapsed...
and how could a 'UFO' have passed over a large city like Norwich
without other reports?

It's also not a unique case and I am aware of other, claimed
'brightly lit triangular UFO' UK sightings, including that
perceived 'interaction'. Any new, comparative, data must be
welcome, even acknowledging why a mundane explanation is almost
certain (keeping in mind the recently mentioned story, where a
fire-balloon was proven to be the 'UFO' which a police
helicopter's crew believed had attacked them!).

We'll hopefully see what Rachel (who did give her full name) has
to say in response.

From: "rotsky" <rotsky@wanadoo.fr>
Date: Tue, 5 Feb 2002 11:03:18 +0100
Subject: RE: [UFORL] 'Triangular UFO' Report

But this is precisely my point. There is no 'data' in this report. The vast
majority of so-called information about UFOs is from eye-witness reports,
much of it unverifiable 'encounters'. And yet, as shown by the ongoing
Rendlesham debate, people will argue over fine points of detail, weaving
them into intricate explanations and plots as though those details
themselves can be taken as given - as though they were data collected and
verified at the time. I've seen arguments about the Rendlesham event in
which the exact colour of the lights was discussed because the precise
colour, say, of a blue light would support one theory or another. Yet we
have no real evidence that there was ever any blue light at all. So what we
get, as in so many UFO reports - perhaps most of them - is theory
constructed on fantasy. This is like discussing the etymology of Klingon
nouns: it passes the time, is quite diverting and may lead to a greater
understanding of the human condition in our examination of people's need to
speak Klingon. But it won't give us any greater insight into Klingons. We
would do better to study the people rather than the event. For my money, any
team investigating a UFO phenomenon should include at least one qualified
psychologist to conduct a full examination of the witnesses without
reference to the event. If eye-witness testimony - the most flawed of all
kinds of evidence - is to have any value, we have to know a very great deal
about the witness.

a+
Steve

not really willing to accept many tales as very accurate that are told more
than a month or two after the event (and that still may be too long). Too
many ways the information can be contaminated/distorted. If you are
interested in collecting stories, these kind of reports are great but they
don't add anything significant. How many years has UFO research collected
such stories and how far has the research progressed? In my opinion, it
seems like it is stuck in the same place it was in the early 50's.


Tim Printy
