From: "James Easton" <voyager@ufoworld.co.uk>
Date: Fri, 8 Feb 2002 02:58:12 -0000
Subject: [UFORL] Re: 'Triangular UFO' Report

Regarding:

>From: <TPrinty@aol.com>
>To: <UFORL@yahoogroups.com>
>Subject: Re: [UFORL] 'Triangular UFO' Report
>Date: 04 February 2002 17:49

Tim wrote:

>I am not so sure about the UK but up here in New England, you
>don't have kids on roller skates outside in December. I did
>visit scotland before in the winter and everyone was inside
>after sunset (and even before that).

Tim,

Sunset, circa November-February in the UK, goes from approx. 5:00
p.m. to 3:30 p.m. and back again.

The upside is... it gets brighter come Spring.

However, no ostensible concerns about children playing outdoors
late at night, beginning of December. 'Winter' is primarily
during those next few weeks, particularly January/February and
even then, unless it's unusually severe weather, kids will still
be making the most of 'winter', albeit perhaps nearer to home.

As an aside, is "up here in New England" still celebrating that
compelling 'you couldn't write the script' superb Patriots' win!


Rachel has now kindly responded in great detail to the questions
asked.

It turns out that, as I suspected, there's maybe more to this
story. There were apparently three witnesses [unfortunately, not
to the entire event] and both a local paper's newsdesk and the
local police station were contacted immediately afterwards.

For now, I've omitted or 'deleted' some information given,
notably concerning the meeting with Camilla 'two years ago' and
why "it all went wrong". Camilla was the other main witness and
her mother, Sandy, reportedly observed the object as it departed.

However, there's no significant evidence missing from what
follows:
Dear James,



Thank you for getting back to me. I feel happy about sharing
further details, and I hope it is useful for research purposes.
This might sound strange but it is a real relief to share this
experience with someone who has had contact with this phenomena.
I have only told very close friends over the years as it is a
very personal experience.

It has only since we got cable that I have started watching
programmes about this phenonmena. It has given me the confidence
to contact you because I have found experiences similiar to what
I saw. Over the years I have avoided UFO programmes or books in
an attemtp to keep my memories clean and avoid scaring myself. I
would be prepared to be hypnotised if in your experience it would
highlight any further details. My only concern with hypnotism is
suggestion and remembering something bad.

I have tried to answer your questions and give an explanation
beneath. Sometimes I have repeated details of environmental
factor for different questions because that's how I remember it.


Q: How can you be so certain of the date?



A: Early December need to check with Sandy. It was close the full
moon of that month.

I have always recalled it as this date. It was a school night
Tuesday or Wednesday? [The 8th was a Monday - James] Camilla's
mum Sandy, who took the event more seriously may have kept a
record of the exact date. Sandy (now known as Louise), may have
the reports we made that night and may have exact date.
Alternatively there may be a telephone enquiry record at the
local [name deleted - James] Police Station.


Q: I would particularly like to know what approximate size the
object was.

A: The object was 3m triangle accompanied by two 'tinkerbell'
scout lights of about 10cm.

The craft's was an equilateral triangle of 3 m lengths. The depth
was tiny, it may have been as much as 10 cm, but in side view it
was opaque and linear seeming more like 1 cm. It is important
not to forget the 'tinkerbell' scout lights which danced up the
street and initially brought our attention up to the craft. They
were different colours - orange/blue and pink, I think they
changed their shades during their tradjectory.

They got our attention, talked about them as being tinkerbell
lights, they were playful. They guided our attention up to the
back of the 3 story houses upon which the tip of the craft made
itself visible to us.

The tip of the triangle crawled behind the roof top and when
adjacent to us rose up over the houses and gracefully made it's
way down to our side of the street.


Q: Where were the spotlights positioned and what size were they
in relation to the object? Can you recall the approximate number
of lights and their colour(s)?

A: Summary: Depends on position and nature of object. 3 main
light sources at tips (red/blue - not avaition lights). Outer
glow and outer rim white lights and inner lights with white
intensity at the centre (think also made up of smaller lights but
made up impression of greater light). Ability to change whole
appearance.

There is no simple answer to this I will try and put the
colour/light mood into context of the story.

When it rose up behind the houses it definitely had red on the
tips bigger than our spotlights at home, with some smaller white
lights towards the centre.

When it was making it's way down to us I recall studying the
glow, of about 50cm? It was so bright and crisp around the whole
craft. I remember trying to work out how it was doing it. I
recall a the inner lights to have a blueish tone as it came down.

Whilst above us everything was lit up, the brickwork detailing on
the house. I remember Camilla saying afterwards that it had blue
and red lights on the tips, which kind of rings true with me, but
I remember maybe 100 white lights of domestic size (but not
depth) spaced on the outer rim of the craft and tighter/brighter
in the centre (possibly tighter packed lights?).

In general when above us the lights were pulsating/throbbing.
Once interupted by the noise factor it turned over with lights
facing upto the sky - slow trajectory. The craft was opaque from
other side, so when took off over house the lights were now
facing upwards.


Q: Were, for example, the triangle's corners at right angles, or
rounded?

A: The object had both during my encounter. It had corners when
interacting and then morphed into rounded departing.

Upon approach and whilst above us I am 99% sure it was a crisp
triangle with corners. Only when it 'morphed' and turned over
did the shape soften with curved edges. If you give me a postal
address I can send you sketches / photographs and maps of the
locations mentioned.


>Duration of its observation of us:
>5 minutes at least (we were put into a kind of trance and lost
>track of time).

Q: What happened during this period - did, for example, the
object simply hover in mid-air? Were the lights changing position
and colour?

A: The lights changed, always in movement but if seen from a
distance it could easily be mistaken as motionless hover.

During this time the object was moving about 1cm a second?
Smoothly, quietly majestic. As I mentioned in question 3 the
lights were throbbing and the emphasis changed towards the
centre. Our minds became transfixed, on details like the brick
work lighting up above the street light.

I find this part of things unnerving because I do not recall
moving during the incident, but the view from which I saw the
object morph etc seems a couple of meters further towards the
wall. I am going back to Norwich tomorrow and will visit the
location to confirm if I'd moved during those 5 minutes.. Also
the loudness of the door banging was intense like a slap round
the face really loud - were my senses hightened?


Q: Is it possible anyone else might have observed this - perhaps
from passing cars?

A: There was no traffic on Sussex St, but St Augustines is a main
road out of the city and I recall cars on it. They might of seen
it whilst it came accross street to us?

It is possible that a passing car on St Augustines Street may
have witnessed the scout lights on sussex street/object when made
it's decent. There was no traffic on Sussex Street during the
incident.

It is scary to think that something like this could be so close
to the back windows of the flats opposite and nobody realise. The
object came from behind the houses (north sussex street 3 story
high weavers cottages renovated into flats) - it must have almost
carressed their windows and nobody realised? Also someone could
have easily looked out of their front windows and seen us on the
street below with the object - nobody ever approached me or asked
about the event.

This aspect of the event still scares me, just shows how
vulnerable you are even in a built up area.


>...it was my friends mother closing her front door about 10
>houses away.



Q: Did your friend's mother see the object? If either yourself of
her daughter immediately (or later) told her about this
experience, what did she suggest the object most likely was?

A: She saw it, and separated us immediately to take reports on
what we'd seen. She thought we should report it, as might be a
UFO.

When Sandy came round the corner the object had just gone over
the roof of my house. (the sky was whispy clouds and the moon was
almost or had recently been full). We asked her if she'd seen and
she said no, so we rushed up to the steps by my house. All of us
watched it in object move over the city towards the city hall
clock, low level, no noise, when it went round the clock and
excellerated south west.

Sandy took us straight to her house. Separated us and took
reports from us both and made us draw diagrams. She then said
that she believed us and we should go straight to my mother to
let her know. When we got to my house, my mother did not take us
seriously and insisted we'd just seen a seagull or something.
Sandy insisted my mother should check with the newsdesk at the
local paper where mum worked to find out if they were running a
story about it. My mother phoned up but was too embarrased to
let her work colleague know her identity. They had not had any
reports, so Sandy said we should phone the local police station
to find out what it was. My mother phoned through and there were
no reports of UFO's in the area. She said we'd imagined it and it
would be silly to take the matter further. She now apologies for
not being supportive during this time, it is only now that I am
still going on about it to her that she thinks there might be
some truth in it.

In the time after the event I experienced hair loss. The doctors
put it down to childhood illness and bad nerves. I also felt as
if I was being monitored - is this something you are familiar
with?


Q: When you say 'morph' - did the object appear to change shape?

A: Yes. As I have mentioned in earlier questions, once we had
been disturbed by the 'bang' it animated and speeded up. It
curved and elongated whilst rotating could see through it, until
reached 180 degrees position with lights facing up (no longer
illuminated the road/tree etc). This is when the true nature of
it's materiality became evident: kind of liquid quality
aluminium/mercury/opaque. It then excellerated with no effort or
noise over my house.


>...over city centre (upside down lights facing upwards when flew
>low level over city around city hall clock and off in a
>southerly direction.

Q: What was the object's approximate speed at this point; did it
slowly manoeuvre towards the city centre, or perhaps suddenly
accelerate?

A: Both.

The distance from my house to the city hall clock is about one
mile. The object travelled in a straight direction towards it.
Arriving there in seconds 5-10? - enough time for Sandy to say
"what the hell is that". It took a sweep round the clock at
level/lower than clock face. Then excellerated at speed off in
south westerly direction. (I will go back to the site and time
the amount of time takes to run to steps + send you details of
the exact distance to town hall clock to give better
understanding of speed of travel).


Q: You were statedly with a friend. Are you still in contact with
them, such that they could provide a secondary account of the
experience?
A: I have asked my mother to find out Sandy's address, I will
pass it onto you by the weekend. I have seen Camilla on one
occasion but she was still too freaked about the whole thing to
talk about it.

I saw Camilla 2 years ago whilst working in Norwich. Invited
round for dinner hoping to discuss the sighting etc. It all went
wrong.

I have since bumped into Sandy (known as Louise) and have
promised to go round for dinner. I no longer live in Norwich, but
my mother has her contact details. I am sure 'Louise' would be
happy to talk to you. I have not spoken to her since in any
detail about events but my mother says she's wanted to talk to me
about what happened. I think it best if you contact her direct
to ensure purity of source.


I hope to hear from you soon.
Yours sincerely,

Rachel.
[END]


It would of course be wonderful if Sandy, who was clearly
thinking 'UFO' from the outset, retains those original December
1980 accounts and sketches [shades of 'Rendlesham' ;)].

There are a number of leads to pursue and although they might not
help to explain what truly occurred, it could be insightful to
document how evidently sincere witness recollections and
perceptions have perhaps altered, or not, over those intervening
years.

It's a peculiar 'UFO' report, especially the object's small size
and stated appearance. However, elements of the archetypal
'triangular UFO' are there - a silent, slow-moving, exceedingly
low altitude object [often described as 'tree top' level], with
bright lights [sometimes compared to a 'Christmas tree'] and
which is also capable of rapid acceleration.


Another intriguing facet to this case are those 'tinkerbell'
lights:

"They got our attention, talked about them as being tinkerbell
lights, they were playful. They guided our attention up to the
back of the 3 story houses upon which the tip of the craft made
itself visible to us".
As some subscribers will appreciate, Jean-Pierre Pharabod is a
French scientist and 'skeptic' who has a thorough knowledge of
the Belgian 1989-90 triangular UFO 'flap'.

We had previously discussed a number of reported cases, during
those incidents and from elsewhere, which allegedly involved
sightings of one or more small lights that separated from the
'triangular object', were seemingly operating under control and
later 'reattached' themselves to the main object.

I dare say children would naturally describe any such comparative
observation as being 'tinkerbell lights'. Indeed, that's the most
apt description I've heard.


It's impossible to reach any conclusions based on current data.
If more evidence becomes available in this instance, it will
doubtless still be inadequate, however, we can only see what
transpires.

I'll firstly ask Rachel if she can expand on her recollection of
those 'tinkerbell lights' and what eventually became of them.


James Easton.

While sitting back in my office having a good rest after a short

Now being involved in the field of Genetics and having spent some
time with Dr Kary Mullis (Nobel Prize winner), I found this snip

investigation.

Read the Fortean Times summary (below) and you will see what I am
on about -

(c) Fortean Times, UK
FT149 Aug 2001,
p14, col 3.

"Alien Genetic Engineering: The Evidence?"

"Australian UFO researcher Bill Chalker has published the results
of a DNA analysis carried out on a strand of hair allegedly left
behind by an alien visitor.

While resting in bed after dropping his wife off at work on the
morning of 23 July 1992, lucky Sydney abductee Peter Khoury was
visited by two naked females. One was Asian in appearance, black-
haired and dark - eyed, the other was 'Nordic', over 6ft (1.8m)
tall, with wispy blond hair and intensely bright blue eyes.

The Nordic attempted to seduce Khoury, who resisted, biting off
one of her nipples in the struggle. This didn't appear to upset
the entity, who did not bleed and only expressed surprise to her
companion. After a coughing fit (caused by choking on the alien's
nipple?) Khoury saw that the two women had vanished and went to
the bathroom. He found urinating difficult and painful, and
noticed a blond hair wrapped around his penis. This he placed
into a specimen bag and eventually submitted to Bill Chalker for
analysis.

Samples were submitted for Polymerase Chain Reaction DNA
profiling to Nobel Prize winner and self-proclaimed abductee Dr
Kary Mullis, with some peculiar results. The hair appeared to
have two different genetic heritages, depending on where along
its length the sample were taken from. The DNA in the shaft came
from someone biologically "close to human", but of an extremely
rare Chinese Mongoloid lineage, despite being blond. This lineage
is, according to Chalker, as far from the human genetic
mainstream as that of the African Pygmies. DNA in the hair's root
section was closer to a Basque or Gaelic lineage.

[...]

These findings, if correct, are leading Chalker and others to
speculate that the hair's alleged alien owner is it/herself the
result of some genetic manipulation. Could this be the evidence
that abduction researchers have been looking for? We'll have more
on the case in a future issue."
[END OF EXTRACT FROM GLEN'S POSTING]


Those are certainly an extraordinary series of claims and some
might conclude, one of the most patently ludicrous 'alien
abductee' stories ever.

In 'Strange Evidence', amongst "compelling evidence" for the
physical "reality of mainstream UFO events", you cite the Tulley,
Australia (1966), Trans-en-Provence, France (1981) and Cash-
Landrum, Texas (1980) cases:

http://www.cufos.org/strange_evidence.pdf

Outwith the fanatical faithful, how many will concur these are
significant indications of ET visitation?

You also reference the "'chupa' encounters in Brazil".
Presumably, these local 'monster' anecdotes are implied to be
serious, scientific, corroborative evidence?


Regarding, "self-proclaimed abductee Dr Kary Mullis", I note an
interesting article which comments:

Remember Kerry [Kary] Mullis? He won it for inventing Polymerase
Chain Reaction. After he got the prize, he quit science and
devoted his life to doing product endorsements and chasing girls.
As for me, I can't understand why a man would want to do product
endorsements.

You all heard about him during the O.J. Simpson trial. The plan
was, the defense would hire him to testify about how inaccurate
PCR is for identifying DNA like O.J.'s. Mullis made millions of
dollars from that invention, but for a little more he's willing
to tell us the method is worthless. Right.

[...]

I think Mullis' attitude is something like, "If you pay me
100,000 dollars, I'll say that PCR can't distinguish O.J. from a
flatworm. And if you pay me half a mil, I'll say O.J. Simpson is
really a thermophilic archaebacteria! Hell, I don't care! I'll
say O.J. is a retrovirus! He's not even a eukaryote! This LSD is
bad s--! Where are the college girls at?"

The supposed witness, Peter Khoury, is a long-time, self-avowed
'alien abductee'. It's no surprise to find he became one along
that familiar route of reading a Whitley Strieber novel and then
being 'hypnotised' by a local 'abductee support group'.

What criteria do you apply to determine if any such 'abductee'
story is or isn't 'real', no matter how seemingly absurd?


In essence, Khoury describes an alleged incident from 1992 when,
at the time, he "was on a lot of medication". He goes to bed,
falls asleep and then 'wakes up' to find himself with two female
aliens who have decided to drop in for a quick 'menage a trois'.

When he bites off part of one girl's nipple, the girls,
understandably, decide to leave and "they just vanished". As if
by magic...

The piece of nipple sticks in his throat for three days, despite
his Mom's advice how to "just eat some bread and wash it down".
Not that he told her what was stuck there.

The tale of how he then found that 'alien hair' is no less
farcical.


In terms of what purportedly constitutes sober, scientific
evidence, can you see why it's the above which has perhaps, in
fact, 'lost the plot' and on page one?

Friends:

In his book, On Pilots and UFOs, Willy Smith is described in the
third person as having recieved his M.S. and Ph.D. from the University
of Michigan. It says that after working one year for the U.S. Atomic
Energy Commission, he worked the rest of his professional career
in education and taught physics at the University of Michigan,
Lycoming College (Williamsport, PA) and at the University of
Valencia. On the back cover it says: "Dr. Smith earned his Ph.D.
from the University of Michigan, and after many years dedicated to
teaching physics at universities in the United States and Europe,
he now devotes most of his time to the study of the UFO
phenomenon, whose reality he considers indisputable." These
cover blurbs are sometimes written by editors or others, although
this book was published in 1997 by his UNICAT Project, described
as "essentially an independant research organization. Copies may
be obtained from booksellers or the author, directly, according to
an announcement after p. 137.

0417 HOURS THEY OBSERVED A LONG GLEAMING SHITE STRIP,
RUNWAY
WIDTH, AND APPROX 5 MILES LONG {ACTUAL ENDS OBSCURED BY
CLOUD}RUNNING NNE/SSW. AT MID POSITION ON EASTERLY SIDE
LARGE
GLEAMING RECTANGLE CONSISTING OF CRISS-CROSS RESEMBLING
ILLUMINATED LATTICE WORK. THIS OBJECT APPROX 2 OR 3 MILES
SQUARE,
EXTENDING AT RIGHT ANGLES FROM FLUSH WITH SIDE OF RUNWAY IN
E TO
SE DIRECTION....WAS THIS UFO SITING ?????????
[END]


Presumably, the "LONG GLEAMING SHITE STRIP" is meant to read
"LONG GLEAMING WHITE STRIP"!

As a photocopy, is the original document known to be publicly

'UFO' sighting?

Given the remarkable claims therein and as it's alleged to be an
'official' RAF report, I would expect to have previously heard
about this case. It surely must have been investigated to some
extent - other witnesses, corroborative radar tracking, etc. What
was the outcome?

Chris,

It looks like, "WAS THIS UFO SITING?" has been added by the
seller and doesn't appear in the document.

I've downloaded a copy from the advertisement and a cursory
examination suggests the document is authentic.

It seems to be headed, "SPECIAL REPORT"; the first word is
"SPECIAL". There's a date stamp which is the standard format
[identifying name, then date, then address] I have seen in use
within other government departments.

There's some text which is partially erased with a red line, as
if this is a document released by HM government - possibly under
the 30 year rule? Yet, the document being shown appears to be the
original copy, of which presumably one or more photocopies are
being sold.

It's not being advertised as 'UFO' related, being sold under the
heading of 'Collectables:Transportation:Aviation'.

I've asked the seller if he can explain the background. As Steve
Mansfield notes, any such document should be traceable via the
Public Records Office.

You might be interested to know the seller's location is given as
Leicester.

<FONT FACE=arial,helvetica><FONT COLOR="#8000ff" SIZE=2>Hi, I've never
seen this document at the PRO and as far as I know the term UFO wasn't in use in the
war either (although there are wartime records at the PRO that refer to "unidentified
objects"). The term "unidentified flying object" was in use in US military circles only
a few weeks after the Kenneth Arnold sighting and one example is contained in a file
I obtained from the FBI. There are a lot of WW2 UFO-style reports at the PRO. Andy
Roberts and Dave Clarke have found a lot (most of which I have now) of Foo Fighter
reports and one report that deals with the sighting of a large UFO (3-400ft long) that
was seen by a British crew both in the air and on the ground. A lot of this material
will be covered in their forthcoming book, Out of the Shadows (Piatkus Books).
Cheers, Nick Redfern.</FONT>

From: "rotsky" <rotsky@wanadoo.fr>
Date: Mon, 25 Feb 2002 00:15:05 +0100
Subject: RE: [UFORL] 1944 UK UFO Case?

If this is a genuine report, I'm inclined to suspect some form of mirage
caused by atmospheric effects. I've seen long bright lines caused by the sun
reflecting off the top of an inversion layer - the 'surface' of the layer
itself looked like a dazzlingly lit silver ocean. The same could happen with
a bright moon (though, admittedly, the presence of an inversion layer would
be less likely). If you saw this from between other cloud layers (the report
mentions cloud), especially if tired after a long and hazardous photo recon
mission... well, you can fill in the blanks.

Alternatively, maybe they saw an actual airfield, perhaps through haze, with
moon shining off wet tarmac. We all know the problems of judging size,
especially from the air and in a fatigued state. Without a *lot* more to go
on (a met report, for example, or some info about the crewmen, the mission,
the altitude, the moon phase... well the list goes on) - all this falls into
the realm of speculation. But we can certainly have some fun with it...

By the way, this is supposed to have been a *night* photo recon mission??

a+
Steve

Y'all,

Regarding the 1944 'UFO' document on Ebay.
I have been in touch with the seller, who tells me the document was
retrieved from a skip at RAF Bentley Priory in the late 1950s/early 1960s,
with a lot of other similar material.
We know this was the time when the Air Ministry were regularly dumping large
amounts of paperwork, including the files on classic UFO incidents such as
the Lakenheath-Bentwaters case.
The seller is not interested in selling the original and has not responded
to my further queries.
Dave Clarke and I are currently in the south of England interviewing a
number of retired RAF aircrew from the 1950s for a forthcoming BBC Radio 4
documentary on RAF UFO encounters.
We can say this type of document certainly existed, as we have collected a
number of similar accounts of foo-fighter type phenomenon from the era
1942-44 in the RAF files at the PRO; these will be detailed in our
forthcoming book Out of the Shadows (published in the UK, May 23, 2002).
On Wednesday we will be at the Public Record Office and will be looking into
the source of the 1944 incident.
Will keep the list notified of what we find.

Happy trails,

Andy Roberts and Dave Clarke

I think Joel asks a very pertinent question. Do we know if
the report itself refers to an "object" or is that just a
term used by the seller? Otherwise, there is really nothing
to suggest that it's in any way aerial.

The observing aircraft is described as being from a "met flight"
- presumably "meteorology". Does anyone know what this actually
entailed? Presumably they would observe the entire sky but they
might be particularly interested in cloud cover over bombing
targets, and so spend a lot of time looking down?

This page describes the 1409 Met. Flight as part of the pathfinders
(ie target markers for the British night bombers): "In 1943 the PFF
was reinforced by two new squadrons and 1409 Met. Flight who provided
daily weather checks over the continent for Bomber Command and the 8th
US Air Force."

<http://www.550sqn.theraf.co.uk/550bkgrd.htm>

be more precise ...

From: cgibson@skomer.u-net.com
Date: Tue, 26 Feb 2002 08:31:08 GMT
Subject: [UFORL] Re: 1944 UK UFO Case?


Met flights were standard procedure, especially at a time when Bomber
Command's operations were at a height (winter 44). We tend to forget how
difficult weather forecasting was before the advent of sats and Crays.

Insufficient weather data led to the largest loss of RAF aircraft in a
single raid, on Nuremburg at the end of March 44. Incidently it was
contrails that caused a problem then as I think the contrail height was
lower than expected. But I'll need to check the relevant books.

When I get home I'll check the Bomber Command war diary for that night and
see what ops were on and if that met flight is listed (document says
Fighter Command, but sometimes the support flights are listed as well)

If this bright strip was on the ground, could it have been a German decoy
structure? I know that one of the large lakes near Berlin was "camouflaged"
to look like a town on H2S radar. Perhaps moonlight was reflecting off the
lake surface below the camouflage nets or whatever. My trusty Psion gives
those co-ords as eastern Germany, not far from Berlin.

As for V-1s. RV Jones et al knew about them and had a ringside seat during
the test flights from 1942 on thanks to Bletchley Park. That's why
Peenemunde was clobbered, setting back the V-1 and V-2 programmes for
months.

Have a nice day. I won't.

Chris

James, Glen & others, you are certainly entitled to your opinions about this
case. It would be nice if they were actually based on the expoused
principles of this list, namely "advocate and adopt a consistent, scientific
appraisal of purported 'UFO' related evidence".
In your response I see little of that, and more of ad hominem attacks on
Kary Mullis, quoting Frank Pettit's own speculative thoughts of what Mullis
might have been on about, as if it was the "facts". As for "facts" maybe it
would be fairer (if science is not the real objective of this list) to at
least quote Mullis's view. Try Mullis's own "take" in his book "Dancing
Naked in the mind field", the cover of which caputures the man a little
"Hunter S. Thompson meets Stephen Hawking", a quote from Gerald Posner.
Its a wild & irreverent book, but great fun. Mullis is certainly a wild and
erratic scientist, but presents a very human story, full of excess. For the
convoluted story on PCR see Paul Rabinow's detailed book "Making PCR - a
story of Biotechnology", an odyssey in "bricolage" Rabinow concludes, in
which Mullis is "a player in a game that was already underway. His rebound
from a blocked course of action turned into a swerve and eventually - a
potential movement." Rabinow shows how complex the saga of PCR was.

Then you suggest my listings of cases such as Tully (not "Tulley"),
Trans-en-Provence & Cash Landrum requires a retort from you of, "Outwith the
fanatical faithful, how many will concur these are significant indications
of ET visitation?" Again little scientific accuracy here. Nowhere did I
say evidence of "ET visitation", thats your invention. I would not
characterise myself as part of "the fanatical faithful" of anything. I try
to be driven by evidence not "armchair pontification" and "it can't be,
therefore isn't" sensibilities. For example I don't agree with Jenny
Randles' "Meaden plasma vortex" analysis of Tully on the basis of field
investigations and fact, but I'm not portraying the 1966 Tully event as ET
evidence either. Re "Trans" 1981, I'm well aware of Maillot & Scornaux's
analysis, but equally there is data collected on the case that is intriguing
and we should not thow out the "baby" with the "bathwater". If anything,
"Trans" while maybe having some evidence of "poor science", the principles
of rapid investigation, field investigation, comprehensive site
investigations, coupled with multidisciplinary scientific and other
enquiries, are laudable, and our aim should be to have them as the norm
rather than the exception. Details of lack of rigour are certainly valid
comments and criticisms, along with Niccolai's vagaries, are further
important points. Still the arguements against "Trans" are far from terminal
and require further debate rather than one sided proselytising. As for
Cash - Landrum, tell me what the problem is there. Sure its not proof of
aliens, but something happened there.

Your belittling, trivialising and superficial "commentary" on Peter Khoury's
case betray's more about a frequent "modus operandi" evident on this list,
that approximates more closely armchair "debunking" than the scientific
principles you claim you want this list to aspire to. I'm all for sceptical
investigations, in fact it was the primary motivation of my DNA
investigation of Peter Khoury's case. Here was a case unlike others that
highlighted some "evidence" that could perhaps be looked at in a scientific
way. My attitude to all UFO reports is most likely IFO first, and let the
quality of the evidence led to any contrary findings, that might suggest
something more impressive. If the "evidence" is impressive or suggestive
then obviously they are the sorts of cases we should concentrate on.

Again you and those on your list that support your view that Peter Khoury's
case is "one of the most patently ludicrous 'alien
 abductee' stories ever", are entitled to your views, but think about how
you come to your views. Perhaps when you air your views your can enlightens
us all to your experience in "abduction" investigations and how many cases
of this type you've actually investigated yourself and where you have
applied your touted list "scientific principles" in the investigation of
them, rather than what seems to me to be "arm chair rants".

As for "medication" and "head injuries" (Glen's belated discovery - he
obviously read my article very closely in the first place?? - I spelt out
all these issues for all to read) tell me where the evidence is that "head
injuries" that occurred months earlier are a cause of "alien abduction"
fantasies. Likewise let me know the evidence for Panadeine Forte and one
tablet of Prozac leading to such fantasies, and while you are at it let me
know how these 2 mechanisms can account for an unusual hair sample wrapped
around the gentleman's penis, that yield unusual DNA results, that
supported, rather than refuted, his bizarre story. I prefer the course of
serious investigation, rather than trivilising and superficial ridicule. If
serious investigation reveals counter arguments you'll hear it first from
me. So far such counter arguments have not been significant, and the case
still is worthy, at least in my humble estimation, of further serious
consideration. Again, for the benefit of the inattentive reader or armchair
commentator, I am not putting the Khoury DNA evidence forward as proof of
aliens. At this stage it is compelling evidence of a possible anomolous
event that deserves further serious investigation, debate and commentary. I
still remain hopeful that this list can provide some of that, but so far I'm
a little disappointed, but hardly surprised.

Regards,

Bill Chalker

Bill wrote:

>Perhaps when you air your views your can enlightens us all to
>your experience in "abduction" investigations and how many cases
>of this type you've actually investigated yourself and where you
>have applied your touted list "scientific principles" in the
>investigation of them, rather than what seems to me to be "arm
>chair rants".

Bill,

I have on video a documentary about Celtic mythology.

It features an ostensible sincere and credible man from Ireland,
who describes his encounter with a leprechaun.

Now, I'm no expert on this subject, however, I can deduce the
story, albeit seemingly told in all honesty, is not trustworthy
evidence that leprechauns are real.

It's called common sense.

Neither would many of us profess to be highly knowledgeable about
crop circles, yet, we can confidently conclude they have no basis
in reality as evidence of ET creativity. That's despite all the
'experts' who proclaim otherwise and castigate those who are more
skeptical (the current fad in UK's 'UFO Magazine').

Same goes for most other facets of ufology.

Do we need to have expertise in document analysis before judging
that the entire MJ-12 bandwagon is baloney? It's actually all
true, according to the 'experts'.

Or is it a prerequisite to be a qualified space historian before
arguing why NASA did not in fact fake the moon landings, although
ufology's 'experts' accuse otherwise.
I'm sure you can think of countless other examples and what they
coincidentally reveal about contemporary ufology's foundations.

So why does one require to have "experience in 'abduction'
investigations" [although I am reasonably well read on this
topic] before commenting on the absurdity of so many instances
where people have been 'hypnotised' until they 'remember' being
kidnapped by fiendish creatures from outer space?


There's an old data processing acronym - GIGO. It stands for,
'garbage in, garbage out', meaning; if your raw data is unsound,
then the outcome will assuredly be.

If you want to believe Peter Khoury's story, that's your
prerogative and it's recognised you do so with the best
intentions. However, you must appreciate why his 'hypnotised'
account is comparative to someone's tale of being abducted by
salacious leprechauns and will be perceived as such.

It's not obligatory we become 'alien abduction investigators'
before common sense applies and we can reason that the ubiquitous
'greys' are an utter myth, significantly constructed by elements
within ufology.

Khoury's supposed sexual adventures did not of course involve the
little grey dudes, however, he had allegedly been in their
custody before. That alone tells us a great deal.


Ultimately, it's not the pre-existing faithful you have to
convince, nor even myself. Your evidence must be persuasive to
science.

How many within that field will read your paper and give it
remotely serious consideration? Or will it be laughed out of town
because it's patently 'garbage in...'.

If the latter, in your position I would want to know why my
research had abjectly failed to make any scientific impact -
there has to be a reason.

Before mandatorily blaming 'debunkers and skeptics', I wouldn't
want to overlook the more obvious possibility I had been
enthusiastically gullible and was, in truth, championing a
fabricated story which had, in all fairness, been highlighted as
nowhere near so plausible or credible as I wanted to believe.

>Again, for the benefit of the inattentive reader or armchair
>commentator...
Your "experience in 'abduction' investigations" and resultant
disdain is no effective barrier to the above possibility, indeed,
perhaps being more likely an inherent cause of it.


Some other points you made, I'll reply to separately when time
permits.



James Easton.

From: "David Clarke" <cd292@crazydiamonds.fsnet.co.uk>

From: James Easton <voyager@ufoworld.co.uk>Sent: Friday, March 01, 2002 10:50
PM
Subject: Re: [UFORL] 1944 UK UFO Case?


> I wasn't aware, as Dave and Andy explained, that such historical
> Air Ministry material is known to have been consigned to the
> waste skip, including "classic UFO files". I thought some of the
> other WWII documents being sold were certainly of historical
> value.
>

Hi James,

Unfortunately, that appears to be the case. The MoD destruction policy
dates from the Grigg Committee of the 1950s which "reviewed the
arrangements for the preservation of records of government departments."
This brought in the system of 'first review' and 'second review' of
documents, five years and 25 years after their closure. Grigg estimated
that 90 percent of documents could be destroyed at First Review to
reduce the amount of paper stored in Government archives.

Individual branches carried out their own reviews "and only records
generally perceived to have possible historical value are transferred to
MoD archives...those records not judged to have historical interest
are destroyed when designed by the local desk officer."

Figures I have for the estimated no of files reviewed and destroyed at
First Review are 2.735 million (195,360 linear feet of paper) - in effect
90 percent of the stuff is shredded before it even reaches 2nd review,
when a decision is taken on whether files are preserved at the PRO.

The simple fact is that there is not the room to preserve this amount
of paper, and hence it has been dumped/shredded/destroyed, removing
the vast majority of MoD UFO files from the historical record. Until
1967, when Merlyn Rees MP demanded that UFO files should be
preserved, all files were shredded at 5 yearly intervals - the few that
slipped through the net are what are now available at the PRO.

It seems that a lot of this stuff, particularly from Fighter Command
HQ, Bentley Priory, ended up in skips or waste dumps where our
friend may have obtained the 1944 report discussed on this list.

Hence, in 1961 when the last destruction was ordered, we lost the
files on the Lakenheath-Bentwaters incident and most of the evidence
for Air Ministry/DDI (Tech) investigations into the classic UFO cases
from thew 1950s. Hence, the earliest files now available for study
at Kew date from 1962, although some material (for instance the
1951 report by the Flying Saucer Working Party) has survived
and was 'lost' for some time in another file relating to scientific
intelligence.

The explanation for this destruction is interesting - UFOs were always
found to have such mundane explanations that records were deemed
to be "of transitory interest"/"no historical interest" by some faceless
bureaucrat. If, they say, any incident was deemed to be of defence interest
then those papers would have been preserved; of course this is a very
subjective viewpoint, but that's what happened whether we like it or
not.

Hope this is helpful.

Dave Clarke

of it."
Sir Walter Ralegh

Subject: [UFORL] 1944 UFO sighting

Just checked the Bomber Command War Diary for the night of 21/22 feb 1944.

"MINOR OPERATIONS

17 Mosquitoes to Duisberg, Stuttgart and 2 flying bomb sites, 1 Serrate partol, 41
aircraft minelaying in the Frisians and off French ports, 10 OTU sorties, 1 Stirling
Minelayer lost."

Serrate was a device fitted to Mosquito night fighters that homed in on the
Liechtenstein radar fitted to Luftwaffe night fighters.

OTU is an Operational Training Unit.

No mention of Met flights, but as the doc says, it was a Fighter Command op.

Next big op was a "maximum effort" to Schweinfurt on Feb 24/25.

Chris

From: "James Easton" <voyager@ufoworld.co.uk>
Date: Sun, 3 Mar 2002 05:17:55 -0000
Subject: [UFORL] 'UFOs, an Air Force Dilemma'

There's an important and hugely interesting publication which is
now online, courtesy of the 'National Institute for Discovery
Science' (NIDS), at:

http://www.nidsci.org/articles/pdf/quintanilla.pdf

Their introduction is self-explanatory:

Preface to "UFOs, An Air Force Dilemma"
by Hector Quintanilla, USAF (retired)

National Institute for Discovery Science

For the first time NIDS is electronically publishing a book
manuscript written in 1975 by Lt. Col. Hector Quintanilla, the
head of the USAF Project Blue Book. Project Blue Book was
supposed to be an objective investigation and documentation of
the UFO phenomenon carried out by the United States Air Force
from March 1952 until December 1969. Project Blue Book was the
successor to Projects Sign and Grudge.

The book is a summary in Quintanilla's own words of his
involvement, as head of project Blue Book, in the investigation
of the UFO phenomenon. "UFOs, an Air Force Dilemma" was also
given the title "UFOs: A $20,000,000 Fiasco" by Quintanilla in a
book proposal to unnamed publishers. NIDS's purpose in making
available this previously unpublished manuscript is twofold: (a)
to demonstrate to the interested public, through the authors own
unedited words, Lt. Col. Quintanilla's attitudes, preconceptions,
and biases that dominated Project Blue Book, and (b) to make
available to historians and to the public the methodology and
practices employed by the United States Air Force in
investigating and cataloging the UFO phenomenon.

NIDS had the choice of introducing editorial changes into the
manuscript. We refrained in order to preserve the historical
accuracy of this document. The manuscript covers the years of
Quintanilla's own involvement from July 1963 to December 1969 in
Project Blue Book and also contains many valuable insights into
the public and media reaction to the USAF funded study, from the
perspective of the author. In particular, Lt. Col. Quintanilla's
antagonistic descriptions of University of Arizona professor
James A McDonald's pursuit of the UFO phenomena as well as Dr. J.
Allen Hynek's relationship with project Blue Book are annotated
for the public record in considerable detail.
[END]
This contains many notable insights, as indicated in the
following preface:

"Tell The Truth and They Will Not Believe You"
Hector Quintanilla, in a private video interview, December 1990

By Alex Chionetti

[...]

"I remember having long conversations with him, in our native
language Spanish. I remember asking him about Roswell, which was
barely mentioned during his time. "Hangar 18," he remarked, "I
went but there was nothing else than an empty structure, nothing
special, no little guys, no ships." We talked about the Socorro
Case, where we both shared frustrated experiences with Lonnie
Zamora. The possibility that the Socorro craft was an
experimental prototype of a lunar module stayed with him for more
than two decades, but he could never prove it. He also told me it
was Blue Book's most important case, as you will see in his
memoirs".


Quintanilla's comments on both the Socorro case and Hynek's
involvement therein are striking.

This is a large document - 131 pages - and I'm surprised its
availability seemingly hasn't been publicised to the extent
merited.

In a decidedly forthright opinion, Quintanilla writes of Hynek:

"Prior to April, 1964, I had very little trouble with Hynek.
He complained to me that Dave Moody was not treating him
according to his scientific stature or some crap like that. I
talked to Dave about it the first couple of times and Dave
would come back that he was too busy to baby sit or kiss the
Doctor's ass and that if he would get busy and evaluate the
cases that were referred to him, that he wouldn't have time to
worry about scientific stature. Dr. Hynek and Dave had a thing
going and I decided to study it. After I analyzed the
situation, I had to agree with Dave. Dr. Hynek would come into
the office and he would spend the first couple of hours
socializing or gossiping or telling us a lot of nonsense about
who was writing books, articles, etc. It was during one of
these distracting sessions that I raised my voice and asked
Dr. Hynek to confine his visit to case studies and let the
rest of the staff proceed with their work.
Our philosophy as to how the program should be administered
differed and we began to polarize during the Socorro sighting.
I wanted publicity kept at a low key until we could finish the
investigation, but he managed to stir up a hornet's nest by
making irrelevant remarks. During the first few days of the
investigation, the telephone lines to my office were backed up
for forty minutes and the lines to the base were backed up for
ten or fifteen minutes. By this time the switchboard operators
were wishing that I'd move my base of operation to Venus or
Mars. They were really very nice and sympathetic, but it
created chaos for them on a number of occasions. Sending Hynek
to investigate the Socorro incident was my mistake and I began
to regret it almost immediately. His part of the investigation
didn't add anything significant to the overall report,
however, he was now in the national lime-light and he managed
to stay there for quite awhile, because the news media
depicted him as the "expert UFO Air Force consultant". This
prestigious title gained him publicity and recognition which
he couldn't possibly get as the chairman of the Dearborn
Observatory. Up to this time, Hynek had taken a fairly stable
stand with regards to UFO's and the associated phenomena. As
the wind changed the desert, so Hynek began to change and I
never knew what was coming next. He embarrassed me and the Air
Force on a number of occasions; but I kept my cool in public,
and wasted no words with him in private. Time and time again I
asked him to clarify his comments and remarks and all I'd get
would be a weasel word explanation. I had become concerned
because at times I couldn't believe what I read in print. For
example: In April, 1966, Dr. Hynek stated before the House
Armed Services Committee that he had twenty cases which he had
"certified as well reported" and was unable to explain. In a
letter to Science Magazine of October 21, 1966, he stated
that, "I have in my files several hundred reports which are
real brain teasers and could easily be made the subject of
profitable discussion among physical and social scientists
alike". In the December 17, 1966 article of the Saturday Post,
Dr. Hynek stated, "of the 15,000 cases that have come to my
attention, several hundred are puzzling, and some of the
puzzling incidents perhaps one in twenty-five, are
bewildering". According to my calculations, this would come to
about sixty cases. I'm not surprised at this statement, some
of the cases that were puzzling to him were not at all
puzzling to me, Dave Moody, Bill Marley, or Dr. Menzel.

The Post article, which was by-lined by "J. Allen Hynek" was
captioned as follows: "For years the Air Force has dismissed
them as hoaxes, hallucinations, or misidentifications. Now the
Air Forces' own scientific consultant on Unidentified Flying
Objects declares that many of the sightings cannot be so
easily explained." I would like to reiterate that Dr. Hynek
was never the Air Force's consultant on UFO's. Dr. Hynek wrote
an article for Playboy Magazines and his title was "The UFO
Gap". The magazines caption for this article was as follows:
"America's leading ufologist-just back from an international
astronomer's conference behind the iron curtain warns that a
new Soviet investigative approach could cost us the race to
solve the flying-saucer riddle." This prognostication, just
like all the others he made throughout the years, fell flat on
its ass because the Soviets weren't interested in flying
saucers. They didn't believe in them as a threat or a
phenomena. I had been getting queries about his unresolved
figures from scientific members and also from the news media,
so for the record I wrote a memo and asked Dr. Hynek to
identify those cases which he considered unresolved and also
to identify the number; was it twenty, sixty, one hundred, or
one thousand? Also, would he identify how many of these were
Air Force cases and how many were from his own personal file.
Just after I had written the memo, I received a block-buster
through the mail. The January-February, 1968, issue of the UFO
Investigator had just been disseminated through the mail and
the front page caption read as follows: "Surprise Warnings: In
a courageous new declaration, Dr. J. Allen Hynek-Air Force
Chief Scientific consultant on UFO's has made this surprising
disclosure: If the Colorado Project's conclusion is completely
negative-denying UFO reality-he will take the wraps off his
personal files of good unexplained cases and make them
public." Once again, he was depicted as the Air Force
consultant, which he was not. I make a point of this, because
I called this to his attention on numerous occasions, but each
time he would advise me that it was the news media who was at
fault and not him. Just for the record I never believed him
and I always expressed dismay and surprise at such
inaccuracies by the news media. As I said before, I had to
make excuses for his remarks and comments, but they always
turned out to be a "misquote".
[END OF EXTRACT]


Recalling standard investigative procedures, he further
explains, "In suspected balloon sightings, we contacted local
airports, local weather stations, the U.S. Weather Bureau,
Holloman AFB Balloon Control Center, the National Center for
Atmospheric Research, General Mills, Raven Industries, Sea
Space Systems, and colleges and universities conducting
balloon research".

Presumably Raven Industries were not asked about a conceivable
'Socorro' connection, as it had, understandably, never been
considered at the time as a 'suspected balloon sighting',
despite Zamora's radio confirmation that the object, "looks
like a balloon".

If Raven Industries had refuted any connection to 'Socorro',
Quintanilla would surely still have welcomed being aware of
those nearby, 'classified', 1963/64 hot-air balloon
'Albuquerque flights'. Even if coincidental, clearly
Quintanilla was oblivious to their existence and I've located
new [to be published in due course] evidence which reaffirms
these were CIA funded 'exercises'.


That aside, Quintanilla's memoirs on the 'Air Force Dilemma' are
a prodigious and profound, landmark, perspective.


James Easton.

February 22, 2205 hours: Large triangular craft approx. 100 feet in length

hissing and crackling from high-voltage electrical pylons.

Neither the local air traffic control or the RAF reported any radar returns.

The "Flying Triangle" has also been seen in land over small town (Wimborne
Minster) near Bournemouth a few years ago at dusk.

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Thu, 7 Mar 2002 17:46:54 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] UK Triangle craft sighting

If it made hissing and crackling sounds, it probably was not as far
away as the witnesses said. Sounds like those do not usually travel
that far audibly.

Again, any unknown object seen against the sky cannot reveal its
altitude, distance, size, or speed to unaided observers.

I would hazard a guess that it was small and closer to the
witnesses. Maybe a fire balloon with some fireworks or flares
attached. Possibly a weather phenomenon.

From: "David Clarke" <cd292@crazydiamonds.fsnet.co.uk>
Date: Sun, 10 Mar 2002 22:43:59 -0000
Subject: [UFORL] Believer into sceptic: Sunday Times article

Sunday Times magazine, 10 March 2002

Brief encounters: Tony Barrell meets his first UFO

Continuing our series on events that changed the lives of Sunday Times
writers, Tony Barrell travels back 25 years, to the day when he spotted a
UFO. He suspects it was this experience that led to his career of
investigating the weird, the unusual and the unexplained ... beginning with
the famous 'flying saucer' crash at Roswell

Guy Fawkes' Night wasn't a big deal for me at the age of 18. As I ambled
home from work on November 5, 1976, I was probably looking forward to a pub
crawl with my friends rather than a few damp squibs in the garden with my
parents. More likely, I suspect my mind was virtually a blank, the kind of
meditative state that often precedes a ghostly experience or a religious
vision.
I certainly wouldn't have been thinking about work: I was a trainee computer
programmer at Crawley Borough Council, a job I was happy to abandon at
5.20pm every evening - or 4.25pm, weirdly, on Fridays like this - for my
10-minute stroll home.

A jovial careers adviser had suggested the job - based, I thought then, on
an inspired reading of the unique potential displayed by my O-levels in
English, Latin, French, maths and art. All too late, I now realise he saw me
as an archetypal nerd, a misshapen peg for a slightly off-square hole. I had
rampaging acne, long hair spilling dandruff down my slouching shoulders, an
addiction to prog-rock records and pints of lager-and-blackcurrant. I was
one of those irritating fools who memorise whole Monty Python sketches.
Girlfriends were something other people had. In my spare time, I laboured
over a shapeless novel about a sinister lobster recipe that was taking over
the world, though most of the action was confined to my home town of
Crawley, West Sussex. I was a Hobbit in all but name. What other choice of
employment could anyone have suggested?

But as I turned the corner into my home territory of Buckmans Road in the
district of West Green, destiny was about to deal me a new role. A mission.
A pointer for the future that I had consistently failed to visualise for
myself.

It was floating above the rooftops of my road - an assemblage of mysterious
lights. It didn't seem to be travelling in a linear way but wobbling from
side to side in the darkness, without making a sound. I stopped and watched
it, dumbfounded. Then I remembered it was Guy Fawkes' Night. Oh, it's a
rocket, I remember thinking. Or an Air Bomb. Or some other firework that
goes up in the air. But when the lights continued to wink and hover for
several minutes, I discounted that theory.
No, this was an unidentified flying object, possibly a spacecraft piloted by
aliens. People see them all the time; it's just that it hadn't happened to
me before. I was excited beyond intelligent thought. I was trembling so
much, I almost shook myself out of my tank top and oxford bags.

There was fear in the excitement, because I was dealing with the unknown.
Who's to say, I remember thinking, that this isn't the start of a full-scale
invasion? It could be The War of the Worlds or, at best, The Day the Earth
Stood Still. People could be massacred; the whole planet could be destroyed
in a flash. It was the kind of day when anything could have happened -
indeed, I have since discovered that on this very same day, a former member
of the band Steps was born.

I hurried home and gibbered to my mother that there was a UFO outside, just
down the road. I was disappointed that she wasn't that bothered; instead of
rushing outside to see it for herself, she suggested I call nearby Gatwick
Airport to see if they had spotted anything on their radar. So I checked the
telephone directory, picked up the receiver on our green Trimphone and
dialled. 'Why do you ask, young man?' an urbane aviation official asked me.
'What have you seen?' I could almost hear his regulation RAF moustache
twitching.

'A UFO,' I replied, helpfully.

'Well, we haven't picked up anything unidentified here. Are you sure?'

'I think so.'

'Don't worry, young man, we'll keep a lookout.'

'Oh. Okay. Thanks.'

When I went back outside to check on the progress of the object, it had
gone. For some reason, my dear old mum thought it would be a good idea to
get in touch with the local paper, the Crawley Observer. Possibly for the
same reason, I agreed, without considering the consequences. A friendly
reporter chap sounded mildly interested and said someone might get back to
me. He didn't say, 'if we don't have any better news this week', but that's
what the cynical, grown-up part of me hears now when I recall the
conversation.

There was a call for me at the office the following week. Was I the
youngster who'd seen the flying saucer? Yes, I said, if that's what it was.
In the cold light of day, I was on the point of disowning the experience and
starting to clutch at rational explanations. I also wished that I hadn't
phoned the paper. I gave a half-hearted and not terribly articulate
interview, mumbling into the receiver lest my story be heard by my work
colleagues, many of whom held diplomas in the art of mickey-taking.
The reporter asked if a photographer could call and take a picture. 'No,' I
said, 'the UFO's not there any more. It disappeared after several minutes.'
No, a picture of me, the local hack patiently explained. 'Oh, okay then,' I
must have said, because a snapper duly turned up on the doorstep one
evening. As a Sunday Times writer I have had the pleasure of working with
some fine photographers since, but this guy had an imagination like no
other. 'Could you pick up something round?' he asked. 'Like a saucer? And
look at it?' The nearest such object was a cheap ashtray with a photograph
of Blackpool Tower in its centre, a souvenir from a distant holiday. I held
it up and smiled, and the flash went off.

'That UFO was no firework,' trumpeted the Observer, above the picture of me
and the ashtray. The anonymous reporter had had some easy fun with the
story: 'Air traffic control at Gatwick missed the scoop of a lifetime on
Friday, when a UFO hovered over West Green...' My age was omitted, giving me
an enigmatic village-idiot quality. Friends and co-workers went through the
whole pantomime of ridicule, the most repeated jest being that I must have
'had a few'. (I still have a problem with this clichŽ that alcohol is a
potent hallucinogenic. When was the last time you 'saw things' after having
one beer too many?) One of my mother's female office colleagues looked at my
photo and commented that I was a 'nice-looking lad', blithely ignoring the
terrible threat of alien invasion implicit in the story.

The sighting 'has certainly increased my interest in these things', I had
told my interviewer. 'Now I would like to find out more about it.' True to
my word, for months afterwards I read every trashy paperback about UFOs and
aliens I could get my hands on. The more I read, the more I was prepared to
believe that not only were we just one of a myriad of intelligent races in
the universe, but also that Stonehenge, the Egyptian pyramids and, in all
probability, the Hanger Lane gyratory system had been built by
extra-terrestrial visitors. The movie Close Encounters of the Third Kind
came out in 1977, and I gorged on that as well.

But like many adolescent enthusiasms, my obsession inevitably waned. I put
away childish things, grew up, switched my career to journalism, and
eventually joined The Sunday Times. In 1997, the editor of this magazine,
unaware of my former life, spontaneously decided I was just the person to
fly to Roswell, New Mexico, to cover the 50th anniversary of the legendary
UFO crash there.

Roswell was the assignment I was born for. I had already done half of the
research, unwittingly, in my teens. The town was packed with nutters in
alien suits, and earnest ufologists arguing the toss about spaceships and
weather balloons, and I could never go far without meeting someone who
wanted to discuss how alien technology was secretly used by modern stealth
bombers, or who needed to offload their own stories of alien abduction. Some
of these tales made The X Files look like Bob the Builder. And not only did
I get to interview the celebrity abductee Whitley Strieber, author of
Communion, but we had an enjoyable if abstruse argument about time travel
after he suggested that the Roswell craft had come from the far future of
our own world.

This was also my first visit to America. Imagine that - your first
impression of the good ol' US of A isn't Manhattan, Disneyland or the Golden
Gate Bridge but a southern hick town in the desert, with pictures of
black-eyed 'greys' gazing out from most of the shop windows.Subsequent
assignments have seen me hunting for ghosts at the site of the Battle of
Gettysburg, attending pagan rituals in Britain, hanging out with Monster
Raving Loonies, and joining an alien-loving religious group for nude
meditation in Canada. Why, people frequently ask me, do I fixate on the
unusual, the offbeat, the unexplained and the paranormal? Let me lie on this
couch awhile and I'll tell you. Well, maybe it makes me feel like a teenager
again. There is also the possibility that the whole experience of November
5, 1976 - the sighting and the humiliation that followed it - intensified my
ability to empathise with people whom many others would dismiss as
crackpots. I've been there, bought the T-shirt: I know what it's like to
confess to unusual beliefs and to suffer mockery for them.

I'm sure that some of the more out-there ufologists I've met would have
another hypothesis: that the craft I saw landed in my street and I was
abducted by the aliens on board, that they programmed me with a mission to
enlighten the world about all kinds of weird and wacky subjects, and then
erased my memory. Perhaps I should have my head examined: it may contain an
elaborate implant fashioned from an otherworldly metal.

But I really don't think so. You see, although my experience was a defining
moment, even perhaps a passport to an unusual career, I have grave doubts
about its authenticity. I have tried over and over again to replay that
memory, clean it up, bring it up to something approaching DVD quality, so I
can determine exactly what I saw. I've tried to revisit those moments
through meditation, and I've been back there in dreams. I can't make myself
18 again, even with a lengthy series of hormone injections, so it's a tough
one. But what follows is the best I can do.

It is already quite dark. The air is heavy with smoke from early bonfires
and fireworks. I can hear them popping and fizzing at regular intervals. My
attention is attracted by lights in the sky, above the rooftops. There is at
least one red light, at least one white light, and they are glowing and
winking eerily. The lights aren't self-contained dots, but trails in the
air. If whatever is responsible for the lights is making a noise, I can't
hear it over the sound of all the bangers and rockets and roman candles.
(This may explain why I told the local paper that the object was hovering
'absolutely silently'.) One of my neighbours is standing outside one of the
houses nearby, but I can't bring myself to speak to him or her; my memory
doesn't make it entirely clear who they are or what sex they are. (My
reluctance to speak to this neighbour may be based on uncertainty as well as
shock: I don't want to share this experience until I have established that
it really is an experience. I am also very shy.)

I continue to watch the object for a few minutes. It doesn't seem to be
moving away from me or towards me, but hovering and wobbling from side to
side. It is at this point that I realise - or rather, believe - that I am
seeing something very special. I begin to worry about alien landings. It has
been a tough week at work, I hate programming computers and I need a break.
Yippee, this is a UFO, and my life will never be the same again.

As special-effects designers know, ordinary lights can appear extraordinary
when they are filtered through smoke. And, as good UFO investigators are
aware, everyday objects may appear alien when they are viewed from unusual
angles, and their trajectory may not be perceived correctly. If a flying
machine were travelling away from me, it might seem to be static or wobbling
from side to side.

The answer is so obvious. But I think I've been in denial for a long time,
because I so wanted that experience to be truly supernatural. Reader, I'm
really sorry. I think it was an aeroplane.

Now that I have the Woolsey letter to Greer, it occurs to me that
perhaps not everybody is familiar with the story and its
significance. I'll use a sequence of posts to display the
documents that tell the story.

Greer's claim to have briefed former CIA director Woolsey in 1993
is one that he repeats at every opportunity. I've heard it in a
1999 presentation at a nearby community college, again during a
radio talk show a few months later, yet again at his "Disclosure
Project" event at the National Press Club last spring, and most
recently in a video interview on YAHOO Finance Vision on March
1st (still accessible; they archive these clips for some
considerable time.) These continuing references to the "Woolsey
Briefing" are a significant image-builder for Greer and his
organization; along with less-frequent claims that he has briefed
congressional staff and members of congress, they imply that
Greer maintains regular contact with high-level federal
officials.

The documents that tell the story of the "Woolsey Briefing" begin
with the introduction to Greer's book, _Extraterrestrial
Contact_. I'll append it to the next post.

This is how Greer described the briefing:

================================================

FROM THE INTRODUCTION OF
EXTRATERRESTRIAL CONTACT: THE EVIDENCE AND IMPLICATIONS
BY STEVEN M. GREER M.D.

Saved from http://www.drgreer.com/excerpts.html

On December 13 1993, my wife and I flew to Washington DC to meet
with President Clinton's first CIA Director, James Woolsey. The
cover story for this meeting was simply a small dinner party
consisting of CIA Director Woolsey and his wife, Dr. Sue Woolsey
(Chief Operating Officer of the National Academy of Sciences) and
our host and his wife. Shortly before the meeting, we learned
that I was to be the first person to brief the Director of
Central Intelligence on the subject of UFOs and extraterrestrial
intelligence: Woolsey had made inquiries but had received no
information on the subject from any official government channels.
Naturally, I came prepared with a large brief case filled with
case evidence, witness testimony, photographs and video footage
of UFOs, government documents and the like. After a few
introductions and pleasantries, we got right to business.

I learned that the CIA Director and his wife had actually seen
one of these UFOs in New Hampshire in the late 1960s, in broad
daylight. So after about 10 or 15 minutes of presenting the
evidence, Mr. Woolsey said, in effect, 'Yes, I know they exist.
Now talk to me about what all of this means'. This book is all
about what does all of this mean. While this book certainly
presents some compelling case evidence, smoking gun government
documents and photographs, the core of this book is really about
meaning. Any open minded person can peruse a handful of these
cases, government documents and authenticated photographs and
conclude, as Mr. Woolsey did, that there is something very real
going on here. But now for the interesting part: Why are they
here, how has the secrecy been maintained, what are the
implications to our society, and what will disclosure of these
facts mean. How do these devices travel through interstellar
space and get someplace in a life form's natural life time and
how can you communicate in real time through many light years of
space, and....

Presented here, then, are a collection of papers which attempt to
elucidate these and many other critical issues. The evidence is
really the easy part: making some sense of it is what is truly
challenging. This book is just such an attempt, one which I offer
with the caveat that this is only an initial attempt to unravel
one of the greatest mysteries of all time. It is a work in
progress. And as we stand on the eve of the next millennium, we
can only peer dimly into a reality that is showing us our future.
And so it was that on that night in December 1993, we spent two
and a half hours with the CIA Director and the Chief Operating
Officer of the National Academy of Sciences discussing the
meaning behind the mysteries. I remember discussing geo-political
implications of disclosing this matter fully to the public. I
remember elucidating the implications of disclosing
extraterrestrial technologies which could replace all of the
sources of pollution in the world. I remember discussing how
religious figures might react to such a disclosure.

But one of my fondest memories is of Dr. Sue Woolsey asking, "But
how do they communicate through the great distances of space?' I
swallowed hard and for an instance contemplated not telling her
the truth. But then quickly I realized that if she was perceptive
enough to ask the question, perhaps she was ready for the answer.
Whereupon I said to her: "Their communications systems are
technologies which interface with aspects of reality closely
associated with what we would call mind and thought, and this
spectrum of reality bypasses linear time and space totally...".
And to my astonishment, Dr. Woolsey smiled and said, "I thought
it had to be something like that."

She got it. And I am sure that you will too.

Steven M. Greer M.D.
February 1999
Albemarle County, Virginia

When Woolsey became aware of Greer's description of the occasion
when they met, he wrote the appended letter, essentially a
blanket denial of Greer's account. It was signed by Woolsey and
his wife, as well as John L. Peterson and his wife. It appears
that Mr. Peterson had arranged for Greer to be invited to the
event:

=======================================================

September 16,1999

Steven M. Greer, M.D.
International Director
Center for the Study of Extraterrestrial Intelligence
P.O. Box 265
Crozet, Virginia 22932

Dear Dr. Greer:

It has just come to the attention of the four of us that you
have, without giving any of us the opportunity to comment,
published a distorted account of a dinner party of some six years
ago at which the four of us, you, and your wife were seated
together.

In the Introduction to your book, Extraterrestrial Contact,
published earlier this year you portray this dinner party
conversation during which the four of us listened to your views
and politely asked questions as a "briefing" with a "cover
story." You further assert that Mr. and Mrs. Woolsey reported a
UFO sighting to you and agreed with your views. You include
specific alleged quotations from them.

None of this is accurate. You have portrayed politeness as
acquiescence and questions as affirmations. Your conduct in this
matter contravenes both accuracy and simple manners.

Sincerely,

John L. Petersen
Diane C. Petersen
R. James Woolsey
Suzanne H. Woolsey
