Subject: Re: [UFORL] OZ "orange lights" & "fire balloons"

Hi Brett & list,

Thank you for pointing out this interesting historical curio. Clearly such
"fire balloons" etc have been around for a long time.

As for whether authorities getting interested in such matters, I tried
precisely that back in 1992 & 1993, with police and the police air wing.
Such "hot air balloons" and their variants were possible air navigation
(they were generally low to nil profiles re radar) and fire hazards. In one
example I had police highlighting one example of one of the "orange lights"
coming down in a tree and it catching fire. Luckily the fire didn't spread,
but I recollect some discussion with police where we were trying to
apprehend the offenders with a view for prosecution on the grounds of public
nuisance and property damage. However resources spread thinly meant that
once the offender lay low for a while the police moved on to other
priorities. Then later the whole cycle would begin again, with authorities
usually gifted with short memories.

I remember thinking during the terrible fire outbreak that followed with the
next (?) summer that some of the fires that ringed Sydney may have been
caused by "orange light"/"fire balloons". Such a connection could not be
proven, but I did notice that the regular "orange light" occurrences that
largely clustered or peaked around the weekends during this period dropped
away to virtually disappearing from the scene. Given the severity of the
fires I suspect, it was quite a while before the "orange light" outbreaks
began again with any regularity.

The perrenial "orange light" outbreaks around Australia and overseas
generally have common causes and hoaxing clearly predominates. A few remain
curious and difficult to explain, but such reports are very much in the
minority.

All I can say is these people should "get a life", but when you come across
instructions on how to create such things in infants school texts on open
education/parents days then you realise that the "education" process starts
pretty young.

While I don't want to throw out the baby with the bath water, if there is
any legitimate UFO "signal" amongst the "orange lights", it is drowning in
the bath, and may have already gone down the plug hole!

While many on this list seem dismissive of any genuine UFO phenomena, from
my obviously naive point of view, there is much of worth to look at beyond
such IFO outbreaks.

Regards,
Bill Chalker

Subject: [UFORL] 'After half a century, it's RIP for the UFOs'

Extracted from 'Sunday Nation' [Africa]:

'After half a century, it's RIP for the UFOs'
By GERRY LOUGHRAN

There is a very popular play here called Peter Pan wherein
Tinkerbell from Fairyland announces she is dying because people
don't believe in her any more. The children in the audience then
clap like mad and call out, "We believe in fairies, we believe in
fairies," and Tinkerbell's light grows bright again and she stops
dying forthwith.

If the modern version of Tinkerbell from Fairyland is ET the
Extraterrestrial, all the clapping and believing in the world
will not keep the little fellow alive. It's official: We don't
believe in aliens any more.

The Ministry of Defence Directorate of Intelligence has declared
that it no longer wishes to be sent any reports of UFOs
(Unidentified Flying Objects) and, perhaps more pertinently, the
enthusiasts of the British Flying Saucer Bureau announced they
are suspending activities because sightings have dried up.
"Perhaps", said a spokesman wanly, "our alien visitors have
completed their survey of earth".
[END]


The full article is online, at:

http://www.nationaudio.com/News/DailyNation/Today/Comment/LettLon
don40.html

From: "James Easton" <voyager@ukonline.co.uk>
Date: Wed, 15 May 2002 02:12:03 +0100
Subject: [UFORL] Alien Skulduggery

The latest edition of 'Fortean Times' features a number of
interesting articles, as always.

One is entitled, 'Keeping an Eye on Cyclops - Strange skulls
found in Bulgaria and the Philippines echo stories of ancient
one-eyed giants'.

It's reported therein:

According to a report in the usually sober Turkish newspaper
'Milliyet' on 4 January, 2002, a very strange skull was found in
southern Bulgaria, near the border with Greece on 21 May, 2001.

An unnamed 38-year-old resident of Plovdiv claimed to have had a
dream in which five aliens dressed in one-piece yellow metallic
suits told him to visit a certain point on Rodop [sic] Mountain,
near Ardino and Madan, about 200km (124 miles) south of Sofia,
and dig.

When he did so, he found the skull and a small elliptical metal
object.

The Bulgarian news agency 'BTA' published a photo of the skull on
31 January, 2002, generating a lot of excitement and speculation
about extraterrestrials. The skull weighs 250 grams (9oz) and has
six orifices in it, but no mouth. The bone is thinner than that
of an average 'Homo sapiens'. 'Milliyet' asserted that 'Prof
Yordan Yordanov, one of the best-known anthropologists in Europe,
claimed that he had never seen a human or animal skull like this
in his life.

The director of the Palaeontology Museum in Asenovgrad, Dimiter
Kovachev, is positive that the find is no fossil and had no
analogy or resemblance to any hominid skull known to science.

The well known Bulgarian psychic Koubrat Tomov said the creature
could be 'a product of the Atlanteans, created to serve man'. DNA
tests and carbon-14 analysis were promised.
[END OF EXTRACT]


Proclaimed 'Bulgarian psychics' and a genesis to 'Atlanteans' can
perhaps be explained by a stated reference to this material
originating from:

'UFO Roundup 7/4, 22 Jan, and 7/6, 7 Feb 2002'.
See:

http://www.ufoinfo.com/roundup/v07/rnd0704.shtml

and

http://www.ufoinfo.com/roundup/v07/rnd0706.shtml


That clarified, our purported 'Bulgarian ET skull', is the same
one, first publicised on UFORL, dated November, 2001, when I
wrote:

I've received a series of photographs which the sender thought
might be of interest - was it possibly the skull of an alien
creature!

The writer claims to be an amateur archaeologist from Bulgaria:

"I am from Bulgaria and found the skull in the Rodopi mountains.
The skull I found by accident, I was on a walk in the mountain
when I almost stepped on it. It is the size of a baby's head. I
thought it was a kind of animal but no animal has such a skull in
the Rodopi mountains. That's the most weird thing".

Although doubtless the skull [if genuine] does comes from an
animal, it is bizarre looking.

[...]

[END OF EXTRACT]


Where and when did the subsequent tale of, "a dream in which five
aliens dressed in one-piece yellow metallic suits told him to
visit a certain point on Rodop [sic] Mountain" originate?


Although the person who contacted myself did reply to early e-
mails, there was no response to further questions raised [I'll
pursue this again].

However, what was provided were several images of the 'skull' and
I made these available at the time.

I did also take a resultant query, 'which animal is this?', to
the foremost 'mammal' mailing list.

Richard W. Thorington, Jr., from the Smithsonian Institution's
Division of Mammals, noted:

"It looks like a cow skull to us".

Stephen Cox Thomas, a 'Bioarchaeological Researcher' from
Toronto, added:

"About the mystery skull, I agree with those who identified it as
Bos taurus.

It looks very much like a calf skull minus the facial portion as
well as the temporals, and much of the occipital--the
basioccipital exoccipitals & outer table of the supraoccipital.
Most of the floor of the brain case appears to be missing.

It is possible that much of the damage was caused by carnivore
gnawing. If so there should be gouges and punctures visible upon
close inspection. The straight anterior edge of what appears to
be remains of the basisphenoid-presphenoid area in profile views
suggests that the anterior portion of the skull could have been
removed by a butchers saw".


Uploaded to the UFORL library is the published photograph of our
'Bulgarian ET' skull, courtesy of 'Fortean Times':

http://groups.yahoo.com/group/UFORL/files/


During related UFORL discussions, I mentioned:

There's also an example of a cattle skull on York University's
web site at:

http://www-users.york.ac.uk/~wjh101/hedbone/Cattle/cattle.htm

The cattle skull featured therein is 'Bos taurus', cited as an
explanation.

I still can't see how it resembles the photographs I received.
Those five pictures are detailed, high resolution close-ups,
showing different profiles of the 'skull' - front, top, bottom
and both sides.

The University of York's online material depicts a "lateral
view". For comparison, I've uploaded to UFORL's library a copy of
the same perspective relating to our enigmatic skull - see:

http://groups.yahoo.com/group/UFORL/files/
Given due copyright concerns, this is presently a much smaller
image than the actual photograph.


Amongst many problems with those changing stories of how the
'Bulgarian skull' was found, is that initial claim, "I almost
stepped on it. It is the size of a baby's head".

Clearly, from the photograph published in 'Fortean Times', it's
significantly larger than a small artefact which could literally
be 'stumbled upon'.

Fundamental anomalies duly noted, I've located a new source which
should offer opinions with a specific expertise in 'animal
skulls'. Feedback on the photographs has simply been invited and
without revealing any background story [perhaps best not to
highlight on a scientific forum that there's a connection with
'five aliens dressed in one-piece yellow metallic suits'].

Resulting developments will be posted to UFORL.

From: "James Easton" <voyager@ukonline.co.uk>
Date: Mon, 20 May 2002 03:24:45 +0100
Subject: Re: [UFORL] 'Flying Saucers' and Where They Came From

Regarding:

>From: YoungBob2@aol.com
>Date: Sat, 11 May 2002 09:30:40 EDT
>Subject: Re: [UFORL] 'Flying Saucers' and Where They Came From

Bob wrote:

>>Can we now duly credit the 'Boise, Idaho Statesman' as first
>>declaring that Kenneth Arnold had seen 'flying saucers'?

>Seem's so. Anybody have anything exculpatory?

Bob,

Yes, I do.

As a result of ongoing research, I've discovered there were two
other newspapers which used the terminology on 27 June.

Current joint-leaders are, the 'Boise, Idaho Statesman', the
'Portland Oregonian' and the 'Portland Oregon Journal'.

More significantly and remarkable, if verified, is that there was
apparently one newspaper which did portray the objects as 'flying
saucers', on 25 June.

This would be two days before, so far as I'm aware, any
previously realised occurrence.

I'm attempting to authenticate the existence and content of this
alleged 25 June article [the newspaper involved is being
extremely helpful]. I've never seen it mentioned in any features
on the Arnold case, even lists of 'all known', contemporary
'flying saucer' newspaper reports.

Hopefully, more on this shortly.


Meanwhile, courtesy of the 'Project-1947' web site:

The June 25, 1947 issue of the Pendleton (Oregon) East Oregonian
carried the very first report of Arnold's sighting at the bottom
of page 1.

_Impossible! Maybe, But Seein' Is Believin', Says Flier_
Kenneth Arnold, with the fire control at Boise and who was flying
in southern Washington yesterday afternoon in search of a missing
marine plane, stopped here en route to Boise today with an
unusual story -- which he doesn't expect people to believe but
which he declared was true.

He said he sighted nine saucer-like aircraft flying in formation
at 3. p.m. yesterday, extremely bright -- as if they were nickel
plated -- and flying at an immense rate of speed. He estimated
they were at an altitude between 9,500 and 10,000 feet and
clocked them from Mt. Rainier to Mt. Adams, arriving at the
amazing speed of about 1200 miles an hour. "It seemed
impossible," he said, "but there it is -- I must believe my
eyes."

He landed at Yakima somewhat later and inquired there, but
learned nothing. Talking about it to a man from Ukiah in
Pendleton this morning whose name he did not get, he was amazed
to learn that the man had sighted the same aerial objects
yesterday afternoon from the mountains in the Ukiah section!

He said that in flight they appeared to weave in an (sic) out in
formation.
[End]


The June 25 issue of the Chicago Daily Tribune quoted Arnold in a
page one story:

"The first thing I noticed was a series of flashes in my eyes as
if a mirror was reflecting sunlight at me... I saw the flashes
were coming from a series of objects that were traveling
incredibly fast. They were silvery and shiny and seemed to be
shaped like a pie plate . . . What startled me most at this point
was . . . that I could not find any tails on them.

I counted nine of them as they disappeared behind the peak of
Mount Rainier. Their speed was apparently so great I decided to
clock them. I took out my watch and checked off one minutes and
42 seconds from the time they passed Mount Rainier until they
reached the peak of Mount Adams . . . All told the objects
remained in view slightly less than two minutes from the time I
first noticed them."
[END OF 'PROJECT-1947' EXTRACT]


Does anyone have a copy of the entire 'Chicago Daily Tribune'
article?
It seems we have two mistakes therein; although Arnold is quoted
as saying the objects, "disappeared behind the peak of Mount
Rainier", that should presumably be, 'behind a peak on Mount
Rainier'. Also, he used the dashboard clock for timing, not his
watch.

Another problem is the dating. According to Brad Sparks, it
should actually be 26 June:

"However, the Chicago Tribune story was published on June 26 not
the 25th, based on phone interview of late the 25th (Loren Gross'
history misdates it). Jan Aldrich of Project 1947 informs me
there was no Tribune article on the case at all on the 25th".

See:

http://www.virtuallystrange.net/ufo/updates/1999/apr/m01-
002.shtml

It's obviously still shown on the 'Project-1947' site as '25
June'.


Arnold recounted in, 'The Coming of the Saucers' [1952]:

It was about four o'clock in the afternoon when I landed at
Yakima and went straight to Al Baxter, general manager of Central
Aircraft.

[...]

The high point of my enthusiasm got its top knocked off when one
of the helicopter pilots said, "Ah, it's just a flight of those
guided missiles from Moses Lake."

I proceeded to gather my scattered wits together, got back in my
airplane, and took off for Pendleton, Oregon.

[...]

When I landed at the large airfield at Pendleton there was quite
a group of people to greet me. When I got out of my plane no one
said anything. They just stood around and looked at me. I don't
recall just how the subject came up in those first few minutes
after I landed, but before very long it seemed everybody around
the airfield was listening to the story of my experience.

[...]

To me, that evening, that was that. They were guided missiles,
robotly controlled.

[...]

After talking to the editor of the East Oregonian newspaper, I
was fairly convinced that it was some new government invention
along the line of guided missiles. I could almost tell what this
editor thought when the story went scudding over the news wires--
that the government had taken this way to announce a new
principle of flight.

I could have gone to sleep that night if the reporters, newsmen,
and press agencies of every conceivable description had left me
alone.
[END OF EXTRACT]


Arnold doesn't clarify when he spoke with the newspaper's editor,
however, it was presumably the following day.

In various accounts, Arnold says his destination was Yakima and
never explains why he then flew on to Pendleton.

It could be that he intended to inform the FBI, as revealed in
Bruce Maccabee's review of Arnold's June 1977 lecture at the
'First International UFO Congress':

"Arnold goes on to say he made the 35 minute flight from Yakima
to Pendleton, Oregon. There were people at the airport. His story
had preceded him. While flying he had figured the speed. He had
measured the distance and minimum 39 miles distance in the time
he measured. He got speeds above 1200 miles an hour. Says he
stopped at Pendleton because he thought he should tell the FBI.
He thought they could possibly be from Russia. Of course, no one
had seen circular aircraft. So at Pendleton he went to the FBI
office but it was locked. So he went to the newspaper office and
told the guy there he wanted to see the FBI. The newspaper man
wanted to know what the story was. He had charts with him and
described it to the newspaper man. Before the evening was over
Arnold was besieged and asked all types of questions".


The Tacoma Public Library has a helpful and lengthy online
feature entitled, 'Unsettling Events', from which the following
is excerpted:

FLYING OBJECTS

Curtis Peebles, "The Age of Confusion begins," Watch the Skies! A
chronicle of the flying saucer myth. Washington and London: The
Smithsonian Institution Press, 1994. p. 8-15.

On the summer day the flying saucer myth began, Kenneth Arnold
was a 32-year-old successful businessman, married with two
daughters. He owned the Great Western Fire Control Supply and
flew his own light aircraft. Kenneth Arnold was, in the
vernacular to come, a reliable witness.

[...]

Arnold did not measure the distance between the two peaks until
he landed at Pendleton, Oregon, later that afternoon. He found it
was forty-seven miles which gave a ground speed of 1,700 mph-more
than twice the speed of sound. No aircraft had yet flown as fast
as the speed of sound. Other pilots suggested the objects might
be guided missiles.

Arnold took his map and calculations to the local FBI office, but
found it closed. He then decided to go to the East Oregonian
newspaper. Arnold talked with Nolan Skiff, the editor of the 'End
of the Week' column.

He said the objects 'flew like a saucer would if you skipped it
across the water.- A report was sent out on the Associated Press
wire. It read:

PENDLETON, Ore. June 25 (AP)-Nine bright saucer-like objects
flying at "incredible speed" at 10,000 feet altitude were
reported here today by Kenneth Arnold, Boise, Idaho, [a] pilot
who said he could not hazard a guess as to what they were.

[...]
[END]

The AP dispatch went out in the late morning of June 25.
Newspapers in the northwestern U.S. carried the report that
evening. The following day (June 26), it had spread nationwide.
[END OF EXTRACT]

Slight typo there; it was intended to read:

Is it also merely coincidental that, once more, the words
'flat/thin' are used in conjunction with a 'disk-like' simile.


There is of course the perfect example of what Arnold attempted
to explain when he said the objects were, "flat like a pie pan"
and "like a big flat disk".

Appended to the report he sent to the Air Force were two
sketches. Firstly, Arnold illustrates how the object looked in
full profile and then shows a "side view" - see:

http://www.project1947.com/fig/ka.htm

It's that side view which he refers to and it is indeed 'saucer-
like'.
For some reason, Arnold chose to accompany this statement with a
drawing which is unlike the "somewhat bat-shaped" object he
described and sketched elsewhere.

In 'The Coming of the Saucers', [which should certainly have been
tiled more accurately], Arnold wrote:

"It was about four o'clock in the afternoon when I landed at
Yakima and went straight to Al Baxter, general manager of Central
Aircraft. I met him in his outer office and rather breathlessly
asked to see him in private. He dropped whatever it was he was
doing and in his private office I related the story of my
observation and drew him pictures of what I had seen".

I understand that it is those same pictures which were reproduced
on the front cover of the 'International UFO Reporter'
[March/April 1995] - see:

http://www.ufoworld.co.uk/arnold/sketch_1.jpg

Arnold actually depicts three different shapes, perhaps because
the objects themselves were changing as they flapped and then
glided, sorry, "fluttered and sailed".

That middle portrayal is the exact same as Arnold later settled
on; those at either side are more like his drawing for the Air
Force.

Note that further to the right, he again shows a side-view and it
resembles an upside-down saucer.


Despite all the desperate efforts we have seen in recent years,
often typically fanatical and ill-mannered, to convince that
Arnold really did see saucer-shaped objects as were reported,
believed in and which are the essential foundation of 'ufology',
'flying saucers' they were not, never had been and the cause of
so much confusion is embedded in those similes Arnold, quite
appropriately, used to describe how flat all nine objects looked.


There's no escaping this and no way back from it.


James Easton.

One further piece of evidence I will now highlight is a somewhat
crucial revelation which came from Arnold in later years.

For some reason, Arnold did not disclose this fact at the time.

Those nine, "bat-shaped", or bird-shaped, fluttering and gliding
objects, actually appeared to be living creatures.


As Arnold confirmed, "They seemed to be alive in the center, to
have the ability to change their density. I know that sounds
strange".

This would explain, as I suggested, why in Arnold's earliest
sketch he shows the objects shape as changing. Strangely, it
resembles a large bird flapping its wings.

I wonder if this was in any way connected with when they
"fluttered".


So, when the evidence is fully digested, there are no saucer-
shipped objects at the heart of 'flying saucers'.

Instead, we have an echelon formation of nine intermittently
fluttering and gliding bird-shaped objects that had a distinctive
undulating flight, were evidently living and which seemed to
"change their density".

That's where 'flying saucers' truly came from, according to the
witness.


I seem to recall publishing evidence which was not a million
light-years away from arriving at that same conclusion.

From: "James Easton" <voyager@ukonline.co.uk>
Date: Wed, 22 May 2002 03:16:26 +0100
Subject: [UFORL] Re: 'Flying Saucers' and Where They Came From

I'm pleased to reveal that I have located a copy of what seems to
now become the first known newspaper use of the terminology,
'flying saucers'.

Although, as mentioned, the reference I found to this news report
dates it as 25 June [and on a specific 'inside page'], the
article which has been unearthed was actually published as a
front page story by the same newspaper on 26 June.

However, it may originally have appeared as a late 'inside page'
news item in an evening edition on the 25th - this is being
further investigated.


Nevertheless, on 26 June, 1947, 'flying saucers' assuredly
entered the media vocabulary in America, not 27 June, as seems to
have previously been accepted.


It's of historical interest, especially as I'm informed the
headline which proclaims Arnold encountered 'flying saucers' is
based entirely on a reproduction of that 25 June AP 'newswire'.

I'm awaiting a scan of the front page story as published and I'll
then confirm this.


In 'Watch the Skies!: A Chronicle of the Flying Saucer Myth',
Curtis Peebles [apparently] wrote, "The AP dispatch went out in
the late morning of June 25. Newspapers in the northwestern U.S.
carried the report that evening".

I have yet to see firm evidence of any newspaper, other than the
'Pendleton (Oregon) East Oregonian', which reported Arnold's
sighting on 25th June, let alone one that interpreted them as
'flying saucers'.

Where are all those stated 25 June news reports documented?

The newspaper which did, on 26 June [and possibly beforehand],
declare that Arnold had observed 'flying saucers', is based in
the Eastern [EDT] time zone.


It should imminently be proven [excepting any evidence ever cited
contrariwise] that 'flying saucers', per se, were evidently first
conceived by a provincial north-eastern newspaper, who have never
been renowned for publishing any contemporary articles about
Arnold's popularised sighting at all!


James Easton.
E-mail: voyager@ukonline.co.uk

Dear List,

Disc-shaped objects were reported generations before
Arnold, and in several different countries, but to
cite a more recent example, I recall Ole Jonny Brænne
found a Norwegian one dating to 1946. There they used
the term "saucer" or at least "plate" (as in dish).

I don't have my archives at hand, so I can't be more
precise right now, but I would suggest we kept our
minds open for a little longer about how much the
media contributed to the creation of the 'flying
saucer'legend.

Best wishes,

Chris Aubeck

From: "James Easton" <voyager@ukonline.co.uk>
Date: Fri, 24 May 2002 05:24:31 +0100
Subject: [UFORL] Re: 'Flying Saucers' and Where They Came From

Regarding:

>From: Ktperehwon@aol.com
>Date: Thu, 23 May 2002 11:04:08 EDT
>Subject: 'Flying Saucers' and Where They Came From

Karl wrote:

>I suppose you're referring to the opening sentence of the
>"briefing document": "On 24 June, 1947, a civilian pilot flying
>over the Cascade Mountains in the State of Washington observed
>nine flying disc-shaped aircraft traveling at a high rate of
>speed."

Karl,

Indeed, plus the claim that one of the discs had been recovered
at Roswell and how "the disc was most likely a short range
reconnaissance craft", etc.

It's all founded on disc-shaped objects, alias, 'flying saucers'.


>At any rate, the foregoing ref. to "disc-shaped aircraft" isn't
>"further proof" that the MJ-12 documents are a hoax (do we need
>anything further?).

NO!

>Other unquestionably genuine formerly classified USAAF/USAF
>documents from the same time period also refer to reports of
>disk-shaped objects, "so-called flying saucers or disks," etc.

Absolutely, however, the US Air Force did not in fact recover an
alien craft at Roswell.

You will doubtless appreciate that fact more than most!

If they had, then, we should find no ambiguity as to whether they
were saucer-shaped, or disk-shaped, or whatever.

>While I find your investigation of the genesis of the term
>"flying saucer" very interesting and historically valuable, it
>certainly doesn't make the case for media hysteria causing
>people to "morph" what they saw into saucers.
I wrote:

"It's additionally been emphasised that immediately ensuing,
seemingly corroborative, reported sightings of 'flying disks',
'flying pie-pans' and of course, 'flying saucers', were not borne
of any media hysteria which followed first newspaper reports of
Arnold's observation.

That's equally exposed and it can also now be proven how in one
instance - there may be others - 'flying saucers' were a direct
consequence of Skiff's AP newswire".

The key phrase here is "any" as in "any media hysteria".

It was intentional and I do not assert 'media hysteria' was
responsible for all which ensued, simply that there is undeniable
evidence the media reporting was influential.

Thanks to your comments, I recognise my own require some
clarification.

I would now revise them to say:

"It's additionally been emphasised that immediately ensuing,
seemingly corroborative, reported sightings of 'flying disks',
'flying pie-pans' and of course, 'flying saucers', were not borne
of _any_ media reporting which followed first newspaper reports
of Arnold's observation.

That's equally exposed and it can also now be proven how in one
instance - there may be others - 'flying saucers' were a direct
consequence of Skiff's AP newswire".

'Hysteria' is perhaps unnecessary, arguably unjustified and duly
amended.

Note also that I only attribute one specifically, proven, example
where "flying saucers" were a direct consequence of Skiff's AP
newswire.

However, I believe it can now be additionally evidenced that the
popularised, underpinning foundation of disk/saucer/pie-pan-
shaped objects originates from a genesis where the entire context
of Arnold's founding sighting report was misunderstood to a much
greater extent than previously realised.

As a direct consequence of your welcome feedback, I've considered
this from another perspective - Kenneth Arnold's.

Summarising readily available data from [known] contemporary
newspaper reports, how did they accurately reflect Arnold's
pivotal sighting?

Is there evidence that 'flying disks', 'flying pie-pans' and
'flying saucers', were significantly a popularised media creation
and do not have any tangible connection to Kenneth Arnold at all?

What might Arnold have said about this, if he had been asked a
few days afterwards.

Perhaps something like...:

[BEGIN]
On 25 June, the 'Pendleton, Oregon East Oregonian' ran the first
story of my sighting and also released it on the Associated Press
(AP) newswire.

In both, they reported that I said the objects were saucer-like.

I actually said they flew in a saucer-like fashion, like a saucer
would skip if you threw it across water.

On 26 June, a United Press (UP) newswire was published in the
'Norman, Oklahoma Transcript' and reported I had observed
"saucer-shaped" objects.

They further misquoted that I told Jack Whitman the objects "were
shaped like saucers".

I never claimed they were even saucer-like, let alone saucer-
shaped.


However, that same day, another newspaper [to be identified -
James] declared in their front page headlines I had encountered
"Flying Saucers".


Bill Bequette also wrote a detailed 26 June article in the
'Pendleton, Oregon East Oregonian' and again published how I had
described the objects as "saucer-like".

Thankfully, he did mention I also described them as "somewhat
bat-shaped", the first time this had been correctly reported.

Unfortunately, that was only to happen once more.


Also on 26 June, the 'Portland Oregon Daily Journal' (AP)
headlined that the "Flying Disk Mystery Grows", the 'Salem Oregon
Statesman' (AP) headlined "Disk-Shaped Objects", the 'Yakima
(Washington) Daily Republic' (AP) headlined I had sighted
"Saucer-Like Objects", the 'Los Angeles Times' (AP) also
headlined that I had seen "Saucerlike Objects", the 'Seattle
Post-Intelligencer' (AP) headlined "Mystery Disks", which were
reportedly "saucer-like" and in the 'Santa Fe New Mexican' (UP)
headlines it was once more proclaimed the objects I observed were
"Saucer-Shaped".

The 'Santa Fe New Mexican' UP article also repeated the misquote
that I had told Jack Whitman the objects "were shaped like
saucers".

Worse yet, the 'Chicago Daily Tribune' misquoted that I said the
objects flew behind the peak of Mt. Rainier - I said a peak _on_
Mt. Rainier - that I used my watch to time them - I used the
dashboard clock - and that the objects were shaped like a pie-
plate.


On 27 June, the 'Boise, Idaho Statesman' (UP) headlined that I
was a "Harassed Saucer-Sighter" and implying a direct quote,
wrote, "Kenneth Arnold said today he would like to get on one of
his 1200-mile-an-hour 'flying saucers,' and escape from the
furore".

They also derided "Arnold's saucers".

The Portland Oregon Journal (AP) headlined the "Flying Disk Case"
and twice referred to "flying saucers", the 'East Oregonian' (AP)
headlines confirmed there was a "'Flying Disc' Mystery" and in a
separate article therein, Bill Bequette maintains I said the
objects were "saucer-like".


On 28 June, another Bill Bequette article replaces "saucer-like"
with a headline which refers to "Flying Discs".

'The Oregonian' headlined that the "Flying Saucer Story Grows"
and referred to my "story of the 'flying saucers'" and "saucer-
like objects" I had reported.


On the two occasions where newspaper stories were based on direct
quotes from interviews actually undertaken with myself
beforehand, I did explain that the objects were "somewhat bat-
shaped", as reported by Bill Bequette and "half-moon shaped, oval
in front and convex in the rear", as reported by the 'Oregon
Journal' (AP) on June 27.
In both interviews I also explained how flat those objects were.

I said to Bill Bequette they were, "flat like a pie pan and
somewhat bat-shaped" and as reported in the Oregon Journal,
"There were no bulges or cowlings; they looked like a big flat
disk".

I did _not_ say the objects were "flat _AND_ shaped like a pie
pan" or "_SHAPED_ like a big flat disk".

Why would I, as in both instances I had already clarified what
the objects did look like.

Is it merely coincidence that the Oregon Journal article, from a
personal interview, seems to be the only one where it was
accurately reported I had observed "crescent-shaped planes or
pilotless missiles".


I also confirmed this in a radio interview with local station
KWRC on 26 June, when I reiterated the objects, "looked something
like a pie plate that was cut in half with a sort of a convex
triangle in the rear".

Subject: [UFORL] Bentwaters - A Suffolk Summer Festival

Courtesy of 'The Guardian':

'The spying game'

Bentwaters Airbase has stored nuclear weapons, been the scene of
UFO sightings and was almost bought by yogic flyers. Now, as part
of the Aldeburgh festival, it is to be the venue for a haunting
piece of music inspired by espionage. Andy Beckett reports...

[...]

The area around Bentwaters is probably the closest Britain comes
to the mysterious military-dominated territories of the American
south-west, made infamous in recent decades by UFO hunters and
conspiracy theorists of all kinds. Next door to the airbase is
another vast former airfield, Woodbridge; a few miles to the east
is Orford Ness, a stony peninsula where British weapons were
secretly tested for 70 years in unexplained pagoda-shaped
bunkers. Originally, the plan was for a conSPIracy cantata to be
performed in one of these, but the logistics of transporting the
audience across the coastal creeks and shingle proved too
difficult. Then Jonathan Reekie, who runs the festival, came
across the "Star Wars building" at Bentwaters.

Inside, it is clammy and cold, even on a mild afternoon. Reekie
is considering installing temporary heaters, but otherwise he
wants the claustrophobic low ceilings and crude breezeblock walls
left as they are. The building was completely stripped when the
Americans moved out in the early 1990s; your imagination is free
to roam the corridors, with their silvery metal doors straight
out of Dr Strangelove.

The history of Bentwaters holds enough riddles to keep
conspiracy-hunters occupied. It was built in 1942 and taken over
by the Americans nine years later. Among its official functions
over the years, it provided the "Soviet" aircraft for Cold War
defence exercises, and housed bombers with nuclear weapons. Its
runway was one of the longest in Europe. In December 1980, an
incident occurred in the woods at the runway's western end that
has provoked speculation ever since. Early one morning, according
to documents released by the Ministry of Defence 20 years later,
"unusual lights" were seen in the sky by American guards at
Bentwaters. "A strange glowing object...metallic in appearance
and triangular in shape" was then spotted above the trees. When
it disappeared from view, the guards searched the woods and found
- depending on which of their accounts you believe - either odd
indentations in the ground and traces of radiation, or a landed
spacecraft complete with "life forms about four feet tall...with
big humanoid heads and dark, catlike eyes."

Five of the MOD documents about all this remain confidential on
the official grounds that they contain secret briefings to
ministers, relate to national security, might alter Britain's
relations with America, or all three. "There are a lot of
military stories and myths about this area," says Reekie.

[...]

[END OF EXTRACT]


For the full story, see:

http://www.guardian.co.uk/friday_review/story/0,3605,724601,00.ht
ml

"Suddenly noted a shiny type object to south about 150 to 200
yards. It was off the road. At first glance, stopped. It looked,
at first, like a car turned upside down. Thought some kids might
have turned over. Saw two people in white coveralls very close to
the object. One of these persons seemed to turn and look straight
at my car and seemed startled--seemed to jump quickly somewhat.

At this time I started moving my car towards them quickly, with
idea to help. Had stopped about only a couple seconds. Object was
like aluminum--it was whitish against the mesa background, but
not chrome. Seemed like O in shape and I at first glance took it
to be overturned white car. Car appeared to be up on radiator or
on trunk, this first glance.

The only time I saw these two persons was when I had stopped, for
possibly two seconds or so, to glance at the object. I don't
recall noting any particular shape or possibly any hats, or
headgear. These persons appeared normal in shape--but possibly
they were small adults or large kids".

In 'Socorro Saucer', Stanford writes:

Zamora further remembered, "Then I saw two small figures in what
resembled white coveralls, pretty close to the object on its
northwest side, as if inspecting it".

In his diagram, Stanford highlights 'footprints'.
Aren't these approximately southwest, not northwest?


Was Zamora's "shiny", 'whitish', 'aluminum-like' yet "not chrome"
enigmatic craft from another realm, or, perhaps a shiny, all-
white, polyurethane-coated nylon hot-air balloon - as it would,
as such, have been in 1964?

Apparently, the only alternative is that it was a 'test flight'
from White Sands which went astray.

Is there any evidence whatsoever to support this premise?

Unless argued otherwise, can we now conclude that Zamora's
sighting [or, more accurately, non-sighting] is a founding 'UFO'
case where the witness encountered either an alien spacecraft, as
perceived, or a hot-air balloon, as evidenced.

Chris wrote:

>Disc-shaped objects were reported generations before Arnold, and
>in several different countries, but to cite a more recent
>example, I recall Ole Jonny Brænne found a Norwegian one dating
>to 1946. There they used the term "saucer" or at least "plate"
>(as in dish).

Chris,

There was a pre-Arnold, 'flying saucer' sighting which originated
in the US and, if I recall, had been reported by a 'cowboy'(?),
circa the 1800s(?).

I can't now locate a source, however, I did see it featured
online by a promotional/tourist web site for a town/city/state -
I believe connected with New Mexico.

It was claimed to be, 'the true first flying saucer sighting'.

If any subscriber recognises this case, please let us know.


What I do specifically remember is that it wasn't actually a
'flying saucer' at all. The witness had reported an enigmatic
aerial object which he described as, 'about the size of a
saucer', or similar. Like Arnold, he didn't say it was saucer-
shaped.


>I don't have my archives at hand, so I can't be more precise
>right now, but I would suggest we kept our minds open for a
>little longer about how much the media contributed to the
>creation of the 'flying saucer' legend.

Comprehensively cited evidence does seem to prove the media did
more than merely contribute - they effectively created a
popularised belief that Kenneth Arnold had seen nine unidentified
objects which were, astonishingly, shaped exactly like
saucers/disks.

Conversely, the premise is that this was irrelevant to 'some'
extent, as there were reports of disk-shaped objects which
predated Arnold's misconstrued comments.

In short; just because the media were initially mistaken in
portraying a scenario where America was being overflown by disk-
shaped (air)craft of unknown origin, doesn't mean that people
were not suddenly witnessing non-earthly [could be from one or
more planets or dimensions, or...] disk-shaped craft(s).


It's an issue which is inherently fundamental to our overall
understanding of 'flying saucers and where they came from'.


Two principal elements therein; firstly, how many comparable
'flying disc' accounts do we, in fact, have documented before 24
June, 1947?

Secondly, to _what_ extent are those likely to explain why
'flying saucer/disk' sightings became so instantaneously prolific
_and archetypal during the next fifty plus years_ [countless
hoaxes acknowledged], following our inaccurate media headline
'flying saucer/disc' descriptions, post 25 June?


The challenge is to evidence why 'flying saucers' - the absolute
essence of ufology - do not have a blatantly recognisable,
specious basis. It's one which I have, equally, duly addressed
and can offer no argument against.

Perhaps I'm simply unaware of the many, significant, pre-Arnold
accounts which might suggest why non-earthly, disk-shaped
vehicles are a, factually, tenable genesis for 'flying
saucers'... and everything built on that foundation.

To begin with - perhaps we can establish and document _all_ of
those apparent pre-Arnold 'disk-shaped' reports.


James Easton.

Here is one "first flying saucer", Texas 1878:
http://www.denisontx.com/history.htm

"Daylight Disk - Denison, Texas, USA - 2 January 1878
The term 'flying saucer' was made popular by a journalist covering Kenneth Arnolds's
Sighting of nine flying disks in June of 1947. A farmer John Martin used the term 70
years earlier to describe what he saw on a hunting expedition in Texas.
John Marton saw a dark object high in the Northern sky. He first noticed it to be about
the size of an orange, that grew in size as it got closer to him. After a while it had
increased considerably in size and appeared to be going quite fast. When it was over
him it was the size of a large saucer and at a great height.
Because this UFO was dark, and not a mysterious light, reflective, or silvery, many
scientists believe he saw a solid object against the sky, with the light behind it."

Jouko Forsstrom

From: chris aubeck <caubeck@yahoo.com>
Date: Fri, 7 Jun 2002 11:50:17 +0100 (BST)
Subject: Re: [UFORL] Re: 'Flying Saucers' and Where They Came From


Hello James,

I have been working exclusively on pre-1940 cases for
over ten years and have gathered what may be the
largest collection of them to date.*

My project, called "Return to Magonia," has received a
great deal of support from other researchers but very
little "publicity" because of the cherished and
overpowering myth that UFOs were first spotted in the
USA in 1947, or, worse still, in the late 19th
century.

I know of many early cases involving circular or
disc-shaped objects. As I see my job as more
descriptive than interpretive I do not seek scientific
explanations for each and every case but I do pride
myself on getting the earliest possible sources for
each report. This often involves translating documents
from Portuguese, French, Spanish and Italian into
English (which I can do okay) and less commonly from
the German (which personally I cannot). It's amazing
to see what other countries are publishing and what is
remains totally unknown to the rest of the world.

Disc-shaped objects were reported in pre-Arnold years
but obviously they had no influence on the post-Arnold
image of the 'flying saucer' as nobody was collecting
them and labeling them as a single item. Therefore, I
would not argue that the modern image of a "saucer"
has been inherited from the remote past (except maybe
in a Jungian sort of way) and I accept that the
popular concept of UFOs as "plate-like craft" began
with Arnold. But this does not mean that sightings of
disc-shaped things in the sky commenced in 1947.

Just as abduction narratives did not begin in the late
1950s and nor did 'implant' stories.

I'll send you the 19th century case you mention later
today if I can.

Best wishes,

Chris Aubeck
*I would like to be proved wrong because I often get
the feeling I'm the only one interested in doing this.

From: Kenny Young <ufo@fuse.net>
Date: Fri, 07 Jun 2002 12:27:40 -0700
Subject: [UFORL] Jackie Gleason update

It has been said that an unusual article appeared in
the BUFFALO NEWS dated Sunday, June 12, 1987. The
article was regarding Beverly McKittrik, the ex-wife of
the late comedian Jackie Gleason. The article
supposedly has McKittrick charging that Gleason was
taken to Homestead AFB by President Nixon to view
unusual creatures held in storage at the facility.

Investigation of this case began in early 2002 by
attempting to locate the original Buffalo News article.

On May 9, 2002, Cincinnati-area researcher Donnie
Blessing filed the following report:

   I contacted the Buffalo News newspaper this
morning. Their number
   is 1-800-777-8680. I spoke to someone in the
newsroom. I explained
   the information I was trying to find. [I asked if
they] Could they tell
   me the reporters name who wrote the Jackie Gleason
article and was
   told that the newspaper only keeps their archives
back to 1997. The
   suggestion was given that I contact the Buffalo
Public Library and
   find out if they could look that information up on
microfilm of old
   newspapers. If I was able to get the news
reporter's name then I
   could call the paper back and they would look to
see if they could
   find the reporter in their files.

   I then placed a call to the Buffalo Central Public
Library. Their
   number is 716-858-8900. I spoke to a Joann who
works in Special
   collections. She told me that she would have
someone to look and
   see if they could find this story tonight on
microfilm. I gave the
   date that I needed. She asked that tomorrow I call
back to see if
   they had found the information. She also said that
if they find the
   information that I could retrieve a copy of the
article for 5 dollars.
   This I will do and hopefully it will include the
reporters name
   which I will ask for on the phone also. Will keep
you updated on
   any info I get tomorrow.

Through follow up inquiry, Donnie learned that the
librarian at the Buffalo Central Public Library could
not locate any such article regarding Jackie Gleason or
Beverly McKittrick from the Sunday, June 12, 1987
edition of the Buffalo News.

Seeking to undertake a more satisfactory and
comprehensive review, Donnie obtained the actual
microfilm of the June, 1987 Buffalo News through
Interlibrary Loan. The microfilm was delivered to the
dowtown, Cincinnati branch of the Hamilton County
Public Library system.

Upon making one search for the Jackie Gleason story in
late May of 2002, Donnie was also unable to locate any
such article on the date in question. Not being
satisfied by her first search, she made another search
effort while the microfilm was being held at the
Cincinnati library. Enclosed below are her comments,
dated Tuesday, June 4, 2002:

  Kenny,

   Just got back from the library and I reviewed the
dates June 11th
   thru the 15th for the Buffalo News for 1987 and did
not find a
   word about the Jackie Gleason article. I scanned
very carefully
   these dates and did not think it was necessary to
go any further.
   The one reel was for the 11th thru the 17th. So
make of this
   what you want but if there is an article out there
its not under
   the 12th for sure. Let me know what you make of
this.

COMMENT:

A total of three (3) searches were made for the Jackie
Gleason article that was said to have appeared in the
June 12, 1987 Buffalo News. One search was made by a
librarian at the Buffalo Central Public Library and two
searches, one very comprehensive, was made by
researcher Donnie Blessing. These three searches failed
to produce the article that was said to have appeared
in this newspaper. At this point it might be necessary
to trace the story back to the source who alleged the
existence of the article to begin with. Perhaps this
source can produce a copy of the article. If so, it is
not likely to be verified as its reference cannot be
located in the microfilmed copy of the June, 1987
Buffalo News.

A Pennsylvania-based private detective is assisting
this investigation and helping us to locate McKittrik.
This phase of the investigation is still ongoing and
details on this will be posted when available.

prepared by Kenny Young
Friday, June 7, 2002

From: chris aubeck <caubeck@yahoo.com>
Date: Sat, 8 Jun 2002 19:06:03 +0100 (BST)
Subject: [UFORL] Pazzaglini, Williamson, Writing, 1937.

Hello list members,

In The Anomalist No. 1, 1994, there appears an
interesting interview with Mario Pazzaglini, a
clinical psychologist who has studied samples of
"alien writing."

One of the samples he mentions comes from the estates
of George Williamson and George Adamski. "The oldest
example Williamson had was from 1937, from pre-flying
saucer days, in other words. But the story involved a
craft that landed in a field. When the farmer went
out, they handed him a piece of paper and there were
symbols on it."

The above is being furnished for your information

NEW YORK - The clamorous cry, "To the moon, Alice", frequently
delivered on the 'Honeymooners' by the late, great Jackie
Gleason, may have been inspired in part by the comic's
fascination with outer space. Gleason was an avowed believer in
UFOs and, according to his ex-wife Beverly McKittrick, he even
got involved in some spaced-out exploits with his friend Richard
Nixon. Beverly was a 37-year-old divorcee with a great golf game
when Jackie met her at Miami country club. Their four year
marriage ended in 1974. In her unpublished biography of the
funnyman entitled 'The Great One,' Beverly, Gleason's second
spouse, describes a bizarre trip Jackie took with the then
President in 1973 to Homestead AFB in Florida to see what see
says were bodies of four dead space aliens recovered by the Air
Force.

[...]

[END]

This article is credited to the 'MUFON Journal', February 1988,
Number 238 and does seem to originate from the same source as
Schuessler's - content in both is almost identical.

In his report, Zamora wrote:

"After the roar and flame, did not note anything, while going up
the somewhat steep rough hill--had to back up and try again, two
more times. Got up about halfway first time, wheels started
skidding, roar still going on, had to back down and try twice and
rock. While beginning third time, noise and flame not noted.

After got to top, traveled slowly on the gravel road westwardly.
Noted nothing for awhile...for possibly 10 or 15 seconds, went
slow, looking around for the shack--did not recall exactly where
the dynamite shack was.

Suddenly noted a shiny type object to south about 150 to 200
yards. It was off the road".

If, "After got to top, traveled slowly on the gravel road
westwardly... Noted nothing for awhile...for possibly 10 or 15
seconds, went slow...", then Zamora [twice noting he was
travelling slowly] might have had that initial glimpse from
approximately where you indicate - maybe slightly further on
[impossible to say for sure].

This early 90's photograph shows a building directly in front of
'X' and presumably it wasn't there in 1964.

Your conclusions effectively agree with Chris Lambright's map -
for which the correct URL is:
http://www.cufon.org/contributors/chrisl/roadmap.htm

However, in 'Socorro Saucer', Ray Stanford provides a map of
events which, interestingly, is quite different and that's only
now evident on seeing the USGS overhead you have provided.

He places, 'Object and two humanoids sighted' as much nearer the
vicinity of Zamora's second observation, with little distance
between both.

Stanford also locates our 'UFO' as close to the dirt road, indeed
only a short distance from it.


Zamora added:

"Stopped car, was still talking on radio, started to get out,
mike fell down, reached back to put up mike, then replaced radio
mike in slot, got out of car and started to go down to where I
knew the object (car) was".

Although Zamora seemingly doesn't confirm how far distant to said
object, Stanford claims in his book, "fifty feet or so away".

Given that Zamora at first, "noted a shiny type object to south
about 150 to 200 yards" - say, 500 feet - then Stanford's
illustration should agree, i.e., Zamora was 'ten times' further
away at his initial sighting of an object in the arroyo.

It clearly doesn't equate, with Zamora being depicted by Stanford
as only about 250 feet from the object when briefly seen at first
glance.


Coming back to the USGS photo as evidence, we have a scenario
where Zamora's first and subsequent observations are separated by
circa a factor of ten.

Or do we.... who says so, except for Ray Stanford and whose own
published research actually corroborates otherwise?

table trying to see something at the base of the leg of the
table. Zamora's line of sight would pass OVER the UFO".

"Then paid attention to road while drove towards scene. Radioed

under the object. Object was starting to go straight up--slowly
up. Object slowly rose straight up. Flame was light blue and at
bottom was sort of orange color.

JIM -- you wrote:

>I have just returned from Show Low, AZ, after evacuating my family from our
>house, 1/2 mile from the fire line....

Glad you and yours are safe. Ditto Mike Rogers. Hope both your homes
ultimately are equally safe, along with the rest of your delightful town.

>Before leaving, I spoke with Mike Rogers, who was also evacuated, and he was
fairly confident that "Turkey Springs," the location of the Travis Walton
incident, has been lost to the fire.

I was afraid of that. Damn!

>Heber, directly to the north, lost several hundred homes in the blaze.

The news we're getting here in New Mexico suggests most of the damage was in
nearby Overgaard and that Heber, while hardly unscathed, managed to get thru
the inferno reasonably well. Any idea what the situation is in the business
district along Hwy 260? Did the (former) gas station where the phone booth
used by Walton--and the phone booth itself--come thru okay? I don't suppose
you have any idea about any of this right now, but I can't help wondering.

>The loss to the state of Arizona in terms of natural beauty is nearly
incomprehensible. I've been to many beauteous locales in my life, and
this area ranks among the top....

The area is one of my wife's and my favorites. In fact, for several years,
we've been toying with the idea of a get-away place there, or even
permanently relocating. Sad, sad, indeed. Let's hope this tragedy will have
a silver lining: that the Forest Service and others finally (!!) will get
the message about failed, foolish forest management/job elimination/fire
kindling policies.

>The loss to ufology may be greater, however, as those trees may have held a
secret that is now forever unrecoverable.... I don't wish to go into more
detail until I have had a chance to find and speak with Mike
again...and...ascertain to what extent he was able to gather evidence from
the Turkey Springs area.

According to Walton's Fire in the Sky (pp. 177-78 of the hardcover ed.), in
1993, he and Rogers returned to the site, where they noted what seemed to be
phenomenal growth of the trees nearest the point where the UFO reportedly
hovered. Walton wrote that Rogers later returned alone, cut down one of the
trees, and examining the stump, studied the tree-ring growth. He interpreted
this as showing that after 1975 (when the Walton incident occurred) the
tree's growth spurted to "four or five times that of any of the tree's
previous years." He also noted that other trees in the general area and
situated in similar conditions showed no change in expected growth rates.
Walton added that Rogers, wondering if there may be some natural explanation,
considered consulting a forestry expert.

Walton also wrote, "...the stump and the other trees are still there." Let's
hope this still is true (even if fire damaged, the stump and associated trees
might still contain valuable information). If not, or even if so, let's hope
Rogers collected and kept physical evidence (e.g., a full-width slice of the
tree trunk/stump), recording his on-site work photographically, etc., and
with detailed notes. Also, did he ever consult a forestry expert and, if so,
with what results?

Many on this list know I think it highly likely that the Walton incident was
a hoax. However, I've definitely not fully closed the door on the possibilty
it was a real abduction event. The "tree-whispered," tree-ring-captured
secret, if any, just might throw the door wide open again. Let's hope it's
not gone with the wind.

Jim, please keep us posted. Meanwhile, may you and your family and Rogers
and his and all your neighbors soon be able to return safely home. -- Cheers,
KARL PFLOCK

exist.&nbsp; The small declivity on the south side of the original site has now been
filled in and is no longer there.&nbsp; The land on the top of the mesa is now all
smoothed for home sites.</EM></DIV>

Buford Street in the Highland Estates development at about 34.04505 degrees north
and 106.90005 degrees west plus or minus about 50 meters.</EM></DIV>

<DIV><EM>There is now a house at the top of the hill at the site on the gravel road
where Zamora said that he stopped and first saw the craft on the ground.&nbsp; The

From: "James Easton" <voyager@ukonline.co.uk>
Date: Tue, 9 Jul 2002 05:35:03 +0100
Subject: Re: [UFORL] Sad Socorro News

Regarding:

>From: "EDWARD BLAIR" <eablair90@hotmail.com>
>Date: Sat, 06 Jul 2002 22:18:58 -0700
>Subject: [UFORL] Sad Socorro News

Ed and list,

In 'Socorro Saucer', Ray Stanford clarified:

"Zamora angled Socorro 2 to the right, off the paved road at a
point just beyond a small church building, the name of which
translates from Spanish as 'Church of the Good Shepherd'."

Later today, I'll scan and upload a copy of Stanford's own map
and some other material which is relevant.

Having visited the site shortly afterwards, Stanford should have
pinpointed its correct location.


I've acquired and await delivery of a book entitled, 'New Mexico
Geological Society: Fourteenth Field Conference, 1963 - Guidebook
of the Socorro Region.'

This contains contemporary maps, including some showing the
location of "Perlite, Mining Districts, Tritium Studies, Ground
Water, Springs, Sais Quartzine, Oil, Gas", etc.

There was a "perlite mill" not far from the site and according to
Stanford, Zamora stated: "I couldn't tell what might have kept
the thing up or going; it was now completely silent. It kept that
same height above the ground - ten to fifteen feet - and never
did get much higher until it got over near the perlite mill on
the west side of US 60, maybe a mile away".

Zamora added, "When there was the 'flame' and roar, the object
rose _slowly_ [Stanford's emphasis is shown underlined], like it
was _heavy_. Seemed like an effort getting up that twenty feet or
so, I'd say. But when there was silence and no roar or 'flame' or
nothing, everything looked _easy_! Looked like no effort to take
off across toward the perlite mill and to climb up at least at a
45 degree angle real fast after that".


There's a significant photograph in 'Socorro Saucer', which shows
the nearby dynamite shack and terrain beyond, in which general
direction the object departed.

If, as Zamora claimed, the object flew directly over that
dynamite shack, then it apparently was not heading towards the
perlite mill.

Stanford realises that Zamora may be mistaken somewhere in his
perceptions and writes in the photograph's caption:

"The dynamite shack which the departing object passed 50 to 100
feet behind and _not over_ as it appeared from Zamora's position,
and terrain over which the object passed during its departure
from the landing site. The general course of departure is
illustrated by the black pointer.

The illusion of passing _over_ the shack was because Zamora was
located 60 to 80 feet northwest of where this photo was taken".

Of course, Zamora had already dropped his glasses and was without
them when watching the object's initial departure. As he wrote in
his formal testimony:

"It did not come any closer to me. It appeared to go in straight
line and at same height--possibly 10 to 15 feet from ground, and
it cleared the dynamite shack by about three feet. Shack about
eight feet high. Object was travelling very fast. It seemed to
rise up, and take off immediately across country. I ran back to
my car and as I ran back, I kept an eye on the object. I picked
up my glasses (I left the sun glasses on ground), got into the
car, and radioed to Nep Lopez, radio operator, to "look out of
the window, to see if you could see an object." He asked what is
it? I answered "It looks like a balloon." I don't know if he saw
it. If Nep looked out of his window, which faces north, he
couldn't have seen it. I did not tell him at the moment which
window to look out of.

As I was calling Nep, I could still see the object. The object
seemed to lift up slowly, and to "get small" in the distance very
fast. It seemed to just clear the Box Canyon or Six Mile Canyon
Mountain. It disappeared as it went over the mountain. It had no
flame whatsoever as it was traveling over the ground, and no
smoke or noise".


If, "the object seemed to lift up slowly" whilst Zamora "was
calling Nep", surely it must be the same moment, as he told
Stanford, when, "it never did get much higher until it got over
near the perlite mill on the west side of US 60, maybe a mile
away".
This would indicate the object had only travelled circa one mile
by the time Zamora had returned to his car and made that call,
bearing in mind his later revelation - not featured in 'Socorro
Saucer' - how the radio would not initially work.

It's also questionable how far distant the object actually was
when it began to ascend - how could Zamora know it wasn't only
half a mile away, or even nearer? Stanford cites that Zamora had
already made an error of judgement, locating the object 50-100
feet closer than factual, when it was approximately just 100 feet
from him.

Stanford's claims are obviously conjecture and required simply to
agree with Zamora's recollection about the perlite mill
trajectory.

What is does alter the context of is Zamora's official statement
and the impression given, albeit sincerely, that our object had
rapidly "disappeared" beyond "Box Canyon or Six Mile Canyon
Mountain".

Where exactly was "Box Canyon or Six Mile Canyon Mountain" in
relation to the landing site and that perlite mill?


James Easton.

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Wed, 10 Jul 2002 09:43:28 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Re: Fantasy Prone Personality Types - Abductions.

My view of abduction and UFO occupant reports:

- Many abduction sequences are generated by improper questioning
under hypnosis. If the hypnotist is expecting alien activity, the
questions asked may be leading enough for the subconscious to
produce an abduction experience.

I consider any case as "tainted" once a hypnotist has plied his trade
on the witness. Hypnotism is not just a viewer of the mind, it is also
an editor.

- There are several cases which resulted from post-hypnotic
suggestion during "party hypnosis".

- I'd say a good portion of abduction cases are people trying to win
the cash prizes the tabloids give away for the "best case of the year".

In one "men in black" case, the police arrested the MIB, and found
a press card for a tabloid on him.

- There are people who are so under stress at the time that the right
stimulus will cause hallucinations. I have also encountered cases
(non-UFO) where allergic reactions caused hallucinations.

- I know of an abduction where the event was staged as a prank on
the victim (who was drunk).

- Some cases were offered as alibis for nonperformance of work, to
get out of contracts, sleeping on the job, speeding, or for ammunition
wasted (security guard).

- I know of at least 3 cases where the abduction or occupant report
came around as a result of a wager. In two of the cases, the bet
was that the case could be pulled off, in the third, it was the payoff
for losing the bet.

- I know of another case where the "victim" was given LSD without
knowing it.

- I personally have known two people who constantly see aliens,
UFOs, fires, and other out-of-place objects, years after sustaining
brain damage in road accidents. Nobody else can see them.

- There are still people who think they can make money by reporting
a bizarre abduction. Usually they find out the hard way that the
trouble they get is not worth what they make in interviews and book
sales.

- Some people report things just to get their names in papers.

From: "James Easton" <voyager@ukonline.co.uk>
Date: Thu, 11 Jul 2002 04:24:39 +0100
Subject: Re: [UFORL] Horten Ho IX V2

Regarding:

>From: "fatrob83" <fatrob83@hotmail.com>
>Date: Thu, 11 Jul 2002 01:52:58 -0000
>Subject: [UFORL] Horten Ho IX V2

Rob wrote:

>Does anyone have any sugestions for sites containing info on the
>craft after it was recoverd by the US?

Rob,

There's helpful information at:

http://www.hotel.wineasy.se/ipms/stuff_eng_detail_hoix.htm

This features a photograph of what was apparently the only V3
captured at Friedrichsroda.

As you will note, what seems to be the untouched airframe can
still be seen in a museum.

>Has it's similarity to Kenneth Arnolds siting in 47 been brought
>up before?

Yes, it's one of several 'flying wings' which have been
investigated by myself and others and dismissed as possible
candidates.

A summary was contained in my November 2000, 'Fortean Times'
article:

As an experienced pilot, Kenneth Arnold seemed to be a reliable
witness; but what could he have observed that so perplexed him?
The most obvious explanation was a formation of military
aircraft, which for some reason he didn't recognise and was
simply mistaken about their airspeed.

On first examination, there are some intriguing possibilities
about this hypothesis. Arnold's crescent-like object resembles
the tail-less 'flying wing' concept pioneered by John 'Jack'
Northrop in the United States. Northrop's XB-35, YB-49 and
particularly YRB-49A were all similar to Arnold's depiction.

However, prior to 24 June 1947, only one XB-35 had been built and
due to several mechanical problems it had been grounded since the
previous September. The second XB-35 to be built made its maiden
flight on 26 June, 1947, two days after Arnold's sighting. The
testing was carried out at Muroc Dry Lake (later re-named Edwards
Air Force Base) in California, far removed from Washington's
Cascade mountain range.

The Northrop YB-49, a jet-propelled derivative of the XB-35,
first flew on 21 October 1948. Only one YRB-49A was built, but
that didn't take off until May 1950.

In Germany, the Horten brothers - contemporaries and counterparts
of Jack Northrop - had also developed innovative 'flying wing'
designs. Their 'Ho IX' (also known as the 'Go 229') was nearing
production as WWII ended. During late April 1945, the Horten
plant at Friedrichsroda was occupied by American troops and one
of the 'Ho IX' airframes was transported back to the US. Its
design is almost identical to Arnold's crescent-like sketch.

So, decades before today's dark rumours about recovered alien
technology at Area 51, could the US Air Force have been indulging
in a spot of clandestine reverse-engineering, not of alien but
German craft? Aviation historians seem satisfied that the looted
'Ho IX' airframe was never completed and test-flown in the US.
Even if it had been, those other eight, tail-less objects that
escorted it and matched its airspeed are not accounted for.

The contemporary similarity between experimental flying wings and
Arnold's 'flying saucers' is therefore a remarkable coincidence
and nothing more. The hypothesis that Arnold witnessed nine such
top-secret, tail-less aircraft is not, evidently, sustainable.
[END]


>...check out the 10th picture down on this site and let me know
>what you think...

It's wonderful to see that someone has actually flown a working
and superbly crafted model of this aircraft.

Amazingly similar to the profile Arnold believed he had observed,
even though it's evidently straightforward why nine 'flying
wings' are not an explanation.

Not as aircraft, anyway.


James Easton.

something does not exist. So you have to assume that it does
not exist until you have proof that it does exist.

real alien
abductions, or even real aliens.

I have an exercise for you: Prove that such a thing as a Smurf does not
exist in the
real universe (other than as a product of a cartoonist's imagination or
artwork).

It was the same with the discovery of new elements. Because it is impossible
to
prove something does not exist, the burden of proof was on those claiming to
have
discovered or prepared a new chemical element. The scientific world had to
assume
that the element did not exist until the proof was completed.

So it is with alien life. You can't prove that it does not exist. So the
default case must
be that alien life does not exist, until someone proves (by demonstrated
example) that
alien life does exist. Anything else is stacking the deck, because if you
assume that
alien life does exist, there is no possible way to disprove it..

Actually, the Army Air Corps didn't exist at that time either. In 1941 it
had become the Army Air Forces and the Air Corps was a branch of the
Army in the way that Infantry, Artillery and Armor were branches of the
Army. As an aside, the aviation portion of the Army is now know as
Aviation.

<DIV><SPAN class=720093002-18072002><FONT face=Arial color=#0000ff
size=2>When
viewed from the side, a "yaw" movement would not involve dipping the
wings.&nbsp; It would involve the nose of the plane tilting towards the viewer,
or away from it, as if the plane were shaking it's head "no".&nbsp; "Pitch"
movement is as if the plane is shaking its head "yes."&nbsp; "Roll" movement
would be as if it were cocking its head back and forth, the "wing-waggling"
motion.&nbsp; But if the plane were to yaw back and forth, it could also reflect
the sun at weird angles.&nbsp; Very rarely does a plane yaw in this way, as
turns normally involve rolling and yawing at the same time.&nbsp; A plane will
change it's yaw angle to compensate for cross-winds.&nbsp; This is called
"crabbing." It will make the adjustment, and then hold it at that angle for an
appreciable period of time. </FONT></SPAN></DIV>
<DIV><SPAN class=720093002-18072002><FONT face=Arial color=#0000ff
size=2></FONT></SPAN>&nbsp;</DIV>

From: "rotsky" <rotsky@wanadoo.fr>
Date: Fri, 19 Jul 2002 10:41:14 +0200
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Re: Horten Ho IX V2

Any appreciable yaw is unusual except with experimental designs where the
problem hasn't been properly addressed (also rare in this computer age). Yaw
is controlled through the use of the rudder, and fast jet pilots can spend
their entire careers without touching the rudder pedals (okay, okay, I'm
kidding, but not much). Aside from deliberate crabbing for crosswind
landings, yaw isn't something that is much of a consideration with fast
jets. (Big difference with gliders, though, whose long, high spect ratio
wings cause a lot of adverse yaw in turns, and also warbirds with their high
torque. Light aircraft come somewhere in between, though the rudder's used a
lot on aerobatics).

That said, your train of thought is still valid. The rolling action (the
dipping of the wings) could easily catch the sun and cause flashing. If
these were aircraft flying near mountains, where you can encounter some
significant air currents, frequent roll corrections would not be uncommon.
PLUS (and this is very important in this scenario), we're presuming that
these were aircraft in formation. Flying in formation demands constant
corrections to maintain position relative to another aircraft: combine this
with mountain currents and you've got aircraft that are bucking about quite
a bit.

And there's another thing about formations of aircraft that's not obvious
when you watch them from the ground. Look at such a formation side-on and
you'll see how the aircraft rise and fall in relation to each other - partly
as a result of hitting the dirty air from aircraft in front (display
formations are usually designed to minimise this - however, we're not
dealing with a display formation here), and partly because each pilot is
trying to stay locked on to another aircraft, following that aircraft as it
rises and falls on vertical air currents and small inputs from the pilot.
But there's a lag in reaction time, so the two aircraft are never at exactly
the same height. Add a bunch more aircraft and you get a distinctive
undulating effect from the whole formation. This is quite evident from any
air-to-air video of formations.

a+
Steve
