From: "James Easton" <voyager@ukonline.co.uk>
Date: Sat, 20 Jul 2002 07:21:23 +0100
Subject: Re: [UFORL] Re: Horten Ho IX V2

Regarding:

>From: "bortaf ----" <fatrob83@hotmail.com>
>Date: Fri, 12 Jul 2002 01:38:19 +0000
>Subject: Re: [UFORL] Horten Ho IX V2

Rob wrote:

>Thanks for the swift reply James,would you say that the number
>of craft observed is the main hiccup in the Horton-Arnold
>connection?

Rob,

There's purely no evidence of any connection.

Separately, the number of objects observed is a major factor,
especially as they apparently flew in a controlled formation.

We can therefore seemingly dismiss 'billowing snow', meteors or
'earth lights', etc. as being candidates.

Just two obvious terrestrial possibilities exist - either the
objects were aircraft or they were birds.


Strictly, we only need one aircraft, not necessarily nine of
them. It could have been a plane which was trailing eight mock-up
models, perhaps to test new developments in radar detection
capabilities, or something similar.

That could explain the undulating flight characteristics and
Arnold's allusion to, 'the tail of a Chinese kite'.

However, there's equally zero known evidence of any such
operations and the Cascades perhaps not an ideal test site.


There's then the crucial issue of airspeed, which is the crux of
Arnold's sighting.

If correct in his perceptions, then the objects couldn't have
been aircraft. If Arnold was mistaken, then they might have a
straightforward explanation, particularly should we know _why_ he
conceivably made an error in judgement.
It comes back to the question which Larry raised - could it have
been a formation of standard military aircraft, which puzzled
Arnold merely because he couldn't observe tails on them.

If Arnold's perceptions were accurate, then the objects could not
have been contemporary aircraft flying at circa 1,000 m.p.h. If
in error, then the entire enigma falls apart and he completely
misunderstood what was being observed.


Perhaps significantly, during his encounter Arnold did not
believe the objects were travelling particularly fast, a point he

mentions on several occasions.

It was only _afterwards_, when he calculated their airspeed,
based entirely on the distance he thought said objects had
travelled, that he realised they must surely be a new type of Air
Force jet.

His calculation comes down to one critical perception; that the
objects momentarily passed behind a "jagged peak" on Mt. Rainer
and consequently must have been some 25 miles distant.

If correct, then we really do have a mystery.

Conversely, if there's reason to conclude Arnold was mistaken,
his calculations and any conundrum are demonstrably specious.


That's the situation which now exists. Not only is there no
"jagged peak" at the altitude Arnold perceived, he was unable to
identify a likely source when this was investigated in later
years and from my own research, local expertise agrees that from
his full descriptions, Arnold is describing the prominent and
distinctive 'Little Tahoma (Tacoma)' peak on Mt. Rainier.

'Little Tahoma' is on the far side of Mt. Rainier from Arnold's
location and although visible, if the objects passed behind it,
they absolutely must also therefore have travelled behind Mt.
Rainier.

However, Arnold reports that the objects flew between himself and
the mountain.


I'm not aware that anyone has suggested an alternative "jagged
peak", even allowing considerable leeway for Arnold's reported
circa 9,500 feet altitude.
The fact that Arnold himself was unable to resolve this, must be
a concern, if not understated.


By default, the evidence indicates that Arnold perceived those
nine objects to briefly pass behind a far distant landmark, when
in fact, they flew in front of it.

If so, then his pivotal premise for an extraordinary observation
collapses - it's that simple.


Where is any 'Arnold's peak' evidence otherwise?

Perhaps someone can highlight it. If not and the foundation of
'ufology' can't even be substantiated to a rudimentary extent,
then why waste time on any further deliberation.

The resultant birth and utterly misconstrued popularisation of
'flying saucers' is evidenced and nothing can ever seriously be
respected as credibly built on _that_ foundation.


Also:

>From: "bortaf ----" <fatrob83@hotmail.com>
>Date: Fri, 19 Jul 2002 01:31:17 +0000
>Subject: Re: [UFORL] Re: Horten Ho IX V2

>Sorry to drag the subject out but James i know you have looked
>into this case extensively, would the fact that Arnold
apparently >turned his plane round whilst taking the timing of
the objects >have affected his calculations?

Arguably it wasn't relevant and what we can now appreciate to be
infinitely more important are Kenneth Arnold's earliest
testimonies.

A foremost difficulty with his various accounts is that some of
the key evidence is contradictory and diametrically opposed.

The quintessential 'Kenneth Arnold story' is usually cited from
his letter/'official statement' to the Air Force, wherein he
wrote:

I flew directly toward Mt. Rainier after reaching an altitude of
about 9,500 feet, which is the approximate elevation of the high
plateau from which Mt. Rainier rises. I had made one sweep of
this high plateau to the westward, searching all of the various
ridges for this marine ship and flew to the west down and near
the ridge side of the canyon where Ashford, Washington, is
located.

Unable to see anything that looked like the lost ship, I made a
360 degree turn to the right and above the little city of
Mineral, starting again toward Mt. Rainier. I climbed back up to
an altitude of approximately 9,200 feet.

The air was so smooth that day that it was a real pleasure flying
and, as most pilots do when the air is smooth and they are flying
at a higher altitude, I trimmed out my airplane in the direction
of Yakima, Washington, which was almost directly east of my
position and simply sat in my plane observing the sky and the
terrain.

[...]

The sky and air was clear as crystal. I hadn't flown more than
two or three minutes on my course when a bright flash reflected
on my airplane. It startled me as I thought I was too close to
some other aircraft. I looked every place in the sky and couldn't
find where the reflection had come from until I looked to the
left and the north of Mt. Rainier where I observed a chain of
nine peculiar looking aircraft flying from north to south at
approximately 9,500 foot elevation and going, seemingly, in a
definite direction of about 170 degrees.

They were approaching Mt. Rainier very rapidly, and I merely
assumed they were jet planes. Anyhow, I discovered that this was
where the reflection had come from, as two or three of them every
few seconds would dip or change their course slightly, just
enough for the sun to strike them at an angle that reflected
brightly on my plane.

These objects being quite far away, I was unable for a few
seconds to make out their shape or their formation. Very shortly
they approached Mt. Rainier, and I observed their outline against
the snow quite plainly.

I thought it was very peculiar that I couldn't find their tails
but assumed they were some type of jet plane. I was determined to
clock their speed, as I had two definite points [Mt. Rainier and
Mt. Adams - James] I could clock them by; the air was so clear
that it was very easy to see objects and determine their
approximate shape and size at almost fifty miles that day.
[END OF EXTRACT]


Let's definitively set this in context and in doing so I will
reveal evidence which seems to have previously been predominately
overlooked.

Arnold, according to his later recollections, is cruising towards
Yakima...

Why?

His ultimate destination was Boise, Idaho.

Why stop at Yakima - was it for refuelling?

There's no indication of that.

As above, Arnold wrote:

"I trimmed out my airplane in the direction of Yakima,
Washington, which was almost directly east of my position and
simply sat in my plane observing the sky and the terrain".

In his early, 26 June 1947, KWRC radio interview, Arnold
confirmed:

Well, about 2:15 I took off from Chehalis, Washington, en route
to Yakima, and, of course, every time that any of us fly over the
country near Mt. Rainier, we spend an hour or two in search of
the Marine plane that's never been found that they believe is in
the snow someplace southwest of that particular area.

[...]

Well, I landed at Yakima, Washington, and Al Baxter was there to
greet me and he said [unintelligible]...

And, he told me, I guess I better change my brand, but he kind of
gave me a mysterious sort of a look that maybe I had seen
something, he didn't know, and well, I just kind of forgot it
then, until I got down to Pendleton and I began looking at my map
and taking measurements on it. And, the best calculation I could
figure out, now even in spite of error, would be around 1200
miles an hour, because making the distance from Mt. Rainier to
Mt. Adams, in, we'll say approximately two minutes, it's almost,
well, it'd be around 25 miles per minute
[END OF EXTRACT]


Again, why stop at Yakima? Arnold's ultimate destination was
Boise, Idaho.

Inbetween, he landed at Pendleton, where his Yakima anecdote had
already been reported to the media and the press awaited...
Arnold states he stopped at Pendleton to inform the local FBI
office.

In that KWRC interview and his co-authored 1952 book, 'The Coming
of the Saucers', Arnold maintains his destination was Yakima,
when the infamous sighting occurred.


Did Arnold in fact land at Yakima for the sole reason to
excitedly report his sighting of new Air Force jets?

If true, it would compel a re-evaluation of his claims in that
respect and beyond.

Any evidence to support why this is the only scenario which makes
sense?

Courtesy of Bruce Maccabee:

Here is a transcript of the germane portion of the tape of
Arnold's speech at the First International UFO Congress in
Chicago, ILL, held on or about June 24, 1977...:

As I came out below on this first sweep I passed over the little
community of Mineral Washington, the pine trees there, and knew
pretty much where I was. I made a turn at probably 2000ft over
Mineral, Washington and started climbing back slowly but
steadily, climbing to gain sufficient altitude to go back on the
high plateau again for another pass at this mountain. As I was
making this turn and of course flying directly toward Mt.
Rainier, at about 9200 ft elevation - it was a beautiful day, in
fact the plane was very stable, I didn't have to fight controls
or weather or anything - a tremendous flash appeared in the sky
and it lit up my whole aircraft, even it seemed the cockpit of
the airplane and I was rather startled. I thought I hadn't seen a
plane that was very close to me, or possibly it had been a
military plane that had dove over my nose and the reflection of
the afternoon sun against his wing surfaces had caused the flash.
Now this just, in less than one tenth of a second, I think, went
through my mind.

I looked all around below me and looked ahead of me. And then the
flash came again and, uh, this very, very bright flash, it was
almost like an arc light, was coming from a group of objects far
up to the north of Mt. Rainier, in the area of Mt. Baker, which
is almost in a line with Mt. Rainier and Mt. Adams. I observed a
chain of very, very peculiar aircraft approaching Mt. Rainier
very rapidly, I think I described them like the tail of a Chinese
kite. They seemed to be in an echelon formation, however, in
getting a look at them against the sky and against the snow of
Mt. Rainier as they approached I just couldn't discern any tails
on them and I had never, never observed an aircraft without a
tail. Particularly these were of fairly large size and there was
nine of them in number. I was good at counting things like this
because I flew missions counting antelope, sheep, cattle, whatnot
in the course of my lifetime and the first craft - I kept
searching for their tails - I was quite surprised that I couldn't
find their tails. I was aware that the military was very clever
at camouflage and I was of course assuming all the time that
these were military craft or at least military missiles.

[...]

This is the reason that gave me the impression that they must be
robotly guided missiles. Anyhow I sort of lost interest in my
search mission [for a missing aircraft, believed to have crashed
in the Cascades - James] and I decided that maybe I ought to go
to Yakima and report it".
[END OF EXTRACT]


So, Arnold did, evidently, land at Yakima for the sole purpose of
making public his perceived observation.

How then, to rationalise Arnold's story about 'cruising to
Yakima' when the incident occurred?


How also, to explain Arnold's subsequent tales of objects which
statedly and in the telling, were ever increasingly so reflective
that they lit up his aircraft and [later] cockpit.

No way these could be birds and doubtless Arnold never remotely
endorsed he thought they might be.

Except for that earliest KWRC interview, when he divulged:

...I was approximately 25 to 28 miles from Mt. Rainier, I climbed
back up to 9200 feet and I noticed to the left of me a chain
which looked to me like the tail of a Chinese kite, kind of
weaving and going at a terrific speed across the face of Mt.
Rainier.

I, at first, thought they were geese because it flew like
geese...
[END OF EXTRACT]


Can we all concur that Arnold was comfortable with aerial
artefacts which "lit up my whole aircraft, even it seemed the
cockpit of the airplane" and he "thought they were geese" or, the
case evidence... and _everything_ built on its foundation, is
inherently fallacious.


James Easton.

From: "James Easton" <voyager@ukonline.co.uk>
Date: Sat, 20 Jul 2002 07:21:23 +0100
Subject: Re: [UFORL] Re: Horten Ho IX V2

Regarding:

>From: "bortaf ----" <fatrob83@hotmail.com>

Rob wrote:

>Thanks for the swift reply James,would you say that the number
>of craft observed is the main hiccup in the Horton-Arnold
>connection?

Rob,

There's purely no evidence of any connection.

Separately, the number of objects observed is a major factor,
especially as they apparently flew in a controlled formation.

We can therefore seemingly dismiss 'billowing snow', meteors or
'earth lights', etc. as being candidates.

Just two obvious terrestrial possibilities exist - either the
objects were aircraft or they were birds.


Strictly, we only need one aircraft, not necessarily nine of
them. It could have been a plane which was trailing eight mock-up
models, perhaps to test new developments in radar detection
capabilities, or something similar.

That could explain the undulating flight characteristics and
Arnold's allusion to, 'the tail of a Chinese kite'.

However, there's equally zero known evidence of any such
operations and the Cascades perhaps not an ideal test site.


There's then the crucial issue of airspeed, which is the crux of
Arnold's sighting.

If correct in his perceptions, then the objects couldn't have
been aircraft. If Arnold was mistaken, then they might have a
straightforward explanation, particularly should we know _why_ he
conceivably made an error in judgement.
It comes back to the question which Larry raised - could it have
been a formation of standard military aircraft, which puzzled
Arnold merely because he couldn't observe tails on them.

If Arnold's perceptions were accurate, then the objects could not
have been contemporary aircraft flying at circa 1,000 m.p.h. If
in error, then the entire enigma falls apart and he completely
misunderstood what was being observed.


Perhaps significantly, during his encounter Arnold did not
believe the objects were travelling particularly fast, a point he

mentions on several occasions.

It was only _afterwards_, when he calculated their airspeed,
based entirely on the distance he thought said objects had
travelled, that he realised they must surely be a new type of Air
Force jet.

His calculation comes down to one critical perception; that the
objects momentarily passed behind a "jagged peak" on Mt. Rainer
and consequently must have been some 25 miles distant.

If correct, then we really do have a mystery.

Conversely, if there's reason to conclude Arnold was mistaken,
his calculations and any conundrum are demonstrably specious.


That's the situation which now exists. Not only is there no
"jagged peak" at the altitude Arnold perceived, he was unable to
identify a likely source when this was investigated in later
years and from my own research, local expertise agrees that from
his full descriptions, Arnold is describing the prominent and
distinctive 'Little Tahoma (Tacoma)' peak on Mt. Rainier.

'Little Tahoma' is on the far side of Mt. Rainier from Arnold's
location and although visible, if the objects passed behind it,
they absolutely must also therefore have travelled behind Mt.
Rainier.

However, Arnold reports that the objects flew between himself and
the mountain.


I'm not aware that anyone has suggested an alternative "jagged
peak", even allowing considerable leeway for Arnold's reported
circa 9,500 feet altitude.
The fact that Arnold himself was unable to resolve this, must be
a concern, if not understated.


By default, the evidence indicates that Arnold perceived those
nine objects to briefly pass behind a far distant landmark, when
in fact, they flew in front of it.

If so, then his pivotal premise for an extraordinary observation
collapses - it's that simple.


Where is any 'Arnold's peak' evidence otherwise?

Perhaps someone can highlight it. If not and the foundation of
'ufology' can't even be substantiated to a rudimentary extent,
then why waste time on any further deliberation.

The resultant birth and utterly misconstrued popularisation of
'flying saucers' is evidenced and nothing can ever seriously be
respected as credibly built on _that_ foundation.

From: "rotsky" <rotsky@wanadoo.fr>

Subject: RE: [UFORL] Re: Horten Ho IX V2

Could be. Same for stealth. The F-117A 'Wobblin Goblin' (it's original and
unofficial name) is - like many fly-by-wire designs - inherently unstable.
It is simply unflyable without the computer to make all those instant little
corrections. (The same, by the way, is NOT true of the A320 and upwards
series of airliners!). One advantage of FBW is that it allows unstable
designs, which in turns allows the designer to use stealthy shapes or - in
the case of fighters - give the aircraft an ability to turn and pitch with a
rapidity that a stable design simply couldn't offer (because stable designs,
by their nature, fight against the turn or pitch movement).

a+
Steve

From: "James Easton" <voyager@ukonline.co.uk>
Date: Thu, 25 Jul 2002 04:48:17 +0100
Subject: [UFORL] 'Rendlesham' and MoD Curios

I've been contacted by someone with an interesting story which,
although having no evident, direct connection to the late
December 1980 incidents, is curious nonetheless.

It might be dated within that general timeframe and apparently
occurred either pre-Christmas late 1970s, or 1980.

I'm optimistic this can be further clarified.

By any default it's a reported 'UFO' sighting and the observation
was on Suffolk's east coast, not that far from RAF Bentwaters and
RAF Woodbridge's twin airbases.

The witness recalls:

It was 4 or 5 pm. and I was waiting for a bus from the dock into
Felixstowe. You could see the bus at the terminus from where I
was and as I looked to see if it was coming I caught sight of a
light in the sky. It was just a point of light, like a star but
moving in a direction from Dovercourt to the entrance of the
Orwell estuary. As I followed it across the sky I caught sight
of a second point of light travelling towards the estuary from
the south, southeast. Just off the point at Harwich. Both
seemed to moving to the same point. A third appeared from the
northeast to the same point where the three met and remained
still. They were a few miles away and just looked like stars.
No coloured lights, no identifiable shapes etc.

At that point I noticed the person stood next to me watching the
same point of the sky as me. Our eyes met as if questioning what
we observed but we said nothing. The bus arrived and we went on
the top deck. Both of us immediately looked and found the three
points of light still stationary. As the bus pulled away the
lights moved together in the direction of where the third
approached from. Suddenly, without any perceived acceleration
they just shot off. I asked the person (she was a switchboard
operator with the Atlantic Steam Navigation Company) whether she
had seen what I saw. She said she had even without me saying
what I saw. We said nothing much else as I recall. I wasn't
shocked at all, just very curious.

Having spent many years as a Coastguard Auxiliary trained to
observe, I can without doubt say what it was not. All that is
left as an option is that it flew and I couldn't identify it. If
there are such things as UFO's, then these were good candidates.
[END OF EXTRACT]
This is comparative to other 'UFO' reports I've seen, including
some originating from the same general area.

Appreciating it's anecdotal evidence, any suggestions for an
explanation?


Although the following can't, at present, be precisely dated,
here's another noteworthy tale from the same source:

During the period between Christmas and the beginning of January
many US airmen used the seafront hotel bars as was usual. On one
of these nights I and a couple of mates were drinking in the
Marlborough Hotel and there were half a dozen or so 'yanks' in
the bar. They were chatting amongst themselves and saying hello
to a few of the locals who they were friendly with. There seemed
to be a bit of anxiety between them and one bloke looked as if he
was getting a dressing down. This bloke took his drink and stood
alone. He was mumbling to himself about something loud enough
for one of the other yanks to go over to him and tell him to keep
his voice down. One or two others went over to him and looked as
if they were trying to console him. At that point we overheard a
bit of their conversation, words like - keep quiet; don't tell
anyone and (craft, spaceship, ufo) unsure of exact term used.
The consoling had no effect and he started to raise his voice
again when he was escorted out of the hotel.

[...]

We heard rumours about what may have happened, but as there were
no reports in the local press we assumed they had been on the
'wacky baccy' and sent back home for being 'bad boys'.

Of course, we never thought much more of it as it was years later
before the UFO story hit the headlines.

At the same period there seemed to be more military vehicles
around Bawdsey Manor which we thought was closed. We could see
them across the river from Felixstowe Ferry but never thought
much of it.

In retrospect, if it was not for the above events, when the news
appeared in the NOTW ['News of the World' - James] I would have
taken the issue with a pinch of salt.
[END OF EXTRACT]


The reported activity at Bawdsey Manor, close to RAF Woodbridge,
is interesting.

Bawdsey Manor was where [Sir] Robert Watson-Watt, born in
Brechin, Scotland and a graduate of St Andrew's University,
effectively invented RADAR - see:

http://www.zephyrus.co.uk/robertwatsonwatt.html

Circa 1980, was Bawdsey Manor still in use by the Ministry of
Defence (MoD)?

Cursory research locates, 'The Essex Yeomanry Journal', 2001,
which seemingly records of the '70 (Essex Yeomanry) TA Centre,
Signal Squadron' [TA = (part-time) Territorial Army - James]:

Early in 1978 the Squadron was informed that Bawdsey would be the
new location for the Armed Forces Headquarters, 4 AFHQ, which it
supported, and on one Saturday afternoon Lieutenant Stephen
Foakes and myself, SSgt David Swann, met Major David Casstles at
Bawdsey to look the place over. It consisted of an old RAF base
with Bawdsey Manor at one end and a two storey underground bunker
at the other. We were told that the RAF would be moving Ground to
Air Missiles in soon and 4 AFHQ would be using the bunker. That
September, 907 Troop occupied the area above the bunker, during
camp 1978 with their D11 HF radio multi vehicles and had one of
the most successful exercises ever. (see EY Journal 1979) Over
the next few years the Squadron made many trips up to Bawdsey not
only for radio exercises but for extremely enjoyable functions as
guests of the RAF.
[END OF EXTRACT]

See:

http://www.essex-yeomanry.org.uk/journal/2001journ.pdf


Some fascinating historical material which may relate to that
'two storey underground bunker', can be found online, at:

http://www.radarpages.co.uk/oral/dbarrett/bawdsey.htm

Also worthy of mention:

'Airfields of Suffolk: A Visitors Guide', by Duncan R. Skeels:

http://www.babergh-south-suffolk.gov.uk/tourism/airfields.pdf


Amongst perhaps a number of questions, why would in 1978 the RAF
allegedly, "be moving Ground to Air Missiles", situated at
Bawdsey?

Presuming the factual dating can be equated, we find:

In August 1979 Bawdsey re-opened as a Bloodhound Mk2 surface to
air missile (SAM) site operated by C flight of No 85 Squadron. It
was divided into 2 missile sections, each equipped with 6
launchers and a Type 87 fire control radar. The Type 84 modulator
building (R17) was retained as a crew room and store for
Bloodhound armament handling flight. It is unclear what part the
R3 bunker played Bloodhound operation if any. The new storage
sheds and storage bays and protective wall are all of Bloodhound
origin.
[END OF EXTRACT]

See:

http://www.subbrit.org.uk/rsg/sites/b/bawdsey/


Occasionally, such eclectic research tangents culminate in a
conceivable new lead.

Consider, in this instance, Victor David Mitchell...

Never heard of him?

Likewise...

Victor evidently claims he was assigned to both 'RAF Bawdsey'
during May 1967 - August 1967 and subsequently, during November
1976 - September 1980, the '4M5/68th', which I can only ascertain
as apparently being connected to the '68th Apprentice Entry, RAF
Cranwell 68th Entry (4m5)':

http://ourworld.compuserve.com/homepages/brian_parkinson_3/68Entr
y.htm


Of foremost significance, is that between November 1976 and
September 1980, Victor David Mitchell statedly:

Held appointment as Ops Ground Environment 2 in MOD Whitehall.
Responsible for operational efficiency of all UK Air Defence
Radar sites worldwide. Represented UK in the final CENTO
conference held in Teheran in 1978.

Was responsible for collating UFO reports and answering
Parliamentary Questions within my sphere of responsibility.
[END OF EXTRACT]
See:

http://homepage.ntlworld.com/barryf/index2.html#12


If, 'Ops Ground Environment 2', were "collating UFO reports",
where is any other reference to 'Ops Ground Environment 2'?

Which Parliamentary Questions?

Yet, otherwise, does Victor's 'Curriculum Vitae' give any
indication of being dubious?

I've been able to locate and contact Victor and his invited
comments will hopefully be insightful.

All others, inherently welcome.

From: "David Clarke" <cd292@crazydiamonds.fsnet.co.uk>
Date: Sat, 27 Jul 2002 12:01:59 +0100
Subject: Re: [UFORL] Final Rendlesham documents released by MOD

Greetings list,

This is a copy of a posting I placed on the UFOIN list this morning:


Further to my posting yesterday regarding the release of the remaining 3
documents from the MOD's Rendlesham forest file, I can now report
that I have received copies this morning, courtesy of Whitehall.

The covering letter reads: "There has recently been an investigation by
the Parliamentary Ombudsman into the decision to with-hold these
documents and the Ombudsman has concluded that the three documents
do fall under the scope of Exemption 2. However, in the particular
cirucmstances of this case he recommended that the documents
should nonetheless be provided to the individual who made the
complaint, and the MOD accepted this. The MOD also agreed to
supply the documents to all those from whom they had previously
been withheld and they are therefore enclosed for your information..."

Credit must go to Eric and Tim for taking the matter this far, and
(political point here) to the Government whose forthcoming FOIA
has made all this possible.

What do the documents contain? Well, not much we didn't already
know. The first is a draft answer to Patrick Wall MP's question in
Parliament in November 1983 (following the News of the World
article), with a briefing attached from Sec AS 2; the second is a
copy of the same briefing to answer a follow up question by Wall;
and the third is a collection of correspondence between David
Alton MP, Michael Heseltine and Ralph Noyes in 1985, with
Noyes making reference to Jenny Randles' seminal work on the
case.

The only document worth quoting in full is the briefing by Sec AS2
given to the Defence Minister John Stanley in 1983, in preparation
for his answer in Parliament. Wall's question was:

"To ask the Secretary of State for Defence, whether in view of the
fact that the United States' Air Force memo of 13 January 1981
on the incident at RAF Woodbridge has been released under the
FOIA, he will now release reports and documents concerning
similar incidents in the UK."

The briefing John Stanley, the Defence Minister, was given, is as
follows:
"These three questions follow from the News of the World
article of 2 October 1983 (Annex A) describing an alleged UFO
sighting by USAF personnel at RAF Woodbridge in Suffolk on
27 December 1980.

"The report of 13 January 1981 (Annex B) was examined by
the Air Staff and DS 8. It was concluded that there was nothing
of defence interest in the alleged sighting.

"There was, of course, no question of any contact with 'alien
beings' nor was any unidentified object seen on any radar
recordings, as alleged in the News of the World.

"A BBC investigation into the incident following publication of
the News of the World article concluded that a possible
explanation for the lights seen by the USAF personnel was
the pulsating light of the Orfordness lighthouse some 6-7 miles
away.

"The sole interest of the MOD in UFO reports is to establish
whether they reveal anything of defence interest (eg intruding
aircraft). MOD investigations are not pursued beyond the point
at which we are satisfied that a report has no defence
implications. No attempts are made to identify and catalogue
the likely explanation for individual reports."

So there you have it folks!

I predict that claims will now be made that the MOD are
continuing to with-hold other papers on the incident. I'd
wager a tidy sum on that.

I hope Eric and Tim will publish the text of the Ombudsman's
judgement soon. This sets quite a precedent in terms both
of the British FOIA itself, and on future applications for
UFO material.

Best,

Dave Clarke
cd292@crazydiamonds.fsnet.co.uk

jrfahlsing writes:
well i thought nothing of it until i found that they
> didn'tr have helicopters,

I assume you mean during the period of US involvement. The North Vietnamese
did have helicopters, including one of the biggest, the Mi-6 Hook that they
rather imaginitively used to move their MiG-17 Fresco interceptors around.
So they had enough. I have a photo if anyone is interested.


One thing mark told me, we, the USA was not allowed
> to engage or chase, fire upon or otherwise harass anything not
> relating to the war itself, in or around the skies in NV!

The rules of engagement were such that all air targets had to be visually
identified before attack and there were numerous bizarre (to current
observers)rules such as a strike aircraft could not fire at a SAM site
until it fired at the aircraft etc etc.

It may be that given the rarity of North Vietnamese helicopters, US forces
considered all helicopters as friendly or there was a blanket ban on
hitting choppers. (I decline to comment further on this)

I'm sure there's some-one out there that will know more detail. Suffice to
say, the sweeping statement that there were no North Vietnamese helicopters
doesn't get off the ground.

Chris

>
> The covering letter reads: "There has recently been an
investigation by
> the Parliamentary Ombudsman into the decision to with-hold these
> documents and the Ombudsman has concluded that the three documents
> do fall under the scope of Exemption 2. However, in the particular
> cirucmstances of this case he recommended that the documents
> should nonetheless be provided to the individual who made the
> complaint, and the MOD accepted this. The MOD also agreed to
> supply the documents to all those from whom they had previously
> been withheld and they are therefore enclosed for your
information..."
>
> Credit must go to Eric and Tim for taking the matter this far, and
> (political point here) to the Government whose forthcoming FOIA
> has made all this possible.
>
> What do the documents contain? Well, not much we didn't already
> know. The first is a draft answer to Patrick Wall MP's question in
> Parliament in November 1983 (following the News of the World
> article), with a briefing attached from Sec AS 2; the second is a
> copy of the same briefing to answer a follow up question by Wall;
> and the third is a collection of correspondence between David
> Alton MP, Michael Heseltine and Ralph Noyes in 1985, with
> Noyes making reference to Jenny Randles' seminal work on the
> case.
>
> The only document worth quoting in full is the briefing by Sec AS2
> given to the Defence Minister John Stanley in 1983, in preparation
> for his answer in Parliament. Wall's question was:
>
> "To ask the Secretary of State for Defence, whether in view of the
> fact that the United States' Air Force memo of 13 January 1981
> on the incident at RAF Woodbridge has been released under the
> FOIA, he will now release reports and documents concerning
> similar incidents in the UK."
>
> The briefing John Stanley, the Defence Minister, was given, is as
> follows:
>
> "These three questions follow from the News of the World
> article of 2 October 1983 (Annex A) describing an alleged UFO
> sighting by USAF personnel at RAF Woodbridge in Suffolk on
> 27 December 1980.
>
> "The report of 13 January 1981 (Annex B) was examined by
> the Air Staff and DS 8. It was concluded that there was nothing
> of defence interest in the alleged sighting.
>
> "There was, of course, no question of any contact with 'alien
> beings' nor was any unidentified object seen on any radar
> recordings, as alleged in the News of the World.
>
> "A BBC investigation into the incident following publication of
> the News of the World article concluded that a possible
> explanation for the lights seen by the USAF personnel was
> the pulsating light of the Orfordness lighthouse some 6-7 miles
> away.
>
> "The sole interest of the MOD in UFO reports is to establish
> whether they reveal anything of defence interest (eg intruding
> aircraft). MOD investigations are not pursued beyond the point
> at which we are satisfied that a report has no defence
> implications. No attempts are made to identify and catalogue
> the likely explanation for individual reports."
>
> So there you have it folks!
>
> I predict that claims will now be made that the MOD are
> continuing to with-hold other papers on the incident. I'd
> wager a tidy sum on that.
>
> I hope Eric and Tim will publish the text of the Ombudsman's
> judgement soon. This sets quite a precedent in terms both
> of the British FOIA itself, and on future applications for
> UFO material.

From: "David Clarke" <cd292@crazydiamonds.fsnet.co.uk>

Subject: Re: [UFORL] Re: Final Rendlesham documents released by MOD

To answer your questions:
As far as I'm aware John Stanley was Under Secretary of State for
the RAF, therefore yes, a junior minister (but still a Defence Minister,
though my mistake if I made this sound ambiguous);
yes, in 1983 DS 8 was the department that would brief ministers
on UFO matters...DS 8 became Sec (AS) 2A in 1984/5.
Re 'other documents relating to who knows what at senior level'
you ough to read my book with Andy Roberts, 'Out of the Shadow'
(London, Piatkus 2002)...this will provide a history of the MOD's
interest in UFO reports from 1942 to present.

Best,

Dave Clarke

From: "Robert Buljevic" <skeptic@s1c.org>
Date: Mon, 29 Jul 2002 12:35:12 +0200
Subject: Re: [UFORL] Re: Fast light in the sky

Irdium was a network of satellites for mobile communications. It failed
because of financial problems. However, the satellites making this network
are still up there, and since they have a high reflective propriety we can
sometimes see the so called "Iridium flares"
I saw one in 2000 and it was a bright light suddenly appearing in the sky
for some 5 seconds, it moved rather slowly.
Later I found on http://www.heavens-above.com/ that it was -7 magnitude
flare, the data corresponding exactly with the time and location of my
observation.
The location data on this web site are really amazing, I even found the
suburb I live in...
go here http://www.heavens-above.com/countries.asp to select the country,
then you type the city and after that you can select the particular part of
the city... for each location there is a range of observational data, among
others the Iridium flare data.

Regards,
Robert Buljevic

the replies actually published in books by me! So much for the need to

In actual fact I first got David Alton involved in the case in February
l985. He was a local MP when I lived on Merseyside. And Ralph and I
subsequently chose to send joint material in order to try to maximise the
opportunity offered by Alton's willingness to assist. Ralph knew that I knew
the facts better than he did at that stage and I knew that he stood a better
chance of getting any serious response out of parliament given his
background.

Alton was then a very liberal minded crusader willing to take up politically
sensitive fights and to be fair to him he did try hard. But in the end
Heseltine shuffled off responsibility to Lord Trefgarne and it was he who
wrote the replies to Alton, not Helseltine.

and I in l985 then that is worth knowing as Alton, of course, is still

The Chinese have had the fire balloon since the 14th century. They have
used it for religious festivals, and also (in recent times) to confuse
enemies, as did the Japanese and French during World War II. I wouldn't
be surprised if that was what was seen at night.

not set off the warhead. It would fall on and destroy an unintended
target.

they look.

Why would a power loss be correlated with a UFO? In most cases of
coincident UFO sightings and power failures, one of these effects
was operating:

1. The power failure caused a visual effect which was reported as
a UFO. Shorting power lines, weather effects, and trees falling
on power lines produce brilliant displays. I once saw a brilliant
orange ball fly into the sky as the lights went out. No aliens. A
large transformer blew up, and the orange ball was a ball of
flame from the ignited transformer oil.

2. The power failure brought people outside to "see what is
happening". They see a mundane light (like Venus) and report it
as the "cause of the power failure". Why? They've been watching
too much science fiction on TV.

3. The UFO was a power company helicopter searching for downed
power lines, a police helicopter dispatched to prevent looting, or
an airplane prevented from landing because of the blackout.

Here is the stupidest comment I ever heard from the 1965 blackout:
"As I stood outside wondering why the lights went out, I saw many
more planes in the sky than usual. Maybe they were looking for the
cause." No, those planes were waiting for instructions on where to
land, since the blackout had shut off the runway lights of all
airports in the area.
I think someone's imagination is overflowing on this light in the
sky. We need to look for mundane causes first:

- Space station
- Satellite
- Lighted weather balloon
- Airplane - you have no idea how far away it is, so you can't
guess at the speed. A small close slow airplane looks just like
a large far fast airplane at night.
- A sailplane carries only white lights, as does a photo mapping
plane.
- If there are arc discharge lamps around (mercury, sodium, or
metalarc, some birds show up as bright dots in the sky.
- Manned and unmanned balloons big enough to be navigation
hazards carry fixed white lights.

I was at the county fair last week. I saw a white fuzzy light
flying over the fairgrounds at a pretty good clip. While I was
pondering what this was, a purple one flew over. Then I realized
that they were just toy balloons which had escaped from children
and were illuminated by the fair's own lights.

There is a fundamental limitation of the human vision system,
which many UFO investigators seem to be grossly unaware of. I
keep bringing it up, because anyone investigating UFOs will
become totally misled if he ignores this limitation:

The human vision system is totally unable to correctly report
the size, speed, distance, or altitude of an UNKNOWN object seen
against the sky, provided that object is at least 30 feet away.

You may ask: How can a pilot report correctly the distance,
speed, and altitude of an airplane? The answer is that he KNOWS
THAT IT IS AN AIRPLANE. If he is good, he can even identify the
type of airplane. Armed with this knowledge, he now has the
true size of the plane, and from that he can make a pretty good
guess of the distance, speed, and altitude by rough trigonometry.

But an unknown object does not reveal its size, so there is no
way for an unaided observer to find out the true distance, speed,
or altitude of it. In UFO cases, the observer then usually
guesses wrong about what the unknown object is, and gives the
investigator erroneous figures of size, distance, altitude, or
speed. These are then printed as "fact", but they are totally
untrustworthy. These "facts" then mislead investigators away
from the true cause of the sighting.

Often the erroneous size chosen by an observer is about the
size of a road vehicle - something capable of carrtying a man.
Only if other aids are used can a person find the true size,
speed, distance, or altitude of an unknown object farther away
than 30 feet. Here are the techniques, and their limitations:

1. Binocular parallax with other objects at known distance
works to about 500 feet away.

2. The object went in front of some objects at known distances
and behind others. For this to work, one object must actually
hide part of the other.

3. Perspective works on the ground, but NOT in the sky. You
can see how far away something is by seeing where it is
touching the ground.

4. The sun or moon casts a shadow of the object in a known
place.

5. Light the object gives off casts shadows.

6. Optical aids are used, like a naval gunnery rangefinder.

7. Multiple witnesses a distance apart can triangulate, but
only if their observations are synchronized in time.

With the data you provided, I decided to use Caen as a point of observation.
Considering that Normandy is not too expansive an area, the time difference
would not be that great between there and any other location for satellite
observations. I then went to www.heavens-above.com (you can easily go there
yourself and run this through) and submitted the location and date. Not
being sure what the exact date was ( I assumed it was saturday night), I
checked both Saturday and Friday evening. Lo and behold, the ISS was visible
on both nights. On Friday it was visible at 23:18 traveling SW to E.
Maximum predicted brightness was -0.2 (brighter than most stars) with a peak
elevation of 38 degrees. The saturday ISS pass is most likely what you saw
(again, your reference to date seemed to imply this). Between 23:56 and
00:03 local (note this is the entire duration of the pass -almost horizon to
horizon), the ISS passed from WSW to ENE with a peak brightness of -0.7
(brighter than Friday's pass and brighter than most stars in the sky).
Maximum elevation was 86 degrees. This seems to be your fast light in the
sky.

This is a great website for tracking down interesting lights in the sky.
About a month ago, while out observing the sky, we had two satellites in
tandem moving across the sky (startled some of my fellow astronomers). A
check found that the satellites turned out to be USA-160 A and USA-160 C
(apparently a classified satellite).

Best of luck watching the skies.

Tim Printy

Irdium was a network of satellites for mobile communications. It failed
because of financial problems. However, the satellites making this network
are still up there, and since they have a high reflective propriety we can
sometimes see the so called "Iridium flares"
I saw one in 2000 and it was a bright light suddenly appearing in the sky
for some 5 seconds, it moved rather slowly.
Later I found on http://www.heavens-above.com/ that it was -7 magnitude
flare, the data corresponding exactly with the time and location of my
observation.
The location data on this web site are really amazing, I even found the
suburb I live in...
go here http://www.heavens-above.com/countries.asp to select the country,
then you type the city and after that you can select the particular part of
the city... for each location there is a range of observational data, among
others the Iridium flare data.

(nibble)

@ VLF / ELF microwave testing.

This phrase doesn't make any sense to an electronics engineer.

VLF and ELF are frequencies below 10 KHz - in the audio range if
played through a speaker.

Microwaves are in the 1 GHz to 100 Ghz range - getting close to
the frequency of light. Red light has a frequency around 430 GHz.

These are at opposite ends of the radio spectrum. They can't be
descriptive of the same signal.

A study a few years ago concluded that 60 Hz power line frequency
has no effect on living beings, plant or animal. This is right in
the middle of the ELF band.

From: "rotsky" <rotsky@wanadoo.fr>
Date: Tue, 30 Jul 2002 23:40:16 +0200
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Fast light in the sky

I don't know about gliders (although gliding at night sounds like a suicidal
occupation to me), but I think you've got your facts wrong about mapping
aircraft.

Federal Aviation Regulations, part 91, sections 205 & 209 refer to lighting
equipment to be carried by powered aircraft for both VFR and IFR night
flights. They stipulate quite clearly that an aircraft must carry an
anti-collision light (normally red, but white for some older aircraft) *and*
the three standard position lights - red, green and white. This requirement
is not one of the sections subject to waiver under Appendix A to part 91.

There is certainly no reference to 'mapping' aircraft - nor would this make
sense. A mapping aircraft would certainly be no slower than, say, a Piper
Cub or loitering helicopter, both of which are required to have the standard
lights.

a+
Steve

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Wed, 31 Jul 2002 14:50:38 -0500
Subject: FW: [UFORL] Triangles in Illinois - Hi-Tech Ballons?

I have a question: How many of those big airships have been built?

I have a simpler hypothesis: A prank in the form of a fire balloon.

Here is info on fire balloons:

http://php.indiana.edu/~lrobins/candbal.htm

http://php.indiana.edu/~lrobins/ufomaneu.htm

And here is info on the innate human depth perception errors that make
this false UFO prank possible:

http://php.indiana.edu/~lrobins/ufopercp.htm

http://php.indiana.edu/~lrobins/distmode.gif

Now, to answer the six questions in the report:

Q(1) Why is it silent?

A(1) Candles don't normally make any noise.

Q(2) Why is it brightly lit, sometimes with blinding light?

A(2) This is a common illusion with the fire balloon. Since the witness
thinks it is much larger and much farther away, the amount of light
emitted also seems disproportionately large. Also, dark adaptation
increases the eye's sensitivity by a factor of about 1000. In the
absense
of other lights, a candle can seem very bright.

Most people are unaware of dark adaptation, usually because they are
always surrounded by bright streetlights and headlights. These destroy
dark adaptation. It takes a good half hour for dark adaptation to fully
resume after an exposure to bright light ends, and most people are in
too big a hurry to stay out in the dark that long.

Q(3) Why is it seen a lot of times near water/lakes?

A(3) Probably because the pranksters launched them where they will be
seen and reported as UFOs.

Lakes also have several properties that make a sighting (not an object)
more likely: people out at night, unobstructed view (no trees growing
out of the lake), no city lights to compete for attention, vacationers
relaxing.

My question: Using the same definition of "near", how much of the area
of the US is NOT "near water/lakes"? I need to travel only one block
to get to open water, two blocks to get to a stream or a swimming pool,
3/4 mile to get to a good sized creek, 2 miles to get to the nearest
lake (a reservoir), 5 miles to get to the largest lake in the area, and
14 miles to get to a major river. There are 5 lakes in my county, and
too many ponds and streams to count. I would have to work at it to NOT
be "near water".

The same thought could be applied to being "near power lines"

Q(4) How does the object appear to accelerate so quickly from a hovering
position?

A(4) Since the lift of a fire balloon is not constant, it can rise into
and fall out of moving currents of air. One common event reported in
fire
balloon sightings is for the balloon to dip down below treetops, hover
around for a while, and then fly away over the trees at "high speed".
Of course, the mistake in depth perception magnifies the departure speed
in the eyes of the witness.

Another commonly reported effect is that the UFO suddenly accelerated
in a direction DIRECTLY AWAY from the witness, and vanished in the
distance. Of course, the clue here is that ALL of the witnesses, on ALL
sides of the UFO, reported the same effect. Therefore, the object did
NOT speed away, since it could not go in all of these different
directions "directly away" at the same time. Instead, the candle simply
dimmed and went out, and the observers took the dimming as an increase
in
distance.

Q(5) How does the object turn without banking?

A(5) It's a balloon, and is at the mercy of the wind. Dirigibles and
helicopters also turn without banking. Banking is necessary only where
air flowing over fixed wings provides the lift. To keep the same amount
of air flowing over each wing, the plane must bank. No banking = no
fixed airfoil for lift. Seagulls bank into turns. But hummingbirds,
which
fly more like helicopters, do not.

Q(6) Why the reported huge size (football field size)?

A(6) NOBODY can visually measure the speed, distance, size, or altitude
of an unknown object seen against the sky, unless it is closer than 30
feet, or unless additional clues give away the position. These reports
are usually based on assumptions by the witness that the object is a
powered, piloted craft. It's not just a matter of training. Humans don't
come equipped with the necessary sensors to make these measurements.
Our eyes were designed for catching prey for food, not tracking UFOs.

A trained aviator can measure the distance, speed, and altitude of a
plane, because he KNOWS what plane it is, and therefore how BIG it is.
The training needed includes knowing all of the aircraft types and
their true sizes. The pilot or spotter can then apply rough mental
trigonometry to the angle subtended by the plane in flight, and get the
other values with reasonable accuracy. Give the observer a sextant and
a chart of known aircraft, and the accuracy is improved

But an unknown object does not reveal its actual size, so the other
values cannot be found.

Guessing that a fire balloon is a plane leads to reports of fantastic
performance, because the speed, distance, size, and altitude are all
grossly overestimated. See the Kentucky helicopter incident in the case
study on the perception page:

http://php.indiana.edu/~lrobins/ufopercp.htm

The reported sizes of UFOs suddenly increased after the TV series "V",
which showed very large flying saucers. They increased again after the
movie "Millennium" was released. Both of these Hollywood creations
changed the expectations of the public about the size of a "UFO".

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Thu, 1 Aug 2002 10:57:02 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Digest Number 261

Ah! The AVRO Disc. Unfortunately, it was unstable when higher than a
few feet from the ground. It is at the Army Transportation Museum
in Ft Eustis VA. The design did have a use. Similar vehicles are used
as ferryboats across the English Channel.

A few other aircraft evolved from this project, with results carrying
forward to today.

These didn't make it:

- The Ryan vertiplane: This was a conventional airplane with the biggest
wing flaps ever made. There were also large downward -pointing vertical
fins at the ends of the wings to contain the air. The propellers, hung
under the wings, pushed against the lowered flaps to make the plane rise
vertically. Raising the flaps allowed horizontal flight. I built a
flying model of this as a kid, and it did work. The problem was what
happened if one engine failed - it fell over sideways before the pilot
could do anything.

- The Super Pogo: This was a tail-sitter, with 4 tail fins and two
wings.
Two large counter-rotating propellers were in the nose. It took off
vertically, and could land either vertically or conventionally (two of
the fins had tail wheels). The hard part was getting it to transistion
back to vertical for landing safely, since it stalled the wings before
the propeller lift took over.

- The Doak 16: This little plane has ducted fan engines on the wingtips
which swiveled from horizontal to vertical flight. The propellers were
linked to a central turboprop-type engine. It had problems maintaining
roll and pitch stability in vertical flight. And if the engine suddenly
failed at low altitude in vertical flight, the plane fell.

- The Hiller Tilt-Wing: On this four-motor craft, the entire wing tilted
from horizontal to vertical. But again, disaster happened if an engine
failed in vertical flight. The pilot could not adjust the throttles in
time to prevent a crash. Control was lacking in vertical flight too.

- The Ryan Vertijet: This was a delta-winged tail sitter which took
off vertically, but landed conventionally. This one worked. Oops.
This one still needs a long runway at the destination - longer, in
fact. So how do you get it into the tight place for the takeoff? On
a truck. Very un-military.

- The Bell X-10: The blast of the wing-mounted jet engines was diverted
to lifting gratings on the bottoms of the wings. Again, there were
control problems in vertical flight, and an instant crash if an engine
quit.

- The Ryan Vertifan: There was a huge ducted fan in each wing, powered
by the wing-mount jet engines. This one had most of the disadvantages
listed above, plus possible failure of the fan covers.

Why doesn't a helicopter crash if the engine quits? The pilot can
release
the drive clutch, and change the pitch of the blades so they auto-rotate
and act like airplane wings. The air flowing up through them spins them,
and then they generate lift. So he can "glide" in to a gentle landing,
if he can find a safe place to set down which is close enough.

Now for the ones which worked:

- The Benson Autogyro: This is an ultralight with a free-spinning rotor
and a pusher propeller. It was the first successful aircraft that met
the criteria. The rotor auto-rotated during flight, but could be given a
quick burst of engine power for a jump into the air (without a tail
rotor, the engine could not power the rotor in the air without spinning
the aircraft). While it was sold primarily for private ultralight use,
the military did buy quite a few. And it appeared in the James Bond
movie "Thunderball" - the jets, LASERs, and bombs were fake, but the
rest was
real.

- The (British) Hawker-Siddely Jump Jet: Basicly an outgrowth of the
Bell X-10, this one was more stable because the engines are in the body,
not on the wings. While it was developed earlier than the Benson, it
didn't go into real use until much later. It is still in use.

- The Bell helicopter with a pusher propeller, a rigid rotor, and wings.

- The jet-propelled helicopters in use today.

- Many STOLs (Short Take Off and Land) aircraft based on the Ryan
Vertiplane. They linked the props together and solved the problem.

- The Osprey: The newer version of the Doak. Enough said.

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Thu, 1 Aug 2002 11:33:53 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] F-16 chase

Here's the rub with those "jets chasing something as seen from the
ground" stories. Were the jets really chasing the object, or did it
just line up with the jets AS SEEN BY AN OBSERVER IN THAT LOCATION?

Remember, our human visual systems cannot make even a rough guess of
the distance, size, altitude, or speed of an object which is in the
sky and is farther away than 30 feet. Unless, of course, the witness
knows what the object is, and thus knows its true size. Our vision
was designed for catching prey, not tracking UFOs.

There are several possibilities:

- A stealth fighter acting as a bogey in an exercise.

- An airplane or helicopter closer to the witness than the jets.

- A child's balloon in the wind (it's that county-fair time of year),
much closer to the witness.

- A bird - extremely close to the witness.

Without a description of the shape, and the relative sizes, I have to
guess at possibilities.

From: "James Easton" <voyager@ukonline.co.uk>
Date: Fri, 2 Aug 2002 06:48:25 +0100
Subject: [UFORL] 'The Socorro, NM UFO - Explained?'

Now online, at:

http://www.nmsr.org/socorro.htm

...is Dave Thomas' above entitled, suggested resolution of
'Socorro'', courtesy of, 'New Mexicans for Science and Reason'.

This reveals the evidence which led Prof. Charles Moore [also (of
course) foremost associated with confirming his involvement with
'Project Mogul' as definitively explaining 'Roswell'], to
seemingly conclude that, "a helicopter used to carry a Lunar
Surveyor around for some tests", was responsible for Zamora's
sighting.

Previously, on UFORL:

http://groups.yahoo.com/group/UFORL/message/572

In essence, I highlighted Prof. Moore's _reported_ claims, as
featured in 'Saucer Smear'.

Dave's article explains and documents precisely _why_ Prof. Moore
had such convictions and perhaps still does.


The evidence is noteworthy and Dave comments of a 24, April,
1964, 'White Sands Missile Range test':

"The timing isn't right for the UFO sighting -- the range log
calls for morning tests, and the sightings occurred in late
afternoon - but then things don't always go 'according to plan,'
and many tests which have defied completion by morning have been
known to somehow get finished up in the afternoon. In fact,
bombing runs scheduled for that part of the range might have
delayed the tests".

He continues:

"There are many other tantalizing bits that might support the
Surveyor explanation for Socorro.

- The Surveyor tests were done with a small Bell helicopter that
supported the craft from its side. The helicopter and spacecraft
would have presented a bizarre profile. The Surveyor's slanted
legs fit Zamora's description well, and are also a match for the
shape of the "landing pod imprints" found later. In Stanford's
1976 book, he mentions Phil Klass' comment that landing pads like
Surveyor's were among the only practical shapes for that
function.

- The spacecraft used vernier engines and attitude jets to probe
and sample soil, which could explain the flames the policeman
saw, and the burn marks many saw. The flames weren't being used
for lift; that was supplied by the helicopter. The burn marks at
the site did not indicate sufficient thrust to lift a large
vehicle, according to Hynek.

- The Surveyor used a mechanical scoop with a shape that matches
a rectangular trough photographed at the Socorro site.

- Zamora described the craft as 'aluminum-white,' which certainly
matched the bulk of the Bell helicopter.

- The tests missions were manned by a helicopter pilot and a
Hughes engineer ... two persons, in white coveralls.

- Most people in Socorro, and several of the investigators,
thought it was most likely a secret government experiment, and
some Blue Book researchers even pinned it down as a tenant
operation run by Holloman, the base for the Surveyor test
flights".
[END OF EXTRACT]


Does, "a helicopter used to carry a Lunar Surveyor around for
some tests", resemble the object Zamora described and its various
characteristics?

The following aspects require to be explained:

1. On descent, the object emitted a 'roaring flame', which Zamora
noted, "changed from high frequency to low frequency and then
stopped". Both apparently ceased, before the object landed.

2. There was no other discernable sound.

3. The object was, "like O in shape" and "like aluminum--it was
whitish against the mesa background, but not chrome".

4. When its 'roaring flame' was next encountered, the object was
slowly lifting off; "At same time as roar saw flame. Flame was
under the object. Object was starting to go straight up--slowly
up. Object slowly rose straight up".

5. The "Object was oval, in shape. It was smooth--no windows or
doors".
If Zamora, somehow, came across a 'Surveyor lunar lander'
[presumably in that era, a 'Surveyor 1' prototype], horizontally
attached to a helicopter, how can this be equated with his
stated, albeit brief, observations?

Alternatively, demanding due consideration in this respect... was
Zamora utterly baffled by a helicopter, to which a 'Surveyor
lunar lander' was horizontally attached?


Amongst many obvious questions:

- how and why was the Surveyor lander firing its 'decent
rockets', when being transported by helicopter?

- how and why was the Surveyor lander then, only circa a couple
of minutes [if even that] afterwards, firing its 'ascent
rockets', when a) it seemingly didn't have any and b), it was
being lifted by a helicopter?

- how could Zamora conceivably fail to notice during his
subsequent, more detailed [although brief], closest observation
that the 'object' was not in truth oval-shaped, did have windows,
exhibited distinctive characteristics of a helicopter and that
there were actually two objects?

- why was the 'Surveyor lander' so far from home?

- did the incoming trajectory of Zamora's cited object coincide
with an origin from White Sands?

- why did it momentarily 'drop in' near Socorro?

- why did it almost immediately depart?

- where was it heading for and why?


Dave Thomas asserts:

1. "The Surveyor tests were done with a small Bell helicopter
that supported the craft from its side".

Where can we find confirmation of this?


2. "The helicopter and spacecraft would have presented a bizarre
profile".
Doubtless so, if these were the sources of Zamora's encounter.

How can this be equated with his factual description of a
singular, oval object, described over the radio as, "It looks
like a balloon"?


3. "The Surveyor's slanted legs fit Zamora's description
well...".

No, they are entirely inconsistent.

How many legs did the Surveyor lander have; how many 'legs' did
Zamora recall?


4. "...and are also a match for the shape of the 'landing pod
imprints' found later".

No, they are not - check it out.


5. "The spacecraft used vernier engines and attitude jets to
probe and sample soil, which could explain the flames the
policeman saw, and the burn marks many saw".

Explain the 'roaring flames' on descent, ascent and [enough for
now]...


6. "The Surveyor used a mechanical scoop with a shape that
matches a rectangular trough photographed at the Socorro site".

Seemingly proposed is that the test-model 'Surveyor lunar lander'
had time and a seemingly unfathomable reason to deploy its
'mechanical scoop', during an otherwise proclaimed fleeting
crisis.

How tenable is this?


7. "Zamora described the craft as 'aluminum-white,' which
certainly matched the bulk of the Bell helicopter".

Zamora _never_ described the object as "aluminum-white", he said
it was, "like aluminum-white" and yet, "not chrome".

This aside, how can it possibly be construed and championed that
Zamora's perceived 'shiny' coloration, "_certainly_ matched the
bulk of the Bell helicopter"?


8. "The tests missions were manned by a helicopter pilot and a
Hughes engineer ... two persons, in white coveralls".

At the outset, a somewhat fundamental problem, to say the least,
with Dave Thomas' proposed explanation is acknowledged. Dave
writes of the White Sands Missile Range 'Log' for 24 April, 1964:

"The timing isn't right for the UFO sighting -- the range log
calls for morning tests, and the sightings occurred in late
afternoon".

Perhaps Dave can at least evidence that, at anytime, on 24 April,
1964, "tests missions were manned by a helicopter pilot and a
Hughes engineer ... two persons, in white coveralls" and they had
any connection whatsoever with the 'Socorro' case.


9. "Most people in Socorro, and several of the investigators,
thought it was most likely a secret government experiment, and
some Blue Book researchers even pinned it down as a tenant
operation run by Holloman, the base for the Surveyor test
flights".

As I previously highlighted:

Is it also little-known that on 3 May, 1964, the 'Post-Standard,
Syracuse, N.Y.' carried an article on the Socorro case which
reported:

"At White Sands Missile Range, meanwhile, Gene Kanoft (?) [I
can't decipher the printed surname], chief of administration for
the National Aeronautics and Space Administration at White Sands
said the lunar excursion module designed for the Apollo moon
flights might fit Zamora's description but won't be built until
later this year. He said it was unlikely the module would be
tested at White Sands".
[END OF EXTRACT]

Noted that he's talking about, "the lunar excursion module
designed for the Apollo moon flights" and not a contemporary,
1964 un-manned Surveyor project.

Of more consequence, why did - only days after 'Socorro' - the
"chief of administration for the National Aeronautics and Space
Administration", statedly have no related explanation?

How is this rationalised?
10. The publicised, 'Socorro solved' contention seems to be based
on a reported claim from Capt. James McAndrew [not exactly a
'stranger to controversy'!] that, "there were special tests being
conducted at the north end of the White Sands Missile Range
(WSMR) involving a helicopter used to carry a Lunar Surveyor
around for some tests".

Where is any meaningful evidence? Said 'range log' merely
documents, 'Surveyor helicopter flights,' which have zilch
evidenced association with later events same day and so many
miles away.


Conversely, we can ascertain online that, during April 1964,
there were indeed cursory tests pertaining to 'Surveyor 1' and
how:

"..in April 1964, ...a test version of the spacecraft, outfitted
with working radars and vernier engines, was suspended from a
balloon and lofted 1,500 feet above the New Mexico desert for a
test of the landing system.

Before the test could begin, a nearby electrical storm triggered
the balloon's electronic release mechanism and the test Surveyor
fell to the desert floor and broke into pieces.

For JPL, Surveyor's troubles worsened an already dire situation.
Ranger 6 had failed that January. The bad news persisted even
after Ranger 7 finally triumphed in July: A second Surveyor drop
test failed in October because of a series of malfunctions. When
engineer Robert Parks took over as project manager of the
Surveyor effort, his colleagues at the lab offered condolences.
"They thought I had taken on an impossible task," he says.

The delays cost the Surveyor team the moon race. On February 4,
1966, a Soviet soft-lander called Luna 9 alighted on the plains
of the moon's Ocean of Storms and radioed back pictures..." -
see:

http://www.airspacemag.com/ASM/Mag/Index/1997/JJ/hdld.html


Dave Thomas' online article is an "edited version" of a July
2001, 'Skeptical Inquirer' feature.

Is it now therefore accepted by the 'Skeptical Inquirer' that
Philip Klass' previously endorsed, advocated and upheld
determination of Zamora's report as a 'hoax', was blatantly
preposterous?


A recipient of my 'Voyager' newsletter, veteran 'sceptic' Steuart
Campbell, recently reminded me that, unmistakably:

"A mirage of Canopus was the object reported by police patrolman
Lonnie Zamora over Socorro (New Mexico) in April 1964".


James Easton.

Subject: Re: [UFORL] silverbug


From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>


> This is the idea they started with. The result (after budget cuts) was
> the AVRO disc.

We have to very clear here. It wasn't simply budget cuts. The AVROCAR was
built to fulfil a totally different requirement from Silverbug. It was
intended to be a ground effect vehicle whereas Silverbug and the other Y2
concepts were supersonic fighters.

I'm sure you know this already, but it's vital to underline this point for
those unfamiliar with the complexities of the work carried out by AVRO
Canada's highly secret Special Projects Group.

There is no way on this Earth that John Frost, the head of the SPG would
have expected the AVROCAR to do much more than it did. It's a common
misconception that it was intended to be a high speed aircraft and was
therefore a total disaster. It wasn't - it was a research vehicle /
technology demonstrator for a surface(ish) craft.

David

From: "Marko Repo" <marko.repo@pp.htv.fi>
Date: Fri, 2 Aug 2002 13:21:05 +0300

>>
> > a+

>>

>
> Hi Steve,
>
> yes. Such ballons are known here in Germany and 20 % of all
> reported UFOs going back to this objects. Last weekend we has
> a small flap of this objects around the whole nation.
>
> WW
>


This kind of fire balloons are sold at least in Sweden by company
Planet-Pluto (http://www.ufo-ballonger.nu/Planet-Pluto).

The price for a 12-balloon package is about 12,60 EUR. This "home-made hot
air balloon" package includes a plastic bag (about 60 liters), two steel
strings and a piece of parafin. Parafin burns about 8 to 10 minutes and will
lift the ball up to 1000 meters. These ufo-balloons should not be used at
the summer time because of the danger of causing fire.

I bought one package a couple of years ago and tried it at winter time in
Finland. The phenomenon is really fascinating even at the day time and it is
no wonder that someone who see it will believe that it is an ufo. Especially
disappearing so suddenly (when parafin burns out) in the middle of the dark
sky makes the phenomenon even stranger than it actually is.

National ufo research organization in Sweden (UFO-Sverige) have some
information (video + pictures) about these fire balloons at their website
http://www.ufo.se/information/misstolkningar/ufoballonger1.shtml.


-------------------------------------------------------

Uforesearcher Marko Repo
Vantaa, FINLAND

marko.repo@pp.htv.fi

<DIV><SPAN class=876370318-02082002><FONT face=Arial color=#000080
size=2>UAVs
are deployed in a variety of ways now - for example as (relatively slow) target
dromes. More common uses, however are for reconnaissance and - increasingly -
integrated with other systems as part of what's known as ISTAR (Intelligence,
Surveillance, Target Acquisition and Reconnaissance). ISTAR systems - like the
UK's forthcoming Watchkeeper - integrate directly into command &amp; control
systems to not just find and identify targets but to guide other 'assets' to
them. However, they don't generally fly in formation with jets - UAVs are
typically quite slow, being typically (though certainly not exclusively)
propeller-driven.</FONT></SPAN></DIV>
<DIV><SPAN class=876370318-02082002><FONT face=Arial color=#000080
size=2></FONT></SPAN>&nbsp;</DIV>
<DIV><SPAN class=876370318-02082002><FONT face=Arial color=#000080
size=2>It's
quite possible that the report you mention was an exercise. Systems like AWACs
and J-STARS form part of the overall ISTAR picture and, of course, aircraft like
the Tornado are at the sharp end of the system.</FONT></SPAN></DIV>

    that occurred as a result of the melting of the ice sheets after the last
    Ice Age. When the ice sheets melted, land that was underneath the ice
    started rising. As the ground rebounded in this fashion, the gravity field
    changed.

From: "James Easton" <voyager@ukonline.co.uk>
Date: Sun, 4 Aug 2002 07:50:28 +0100
Subject: [UFORL] Occam's Razor

In, 'The Socorro, NM UFO - Explained?'...:

http://www.nmsr.org/socorro.htm

...Dave Thomas concludes:

A lot has happened since 1964, and it's difficult to reconstruct
events from that long ago, especially events with strong
implications. Was it a college prank? A hoax? A balloon? An alien
craft from another world? Perhaps we'll never really know.
Gildenberg is confident that William of Occam, of Occam's Razor
fame, would think kindly of the Surveyor explanation, especially
over some of the other contenders.
[END OF EXTRACT]


I propose that 'William of Occam' would be dismayed to see the
'Surveyor explanation', cited as substantiation of 'Occam's
razor'.

Not only is there zero evidence, whatsoever, of any 'Surveyor'
connection to Zamora's reported observations, the proclaimed
evidence is both entirely circumstantial and an antithesis to
Zamora's fundamental, witness testimony.


Yet, moreso, what exactly is 'Occam's Razor', beloved of
'supporting' a mundane explanation, as opposed to one which is
otherwise 'not so straightforward'.

Quoting:

http://wotug.ukc.ac.uk/parallel/www/occam/occam-bio.html

William of Ockham, born in the village of Ockham in Surrey
(England) about 1285, was the most influential philosopher of the
14th century and a controversial theologian.

He entered the Franciscan order at an early age and took the
traditional course of theological studies at Oxford. Strong
opposition to his opinions from members of the theological
faculty prevented him from obtaining his Master's degree. His
teaching had also aroused the attention of Pope John XXII, who
summoned him to the papal court in Avignion (France) in 1324.

The charges against him were presented by Jogh Lutterell, the
former chancellor of the university of Oxford. Ockham was never
condemned, but in 1327, while residing in Avignion, he became
involved in the dispute over apostolic poverty. When this
controversy reached a critical stage in 1328, and the Pope was
about to issue a condemnation of the position held by the
Franciscans, Ockham and two other Franciscans fled from Avignion
to seek the protection of Emperor Louis IV, the Bavarian.

They followed the emperor to Munich (Germany) in 1330, where
Ockham wrote fervently against the papacy in a series of
treatises on papal power and civil sovereignty. The medieval rule
of parsimony, or principle of economy, frequently used by Ockham
came to be known as Ockham's razor. The rule, which said that
_plurality should not be assumed without necessity_ (or, in
modern English, keep it simple, stupid), was used to eliminate
many pseudo-explanatory entities.

It is believed that he died in a convent in Munich in 1349, a
victim of the Black Death. His name, spelled Occam, lives on in
the names of streets and restaurants in Munich ... and in the
brave new world of high-performance safety-critical parallel
computing.
[END OF EXTRACT]


So... 'Occam's razor' was, apparently, in truth a comment on 14th
century religious persuasions?

How did this become a 'skeptic' edict?


As opposed to a conviction that 'Occam's Razor' proclaims,
"Entities should not be multiplied unnecessarily", we find:

'Pluralitas non est ponenda sine neccesitate'' -

"Plurality should not be posited without necessity...".

or:

'Entia non sunt multiplicanda praeter necessitatem' -

"No more things should be presumed to exist than are absolutely
necessary...".


Why the discrepancies and how did this evolve?
From: "rotsky" <rotsky@wanadoo.fr>
Date: Sun, 4 Aug 2002 12:09:16 +0200
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Occam's Razor

Actually, those explanations make it clear why Occam's razor is so apt as a
sceptical principle. For any given 'event', it is better to accept
explanations based on accepted or proven phenomena (Venus, fire balloons
etc) that an explanation which demands the unproven existence of
extra-terrestrials or fantastic technology. In other words, if there is a
workable mundane explanation, this is far more likely to be the truth than
something supernatural. That doesn't necessarily 'prove' the case, of
course, but this is an area where belief is important and scientific
standards of proof are often impossible or (in so many cases, IMHO)
irrelevant.

a+
Steve

Announcing the opening of the UFO Data Exchange
Website:

http://wakeup.to/ufos

The UFO Data Exchange Website has been developed to
fill a need in the ufological community for an online
meeting place to exchange ideas and information. The
primary focus of the site is to serve established
researchers, but we also offer resources specifically
for the individual with a casual interest in ufology.

The UFO Data Exchange is a FREE service. All costs
associated with maintaining the site are paid for by
private contributions and by any funds obtained
through affiliate program links at the site. Some of
the resources offered to the general public are hosted
by third party providers, and may include advertising.


Resources offered to researchers are free of
advertising.

Free Resources offered to the general public: Public
message forum, the option to join several topical
e-lists, a public web-utility for posting links to
interesting websites, the option to subscribe to a
quarterly newsletter, a post-your-own classified ad
utility (items related to ufology, only), constantly
updated physical, space-science, and NASA headlines,
plus a lot more!

Free Resources offered to UFO researchers: A private,
password-protected area of the site incorporating: a
private message forum, a private chatroom, a private
web-utility for posting links to interesting websites,
 a private image bank where researchers may upload
images of interest, over 200 megabytes of webspace
reserved specifically for researchers to post
documents of interest to other researchers, and the
option to join several private, topical e-lists.
Researchers are also free to make use of the public
resources offered by the UFO Data Exchange.

Additionally, the official publication of the UFO Data
Exchange Website, Nocturnal Lights
[http://nocturnal_lights.tripod.com] is currently
under development, and is now accepting submissions
from writers.

We encourage you to explore all that we have to offer,
and if you like what you see, tell your friends and
associates about us!

Oh, yes! The Aurora case.

There are a few little bits of relevant info:

1. H.G. Wells' "War of the Worlds" was new then.

2. The new railroad company had just decided to take a route which did
not include Aurora.

3. The hoax was concocted by the newspaper to bring people to the town.

4. The "airship sightings" were at their peak in the west then. Many of
them were fire balloons launched by pranksters.

5. The windmill supposedly knocked down by the spaceship never existed.

6. A few years ago, UFOlogists sued to open the grave they thought
contained the alien.

Subject: [UFORL] Ufology in Perspective



Compliments from the Mendoza remuda:

>Subject: ufology in perspective
>Sent:    14/08/20 02:43
>Received: 20/08/02 01:14
>From:     Jerome Clark, jkclark@FRONTIERNET.NET
