Perhaps Jerry is feeling the pinch, not having had anyone
to pontificate at for a few days, but surely this is either
a wind-up or a desperate attempt at cheerleading.

Knees up and twirl the pom-poms, then.

Zetetic is not Greek, ancient or demotic, for "skeptical
enquirer". Liddell & Scott give several ancient Greek words
from the zeta-ita-tau-ita root (which suggests "zetetic"
should be pronounced zEEteetik -- I can see that catching
on). The "ita" is here transliterated as an "i", but should
be pronounced long, as in "geek". The verb zitéo means
variously to seek, search out, inquire into, examine or
investigate. A "zititís" (accent on the final syllable) is
a seeker, searcher, or examiner. L&S add that zititai
were commissioners appointed to investigate state offences!
In modern demotic Greek the meaning has changed somewhat,
and the accent has shifted to the first syllable: zíteia
means begging, zítima is a problem, zítisis is a demand
(as in "the global demand for petroleum") or quest for truth,
and zitao means to look for ("Zitao ton gatton mou", I am
looking for my tomcat) -- or to beg, or to ask *for*
something ("I asked him for a meal").

English "zetetic" need imply no more than an enquiring
mind. In an ideal world the term "zetetic scholar"
would contain an otiose redundancy [yes, this is a self-
referring sentence].

There is no suggestion of "skepticism" in either the
ancient or the current usages. Ancient Greek had a good
word, "skeptomai", I look about, watch, look carefully or,
when applied to mental activity, I view, examine, or
consider. In demotic Greek one might use "skeptomai" to
mean "it is my considered opinion that" or "to reflect
on" something. "Skeptikos" means pensive. Those who know
the history of "skeptic", as Sir W. Raleigh did, use it
in this sense. Ignorant persons, among whom I would count
some members of CSICOP as well as purveyors of terms such
as skeptibunker and pelicanist, use it in a peculiarly
destructive sense, which is a pity, because it muddies
the waters of meaning. We have been through this one
before, so I won't rant about the abuse of the word
"debunker" by the ignorati.

Truzzi mostly sets up easy targets among allegedly
scientific pursuits in comparison with anomalistic ones.
It ought to be obvious to anyone that electronic SETI is
a matter of naive (and ethnocentric) faith, or that economics,
sociology, and psychotherapies are bogus sciences -- the first
two are descriptive, not predictive, disciplines, and the
third are sheer hokum, invented on the hoof by such as
"pioneers" as Freud and Jung. This last is perhaps more
obvious in 2002 than it was in 1987. But there is
no comparison between Nessie (anecdotal evidence, photos
of socks on poles etc) and the big bang and black holes
-- I see no subtle mathematics taking place on the shores
Loch Ness. I'm not arguing against the monster: I am just
pointing out the falsity of the analogies that Truzzi
wants to draw.

Insofar as Truzzi (in 1987) wanted to cock a snook at
science, he failed; and to that extent he also failed to
put ufology in context, pace one of its senior theologians.
Ufology can't predict anything, unlike a real science,
and cannot logically link cause (anecdote) and effect
(belief), and often can't tell which is cause and which
is effect. No question, it has dedicated scholars. On
the other hand it is not always clear what those scholars
are recording, or what gives them ultimate impulsion.

best wishes
Prosciuttio D. Melone, HTML (failed)
Weighing In At 11st 7lb

>The reason that the zetetic [Greek for "skeptical inquirer"] may appear to
>take a softer critical line may be the result not so much of a less critical
>view of the extraordinary but of a more critical view of the ordinary with
>which it is contrasted. Those who leap to call parapsychology a
>pseudoscience might do well to look more closely at the social sciences
>in general. Those who laugh at the implausibility of a possible plesiosaur
>in Loch Ness should take a close look at the arguments and evidence
>put forth for the Big Bang or Black Holes. Those who think it unreasonable
>to investigate reports of unidentified flying objects might do well to look
>carefully at arguments and evidence of those who promote current attempts
>at contacting extraterrestrial intelligence allegedly present in other solar
>systems. Those who complain about the unscientific status of psychic
>counselors should be willing to examine the scientific status of orthodox
>psychotherapy and make truly scientific comparisons. Those who sneer at
>phoney prophets in our midst might also do well to look at the
>prognosticators in economics and sociology who hold official positions as
>"scientific forecasters." Those who concern themselves about newspaper
>horoscopes and their influence might do well to look at what the "real"
>so-called helping professions are doing. The scientist who claims to be a
>true skeptic, a zetetic, is willing to investigate empirically the claims of
>the
>American Medical Association as well as those of faith healers; and, more
>important, he should be willing to compare the empirical results for both
>before defending one and condemning the other.
>
>-- Marcello Truzzi, in "Zetetic Ruminations on Skepticism and Anomalies
>in Science." Zetetic Scholar 12/13 (1987): 7-20,

Anthony:

That is the $64,000 question (a popular 1950s American quiz show
which turned out to be rigged). I am not aware of any proven
_physical_ evidence. The Sturrock Panel report is on a website,
you might start there:

http://www.scientificexploration.org/jse/articles/ufo_reports/sturrock/toc.htm
l

Please note the following conclusion in the abstract:

"A review panel was composed of nine scientists of diverse
expertise and interests. The panel offered comments and
criticisms concerning the investigations that were presented,
and also prepared a summary of their overall response, with the
following key elements:

Concerning the case material presented by the investigators, the
panel concluded that a few reported incidents may have involved
rare but significant phenomena such as electrical activity, but
there was no convincing evidence pointing to unknown physical
processes or to the involvement of extraterrestrial intelligence."

From: "James Easton" <voyager@ukonline.co.uk>
Date: Fri, 23 Aug 2002 07:12:30 +0100
Subject: [UFORL] The Birth of the 'Greys'

Taking the synopsis from a readily available, acknowledged
unverified, online source:

The story of Betty and Barney Hill begins in September 1961, in
the state of New Hampshire. Barney had recently developed an
ulcer, and he and his wife Betty decided to take a short vacation
to Canada. The couple had visited Niagara Falls, and Montreal,
and on the 19th of the month, they began their journey back home
to Portsmouth. The night was clear, with a crescent moon shining
on the heavily wooded landscape, that surrounded US Route 3 in
the central part of New Hampshire. At about a quarter past 10:00
P.M., three miles south of the city of Lancaster, Barney noticed
what appeared to be a bright star, or planet which seemed to move
erratically. Barney pointed this out to Betty, and they both
began to keep track of the object.

The couple began to believe that they were watching a plane,
appear and disappear, as the movement of their vehicle caused the
trees to come and go in obstructing their view. Later Barney
would state that he tried to convince himself that the object was
a plane, but that Betty thought it to be something else; an
unidentified craft of some kind. As the two continued to the
Flume, just north of North Woodstock, the object appeared to move
in an odd way. As they reached Indian Head, Barney actually
stopped the car to have a look at the object with his binoculars.
He saw multicolored lights, and rows of windows on a flat-shaped
object, which now seemed to be moving toward him. As the object
moved to within a hundred feet of him, he could see occupants
inside. Frightened, he ran back to his car where Betty waited.
They climbed inside and sped away. Soon, two hours of their lives
would vanish into oblivion.

After resuming their journey home, they were not able to see the
strange craft anymore. Oddly though, they heard a beeping sound.
They then heard the beeping a second time, noticing that they
were suddenly thirty-five miles farther down the road than a
minute or two ago. They were now in Ashla. The mood in the car
was quiet as they proceeded home, and went to bed. They both
slept until the next afternoon. When Betty got up, she called her
sister Janet, and told her what had happened. Janet told her to
call nearby Pease Air Force Base, and report what she had seen.
Betty reported the incident, speaking to Major Paul W. Henderson,
who told Betty; "The UFO was also confirmed by our radar." It is
important to note at this point that Barney was against calling
the sighting in to the base, hoping to keep it quiet.
At this time, neither Betty nor Barney recalled any abduction.
Soon, Betty began having nightmarish dreams of her and her
husband being taken aboard a craft of some kind, against their
will. In a matter of weeks, two writers got wind of the story,
and after interviewing the Hills, made an intensive log of the
events of the night. They discovered that there were two hours of
unaccounted time in the Hill's story, even allowing for stops for
the Hills, and breaks for their dog, who also had made the trip
with them. Another interesting note that I should interject here
is that these "two writers," which are mentioned in almost every
report of this incident, (and there are literally thousands of
them), have not been named, or I cannot find their names.

However, the story is true, because their interview was attended
by Major James MacDonald, a former Air Force Intelligence
Officer. Shortly after Betty began having these disturbing
dreams, she wrote a letter to Major Donald Kehoe, who passed her
information on to one Walter Webb, who was on the staff of the
Hayden Planetarium. Webb, at the time, was a scientific advisor
for the National Investigations Committee on Ariel Phenomena.
(commonly referred to as NICAP). What he did with the report is
unknown.

It was Major MacDonald who made the suggestion to the Hills that
regressive hypnosis might account for the two hours of missing
time. In the spring of 1962, the Hills contacted a psychiatrist
about the hypnosis sessions, but decided to put it off for a
time. All the while, Betty was still haunted by the dreams, and
Barney's ulcer was worse, and he was again suffering from
hypertension. After dodging reporters, and doing some research on
psychiatrists, the Hills made a decision to contact well-known
Boston psychiatrist and neurologist, Dr. Benjamin Simon, who was
one of the most respected doctors in his field. After a couple of
initial interviews, Dr. Simon's preliminary diagnosis was
"anxiety syndrome," relating to the incidents of the night of
September 19, 1961. His next step was to find out what those
events were.
[END OF EXTRACT]

See:

http://bjbooth.topcities.com/Hill.html


Continuing:

The method of treatment that Dr. Simon chose for the Hills was
regressive hypnosis, which was meant to get to the source of
their problem, whatever that may have been. He began the sessions
on Barney, and then followed up with the same treatment for
Betty. The process was slow, but after six months, it was Dr.
Simon's expert opinion that the Hills had been abducted, and
taken aboard an unknown flying craft on the night in question.
Anyone who is deeply interested in these sessions, can see
transcripts of them in an excellent book on the entire Hill
story, "The Interrupted Journey," written by award-winning
investigative author John G. Fuller. The Hills' story was also
included in a two-part article in "Look" magazine, and a movie,
"The UFO Incident," a made-for-TV production. The movie was
released in 1976, and starred Estelle Parsons as Betty, and James
Earl Jones as Barney.

After the many sessions with Dr. Simon, the following details
became evident. The Hills related that their car had stalled, and
then the alien craft landed on the road in front of their
vehicle, forming a kind of roadblock, hailing them down. They
were taken into the craft, and given medical examinations by
these aliens, and before being released, were ordered under
hypnosis not to recount any of the details of their incident. The
entities were described by the Hills as "....bald-headed alien
beings, about five foot tall, with greyish skin, pear shaped
heads and slanting cat-like eyes."-- This was the very first
mention in UFO folklore of the so-called "greys." The Hills were
taken into separate rooms during their examinations. These
"tests" involved both physical and mental procedures.

As part of these tests, skin, hair and nail samples were taken.
Betty had a long needle inserted into her navel, and was told it
was a pregnancy test. Under duress, Barney related that he had
given a semen specimen. Betty stated that she was given a kind of
book as a token of her visit, but this item was later taken back.
Another odd fact related under hypnosis was that the aliens
seemed to have no conception of time, or of colors, whatever this
may mean. At one point, the aliens seemed surprised to find that
Barney's teeth (dentures) could be removed and replaced. Betty
asked one of her abductors where they were from, and in reply,
she was shown a star map of sorts, which will be discussed in
more detail later. After these events, the Hills were taken back
to their car, and the last thing they remembered was an orange
glow disappearing into the night sky. It is very important to
note that the Hills tried to keep these events out of the press,
but unfortunately, an inaccurate version of the events was leaked
to the press, after which, the Hills decided to come forward with
the true events of the case.

Dr. Simon was under a great amount of pressure to release
whatever information the Hills authorized about their case. This
was considered prudent, not to exploit the story, but to stop
speculation that the absence of a statement by him would seem to
shed a negative light on the Hills' story. Simon concluded that
the Hills were not fabricating their story. He further stated
that he there were several conclusions that could be reached. [1]
"The experience actually happened, or, [2] some perceptive and
illusory misinterpretations occurred in relationship to some real
event." What the "real event" may be, I do not know.

As the facts of the Hills' case came to public knowledge, two
notable, respectable professionals investigated the story, and
made their conclusions. One was Dr. J. Allen Hynek, who was at
the time, Professor of Astronomy at Northwestern University, and
later to be an Air Force Consultant on Aerial Phenomena. He
eventually would create his own "Center For UFO studies." The
other was Stanton T. Friedman, a nuclear physicist and the
nation's only space scientist devoting full time to researching
the UFO phenomenon.

As a consultant to Project Bluebook, Hynek later released the
book, "The UFO Experience," in which he discussed the Hills'
case. I will insert his own words here; "Under repeated hypnosis
they independently revealed what had supposedly happened. The two
stories agreed in considerable detail, although neither Betty nor
Barney was privy to what the other had said under hypnosis until
much later. Under hypnosis they stated that they had been taken
separately aboard the craft, treated well by the occupants -
rather as humans might treat experimental animals - and then
released after having been given the hypnotic suggestion that
they would remember nothing of that particular experience. The
method of their release supposedly accounted for the amnesia,
which was apparently broken only by counterhypnosis".
[END OF EXTRACT]

See:

http://bjbooth.topcities.com/Hill2.html


Although claimed, "It was Major MacDonald who made the suggestion
to the Hills that regressive hypnosis might account for the two
hours of missing time", according to Ben H. Swett, he was the
catalyst:

On 7 September 1963, I gave a talk on hypnosis to one of the
adult study groups at a Unitarian Church in Portsmouth, New
Hampshire. Afterward, two people came up to me, introduced
themselves as Betty and Barney Hill, and asked me if hypnosis
could be used to recover lost periods of memory. I wondered why
they asked that question, because I had mentioned it in my talk,
but I said, "Yes, that's one of the classical uses of clinical
hypnosis."
They started telling me about something that happened to them as
they were driving home from Canada on the night of 19-20
September 1961 -- a light in the sky that seemed to follow them
and then circled them, and being stopped on the road, and how
they later realized they had a three-hour gap in their memories.
As they told their story, Barney's face kept twitching
spasmodically on one side. I didn't like the looks of that.

They said some of their friends thought the light that followed
them was a UFO, and asked me what I thought about UFOs. I said,
"There are a lot of reports by credible people." Then they asked
me if I would hypnotize them to recover that three-hour gap in
their memories. My first thought was: "I don't want to wade into
whatever is making his face twitch like that. I'm not a
psychiatrist." Then I thought: "UFOs ... I'm an Air Force officer
... hypnosis ... I have no credentials." So I said, "No, I'm not
qualified to do that." But I strongly encouraged them to find a
reputable psychologist or psychiatrist who used hypnotherapy.
They said that several people had suggested they try hypnosis,
and since I had studied hypnosis and recommended it for that
purpose, they thought they would go ahead with it. I answered a
few other people's questions about my talk, and went home.

I didn't hear anything about the Hills for the next nine months.
It was only later that I learned they had acted on my
recommendation and were referred to Dr. Benjamin Simon, a well-
known psychiatrist in Boston. They first met with him on 14
December 1963.

Hopkins once got a letter from an oncologist in Canada. This gentleman uses
hypnosis to relieve his patients' anxiety, and was amazed one day to find an
abduction scenario emerge. He'd never heard of such a thing. After doing some
research, he discovered that abduction stories had emerged before, and contacted
Budd, mostly to find out what he should do. </SPAN></FONT></DIV>
<DIV><FONT face="Book Antiqua" size=2><SPAN

<DIV><FONT face="Book Antiqua" size=2><SPAN class=183451820-
23082002>Another
example, from a book by a hypnotherapist named Michael Nash. Nash had a patient
suffering from anxiety because of consciously recalled abduction memory. Nash,
who apparently had never heard of the abduction phenomenon, assured the patient
that the memories couldn't possibly be of real events. He hypnotized the
patient, and was astonished to find more abduction details emerge, even though
he'd told the patient that none of it really happened. The patient, who believed
that the events were in fact real, eventually got over the anxiety, and warmly
thanked Nash -- who, utterly astonished, concluded that it was possible to
relieve anxiety even while the patient still believed in the fantasies (as Nash
saw it) that were associated with it. </SPAN></FONT></DIV>
<DIV><FONT face="Book Antiqua" size=2><SPAN
class=183451820-23082002></SPAN></FONT>&nbsp;</DIV>
<DIV><FONT face="Book Antiqua" size=2><SPAN class=183451820-
23082002>Besides, as
many of us have observed before (perhaps a little wearily), abuduction accounts
also show up outside hypnosis, recalled from conscious memory. Eddie Bullard
wrote a paper comparing the stories told with and without hypnosis, and found no
substantial difference. </SPAN></FONT></DIV>
<DIV><FONT face="Book Antiqua" size=2><SPAN
class=183451820-23082002></SPAN></FONT>&nbsp;</DIV>
<DIV><FONT face="Book Antiqua" size=2><SPAN class=183451820-
23082002>Of course,
many of these stories are told to abduction researchers, so there's always a
possibility that abduction researchers are somehow shaping the account. Here,
then, from a fairly amazing piece of current research, is a situationwhere that
doesn't seem to be true. More than a dozen American physicians, associated as
part of the same medical group, have discovered that all of them have patients
with abduction memories. All of these patients had told their abduction stories
to the physicians, apparently looking for help. I hope it goes without saying
that none of these doctors are abduction researchers, or even had any interest
in abduction phenomena before. None of them had asked their patients about
abduction memories. The patients took the intiative. One patient became active
in abduction affairs, and presented anomalous physical symptoms, which got his
doctor's attention. This doctor than consulted his colleagues, and was amazed to
find that every one of them had heard abduction stories from their patients. I
don't know what involvement the other patients may have had with the organized
abduction world, but I doubt it was very great. The doctors, from what I've
heard of them, would have been suspicious if the patients had, let's say, been
in abduction support groups, precisely because that might explain where the
abduction reports came from.</SPAN></FONT></DIV>
<DIV><FONT face="Book Antiqua" size=2><SPAN
class=183451820-23082002></SPAN></FONT>&nbsp;</DIV>
<DIV><FONT face="Book Antiqua" size=2><SPAN class=183451820-23082002>I
can't say
more about this right now. The doctors involved -- who don't hold any opinion
about what all this might mean -- are starting some research on the phenomenon.
As I understand it, they're trying to find out if the patients reporting
abduction stories have any physical characteristics in common that might set
them apart from the population at large. I know of this through one of the
abductees involved,, and from someone I trust who's talked to some of the
doctors. Maybe the doctors will eventually publish something, and allow this to
be publicly discussed. </SPAN></FONT></DIV>
<DIV><FONT face="Book Antiqua" size=2><SPAN
class=183451820-23082002></SPAN></FONT>&nbsp;</DIV>
<DIV><FONT face="Book Antiqua" size=2><SPAN class=183451820-
23082002>Finally,
about hypnotists putting ideas in peoples' heads...many of us may know about
research done by psychologists, which seems to show that hypnotism doesn't help
people recall events accurately. Somewhere in the 1990's psychology literature I
found a journal article questioning this research, precisely because the
researchers&nbsp;-- many of whom were quite outspoken in their belief that
hypnosis can't aid in accurate recall -- had subliminally influenced their
subjects not to remember things accurately! I'm sorry that I don't recall the
citation, but what's sauce for the goose....</SPAN></FONT></DIV>
<DIV><FONT face="Book Antiqua" size=2><SPAN
class=183451820-23082002></SPAN></FONT>&nbsp;</DIV>
<DIV><FONT face="Book Antiqua" size=2><SPAN class=183451820-
23082002>Greg
Sandow</SPAN></FONT></DIV>

From: "Greg Sandow" <greg@gregsandow.com>
Date: Fri, 23 Aug 2002 18:59:10 -0400
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Best Evidence

My memory failed me here. Michael Nash is a psychology professor at the
University of Tennessee, and editor of the International Journal of
Clinical and Experimental Hypnosis. He's an important hypnosis
researcher, but he's not the author of the book I was talking about.

My notes on that book aren't with me at the moment, but I believe it's
Michael Yapko's"Suggestions of Abuse: True and False
Memories of Childhood Sexual Trauma" (New York: Simon and Schuster,
1994). To verify this, though, I'll have to find my notes (which are on
a floppy disk that I believe is in my country house), or else make
another visit to the NY Public Library, and search their psychology
citations, where I found this book in the first place.

My apologies for the mistake. Yapko, by the way, is a clinical
psychologist currently famous for his use of hypnosis to treat
depression. The book I've cited was Yapko's angry response to the
recovered memory movement, and especially to the many therapists who
claimed to help their patients recover memories of sexual abuse.

Greg Sandow

From: "Greg Sandow" <greg@gregsandow.com>
Date: Fri, 23 Aug 2002 19:18:59 -0400
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Best Evidence

Yes, of course this has been attempted.

Normally, people have tried electronic monitoring, sometimes by methods
as simple as leaving a video camera trained on their beds while they
sleep at night. Allegedly, the monitoring devices malfunction, at times
(or so it's said) in inexplicable ways. David Jacobs tells a story about
a video camera that showed a woman sleeping, then stopped, then showed
the woman sleeping again. It allegedly didn't show her or anyone else
approaching it to turn it off. Nor did it show her leaving her bed. And
of course the woman involved claims she didn't do it. I believe she was
supposedly alone in her house.

An account of one monitoring attempt is in "Connections: Solving Our UFO
Abduction Mystery," by Beth Collings and Anna Jamerson.

There's a systematic monitoring study going on how, with respectable
double-blind methodology. I don't know when it's scheduled to conclude,
or when results will be published. Though I know details of the study
(who's doing it, how it's being done), these details are confidential
until the results are published. One thing I'll say, though -- abduction
researchers aren't involved. Or, to be precise, they were asked to
recommend abductees for the study, but they weren't and won't be
involved in planning, executing, or evaluating the work.

Greg Sandow

Karl,

Thanks for the feedback.

My understanding was that there were no reports involving 'greys'
and especially outwith 'hypnosis', before the Hills' 'regressive
hypnosis' story was known.

Fuller's 'The Interrupted Journey' was apparently first published
in 1966.

One reason I highlighted this issue is that I was a surprised to
see an 'alien art bust', for sale on eBay and which does look
similar to the archetypal 'grey', particularly those slanted,
'cat-like' eyes.

This model is inscribed and dated to 1961.

Although being sold as an 'alien art bust', it may not have any
'alien' connotations at all and merely be a stylised sculpture -
are those two trailing 'tendrils' a representation of long hair?

See:

http://cgi.ebay.com/ws/eBayISAPI.dll?ViewItem&item=900952487

This can only be resolved with more background information and
that might be difficult to obtain now.

One clue is the full inscription; 'Austin Inc. (copyright) Prod.
1961'.

If it _was_ intended to depict an alien and inspired by someone's
claimed experiences, it would certainly be an interesting,
historical 'UFO' artefact.

From: "James Easton" <voyager@ukonline.co.uk>
Date: Sat, 24 Aug 2002 06:48:09 +0100
Subject: Re: [UFORL] Ufology in Perspective

Regarding:

>From: Mendoza <Horseman@onetel.net.uk>
>Date: Tue Aug 20, 2002 3:07 am
>Subject: Ufology in Perspective

Peter wrote, in a 'cross-post':

>Posted to the Project 1947 List in response to:
>Subject: ufology in perspective
>From: Jerome Clark, jkclark@FRONTIERNET.NET
>To: Project-47, PROJECT-1947@LISTSERV.AOL.COM

>There is no suggestion of "skepticism" in either the ancient or
>the current usages. Ancient Greek had a good word, "skeptomai",
>I look about, watch, look carefully or, when applied to mental
>activity, I view, examine, or consider.

Peter,

Pyrrho was a Greek philosopher from Elea, and founder of the
Greek school of skepticism.

In his youth he practiced the art of painting, but passed over
this for philosophy. He studied the writings of Democritus,
became a disciple of Bryson, the son of Stilpo, and later a
disciple of Anaxarchus. He took part in the Indian expedition of
Alexander the Great, and met with philosophers of the Indus
region. Back in Greece he was frustrated with the assertions of
the Dogmatists (those who claimed to possess knowledge), and
founded a new school in which he taught that every object of
human knowledge involves uncertainty. Thus, he argued, it is
impossible ever to arrive at the knowledge of truth (Diog. Laert,
58).

It is related that he acted on his own principles, and carried
his skepticism to such an extreme, that his friends were obliged
to accompany him wherever he went, so he might not be run over by
carriages or fall down precipices.

It is likely, though, that these reports were invented by the
Dogmatists whom he opposed. He spent a great part of his life in
solitude, and was undisturbed by fear, or joy, or grief. He
withstood bodily pain, and when in danger showed no sign of
apprehension.
In disputes he was known for his subtlety. Epicurus, though no
friend to skepticism, admired Pyrrho because he recommended and
practiced the kind of self-control that fostered tranquillity;
this, for Epicurus, was the end of all physical and moral
science. Pyrrho was so highly valued by his countrymen that they
honored him with the office of chief priest and, out of respect
for him, passed a decree by which all philosophers were made
immune from taxation. He was an admirer of poets, particularly
Homer, and frequently cited passages from his poems. After his
death, the Athenians honored his memory with a statue, and a
monument to him was erected in his own country.

Pyrrho left no writings, and we owe our knowledge of his thoughts
to his disciple Timon of Phlius. His philosophy, in common with
all post-Aristotelian systems, is purely practical in its
outlook. Skepticism is not posited on account of its speculative
interest, but only because Pyrrho sees in it the road to
happiness, and the escape from the calamities of life.


The proper course of the sage, said Pyrrho, is to ask himself
three questions.

Firstly, we must ask what things are and how they are
constituted.

Secondly, we ask how we are related to these things.

Thirdly, we ask what ought to be our attitude towards them.


As to what things are, we can only answer that we know nothing.
We only know how things appear to us, but of their inner
substance we are ignorant. The same thing appears differently to
different people, and therefore it is impossible to know which
opinion is right.

The diversity of opinion among the wise, as well as among the
vulgar, proves this. To every assertion the contradictory
assertion can be opposed with equally good grounds, and whatever
my opinion, the contrary opinion is believed by somebody else who
is quite as clever and competent to judge as I am.

Opinion we may have, but certainty and knowledge are impossible.
Hence our attitude to things (the third question), ought to be
complete suspense of judgment. We can be certain of nothing, not
even of the most trivial assertions. Therefore we ought never to
make any positive statements on any subject. And the Pyrrhonists
were careful to import an element of doubt even into the most
trifling assertions which they might make in the course of their
daily life. They did not say, "it is so," but "it seems so," or
"it appears so to me." Every observation would be prefixed with a
"perhaps," or "it may be."

This absence of certainty applies as much to practical as to
theoretical matters. Nothing is in itself true or false. It only
appears so. In the same way, nothing is in itself good or evil.
It is only opinion, custom, law, which makes it so. When the sage
realizes this, he will cease to prefer one course of action to
another, and the result will be apathy (ataraxia). All action is
the result of preference, and preference is the belief that one
thing is better than another.

If I go to the north, it is because, for one reason or another, I
believe that it is better than going to the south. Suppress this
belief, learn that the one is not in reality better than the
other, but only appears so, and one would go in no direction at
all. Complete suppression of opinion would mean complete
suppression of action, and it was at this that Pyrrho aimed.

To have no opinions was the skeptical maxim, because in practice
it meant apathy, total quietism. All action is founded on belief,
and all belief is delusion, hence the absence of all activity is
the ideal of the sage. In this apathy he will renounce all
desires, for desire is the opinion that one thing is better than
another. He will live in complete repose, in undisturbed
tranquillity of soul, free from all delusions. Unhappiness is the
result of not attaining what one desires, or of losing it when
attained.

The wise person, being free from desires, is free from
unhappiness. He knows that, though people struggle and fight for
what they desire, vainly supposing some things better than
others, such activity is but a futile struggle about nothing, for
all things are equally indifferent, and nothing matters. Between
health and sickness, life and death, difference there is none.
Yet insofar as we are compelled to act, we will follow
probability, opinion, custom, and law, but without any belief in
the essential validity or truth of these criteria.
[END OF EXTRACT]


I know all of this be true, as I found it on a web site. ;)

See:

http://www.utm.edu/research/iep/p/pyrrho.htm


Does Jerome Clark seriously argue that, "Those who laugh at the
implausibility of a possible plesiosaur in Loch Ness should take
a close look at the arguments and evidence put forth for the Big
Bang or Black Holes"?

It's long been, scientifically, proven that Loch Ness does not
factually have a 'food-chain' which could ever sustain even one
'plesiosaur'.


This is evidently the same Jerome Clark who once professed:

Many years later I read Jacques Vallée's Passport to Magonia and
was taken with his attempt to link traditional fairy lore to
modern flying saucer lore.

I began reading in the considerable scholarly literature on fairy
beliefs. In one of these books, Katharine Briggs's 'The Fairies
in Tradition and Literature', I came upon a brief account of the
Cottingley episode, about which Dr Briggs, one of Britain's
leading folklorists, wrote: "As one looks at these photographs,
every feeling revolts against believing them to be genuine. Yet,
noting some of the unexplained aspects of the affair, she went on
guardedly to suggest that the pictures might be psychic
photographs".

She was troubled by a few odd items of evidence, such as the
testimony of three photographic experts who said they didn't know
how the pictures could have been faked.

Intrigued, I reread Doyle's book and two others on the subject. I
was impressed not so much by the testimony of the photographic
experts as by the demonstrated inability of would-be debunkers to
come up with plausible, non-extraordinary explanations. Typical
of the blunders was Houdini's bold assertion that the models for
the fairy figures came from a certain advertising poster. This
allegation was widely published and uncritically accepted. But
eventually, when investigators located copies of the poster in
question they found that the fairies depicted on it looked not at
all like those in the Cottingley pictures.

I was also interested to read that as late as the early 1970s,
over 50 years after the events in question, the two
photographers, both now elderly women, seemed to stand by their
earlier testimony.

So, following Briggs's lead, I cast all caution to the wind. I
was at least wise enough to concede that the Cottingley fairies
didn't look real but dismissed that as a subjective
consideration. To me the absence of convincing negative evidence,
coupled with the presence of positive evidence (however thin),
added up to the conclusion that these might be authentic
thoughtographs much like those Ted Serios is said to produce.

To this day I can't believe how stupid and how credulous I was.



As we know now beyond any reasonable doubt, the Cottingley
pictures are clumsy and absurd fakes. In his 1978 book 'Ghosts in
Photographs'; Fred Gettings reveals that the models from the
figures came from a popular children's book of the period. Photo-
analysis by William Spaulding's Ground Saucer Watch has shown
that, yes indeed, the figures are of cardboard, just as my 11-
year-old eye had told me many years ago.

Robert Sheaffer, in his effort to debunk the story, contributed
to the grand tradition of misleading nonsense by claiming, on the
basis of the thinnest possible circumstantial evidence, that
Theosophical writer Edward Gardner was the mastermind behind the
hoax - an assertion that quickly fell victim to Occam's Razor,
but not before proving once again that the Cottingley affair
could as easily make fools of disbelievers as of believers.

In their recent books, non-admirers of mine like Sheaffer and
Martin Gardner have resurrected my foolish remarks on these non-
fairy/non-thoughtograph pictures in an effort to discredit me.

Sheaffer even claims that he, as the man who commissioned
Spaulding to analyse the pictures in 1977, forced me to
relinquish my support. He doesn't mention that, on the contrary,
I accepted this first truly solid negative evidence with almost
unseemly haste, in part because I like to think I am
intellectually honest and in part because on some level -
specifically the level of my psyche at which the embers of common
sense still glowed, however faintly - I had long suspected that
in taking the pictures seriously I was making a very, very dumb
mistake.

Another mistake was in assuming the existence of thoughtographs ,
the evidence for which is shaky at best. In other words, I had
attempted to explain a dubious claim with another dubious claim.
Realising belatedly that I was lost deep in a jungle of Fortean
unreality, I decided that it was high time to cut and slash my
way through the undergrowth and return to safety, sanity and
scepticism. At the end of my harrowing adventure my hair was
whiter but my head was clearer.

The moral of the story is this:

(1) There is something to be said for common sense.
(2) Just because the debunkers are wrong, it doesn't necessarily
follow that therefore the proponents are right.

(3) The time had come for this proponent to do some serious
rethinking of his position.
[END OF EXTRACT]

See:

http://www.magonia.demon.co.uk/arc/80/confessions.htm

It dates from 1983, under the heading, 'Confessions of a Fortean
Sceptic', by Jerome Clark.

Yes, but we should be careful to distinguish between the stimulus
and today's latest mythology to explain it.

Bob Young

From: YoungBob2@aol.com
Date: Sun, 25 Aug 2002 13:29:28 EDT
Subject: Re: [UFORL] The Birth of the 'Greys'

In a message dated 8/23/2002 2:19:01 AM Eastern Daylight Time,
voyager@ukonline.co.uk writes:

<< The story of Betty and Barney Hill begins in September 1961, in
the state of New Hampshire. Barney had recently developed an
ulcer, and he and his wife Betty decided to take a short vacation
to Canada. The couple had visited Niagara Falls, and Montreal,
and on the 19th of the month, they began their journey back home
to Portsmouth. The night was clear, with a crescent moon shining
on the heavily wooded landscape, that surrounded US Route 3 in
the central part of New Hampshire. At about a quarter past 10:00
P.M., three miles south of the city of Lancaster, Barney noticed
what appeared to be a bright star, or planet which seemed to move
erratically. Barney pointed this out to Betty, and they both
began to keep track of the object.
 >>

Good Morning James, other Listers:

Robert Sheaffer, in his book, The UFO Verdict - Examining the
Evidence (Prometheus Books, 1981) pp. 34-36, says that the
Hills actually noticed the "star" below the moon. Shortly afterward,
according to Sheaffer, Betty reportedly spotted a second object,
which she described as a bigger or brighter star, above the first
star. It was this second brighter object which she thought was
a UFO.

Sheaffer notes (p. 35) that this exactly matches the configuration
of the moon, Saturn and brighter Jupiter.

I just checked these objects in a planetarium program, Cartes du
Ciel, and see that at 11 PM they would have been visible less than
15 degrees high in the South West, out Betty's side window, as
seen travelling South on Route 3 through the White Mountains
(I assumed a location near Woodstock, N.H. at 44 deg N,
71 deg 45' W).

Object       Azimuth Altitude

Moon         226 deg    13 deg
Jupiter (UFO?) 224 deg    11.5 deg
Saturn      228 deg    9 deg

If the original stimuli for this incident can be attributed to these
astronomical objects, it suggests a Psycho-Social cause.
Clear skies,
Bob Young

caused them. I spent some time, a few years back, watching Budd Hopkins work --
attending his support group meetings (very infrequent, by the way), and sitting
in on both initial interviews with people who wanted to work with him, and
hypnosis sessions.</SPAN></FONT></DIV>

26082002>The support
group meetings and informal conversation with the abductees was the most
revealing (though of what, I couldn't say). Abductees routinely will say, for
instance, that they woke up in the morning wearing clothes they hadn't been
wearing when they went to bed. Or that they woke up with unaccountable stains on
their hands, clothes, or bodies. To say that they report these things in a
matter-of-fact way wouldn't be accurate. Obviously, they're concerned and to
some degree upset. But on the other hand, they don't talk about these things
with wild affect, or with any great sense of self-importance or revelation.
There's something factual in the tone they use -- which, again, is not to say
they have to be reporting the literal truth, but that they say these things in a
tone that wouldn't surprise us if they were reporting something we wouldn't
hesitate to accept as true. They might just as well be saying that they'd seen
something unusual, but not shocking or unheard of -- a police car involved in a
chase, for instance. (This all happens in NY City, where we do see things like
that.)</SPAN></FONT></DIV>

children! You know tenants aren't allowed on the roof!" Plus cases of family

From: "Greg Sandow" <greg@gregsandow.com>
Date: Mon, 26 Aug 2002 15:10:57 -0400
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Best Evidence

Good thought. There may have been something more anomalous about what
the camera showed, but I don't remember all the details.

What would be interesting, of course, would be to monitor with a video
camera for many months, and (using proper double-blind procedures)
compare anomalies in what the camera showed with the abductee's reports
of alleged abductions. Maybe the circuit breaker would oddly assert
itself only on abduction nights -- which, of course, might also suggest
some kind of electrical source for the abduction experience.

One test like that was done by William Levengood, a retired plant
physiologist. He found a female abductee, who slept each night with her
hair in curlers. Levengood put a plant seed (a wheat seed, I think) in
the curlers each night for a month. The seeds were put into containers,
labeled with the day they were used. The abductee kept a log of possible
abductions. At the end of the month, with proper double-blind
procedures, the log and the seeds were compared. The abductee reported
an abduction on one of the nights. The seed from that night differed
from all the other seeds. It appeared, at least to Levengood, to have
been subjected to high heat. And it germinated faster than the seeds
from non-abduction nights.

I don't know whether this research has been published. I've read about
it in informal accounts, which I've verified with an associate of
Levengood's. Certainly this work needs to be replicated before it's
taken as serious evidence of anything.

Greg Sandow

From: "Jim Speiser" <jimspeiser@yahoo.com>

Subject: [UFORL] Turkey Springs Incident Update

Regrettably I bear the sad news that the Rodeo-Chediski wildfire did in fact
go through Turkey Springs, Arizona, and the TSI/Walton site was affected.
HOWEVER, the good news is that the site was not thoroughly consumed, and the
trees, though charred, are still standing, and are still viable for future
evidence collection.

Mike Rogers and I made the 45 minute drive from Show Low to visit the site
yesterday. As far as we know, we were the first to set foot on Ufology's
second most hallowed ground since the wildfires of June/July. Besides
historical curiosity, our purpose was to follow up on previous site
investigations which indicate anomalous growth patterns in the trees
immediately surrounding the site. In the near future I intend to post more
details on this possible evolution of the TSI CE-I into a CE-II. Suffice it
to say that the investigation is ongoing...thanks to the hardiness of the
Ponderosa Pine.

that, would he not have simply mentioned that the binocs were out of focus
during one of his interviews? I've looked at stars through unfocused
binoculars. They look......unfocused.


<<Again, bright stars are responsible for many Nocturnal Lights cases, but I
think IN GENERAL we have to draw the line at Close Encounter cases and say
that the stimulus has to be something else....or else we go back to Human
Perception 101 and start writing the books all over.
 >>

<<Problem is that Betty reported seeing the Moon and a bright star
below it and the brighter UFO next to the Moon. That would have
been Jupiter. She didn't report seeing one star below the Moon and
a brighter one next to it, and the UFO.>>

Unless, of course, the UFO were obscuring Jupiter...

The first thing a good ufologist should do when investigating a nighttime
UFO report is get out his star charts. The problem is that some people
don't know when to put them away. Has anyone noticed how many "bright"
stars there are, scattered throughout the night sky? There seems to be
enough such that one can find a candidate star for just about any viewing
angle...depending on how flexible one wants to be about the precision of
reported viewing angles...


<<Well, I don't think that one can say anything IN GENERAL about UFO
sightings. Each one is different. The history is clear, though: close
encounters can be caused by astronomical IFOs.>>

Only if one persists in assuming that nighttime UFOs are bright stars, and
then just finds the nearest candidate, then -assumes- that that is the
explanation.

<<Once one "draws a line" based upon a criteria selected by the
investigator, mysterious causes will be left, because it can't be
prosaic.>>

First, my criteria is not self-selected, it is selected by common sense. As
a rule, people don't generally mistake distant celestial bodies for
structured craft less than 500 feet away. Remember, that's the criteria for
a CLOSE encounter. In those cases where the observer is being fooled by a
bright celestial object, they generally describe something much further
away. Now I know you'll be full of counter-examples, but I've heard very
few that weren't merely restatements of the _assumption_ you try to put
forth as an explanation, to wit, that astronomical IFOs can be the stimulus
for Close Encounter reports...and (the unspoken part) therefore are.

Second, I can't help what's left. If it's mysterious and can't be
"prosaic," maybe it's because we're dealing with a mysterious and
non-prosaic phenomenon?

Bob,

The Hills' case is one I have never previously looked at in any
detail.

Some further, still cursory research, unearths apparently glaring
discrepancies within published and accepted case evidence.


As our 'incident', reportedly occurred on September 19, 1961 and
the Hills weren't first 'regressed' until January to June 1964,
during which time they doubtless discussed recollections and
professed, subsequent 'nightmares', any images which emerged
under 'hypnosis' are, by default, of no scientific research value
whatsoever.


Much more interesting would be any available evidence of what was
initially reported and there is fortunately, considerable, early
documented material.

Available online, is a helpful, detailed analysis of foremost
case evidence, as discussed in:
AIR COMMAND AND STAFF COLLEGE
RESEARCH STUDY
AIR UNIVERSITY
REPORT NO. 0450-74
SHOULD THE USAF REOPEN PROJECT BLUE BOOK?

By William E. Brummett, 310-40-5845FR, Major, USAF
And
Ernest R. Zuick, Jr., 549-46-3888FR, Captain, AF, CA ANG

See:

http://www.geocities.com/hooch43us/afu-ufos.html


Their study highlights evidence for and against Jupiter being
responsible for the Hill's sighting.

One question which I hoped to answer is whether the following was
accurate:

"He saw multicolored lights, and rows of windows on a flat-shaped
object, which now seemed to be moving toward him. As the object
moved to within a hundred feet of him, he could see occupants
inside. Frightened, he ran back to his car where Betty waited".

See:

http://bjbooth.topcities.com/Hill.html


Did Barney Hill believe, at the outset, he could see occupants
and was this reported to the USAF?

According to Brummett and Zuick [B&Z], Barney apparently did not
tell the USAF he might have seen occupants [for 'fear of
ridicule'] and at nearest perceived proximity, the object was not
"within a hundred feet of him", but "'hundreds of feet' above
their car".

However, there may be inherent contradictions. In summarising the
overall story, B&Z state:

The couple lost sight of the object temporarily until it
suddenly appeared approximately 300 feet to the right of their
car.(10:46) At this point Barney stopped the car, grabbed his
binoculars, and walked toward the object, which he now realized
was a spacecraft. Barney stopped approximately fifty feet away
from the object and began viewing the UFO through his binoculars
and noticed at least six living creatures staring back at him
from behind the craft's windows. Barney immediately ran screaming
toward his car. Reaching his automobile in a state of near
hysteria, he jammed the car into gear and sped toward his
original destination.
[END OF EXTRACT]


Later, B&Z write:

Betty Hill talked with Major Paul W. Henderson of the 100th Bomb
Wing (SAC) at Pease AFB and relayed the bare outline of their
sighting. Since Barney was concerned about being considered
irrational, he purposely avoided mentioning the figures observed
in the craft. (10:47) The official Air Force Form 112, report No.
100-1-61, as transcribed by Major Henderson appears in Project
Blue Book files as follows:

They report that the object was travelling north very fast. They
report it changed directions rather abruptly and then headed
south. Shortly thereafter it stopped and hovered in the air.
There was no sound evident up to this point. While hovering,
objects began to appear from the body of the "object" which they
describe as looking like wings which made a V-shape when
extended. The "wings" had red lights on the tips. At this point
they observed it to appear to swoop down in the general direction
of their auto. The object continued to descend until it appeared
to be only a matter of "hundreds of feet" above their car.

At this point they decided to get out of that area, and fast. Mr.
Hill was driving and Mrs. Hill was prevented from observing its
full departure by her position in the car.
[END OF EXTRACT]


In our 'ET kidnap/medical examination' context, there's a
significant difference between a proclaimed aerial object,
originally 'star-like' and then appears to be much lower
overhead...as opposed to one which now seems to be, "300 feet to
the right of their car" and the Hills then approach to a distance
of only 50 feet.

Presuming early USAF documentation to be more accurate than later
retellings of the story, it's nowhere near so dramatic.

I would like to know when Barney first reported the occupants and
if it was indeed pre-hypnosis.


Obviously, it's hardly probable the Hills observed an object,
which Betty statedly thought from the beginning to be 'a star-
like UFO', was an 'alien spacecraft'... that coincidentally
happened to be on a mission to kidnap Betty and Barney.


What about corroborative witnesses?

Doubtless, avowed sky phenomena was seen and mentioned by
numerous others?

Did no-one else on that same road, or nearby, during a stated and
astonishing thirty minute observation, notice the 'UFO',
especially when it supposedly descended and hovered?

Moreso, if an ET spaceship had, as 'recalled under hypnosis',
landed on the road in front of the Hills, forming a roadblock and
they were then taken on-board, etc., was there no other traffic
within, say, a mile or so during that entire period?

The same question relates to how the Hills were 'returned'.


As for those critical, proclaimed, two hours of 'missing time',
there seems to be a fundamental variance concerning the
background to any such 'realisation'.

So far as I can see, neither Betty or Barney Hill thought any
time was unaccounted for, until they were subsequently encouraged
to believe this...


There are so many different online versions of the popularised
story, however, what seems to have happened is this typical
mythology:

"When they awoke, they found themselves driving near Ashland, two
hours later. Ashland is 35- miles south of Indian Head, a twenty
or thirty minute drive. They continued their drive home, feeling
somewhat uneasy and confused about their missing two hours".

See:

http://www.qtm.net/~geibdan/a1999/hills/

It's a claim repeated elsewhere.


Yet, alternatively...

"At this time, neither Betty nor Barney recalled any abduction.
Soon, Betty began having nightmarish dreams of her and her
husband being taken aboard a craft of some kind, against their
will. In a matter of weeks, two writers got wind of the story,
and after interviewing the Hills, made an intensive log of the
events of the night. They discovered that there were two hours of
unaccounted time in the Hill's story, even allowing for stops for
the Hills, and breaks for their dog, who also had made the trip
with them. Another interesting note that I should interject here
is that these "two writers," which are mentioned in almost every
report of this incident, (and there are literally thousands of
them), have not been named, or I cannot find their names.
However, the story is true, because their interview was attended
by Major James MacDonald, a former Air Force Intelligence
Officer. Shortly after Betty began having these disturbing
dreams, she wrote a letter to Major Donald Kehoe, who passed her
information on to one Walter Webb, who was on the staff of the
Hayden Planetarium. Webb, at the time, was a scientific advisor
for the National Investigations Committee on Arial Phenomena.
(commonly referred to as NICAP). What he did with the report is
unknown".

See:

http://bjbooth.topcities.com/Hill.html


I can identify who those two writers were and instantly, this
pillar of belief in 'UFOs', 'alien abductions' and the 'greys',
begins to alarmingly collapse...

Taking up the story, from elsewhere:

"Meanwhile, Betty's letter to Kehoe had been passed to Walter
Webb, a lecturer on the staff of the Hayden Planetarium in
Boston. Webb was a scientific advisor for NICAP (National
Investigations Committee on Aerial Phenomenon), Kehoe's UFO
organization. Webb was asked to interview the Hills. He drove up
to Portsmouth and spent several hours interviewing them. He was
much impressed with their sincerity and with the detail they
provided, and he wrote a long report for NICAP.

After talking to Keyhoe, and after reading Webb's report, two
technical writers who were interested in UFOs, Robert Hohman and
C.D. Jackson, made arrangements to interview the Hills in
November. It was during this interview that one of the writers
asked a key question: Why had it taken the Hills so long to get
home? Calculating the time and the mileage from Colebrook to
Portsmouth showed that they should have gotten home two hours
sooner than they did, even allowing for stops. Also present at
this interview was Major James MacDonald, a former Air Force
Intelligence officer and close friend of the Hills. It was he who
first suggested hypnosis to recover their memory of the missing
time period.

In March of 1962, they spoke to a psychiatrist about hypnosis,
but decided to put it off until a later date. That summer,
Barney's ulcers returned, and his recurring hypertension
returned. Feeling that his problems were emotional in origin, he
began therapy with a psychiatrist in Exeter, Dr. Stephens. He
continued this therapy through the next year, but the UFO
sighting was not explored as part of this treatment at first.

But, not long after Betty and Barney had been asked to speak to a
church group about their sighting, Dr. Stephens decided that the
sighting was important. He also decided that hypnosis was needed
to help Barney deal with the incident. Not being proficient in
hypnosis himself, he referred Barney to Dr. Benjamin Simon, a
well-known Boston psychiatrist and neurologist.

[...]

He began by hypnotizing Barney, then Betty. Over the next six
months, the story of the two hours of missing time began to
emerge. Betty and Barney Hill told of being stopped at a
roadblock and being taken onto the UFO, where they were given
medical examinations before being returned to their car. Betty
reported being shown a "star map" that was later interpreted to
mean that the aliens came from Zeta Reticuli. Their story was
later written into a two-part article in Look magazine, a book
titled The Interrupted Journey by John G. Fuller, and later a TV
movie called The UFO Incident starring Estelle Parsons and James
Earl Jones as the Hills.

The Hill's story was the first "modern" abduction story. There
was no Communion back in 1961, and no X-Files. Abduction stories
had not become part of the popular culture yet. People had
claimed to have contact with aliens, but they were "contactees"
in the mold of George Adamski, who claimed to have been visited
by friendly Venusians with long blond hair who gave him a warning
for all mankind about nuclear war. Skeptics such as Martin S.
Kottmeyer claim that the elements of the Hill abduction could be
found in movies like 1953's Invaders
From: "Greg Sandow" <greg@gregsandow.com>
Date: Tue, 27 Aug 2002 11:47:54 -0400
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Best Evidence

Why would we expect subconscious responses to cultural stimuli to be
similar to each other? Seems to me that's an unwarranted assumption.

Eddie Bullard, for whatever it's worth, makes the opposite assumption,
drawing on professional experience as a folklorist. He takes for granted
that folklore -- a response, generated unconsciously, even if
consciously expressed, to cultural stimuli -- changes greatly over time.
He specifically contrasts this to abduction stories. He may or may not
be right, but if we're going to discuss these things, we at least should
join the ongoing debate.

From: "Greg Sandow" <greg@gregsandow.com>
Date: Tue, 27 Aug 2002 11:55:17 -0400
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Best Evidence

Like much of ufology, abduction research is a cottage industry. The
people I know who engage in it -- Budd Hopkins and Dave Jacobs,
primarily -- do it on their own time, with their own money, with notable
damage to their mainstream careers. I don't say this to praise them or
get sympathy for them. I just want to note the context in which things
do or don't get done. Another factor is scientific help. There are
scientists who help both Budd and Dave, but almost always they'll only
do it secretly, for fear of damage to their own careers. That greatly
limits what they can do.

If I were going to make a list of abduction work that ought to be done,
I'd start with something relatively simple -- publication of data. A lot
of major information remains unpublished.I understand why that is, but
it's sad. And yes, this means I wish the books Budd and Dave have
written took a somewhat different approach, but that's another story.

-----Original Message-----
From: Greg Sandow [mailto:greg@gregsandow.com]
Sent: 27 August 2002 17:48Subject: RE: [UFORL] Best Evidence


Why would we expect subconscious responses to cultural stimuli to be
similar to each other? Seems to me that's an unwarranted assumption.

Eddie Bullard, for whatever it's worth, makes the opposite assumption,
drawing on professional experience as a folklorist. He takes for granted
that folklore -- a response, generated unconsciously, even if
consciously expressed, to cultural stimuli -- changes greatly over time.
He specifically contrasts this to abduction stories. He may or may not
be right, but if we're going to discuss these things, we at least should
join the ongoing debate.

<FONT FACE=arial,helvetica><FONT COLOR="#0000ff" SIZE=2>"Betty and
Barney Hill go for a nice leisurely drive in New England.&nbsp; Suddenly Betty sees
the planet Jupiter, which she instantly mistakes for an interstellar spacecraft.&nbsp;
Later, Barney views an advertising plane through cheap, unfocused binoculars and
becomes so convinced he sees aliens that he jumps back in the car and starts
driving."<BR>
<BR>
</FONT><FONT COLOR="#000000" style="BACKGROUND-COLOR: #ffffff"
SIZE=2 FAMILY="SANSSERIF" FACE="Arial" LANG="0">Don't downplay the
use of binoculars in misidentifying stars as UFOs.&nbsp; Perhaps you should read,
Hendry's "The UFO Handbook"&nbsp; Chapt 15 "Tools: Optics". I could quote the
text on numerous cases he points out but one has to keep in mind one conclusion that
he reached, "...optics can play a role in enhancing distortion rather than penetrating
it..."<BR>
<BR>
If Barney used simple 7X35s or 7X50s, I doubt he would have been able to resolve
much more than a slightly larger light (assuming it was a star-like point visually) if he
even used them correctly.&nbsp; Exactly how Barney was able to determine that this
star-like object suddenly was an alien craft of some kind with such a low power
instrument is hard to understand. If it were Jupiter, then he probably would have seen
a brighter center dot (Jupiter) and several smaller lights in a row (between 1 and 4
moons could have been present) giving the impression of some larger dark craft with
running lights.&nbsp; Additionally, setting the diopter correctly, steadying the
binoculars, and even getting the focus correct could have given Barney
problems.&nbsp; These are all pointed out by Hendry and are based on my own
personal astronomical experience using these instruments for almost thirty
years.&nbsp; I would be careful in accepting Barney's observations as an accurate
representation!
 as what he saw just because he used binoculars.&nbsp; <BR>

Of course they were stressed. After all, a flying saucer was
following them, zig zagging back and forth so as to precisely
cover the planet Jupiter. Then when it went behind trees or
a hill, it suddenly appeared in front of them. Of course, they

star.

movie Interrupted Journey, after she was asked by Tom Brokow
if this really happened to her, Dr. Simon looked over and said
(I'm paraphrasing from memory) something like, "It didn't
happen, Betty, it was a fantasy."

a flying saucer filled with Jimmy Durantes, or Greys, or whatever,
is at the crux of it. There seems no question that the initial
sighting was of Jupiter, Saturn and the Moon. If we knew the
reasons for the rest, we could all go out and write a paper for one
of the peer reviewed UFO magazines. Yeah, that's the ticket.

I see where this might be confusing so... what it means is that on the night
of the sighting, the two witnesses reported points of light, like stars in the
distance falling toward the ground (in reality they were the landing lights of
aircraft going into the local airport), but during subequent interviews, one
of
the witnesses produced a sketch that showed a domed disk and in another,
later interview, produced another sketch of the domed disk but this time
with shapes on the inside. The story evolved from points of lights to a domed
disk with "creatures" in a matter of weeks.

From: "Greg Sandow" <greg@gregsandow.com>
Date: Thu, 29 Aug 2002 12:06:11 -0400
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Best Evidence

> People who share a culture share the same stimuli, no?

Not necessarily. It depends on what you define as a culture, and what
you define as a stimulus. It's tempting to reason something like this:
"I'm an American, and I'm interested in the UFO abduction phenomenon.
And I see a lot about it on TV, in the movies, and in the press. I
notice these things. Therefore most other Americans notice them, too,
and know something about abductions."

(By the way, I'm not assuming that everyone reading this, or Steve who
I'm responding to, is American. I'm just using this as a convenient
example, probably because I'm American, and we all know that there's a
lot of talk about abductions in America.)

But what this ignores is many things familiar to social scientists,
demographics experts, cultural theories, and -- much more simply --
people in business who do marketing. For instance, there's the well
known phenomenon of subcultures. Much talk about that from social
scientists and cultural theorists. People who belong to a large cultural
group in modern western society don't necessarily share a common
culture. They fragment into smaller subcultural groups.

Allied with this is something marketers talk about -- "psychographics."
Psychographic factors cut across demographic groups. People who are
outwardly similar -- in, for instance, income, occupation, and many
external factors of lifestyle -- may have very different mindsets. These
mindsets, in turn, make them interested in different things. Very
important, for example, for people marketing pop music. Familiar
demographic distinctions don't begin to tell you who's going to be
interested in specific pop groups.

If all this seems a little abstract, here's an example from my own
experience. Recently I read a rather famous book about jazz, Ashley
Kahn's "Kind of Blue." It's about the Miles Davis album by that name,
and among other things it spends a lot of time establishing how popular
-- and how widely familiar -- the album is. There's even a story about a
jazz musician who lost his copy, and, needing to hear the music, knocked
on the door of a neighbor he didn't know, confident that this neighbor
would have the album. Which the neighbor did.

My wife, however, is an educated, musical, upscale professional,
culturally aware -- and in fact a music professional, a classical music
critic for the NY Times. When I mentioned the book to her, it turned out
she'd never heard of the album. Now, obviously, my wife might be an
exception, and, on the other hand, the jazz musician Kahn talks about
might have been wildly optimistic in assuming his neighbor would have a
copy.

But then maybe that jazz musician knew what the neighbor looked like,
and maybe they lived somewhere -- like, maybe,
Berkeley, CA, or Cambridge, MA -- where you really could assume that
people who looked a lot like you would share your musical subculture.
When I lived in Cambridge in the '60s, I could reasonably assume that
any of my neighbors who bought records would have the Band's "Music
from Big Pink," for instance, or (the most obvious example), the
Beatles' "Sgt. Pepper."

The point of this, though, is that Kahn, from his vantage point in the
jazz world, takes more or less for granted that "everyone" in mainstream
American culture knows the album; my wife, from her vantage point in the
classical music world, had never heard it so much as mentioned. Both
these positions may be unusual; the truth may lie somewhere in the
middle. But are we in any position to know what that truth is? What
percentage of culturally-aware Americans do in fact know "Kind of Blue"?
And -- a very important question for anyone at Sony Music marketing a
reissue of the album, or for Ashley Kahn's publisher, marketing the book
-- which culturally-aware Americans would these be? Which subculture,
which demographic, which psychograpic, would you go to if you wanted to
find people who'd respond to this marketing?

These are serious, real-world questions that arise every day. I'm
involved, in my own professional work, with various attempts to
determine who the audience is in America for classical music. Who are
the people who go to classical concerts regularly? How do they differ
from people no different from them demographically, who go to classical
concerts occasionally, or not at all? I know two serious studies of
these questions, one by the Knight Foundation, the other by the American
Symphony Orchestra League. Neither group assumes that "people who share
a culture share the same stimuli." Even more importantly, they don't
assume that people respond to the stimuli in the same way. They can't
afford to make these assumptions. They have to know -- to put this in
the most basic, bottom-line terms -- who to go out and sell tickets to.

It's easy to see how this is relevant to UFOs and abductions. Obviously
a lot of people in America (again, I'm using the US just as an example,
because I'm familiar with it) know about abductions. But which
Americans, precisely, are these? What subculture, what demographic, what
psychographic do they belong to? How -- using whatever tools social
science offers -- can they be defined as a group?

Once we've done that study, we could then look at abductees, who of
course form yet another of the many subcultures in America. (And who, in
my experience, anyway, have a few subcultures splitting them into
further subgroups.) What defines abductees, culturally?

Having done _that_ study, we could then compare people interested in
abductions with abductees. Do they belong to the same subculture? Or are
they, subculturally, rather different? Maybe there's no subcultural
connection between them at all. This information wouldn't prove anything
conclusively, but it certainly would be interesting to have. For
instance, suppose abductees turned out to be very different, culturally,
from people who follow abduction material in the media. This might
suggest that abduction accounts can't readily be said to derive from
media information. Or at least we'd have to take the data into account
in considering that question.

I've written far too long, far longer than I expected to, and I'll bring
this to a halt. I'll add just one thing -- that on UFO lists like this
one, we take physical science very seriously. We don't go around making
assumptions --at least not if we're serious people -- that physical
scientists would say are unsupported. But we _do_ fling social science
concepts around really carelessly, at least in my opinion. We make
blanket statements about things that social scientists have considered
in great detail, and only rarely do we even mention that there might be
a body of literature on the concepts we carelessly take for granted.

Disclaimer: I'm not a trained social scientist. I do read widely,
though, and because of my professional work in both pop and classical
music I've had to deal with some of the social science discussion of
cultures and subcultures.

Greg Sandow

From: "Greg Sandow" <greg@gregsandow.com>
Date: Thu, 29 Aug 2002 14:03:48 -0400
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Best Evidence


> @ Which explains Betty and Barney Hill....how?
>
> "The Day the Earth Stood Still" 1951
> "It Came from Outer Space" 1953
> "Earth VS The Flying Saucers" 1956
>
> Everything the Hills reported was similar to items seen in
> these movies. All three contain abduction sequences and mind
> control, two contain medical procedures aboard a saucer, and
> one contains EM effects (power and auto failure).

Depends on how you define "everything" and "similar." Obviously, some
things the Hills reported weren't in these movies. Driving around in the
mountains, pursued by a light in the sky that turned out to be a craft.
Having a sperm sample taken from Barney. (Suppressed in the original
reports of the case, but it emerged later.) Marks on the car. Betty
seing a star map, being offered a book. Etc.

And then the capture of humans by aliens in these movies wasn't much
like the capture of the Hills. The ambience/feel/stories of the movies
are very different. Where, for instance, in the Hills' account is the
support for world peace that's central to "The Day the Earth Stood
Still"? Where's the massive robot? Where's the alien living in a
peaceful urban boarding house?

There are, in other words, great differences between these movies and
the Hills' story. Whether the smiliarities seem more important than the
differences is a highly subjective call. The objective study of whether
the films could have influenced stories like the Hills' is a complicated
matter. See my comments on social science in another post.

Greg Sandow

From: "Greg Sandow" <greg@gregsandow.com>
Date: Thu, 29 Aug 2002 14:15:19 -0400
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Best Evidence

Larry,

Re birth memories: With all respect, and taking you very seriously, what
you report here reminds me of what abductees report. Both you and many
abductees are very serious, wholly sincere, and as objective as you're
able to be. You don't mean to be making unsupported assertions.

And on the other hand, what you say here and what abductees report are
both outside the frontiers of accepted science. And there's no objective
corroboration for what you say here, or for what abductees say.

One statement you make is almost exactly like the way many abductees
talk. "Nothing happened until I came to 'In the Mood' (which I know my
dad has a 78 of). Suddenly the whole memory came back to me..."
Abductees, too, say that memories suddenly flood back into
consciousness. For instance, when the Hills thought they stumbled on the
place where they'd been abducted. Or in many other cases I've heard
about from abductees. "I saw the picture of the alien on the cover of
'Communion,' and suddenly the memory of seeing exactly that alien came
back to me...I drove past the spot where I now know I was abducted, and
the memory came back to me....Someone in my abduction support group
talked about the cold metal table he was examined on, and suddenly I
remembered lying on a table exactly like that....I saw fireworks in the
sky, and suddenly remembered the bright UFO that swept down from the sky
to abduct me......."

Larry, I'm not challenging your memories, and certainly not demeaning
their importance to you. I'm only saying that we're in a gray area here
(no pun with alien grays intended!), where strongly held and very
personal beliefs conflict with established science, and may be hard to
corroborate.

A related area, for what it's worth. Therapists who work with trauma
victims often find that the trauma victims have detailed memories of the
traumatic event. The therapists take these memories seriously, in their
work with the trauma victim. They may help the victims explore the
memories in many ways, occasionally even with hypnosis. But the
therapists don't necessarily believe the memories are true, no matter
how strongly the patient believes in them. The truth of the memories may
have nothing to do with how important they seem to be, or how strongly
the person believes in them.

Greg Sandow

From: "rotsky" <rotsky@wanadoo.fr>

Subject: RE: [UFORL] Best Evidence

Actually, I'm not assuming anything that specific. The cultural stimuli we
share are often far more subtle than this. You don't have to have any
specific interest in UFOs, abductions, greys etc to be aware *at some level*
that these things exist. These stimuli might be as fleeting as an
advertising image that you are not aware of having seen, but which passes
through your gaze many times; it might be a TV news item to which you
thought you paid no particular attention and may have forgotten seeing.
These are the stimuli we share because they cannot be avoided.

I've often read, in UFO or abduction accounts, that so-and-so described a
craft/entity that matches others but can't have been influenced at all by
previous accounts because 'they had no previous interest in UFOs etc'. This
simplistic reasoning just doesn't hold up. I have absolutely no interest in
sport, and consciously try to avoid all sports programmes, will change
channel when the news switches to sports coverage, never read the sports
pages. But I still absorb information one way or another - I know when
there's a World Cup and even where it is, that there is such a person as
Beckham etc.

Obviously, different people have different interests, but we share a
cultural environment and the stimuli we receive are never limited solely to
those areas in which we are interested. If only...

a+
Steve

OK, let's stop for a moment and take a look at what we have so far.

Betty and Barney Hill go for a nice leisurely drive in New England.
Suddenly Betty sees the planet Jupiter, which she instantly mistakes for
an interstellar spacecraft. Later, Barney views an advertising plane
through cheap, unfocused binoculars and becomes so convinced he sees
aliens that he jumps back in the car and starts driving. Both of them
then experience two hours of missing time - years before that term was
even invented - perhaps because they pulled over to read an obscure 1934
science fiction novel and fill their minds with subliminal images of
gray aliens.

Months later, Betty starts having nightmares about being abducted, and
because she describes them to Barney, he begins having the same
nightmares. That happens all the time, right? They get regressed, and
begin recalling images of their births which they mistake for a medical
exam by aliens. During one session, Barney screams in utter panic,
presumably because he remembers how frightened he was by Klaatu in "The
Day The Earth Stood Still." His unconscious mind conjures up a
suggestion planted by a party hypnotist years earlier that gray beings
were taking him aboard a flying saucer. Meanwhile, Betty recalls one of
the gray beings sticking a needle in her abdomen to do a pregnancy test.
This, of course, was something she must have seen on "The Outer Limits."


That sound you hear is William of Ockham pirouetting in his grave....

==JJS==

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Fri, 30 Aug 2002 12:23:31 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] The Birth of the 'Greys'

OK, how many pieces do you have to hammer into place to get the alien
abduction scenario to work?

- Space aliens have to exist. You can't even assume that, until we have
proof.

- Space aliens must be coming to earth. You can't assume that either.

- They would have had to get through NORAD, which came on-line the
previous year, without being detected. (Please, no ad-hoc postulations
of alien technology able to evade RADAR. That's right out of sci-fi.
You cannot assume that "they" even know what RADAR is, let alone that
they know how to hide from it.)

- They would have had to be able to hide their vehicle from everyone
else on the road and in the air. (The same ad-hocracy rule applies.)

- They would have to have a form of telepathy and mind control. (Ditto.)

- They would need to temporarily be able to hide the planet Jupiter.

- They would have to be able to navigate in three-dimensional space from
a flat chart.

By this time, the pounding loosened the head of the hammer. It flew off
of the handle during a swing, and smashed the mirror by which we must
periodically examine ourselves in (looking for the presence of reality).
Without that, an X-acto knife is then used to cut the pieces into shape.

My, what a funny looking scene. A collage?

It looks just like the one the Evolution scientists pasted together.
