@ And then the capture of humans by aliens in these movies wasn't much
@ like the capture of the Hills. The ambience/feel/stories of the movies
@ are very different. Where, for instance, in the Hills' account is the
@ support for world peace that's central to "The Day the Earth Stood
@ Still"? Where's the massive robot? Where's the alien living in a
@ peaceful urban boarding house?
@

@ the Hills' story. Whether the smiliarities seem more
@ important than the

@ of whether

@ complicated

Firelight

The date was March 24, 1964. The movie was
"Firelight." Its production cost was under $600, and
it was the first feature-length film written and
directed by a high school junior named Steven
Spielberg. After becoming a professional filmmaker,
Spielberg publicly disparaged "Firelight" as "one of
the five worst films ever made anywhere." But his
extraordinary promise was obvious to everyone who
attended the Phoenix premiere of the 8mm production.
"`Firelight' is just as good, although this may be
construed as criticism, as some of the science-fiction
movies seen by the late-late television viewers,"
wrote Arizona Journal reviewer Larry Jarrett. "The
plot, the action, the basic material of the movie, is
sound and not as far out as some of Hollywood's
fantasies-de-science."
   Allen Daviau, the cinematographer who has shot such
Spielberg films as "E.T.--The Extraterrestrial," "The
Color Purple," and "Empire of the Sun," was shown
"Firelight" by Spielberg in the late 1960s. "It's what
you expect with a kid's film, the acting and so on,
but oh, God! Some of it was so audacious," Daviau
says. "The effects were what was really
amazing--that's what his heart was in. What he did
with crumpled aluminum foil and bits of Jello on a
kitchen table was pretty amazing."
   The stimulus for "Firelight" was an unidentified
flying object Spielberg did not see when he was
growing up in Phoenix. Fascinated by heavenly lights
ever since the night in 1957 when he and his father
saw a meteor shower in the desert, Steve, like
virtually every American boy growing up in the '50s,
was intrigued by reports of flying saucers and other
UFO's. He longed for the real thing--the chance to see
a UFO with his own eyes. So he was devastated when he
missed a Boy Scout outing, "the only overnight I
missed the entire year. Wouldn't you know," and his
fellow Scouts came back and told him how, at midnight
in the desert, they all saw "something they couldn't
explain...a blood-red orb rising up behind some
sagebrush, shooting off into space. I felt so left out
not being there." Patrol leader Bill Hoffman says,
"One overnight Spielberg was absent out in the desert.
I don't recall who did it, but the story was told to
Spielberg that someone had seen a flying saucer.
Spielberg was very interested. It wasn't true at all.
As far as I can tell, it was a complete fabrication."
  Steve's 67-page, fully dialogued screenplay for
"Firelight" was completed in early 1963, near the end
of his sophomore year at Arcadia High School. He spent
about six months shooting the film, from June through
December of that year, with collaborators recruited
from his fellow actors and crew members in "Guys and
Dolls" and other school plays. Postproduction,
including post-synchronization of dialogue and
recording of a musical score, continued until the
March premiere. "I used the high school band to score
[the] movie," Spielberg recalled. "I played clarinet
and wrote a score on my clarinet and then had my
mother [who played piano] transpose it to her key. We
made sheet music, the band recorded it, and I had my
first original soundtrack."
  Spielberg had been making amateur films since he
was 10 years old; his mother proudly called him "Cecil
B. DeSpielberg." "Firelight" was his first film with
trained actors and a carefully detailed screenplay,
and he had not yet developed into much of an actor's
director. But his innate narrative sense, his
precocious flair for visual storytelling, and his
already evident ability to orchestrate complex
movement and character interaction (as outlined in the
script) made "Firelight" a gripping, well-constructed
(if overlong) yarn about a small group of scientists
investigating mysterious red, white, and blue balls of
moving light coming from the Arizona sky to abduct
people, animals, and objects.
  "Close Encounters of the Third Kind," Spielberg's
1977 sci-fi masterpiece, "was actually a remake of
`Firelight,'" says Jean Weber Brill, a Spielberg
classmate who did the makeup for "Firelight." "There
were scenes in `Close Encounters' that were almost
direct copies from `Firelight,' such as the lights
appearing on the highway and the scene when the little
boy looks out the door at the bright light. The
storyline of `Close Encounters' was very similar, but
obviously rewritten and more sophisticated."
  "Firelight" introduces the themes of supernatural
intruders, suburban alienation and escape, broken
families and abducted children, scientific adventure,
and spiritual renewal that would become familiar in
Spielberg's mature work. But unlike "Close
Encounters," which radically departed from sci-fi
movie tradition to depict its extraterrestrials as
benign rather than menacing, "Firelight" derives in
large part from the mood of anxiety and paranoia that
characterized the genre in the 1950s, when Spielberg
became hooked on sci-fi. "It was a Cold War movie,"
says cast member Clark (Lucky) Lohr. "They talk about
it being his [first] version of `Close Encounters,'
and it was, in a sense--a sky movie, about sky
gods--but the `cinematic vision' of `Firelight' owed
more to horror movies about aliens dusting humans."
   Arnold and Leah Spielberg bankrolled the production
of their son's first feature. "Steve's parents were
totally behind the film," Jean Weber Brill remembers.
Leah not only kept the cast and crew supplied with
snacks, but cheerfully put up with "constant commotion
at her home" weekend after weekend, the Arizona
Republic reported in a feature about the production.
She even allowed Steve to set up a flashing red light
by the carport door to signal the neighbors to keep
quiet while filming was in progress. People in Phoenix
still speak in awestruck tones of how Spielberg talked
his way into shooting scenes for "Firelight" at
Baptist Hospital and Sky Harbor Airport, using an
actual jet plane. But much of the film was shot in and
around the Spielberg home at 3443 North 49th Street in
the city's Arcadia neighborhood, with the family
carport used as a studio for both interior and
"exterior" shots. The summer shooting mostly took
place at night, because of the heat. After school
resumed, Steve had to film mostly on weekends.
   Arnold Spielberg, a pioneer in the field of
computer engineering and himself a longtime amateur
filmmaker, helped on many of his son's early films.
For "Firelight," Arnold rigged the lights for scenes
filmed in the carport, helped design miniature sets,
and built a dolly for the elaborate tracking shots
that were already a hallmark of the Spielberg visual
style. Steve enlisted his three younger sisters, Anne,
Sue, and Nancy, into the production as well. Anne
served as a script supervisor, Nancy played the key
role of a little girl abducted by aliens, and all
three of them bounced up and down on the hood of the
jeep inside the carport to make the jeep look like it
was speeding through the desert night around Camelback
Mountain.
   Steve and Arnold gave the shoestring production the
illusion of a Hollywood spectacle with ingeniously
designed visual effects. These included optical tricks
to conjure up supernatural firelights and the filming
of some elaborate miniatures, including a map of the
area with flashing lights to show where the firelights
were attacking, an Arizona town under glass, and a
papier-maché mountain for a stop-motion sequence of
firelight disintegrating National Guardsmen, tanks,
and jeeps.
   For the visual effects involving the firelight,
Steve employed a variety of simple but effective
techniques. Charles G. (Chuck) Case II, now a federal
judge in Phoenix, played a love scene with Dede Pisani
in an orange grove. The scene ends with the young
couple being chased by a firelight and Case calling
the police. "The firelight was just a red gel on a
light," Case recalls. "It descended from the trees,
and the illusion was effective. In the film it really
looked like something strange was happening." Arnold
Spielberg explains how Steve showed "the firelight
picking up Nancy. She was crawling along the ground.
He had her crawl from here to a tree, and he timed it
in his head, backed up the film, then re-exposed the
same thing, but with a firelight coming right down to
where Nancy was. In order to get this effect of a
whirling piece of flame, of energy, he took two glass
plates and a red gel and put Vaseline between the
plates. Sue or Anne would take the plates and pull
them back and forth, and that would make the jelly
wiggle and move, and then he'd film through it. If you
imagine a bunch of clouds in fast motion whirling
around, that was his effect of firelight. And it came
out! It looked like it took her and she disappeared."

   "I was intrigued by the contraptions [Steve]
dreamed up," says cast and crew member Warner
Marshall. "The one I remember most vividly was a scene
in his parents' carport. Somebody was sitting on the
hood bouncing the jeep, and he had pullies with a
couple of white Christmas lights--a clothesline of
lights would move past the jeep so it would look like
the jeep was driving in the country passing a house.
He had floodlights shining down on the jeep to make it
look like moonlight. He had a big piece of cardboard
with triangular holes in it that would pass in front
of the light to make shadows. He conceived all that!
It made a heck of an impression on me when I was 15
years old--this guy really knew what he was doing. But
he didn't exude an air of a guy who knew exactly where
he was going and what he was doing. He was humble and
kind of quiet."
   Perhaps the most remarkable visual effect was
Steve's use of a series of quick lap dissolves in
showing the attack of the firelight on a UFO expert
played by Lucky Lohr. "He collapsed on the floor and
we filmed him disintegrating," makeup artist Jean
Weber Brill recalls. "We filmed the scene in the
Spielbergs' front room. Steve had the camera on a
tripod and we filmed about eight frames at a time,
then we would change the setup and the makeup and film
another eight frames. We did that all day long." "They
had red and brown makeup and wet Kleenex on my face,"
Lohr remembers. "I had a cold at the time, so I was
shivering. I thought I was being a real trouper. At
the end of the scene, Steve pulled out a plastic
skull, moved me out, set the skull down, and shot a
couple of frames of the skull." Spielberg redid that
scene at the end of "Raiders of the Lost Ark," when
the blazing light from the Ark of the Covenant hits a
Nazi and disintegrates him right down to his skull.
   Throughout the protracted making of "Firelight,"
even when the two actors originally cast in the lead
roles (Carol Stromme and Andy Owen) quit after the
first two weeks of shooting, Spielberg did not become
discouraged. He recast those parts with Beth Weber and
Bob Robyn and reshot the opening scenes in December.
"I remember the energy level starting to flag, people
starting to wonder, `Gee, do I want to spend my entire
Saturday doing this?,'" says Warner Marshall. "He was
having a great time. He'd say, `I want to get this one
last thing. Would you mind staying?' He was extremely
gracious. He created an atmosphere where everybody had
an affectionate respect for him."
   "It was a huge undertaking," marvels Spielberg's
classmate Rick Cook, who now writes science-fiction
novels. "He wrote a professional-looking script, he
had to be the production manager, he had to scare up
props, he had to convince actors to be in it--although
that wasn't too hard--he had to juggle everything. He
was the damnedest promoter. He knew how to get things
out of people, and he did it without being pushy or
obnoxious. He was not a braggart, he was not one who
would talk about what he was going to do. He just did
it. He knew what he wanted, he was young and kind of
attractive, and it was a matter of enthusiasm and
dedication being contagious."
   Betty Weber, whose daughters Beth and Jean worked
on "Firelight," was a volunteer stage manager at the
nonprofit Phoenix Little Theatre. She cajoled the
theatre's board members into donating their facilities
for the premiere. She also barraged the local
newspapers and radio stations with announcements about
the young filmmaker, arranged for photo spreads in the
Republic, and made sure the title of "Firelight" was
displayed on billboards at businesses all over town.
  Leading lady Beth Weber typed and mimeographed the
programs distributed to the opening-night audience.
The limousine that brought Steve and his actors to the
theatre was supplied and driven by a cast member's
father who owned a local brewery. The searchlight was
borrowed from a nearby shopping center. Arnold
Spielberg helped Steve play the complicated
sound-track for the movie, and Leah Spielberg climbed
a ladder to put the title of her son's first feature
on the marquee. As she did so she was thinking, "This
is a nice hobby."
  That triumphant evening in March 1964 marked a
coming of age for Steve Spielberg. His debut as a
feature film-maker was also his farewell to his
boyhood years in Arizona. The day after the premiere,
he and his family moved to California. Before leaving,
Spielberg told a local reporter that making movies
"grows on you. You can't shake it...I want to write
movie scripts, but I like directing above all. All I
know for sure is I've gone too far to back out now."

Adapted by the author from Joseph McBride's "Steven
Spielberg: A Biography," published by Simon &
Schuster. Photos pgs. 11-14 are from the book,
courtesy Simon & Schuster.

From: KRandle993@aol.com

Subject: Re: [UFORL] The Birth of the 'Greys'

Good Morning -

>It's clear that detailed notes from a sequence of interviews was
>important. How important do you think continued interviews, perhaps
>years later, are to illuminating the original event?

For those of us who read history, we're bombarded with articles and books
written years after an event in which the participants recall that event. We
accept this testimony as accurate, rarely questioning the views of those
who claimed to have been there.

I have an article coming out in MHQ (The Quarterly Journal of Military
History) about the claim that Davy Crockett surrendered at the Alamo. Most
of this claim is based on a document that surfaced in 1956. It was the diary
of one of Santa Anna's officers but is relevant to us because the forensic
evidence suggests it is a hoax. Faked documents plague the UFO field,
but seem to plague history as well. This means that we must continually
evaluate the information as we search for the truth.

We also have an opportunity to study how memories of traumatic events
are stored in the human brain. Within days of the sinking of Titanic, many of
the survivors were called to testify in front of an American investigation.
And
I mean days. The survivors were pulled from the lifeboats on Monday and by
Friday they were telling their stories in front of the Senate investigation.
And,
then, over the years, they provided to reporters and historians, their
memories
of what happened that night. It would be interesting to see how the stories
evolved over time, if they did evolve, and how that evolution might color our
impressions of that night.

The article I did for IUR looked at one UFO sighting because there were two
witnesses who were not in communication with one another after the event,
we had the drawings made at different times... the first on the night of
the event, and we had the stories as told by both witnesses at a later date.
One claim went from bright lights in the distance to a domed disk with
occupants and that evolution didn't take long. This is illustrative
because it tells us that the mind sometimes adds details that weren't
observed originally and that complicates our search.

All this is relevant to the Hill case because the story as we have come to
understand it was not given to us within days, but evolved over a period of
years and was complicated by the nightmares of Betty and the use of
hypnosis. And this means we must be very careful as we study events from
the past.
KRandle

y1.html</A><BR><BR>I'd
 love top see a photo of the
aliens!<BR><BR>Chris<BR><BR>Firelight<BR><BR>The
 date was March 24, 1964. The movie was<BR>"Firelight." Its production cost was
 under $600, and<BR>it was the first feature-length film written
 and<BR>directed by a high school junior named Steven<BR>Spielberg. After
 becoming a professional filmmaker,<BR>Spielberg publicly disparaged
 "Firelight" as "one of<BR>the five worst films ever made anywhere." But
 his<BR>extraordinary promise was obvious to everyone who<BR>attended the
 Phoenix premiere of the 8mm production.<BR>"`Firelight' is just as good,
 although this may be<BR>construed as criticism, as some of the
 science-fiction<BR>movies seen by the late-late television viewers,"<BR>wrote
 Arizona Journal reviewer Larry Jarrett. "The<BR>plot, the action, the basic
 material of the movie, is<BR>sound and not as far out as some of
 Hollywood's<BR>fantasies-de-science." <BR>&nbsp;&nbsp; Allen Daviau, the
 cinematographer who has shot such<BR>Spielberg films as "E.T.--The
 Extraterrestrial," "The<BR>Color Purple," and "Empire of the Sun," was
 shown<BR>"Firelight" by Spielberg in the late 1960s. "It's what<BR>you expect
with a kid's film, the acting and so on,<BR>but oh, God! Some of it was so
audacious," Daviau<BR>says. "The effects were what was
really<BR>amazing--that's what his heart was in. What he did<BR>with crumpled
aluminum foil and bits of Jello on a<BR>kitchen table was pretty
amazing."&nbsp; <BR>&nbsp;&nbsp; The stimulus for "Firelight" was an
unidentified<BR>flying object Spielberg did not see when he was<BR>growing up
in Phoenix. Fascinated by heavenly lights<BR>ever since the night in 1957 when
he and his father<BR>saw a meteor shower in the desert, Steve,
like<BR>virtually every American boy growing up in the '50s,<BR>was intrigued
by reports of flying saucers and other<BR>UFO's. He longed for the real
thing--the chance to see<BR>a UFO with his own eyes. So he was devastated when
he<BR>missed a Boy Scout outing, "the only overnight I<BR>missed the entire
year. Wouldn't you know," and his<BR>fellow Scouts came back and told him how,
at midnight<BR>in the desert, they all saw "something they
couldn't<BR>explain...a blood-red orb rising up behind some<BR>sagebrush,
shooting off into space. I felt so left out<BR>not being there." Patrol leader
Bill Hoffman says,<BR>"One overnight Spielberg was absent out in the
desert.<BR>I don't recall who did it, but the story was told to<BR>Spielberg
that someone had seen a flying saucer.<BR>Spielberg was very interested. It
wasn't true at all.<BR>As far as I can tell, it was a complete fabrication."
<BR>&nbsp;&nbsp; Steve's 67-page, fully dialogued screenplay
for<BR>"Firelight" was completed in early 1963, near the end<BR>of his
sophomore year at Arcadia High School. He spent<BR>about six months shooting
the film, from June through<BR>December of that year, with collaborators
recruited<BR>from his fellow actors and crew members in "Guys and<BR>Dolls"
and other school plays. Postproduction,<BR>including post-synchronization of
dialogue and<BR>recording of a musical score, continued until the<BR>March
premiere. "I used the high school band to score<BR>[the] movie," Spielberg
recalled. "I played clarinet<BR>and wrote a score on my clarinet and then had
my<BR>mother [who played piano] transpose it to her key. We<BR>made sheet
music, the band recorded it, and I had my<BR>first original soundtrack."&nbsp;
<BR>&nbsp;&nbsp; Spielberg had been making amateur films since he<BR>was 10
years old; his mother proudly called him "Cecil<BR>B. DeSpielberg."
"Firelight" was his first film with<BR>trained actors and a carefully detailed
screenplay,<BR>and he had not yet developed into much of an
actor's<BR>director. But his innate narrative sense, his<BR>precocious flair
for visual storytelling, and his<BR>already evident ability to orchestrate
complex<BR>movement and character interaction (as outlined in the<BR>script)
made "Firelight" a gripping, well-constructed<BR>(if overlong) yarn about a
small group of scientists<BR>investigating mysterious red, white, and blue
balls of<BR>moving light coming from the Arizona sky to abduct<BR>people,
animals, and objects. <BR>&nbsp;&nbsp; "Close Encounters of the Third Kind,"
Spielberg's<BR>1977 sci-fi masterpiece, "was actually a remake
of<BR>`Firelight,'" says Jean Weber Brill, a Spielberg<BR>classmate who did
the makeup for "Firelight." "There<BR>were scenes in `Close Encounters' that
were almost<BR>direct copies from `Firelight,' such as the lights<BR>appearing
on the highway and the scene when the little<BR>boy looks out the door at the
bright light. The<BR>storyline of `Close Encounters' was very similar,
but<BR>obviously rewritten and more sophisticated." <BR>&nbsp;&nbsp;
"Firelight" introduces the themes of supernatural<BR>intruders, suburban
 alienation and escape, broken<BR>families and abducted children, scientific
 adventure,<BR>and spiritual renewal that would become familiar
 in<BR>Spielberg's mature work. But unlike "Close<BR>Encounters," which
 radically departed from sci-fi<BR>movie tradition to depict its
 extraterrestrials as<BR>benign rather than menacing, "Firelight" derives
 in<BR>large part from the mood of anxiety and paranoia that<BR>characterized
 the genre in the 1950s, when Spielberg<BR>became hooked on sci-fi. "It was a
 Cold War movie,"<BR>says cast member Clark (Lucky) Lohr. "They talk
 about<BR>it being his [first] version of `Close Encounters,'<BR>and it was, in
 a sense--a sky movie, about sky<BR>gods--but the `cinematic vision' of
 `Firelight' owed<BR>more to horror movies about aliens dusting humans."&nbsp;
 <BR>&nbsp;&nbsp; Arnold and Leah Spielberg bankrolled the production<BR>of
 their son's first feature. "Steve's parents were<BR>totally behind the film,"
 Jean Weber Brill remembers.<BR>Leah not only kept the cast and crew supplied
 with<BR>snacks, but cheerfully put up with "constant commotion<BR>at her
home"
 weekend after weekend, the Arizona<BR>Republic reported in a feature about the
 production.<BR>She even allowed Steve to set up a flashing red light<BR>by the
 carport door to signal the neighbors to keep<BR>quiet while filming was in
 progress. People in Phoenix<BR>still speak in awestruck tones of how Spielberg
 talked<BR>his way into shooting scenes for "Firelight" at<BR>Baptist Hospital
 and Sky Harbor Airport, using an<BR>actual jet plane. But much of the film was
 shot in and<BR>around the Spielberg home at 3443 North 49th Street in<BR>the
 city's Arcadia neighborhood, with the family<BR>carport used as a studio for
 both interior and<BR>"exterior" shots. The summer shooting mostly
 took<BR>place at night, because of the heat. After school<BR>resumed, Steve
 had to film mostly on weekends. <BR>&nbsp;&nbsp; Arnold Spielberg, a pioneer
 in the field of<BR>computer engineering and himself a longtime
 amateur<BR>filmmaker, helped on many of his son's early films.<BR>For
 "Firelight," Arnold rigged the lights for scenes<BR>filmed in the carport,
 helped design miniature sets,<BR>and built a dolly for the elaborate tracking
 shots<BR>that were already a hallmark of the Spielberg visual<BR>style. Steve
 enlisted his three younger sisters, Anne,<BR>Sue, and Nancy, into the
 production as well. Anne<BR>served as a script supervisor, Nancy played the
 key<BR>role of a little girl abducted by aliens, and all<BR>three of them
 bounced up and down on the hood of the<BR>jeep inside the carport to make the
 jeep look like it<BR>was speeding through the desert night around
 Camelback<BR>Mountain. <BR>&nbsp;&nbsp; Steve and Arnold gave the
shoestring
 production the<BR>illusion of a Hollywood spectacle with
 ingeniously<BR>designed visual effects. These included optical tricks<BR>to
 conjure up supernatural firelights and the filming<BR>of some elaborate
 miniatures, including a map of the<BR>area with flashing lights to show where
 the firelights<BR>were attacking, an Arizona town under glass, and
 a<BR>papier-maché mountain for a stop-motion sequence of<BR>firelight
 disintegrating National Guardsmen, tanks,<BR>and jeeps. <BR>&nbsp;&nbsp; For
 the visual effects involving the firelight,<BR>Steve employed a variety of
 simple but effective<BR>techniques. Charles G. (Chuck) Case II, now a
 federal<BR>judge in Phoenix, played a love scene with Dede Pisani<BR>in an
 orange grove. The scene ends with the young<BR>couple being chased by a
 firelight and Case calling<BR>the police. "The firelight was just a red gel on
 a<BR>light," Case recalls. "It descended from the trees,<BR>and the illusion
 was effective. In the film it really<BR>looked like something strange was
 happening." Arnold<BR>Spielberg explains how Steve showed "the
 firelight<BR>picking up Nancy. She was crawling along the ground.<BR>He had
 her crawl from here to a tree, and he timed it<BR>in his head, backed up the
 film, then re-exposed the<BR>same thing, but with a firelight coming right
 down to<BR>where Nancy was. In order to get this effect of a<BR>whirling piece
 of flame, of energy, he took two glass<BR>plates and a red gel and put
 Vaseline between the<BR>plates. Sue or Anne would take the plates and
 pull<BR>them back and forth, and that would make the jelly<BR>wiggle and move,
 and then he'd film through it. If you<BR>imagine a bunch of clouds in fast
 motion whirling<BR>around, that was his effect of firelight. And it
 came<BR>out! It looked like it took her and she disappeared."
 <BR><BR>&nbsp;&nbsp; "I was intrigued by the contraptions
[Steve]<BR>dreamed
 up," says cast and crew member Warner<BR>Marshall. "The one I remember most
 vividly was a scene<BR>in his parents' carport. Somebody was sitting on
 the<BR>hood bouncing the jeep, and he had pullies with a<BR>couple of white
 Christmas lights--a clothesline of<BR>lights would move past the jeep so it
 would look like<BR>the jeep was driving in the country passing a house.<BR>He
 had floodlights shining down on the jeep to make it<BR>look like moonlight. He
 had a big piece of cardboard<BR>with triangular holes in it that would pass in
 front<BR>of the light to make shadows. He conceived all that!<BR>It made a
 heck of an impression on me when I was 15<BR>years old--this guy really knew
 what he was doing. But<BR>he didn't exude an air of a guy who knew exactly
 where<BR>he was going and what he was doing. He was humble and<BR>kind of
 quiet." <BR>&nbsp;&nbsp; Perhaps the most remarkable visual effect
 was<BR>Steve's use of a series of quick lap dissolves in<BR>showing the attack
 of the firelight on a UFO expert<BR>played by Lucky Lohr. "He collapsed on the
 floor and<BR>we filmed him disintegrating," makeup artist Jean<BR>Weber Brill
 recalls. "We filmed the scene in the<BR>Spielbergs' front room. Steve had the
 camera on a<BR>tripod and we filmed about eight frames at a time,<BR>then we
 would change the setup and the makeup and film<BR>another eight frames. We did
 that all day long." "They<BR>had red and brown makeup and wet Kleenex on my
 face,"<BR>Lohr remembers. "I had a cold at the time, so I was<BR>shivering. I
 thought I was being a real trouper. At<BR>the end of the scene, Steve pulled
 out a plastic<BR>skull, moved me out, set the skull down, and shot a<BR>couple
 of frames of the skull." Spielberg redid that<BR>scene at the end of "Raiders
 of the Lost Ark," when<BR>the blazing light from the Ark of the Covenant hits
 a<BR>Nazi and disintegrates him right down to his skull. <BR>&nbsp;&nbsp;
 Throughout the protracted making of "Firelight,"<BR>even when the two actors
 originally cast in the lead<BR>roles (Carol Stromme and Andy Owen) quit after
 the<BR>first two weeks of shooting, Spielberg did not become<BR>discouraged.
 He recast those parts with Beth Weber and<BR>Bob Robyn and reshot the opening
 scenes in December.<BR>"I remember the energy level starting to flag,
 people<BR>starting to wonder, `Gee, do I want to spend my entire<BR>Saturday
 doing this?,'" says Warner Marshall. "He was<BR>having a great time. He'd say,
 `I want to get this one<BR>last thing. Would you mind staying?' He was
 extremely<BR>gracious. He created an atmosphere where everybody had<BR>an
 affectionate respect for him." <BR>&nbsp;&nbsp; "It was a huge undertaking,"
 marvels Spielberg's<BR>classmate Rick Cook, who now writes
 science-fiction<BR>novels. "He wrote a professional-looking script, he<BR>had
 to be the production manager, he had to scare up<BR>props, he had to convince
 actors to be in it--although<BR>that wasn't too hard--he had to juggle
 everything. He<BR>was the damnedest promoter. He knew how to get
things<BR>out
 of people, and he did it without being pushy or<BR>obnoxious. He was not a
 braggart, he was not one who<BR>would talk about what he was going to do. He
 just did<BR>it. He knew what he wanted, he was young and kind
 of<BR>attractive, and it was a matter of enthusiasm and<BR>dedication being
 contagious." <BR>&nbsp;&nbsp; Betty Weber, whose daughters Beth and Jean
 worked<BR>on "Firelight," was a volunteer stage manager at the<BR>nonprofit
 Phoenix Little Theatre. She cajoled the<BR>theatre's board members into
 donating their facilities<BR>for the premiere. She also barraged the
 local<BR>newspapers and radio stations with announcements about<BR>the young
 filmmaker, arranged for photo spreads in the<BR>Republic, and made sure the
 title of "Firelight" was<BR>displayed on billboards at businesses all over
 town. <BR>&nbsp;&nbsp; Leading lady Beth Weber typed and mimeographed
 the<BR>programs distributed to the opening-night audience.<BR>The limousine
 that brought Steve and his actors to the<BR>theatre was supplied and driven by
 a cast member's<BR>father who owned a local brewery. The searchlight
 was<BR>borrowed from a nearby shopping center. Arnold<BR>Spielberg helped
 Steve play the complicated<BR>sound-track for the movie, and Leah Spielberg
 climbed<BR>a ladder to put the title of her son's first feature<BR>on the
 marquee. As she did so she was thinking, "This<BR>is a nice hobby."
 <BR>&nbsp;&nbsp; That triumphant evening in March 1964 marked a<BR>coming
of
 age for Steve Spielberg. His debut as a<BR>feature film-maker was also his
 farewell to his<BR>boyhood years in Arizona. The day after the premiere,<BR>he
 and his family moved to California. Before leaving,<BR>Spielberg told a local
 reporter that making movies<BR>"grows on you. You can't shake it...I want to
 write<BR>movie scripts, but I like directing above all. All I<BR>know for sure
 is I've gone too far to back out now."<BR><BR>Adapted by the author from
 Joseph McBride's "Steven<BR>Spielberg: A Biography," published by Simon
 &amp;<BR>Schuster. Photos pgs. 11-14 are from the book,<BR>courtesy Simon
 &amp; Schuster.

Is this a fair characterisation, or am I simply not reading the
right reports?

STRANGE HAPPENINGS ON THE EARTH ENERGY SYSTEM

Black Spirals, Ill Health and Apparitions

"The lodestone causes mental disorders, makes people
melancholic and is often fatal. With a sort of fumes
it can greatly affect the mind."

WILLIAM GILBERT, DE MAGNETE, 16oo

Earth energies play a part in phenomena of various types. The
apparitions, poltergeists and strange phenomena with which i have
been involved seem to be broadly divided into three categories:

1 Holograms, where the image of a person or object is captured in
crossing energy leys.

2 Earth energy spirals (blind springs), where spirits appear to be
trapped.

3 Hallucinatory experiences caused by telluric spirals, 'hot spots'
from modern electrical sources, natural Earth and seismic energies
(including outgassing (the releasing of gas) from the planet).

The first, the hologram, is an automatic repeat performance of an
event. The second is where an apparition sometimes shows awareness.
The third, the hallucinatory experience, may be caused by an input
of external extremely low frequency (ELF), radio frequency or
microwave energy into the brain, causing the temporal lobes to
produce powerful hallucinatory images. These, and seismic energies
and outgassing, will be discussed in more detail in later chapters.

p. 172

Earlier I explained how leys were formed from standing stones
situated on 'hot spots' directly above at least two veins of water
crossing underground at different depths. Energy from a vein,
fissure or pipe, is emitted vertically to the surface. There are
also two other waves, at an angle of 45º on each side, which
together form three parallel lines on the surface, down the length
of the vein. The centre line is the centre of the interconnecting
spirals and the width of the spirals is determined by the outside
lines. The spirals may be healthy (white spirals) or unhealthy
(black spirals), depending upon the subterranean rock and other
factors. The distance from the centre line directly above the water
to the outer parallel is the same as the depth of the vein (see
Figure 61). This is used by water diviners to gauge the depth of
subterranean water sources.

When some types of ley comprising individual vertical waves
(overgrounds) encounter the outside of such a spiral, they
automatically tune into its centre, giving a powerful 'hot spot' A
few decades ago, these overgrounds were mainly natural and the
spirals were comparatively weak, but in this modern age we
have 'artificial leys' from other sources: nuclear submarines and
missile stores, radar stations, microwave towers, television
repeater stations, electric sub stations and power station
generators, for example. In addition, we have an increasing amount
of disturbed Earth energies from quarrying, deep mining and in
particular open cast coalmining (oil drilling may also be bad,
judging from a conversation with an oil rig employee). These
activities create micro seisms and draw unhealthy sub surface Earth
currents to the surface and on their journey across country to
eventually earth themselves, perhaps in a quarry, they focus on the
centre of black spirals. Basically, the more electricity we use and
the more we disturb the planet, the more powerful these telluric
spirals, both black and white, become.

p. 173

Living, and especially sleeping, above a subterranean fissure
emitting such vortices can have a profound effect on our brainwave
patterns, as you can readily observe in Figure 62. The top scan was
taken in the clinic of a complementary practitioner and shows the
normal electroencephalograph readout of a patient. Knowing about
geopathic stress, the practitioner took another EEG, this time with
the patient lying on his bed, below which a water diviner had
previously discovered an underground stream. The lower scan is the
result. As can be seen, the difference is marked, to say the least,
and anyone sleeping in such a place will suffer depressed brainwave
activity which can only result in an eventual illness, as one of the
purposes of sleep is to enable the body to repair cellular damage.
The patient's wife, not surprisingly, had ME.

....................

p. 180
CAUGHT IN A BLACK HOLE

1 have already mentioned the powerful energy ley which runs from
Comrie's Braefordie standing stone down Crieff High Street to two
standing stones in tandem, one at Aberuffiven and the other at
Dunning. This also passes through Crieff 's old parish burial ground
(see Figure 54). A local lady, walking past this disused burial
ground with her husband, suddenly found herself enveloped in almost
pitch darkness, even although it was a bright November afternoon.
Terrified, she could just see in front of her a young girl, aged
about eight, whom she instinctively knew was herself (she had had a
frightening experience at this age). Eventually, after about five
minutes, she managed to free herself and walked through into the
light again, to find her husband walking a few yards in front of her
as if nothing had occurred. When she asked him what had happened he
was quite puzzled he had noticed nothing at all. Time, apparently,
had stood still for her in these few minutes.

When I checked the site of this occurrence I found that not only had
she been on the Braefordie/Dunning energy ley, but also that she had
been standing above one of the many underground streams which run
under this hill town.

Another surprise was in store for me when 1 checked her house
there was a black spiral in her bed, at her head. Sleeping under the
influence of this black spiral for some eight years, she could well
have become hypersensitive to such unhealthy energies, and walking
into an even more powerful spiral from the underground stream next
to the old parish burial ground could have triggered the
hallucination, which to her was very real.

Another fact which may be relevant is that the burial ground had
recently been landscaped using heavy machinery and the gravestones
removed to the side, which might conceivably have disturbed
something who knows what?

Four months later, the lady was still in a state of shock and spent
much of her time in her house lying on a settee, crying. Shortly
after I had shown her what had happened and referred her to others
who had shared a similar experience, she recovered.

It is an intriguing possibility that people who believe they have
been abducted by aliens or suffer other phenomena of a bizarre
nature might also be under the influence of nature's energies, the
event itself taking place not necessarily in bed, where they may
have been sensitised to these malevolent energies, but at another
power point elsewhere which they happen to walk into at the wrong
time.

Jim,

Will 'Creation Scientists' ever be dissuaded from their beliefs,
any more than the mainstream of those who populate 'ufology' can
be persuaded their convictions in hoaxed 'flying saucer'
photographs, escalating bogus 'MJ-12 documents', 'paranormal crop

and 'non-existence'?

hope there's 'more to life than we know - certainly greater than

nationwide broadcast declared, "except for space travel,
actually, we know no more than you do...".

If, 'nothing in it for me...' how many would be interested... or
would switch over to the live game on the sports channel?

One of the fascinating things about UFO reports is that they do seem to be
subject to fashions. The definitive report on how fashions in ufology change
and develop has yet to be done, but I think this would be a great subject
for someone with the right knowledge. Of course, the classic case is that of
the saucers - where suddenly the majority of sightings were of saucer-shaped
objects after Arnold was misreported as having seen such things.

From: Mendoza <Horseman@onetel.net.uk>
Date: Mon, 2 Sep 2002 01:56:57 +0100
Subject: Re: [UFORL] The Birth of the 'Greys'


Compliments of the Duke:

At 14:26 +0100 31/08/02, KRandle993@aol.com wrote
(among other things):

>All this is relevant to the Hill case because the story
>as we have come to understand it was not given to us
>within days, but evolved over a period of years and was
>complicated by the nightmares of Betty and the use of
>hypnosis. And this means we must be very careful as we
>study events from the past.

I have been half-following this thread over the last
few days, so apologies if these points have been made
already by someone else.

First, yea bro, and so on: well said Kevin. Second off,
the apparently web-based account that James posted of the
Hill case is a prime example of "evolution". There are
so many errors of detail in that account that it is not
worth anything to anyone wanting to consider the Hill
case dispassionately. John Fuller's book is more reliable,
and that is not very reliable at all in important respects.

For example. Betty Hill wrote to Donald Keyhoe, having
read his book and (a somewhat overlooked fact) various
others and even then, but a few weeks after the sighting-
cum-encounter, remarking that hypnosis might be a way
to discover what had actually happened to her and Barney.
Exactly" "We are considering the possibility of a competent
psychiatrist who uses hypnotism." Fuller suppressed this
sentence, presumably for dramatic reasons. But it reveals
that the idea came from the Hills themselves. This may or
may not tell us something about Betty's attitude when the
couple finally wound up with Doc Simon.

Betty & Barney approached Patrick J. Quirke, M.D. of
Georgetown, Mass., with the same idea in March 1962. He
counselled against hypnosis and suggested that memories
of the events would surface over time. (This is a line
Betty takes today.)

Meanwhile Barney was being treated by a Dr Stephens for
various stress-related symptoms, including an ulcer.
(Ulcers are now known to be caused by bacteria and are
not necessarily psychosomatic in origin.) Acting on a
third party's suggestion - which we have to assume only
reinforced the Hills' own original idea - Barney put the
possibility of hypnosis to Dr Stephens, who passed the
Hills on to Doc Simon. Whatever else is pertinent,
Barney was under massive stress during that period of
time. Consider his career as a civil-rights campaigner
in a state approximately 98% white, for starters...

Simon had used hypnosis to resolve various behavioral
problems exhibited by WW2 combat veterans. His work was
documented by John Huston in "Let There Be Light", made
for the US Army Signal Corps, if memory serves. It is an
extraordinary film, notable for Simon's brusqueness with
his patients. He was not interested in whether or not
they were recalling events accurately, but in evincing
some memory, real or false, that would enable them to
confront their current inadequacies and rise above them.
This is important when considering his role in the Hill
case.

The apparent discrepancy between Barney Hill's initial
account to the USAF of seeing the UFO "some hundreds of
feet away" and his later description of it being within
only 50 feet (yet still using binoculars to view "the
leader" whose gaze so entranced him) is a classic of
ufological ambiguity. The extra distance in the earlier
report *may* be a product of his not wishing to discuss
the UFO's apparent occupants with the USAF. In other
words, he may have been economic with the truth. Thus the
later account may be more accurate. On the other hand it
may be contaminated, tho' innocently, through discussion
with Betty. It is absolutely certain that Barney (despite
Betty's repeated claims to the contrary over the years)
knew of her dreams in detail, for example. I would argue
that his own account of the abduction took off from that
(I do not suggest his account follows hers, but that it
was inspired by it).

The behaviour of the UFO during the first close encounter
is not consistent with *merely* an astronomical sighting,
and there is no reason to suppose (there again, one can't
entirely eliminate the opposite) that an advertising plane
would be flitting around one of the least inhabited parts
of New Hampshire fully lit. The two red lights on the UFO
actually suggest a military lighting configuration - not
impossible, but one does wonder from where and to where
such a plane might have been going (NH is not NM) and why
it would bother to cross Rte 3 just where it did. And so
on. I don't know how to explain the first CE-III, taking
all things into account, tho' I would temperamentally
plump for a prosaic explanation. However, no supporting
evidence exists for one, however one might enjoy speculation.

I can account to my own self-critical satisfaction for
the couple of hours of alleged missing time during the
rest of their journey, having driven the route myself.
Karl Pflock can equally well defend his case for the Hills'
being inordinately slow on that leg of their journey and
thus there being an element of "missing" time. (He's done
that trip too.) We are both agreed that the exact route
the Hills took can no longer be precisely established,
but it may come as a surprise to some to learn that their
deviation from their planned course added perhaps three
miles to their total journey.

It's unlikely anyone would have witnessed their various
stops and starts. This really was a desolate region in
1961, and even today people seem to get abed early. If
the Hills were either abducted, or got lost, but in either
case ended up on Mill Brook Road where Betty now believes
they met the ufonauts, traffic would be non-existent at
that time of night. (The road is a dead end, or as we
say in English, a cul-de-sac.) When Karl and I poked
around up there two years ago, in the middle of the day,
we met *one* passing pick-up truck, whose occupants wanted
to know if we'd stopped because we'd seen a moose.

The argument that there must be something to the Hills'
story because of their (or Barney's) emotional reactions
under hypnosis is not worth pursuing. One of the classic
cases of false (not fake!) emotion under hypnosis is that
of Jane Evans (aka Janet Jones) who shrieked and screamed
while describing horrible scenes from a regressed past
life, but had actually culled her material from a novel.
This was thoroughly documented by Melvyn Harris, as cited
in one of my books (unlike Clark, J., I can't remember
which one). John Mack, whose logic escapes both me and
professional psychologists of my acquaintance, still trots
this discredited argument forth from time to time. It is
bullshit. If you want to give credit to the Hills, there
are better lines of argument to follow.

And finally. The cranially-enlarged anemic "gray" of
current abduction lore did not, as Karl has pointed out,
emerge with the Hill case. There are certain superficial
resemblances in the Hills' aliens, but one has to recall
that even they changed over time (remember those noses).
The "gray" we know today is a crystallization of a floating
folk motif whose roots are in science fiction, as Ed
Stewart has documented and whose evolution Marty Kottmeyer
has pursued in almost painful detail in various notes and
papers, some of which he has published.

In REALL News (try Google) Martin recently also addressed
the little-known issue of Barney's anal rape featuring in
his abduction account, but suppressed in Fuller's book for
reasons of sensitivity. I don't think anyone would go as
far as to claim that that is an event known only to
victims of "alien" intervention. Or would they?

best wishes
Peter B

@ (see Figure 54). A local lady, walking past this disused burial
@ ground with her husband, suddenly found herself enveloped in almost
@ pitch darkness, even although it was a bright November afternoon.
@ Terrified, she could just see in front of her a young girl, aged
@ about eight, whom she instinctively knew was herself (she had had a
@ frightening experience at this age). Eventually, after about five
@ minutes, she managed to free herself and walked through into the
@ light again, to find her husband walking a few yards in front of her
@ as if nothing had occurred. When she asked him what had happened he
@ was quite puzzled he had noticed nothing at all. Time, apparently,
@ had stood still for her in these few minutes.
@
@ When I checked the site of this occurrence I found that not only had
@ she been on the Braefordie/Dunning energy ley, but also that she had
@ been standing above one of the many underground streams which run
@ under this hill town.
@
@ Another surprise was in store for me when 1 checked her house
@ there was a black spiral in her bed, at her head. Sleeping under the
@ influence of this black spiral for some eight years, she could well
@ have become hypersensitive to such unhealthy energies, and walking
@ into an even more powerful spiral from the underground stream next
@ to the old parish burial ground could have triggered the
@ hallucination, which to her was very real.
@
@ Another fact which may be relevant is that the burial ground had
@ recently been landscaped using heavy machinery and the gravestones
@ removed to the side, which might conceivably have disturbed
@ something who knows what?

@ much of her time in her house lying on a settee, crying. Shortly

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Tue, 3 Sep 2002 10:40:49 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] The Birth of the 'Greys'

Of course, you can't prove the Creation vs Evolution question either
way,
in the same way that you can't prove that space aliens don't exist.
There
are 4 reasons why:

1. Evolution as the origin of species is the null hypothesis. Since
random chance is usually the hypothesis that other theories are tested
against, there is nothing to test Evolution against except itself.
Therefore, no proof can exist that shows that Evolution is the origin of
species.

2. You can never prove that something (such as space aliens, or in this
case, God) does not exist.

3. Since God is defined as all powerful, there is no way that you can
prove that God did not arrange everything as it is, just to fool the
"foolish unbelievers" into wasting their time on Evolution. You must
admit, it IS a possibility.

4. Actually, nobody has ever proven the existence of random chance.

So while Evolution is the "Occam's Razor" case of simplicity, it cannot
ever be proven to be true, just as the total absence of alien visitors
on
Earth can never be proved.

However, it does place the burden of proof on those claiming that aliens
have landed, and on those claiming Creation Science. And the test is
nearly the same in each case: They need only one example showing where
the null hypothesis fails.

- In the case of space aliens, all they have to do is produce just one
specimen before the press, for all to see.

- In the case of Creation Science, the Bible says that no proof will be
given to unbelievers until the end. But believers are given the proof
they need (the trouble is, they can't ever prove it to anyone else). So
you will have to either wait until the end of time, or become a
believer,
to find out.

Of course, the problem I have with the Evolutionists is the hate many of
them display toward people who disagree with them. They get very angry
whenever someone speaks up for their right to freedom of religion at the
school board or state house meetings which decide curriculum. In the US,
there is a Constitutional right to freedom of religion. This means that
the schools cannot take sides on any religious question.

Hate is not a scientific mode of argument. So why are the Evolutionists
using hate as a means to get school systems to comply with their
demands?
Are they being scientific when they use hate tactics to try to get their
way? They constantly demand that their unproven belief be allowed in the
schools, but that the opposing Creationist belief be banned. The correct
response is to ban both, since it takes a religious decision to choose
between them.

Usually, hate appears when a minority group wants to impose its beliefs
on the majority, and has no valid argument for doing so. We see it time
and time again, with terrorism (Bloomington Indiana has had about 30
cases of Environmentalist terrorism over the past two years),
disruptions
of government meetings, destruction of the campaign signs of opponents,
and graffiti on public and private property. Environmentalists,
Evolutionists, the Taliban, the anti-war pacifists, homosexual rights
groups, and many other factions display these tactics.

Actually, I can usually tell when a group has no valid argument. That
group
is usually the one disrupting the meeting with boos, name calling, and
attempts to drown out the speaker with noise.

Subject: RE: [UFORL] Over the years

I suggest that you compare the observations of each period to the
science
fiction films which were popular then.

- EM and occupant cases rose after "The Day The Earth Stood Still".

- Disk shaped UFOs started rotating after "Earth vs the Flying Saucers".

- Disk UFOs started looking like upside-down bowls after "The Invaders"
TV show.

- Aliens in different countries looked like the aliens in those
countries'
sci-fi movies and books. Thus, in the late 1950s, we were seeing "people
of the future" with large evolved brains, while in South America, they
were seeing hairy dwarfs come out of their OVNI.

- After "Close Encounters of the Third Kind" and "ET", the grays started
showing up, abductions became popular, and strange UFO shapes started to
be commonly reported.

- After "V", very large UFO sizes started appearing in reports.

@ report *may* be a product of his not wishing to discuss

It's probably more an inability to measure distance.

NOBODY can report accurately the distance of an object in
the sky if it is more than 30 feet (1.2 parking space lengths)
away, UNLESS he knows what the object is, and thus its true
size.

An object 50 feet away is just a little farther away than
two city parking space lengths.

But most people can't even tell (in feet or meters) how far
away something they know about is, even when it's on the
ground. They have never learned to estimate distance except
relative to something else.

I suggest that you compare the observations of each period to the
science
fiction films which were popular then.

- EM and occupant cases rose after "The Day The Earth Stood Still".

- Disk shaped UFOs started rotating after "Earth vs the Flying Saucers".

- Disk UFOs started looking like upside-down bowls after "The Invaders"
TV show.

- Aliens in different countries looked like the aliens in those
countries'
sci-fi movies and books. Thus, in the late 1950s, we were seeing "people
of the future" with large evolved brains, while in South America, they
were seeing hairy dwarfs come out of their OVNI.

- After "Close Encounters of the Third Kind" and "ET", the grays started
showing up, abductions became popular, and strange UFO shapes started to
be commonly reported.

- After "V", very large UFO sizes started appearing in reports.

From: TPrinty@aol.com
Date: Wed, 4 Sep 2002 12:34:27 EDT
Subject: Re: [UFORL] The Birth of the 'Greys'

"There are unexplained cases that defy mundane solutions."

There are also ghost stories, miracles, etc that also defy mundane solutions.
 However, these are not proof that the events occurred as described. It is
the person who has presented such story that is the center of the report and
its weakest link. Any misinterpretation/misrepesentation of what actually
occurred can possibly turn an easily explained case into one that defies
mundane solutions simply because the witness stated something happened that
actually did not. Perhaps RV Jones put it best to interpreting eyewitness
testimony in WWII, "...witnesses were usually right when they said that
something had happened at a particular place, although they could wildly be
wrong about what had happened. "

Recent events with Hickman and Maccabee with the "Lawton Triangles"
demonstrates that UFOlogists tend to be still credulous of a good story which
had a photograph to go with it. This is very similar to the Warminster
experiment conducted in 1970. Sometimes hoaxes are exposed and other times,
they are not. This is all dependent on the hoaxer. Ed Walters is considered a
hoaxer by some and not a hoaxer by others. Does his photographs go into the
column of "unexplained cases" or into probable hoax? Depends on which
UFOlogist you ask. Same thing can be said for the Carp video.

One can never explain away 100% of the cases simply because the best hoaxes
are not easy to uncover and that misperceptions/misrepresentations of what
actually happened can make a case defy explanation.

If UFO cases are as numerous as we are to believe (every week Filer's files
is full of UFO reports and NUFORC reports dozens as well), why isn't there
more solid evidence of their existence? After 50+ years, we are still stuck
with the same basic data that was present at the beginning. Simply put,
people report seeing objects in the sky that can not be routinely explained.
I think the challenge of UFOlogy is to move beyond this simple gathering of
reports (it has not done anything but sell books and magazines) to a more
serious effort of trying to establish the existence of UFOs as an actual
phenomena. The failure of UFOlogy to move beyond this point is their own
undoing. As long as they rely on this "unexplained cases" idea as their
cornerstone of evidence, then it will not move forward in resolving the
issue.

Tim Printy

From: TPrinty@aol.com
Date: Wed, 4 Sep 2002 17:53:16 EDT
Subject: Re: [UFORL] The Birth of the 'Greys'

"Name one"

Off the top of my head, Fatima is a good instance for a "miracle".

"How does this apply to multiple-witness cases with corroborating evidence?"

Exactly what do you define as corroborating evidence? A video of lights in
the sky? What does that prove? All it proves is that there were lights in
the sky. Does it compute the actual size? Mexico city in 1997 supposedly
had multiple witnesses but this was a hoax! For that matter, the 1991 videos
of a UFO during an eclipse seem to be showing Venus for the most part
(interesting that all the astronomers in Mexico city watching the eclipse did
not see the UFO and neither did I from Baja).

"By golly there's definitely something going on up there that science needs
to look at?"

Let's try multiple videos/photographs of the same object at the same time
from different locations that show something other than a light in the sky or
something at the limits of resolution for the recording device. This would
have to be supported by eyewitness testimony all suggesting the same thing.
There have been multiple witness cases, but I have yet to see anybody do a
real bang-up job on investigating them. Nobody seems to be interested in
presenting flight paths, angular size, angular elevations, etc in such
reports of "mass" sightings. This would be the first thing I would think of
doing. Instead we have the witnesses telling us how high it was and how big
it was. A proper investigation would ignore such estimates and go for the
angular sizes and elevations to compute the true size and heights.

"As I say, it may be in the nature of the phenomenon not to leave much in the
way of solid evidence behind. This is true for accepted phenomena such as
ball lightning, for example."

If UFOs are something as transient as ball lightning or some form of
electromagnetic energy that is short-lived but this is not generally the
case. Examining the bluebook files and many of the reports I see in
databases, the phenomena is usually around 3-10 minutes in duration. Also,
it is the popular theory that they are actual physical craft that may be
landing from time to time. These craft should leave physical evidence that
would be convincing. However, even in the most promising physical trace
case, there is nothing to suggest that this was caused by something outside
the earth. If so, such evidence should be presented in a manner that is
better than the MUFON journal/IUR. It should be sent to the appropriate
journal so experts can examine the data and render their opinion. If the
evidence was convincing, then you might get your response that "by golly
something is happening".
Tim Printy

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Thu, 5 Sep 2002 10:49:10 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Best Evidence

Actually, I have seen a UFO, using the real meaning of the term. See the
"Summer 1976" entry on my web page:

http://php.indiana.edu/~lrobins/uforogue.htm

It remains unidentified. All of the other sightings listed were "UFOs"
until I was able to identify them.

Maybe the following experience gave me the tools to be able to identify
objects easier:

- As a kid, I was fascinated by light and optical illusions.

- I have always had a lot of technical experience (I built a working
traffic light at age 13). Look at my page about the record changer I
heavily modified, at http://php.indiana.edu/~lrobins/collaro.htm .

- My brother studied film production in college and asked me for
technical help at that time.

- We study perception where I work.

- For several years, I tutored computer, math, and science to college
students who did not understand them.

Also, if you will notice, in each case, I stayed there and watched the
object until I identified it. In many UFO cases, the observer got
excited or scared, and left the scene before the UFO did.

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Thu, 5 Sep 2002 12:09:02 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] The Birth of the 'Greys'

This year, the Kansas statehouse was surrounded by pickets protesting
the possibility of a law being passed which allows Creationism to be
taught alongside Evolution as an alternate theory. Notice that the
protestors were against Creationism, not for it.

There was a very hateful article in Scientific American earlier this
year, which demanded that all religious beliefs (including Creationism)
be removed from our culture "through education". It also demanded that
Evolution be taught in all public schools (many states rightly don't
teach anything about the origin of life).

You haven't been around here. We have had the following "terror events"
in Bloomington in the last few years:

- At least 10 fires were set at new construction projects. Three new
houses were burned down, because they were built in a watershed. The
Earth Liberation Front (ELF) claimed responsibility for some of these
acts of terror. The FBI is still investigating to find the people
responsible.

- ELF also set fire to the local Republican campaign headquarters.

- A solar collector system was destroyed by persons unknown.

- The Animal Liberation Front set gasoline bombs at a chicken packing
plant. A truck was destroyed, but the other bombs were defused by the
bomb squad before they could go off.

- Democrats accused some Republicans running for School Board of trying
to bring the Bible back into schools. It wasn't true, but the tactic
won the election for the Democrats.

- Demonstrators stormed a school board meeting to protest the fact that
someone had asked that teaching Creationism be placed on the agenda. It
wasn't even on the agenda.

- After a member of a racist religious group went on a killing spree in
1999, all religions were portrayed as "hate groups" by the liberals.
Then
several churches were broken into and vandalized.

- Someone threw food on the windows of all of the vans and SUVs in my
neighborhood.

- Demonstrators totally disrupted a public meeting on extending
Interstate 69 from Indianapolis IN to Evansville IN. Anyone who spoke
in favor of the highway was heckled and not allowed to speak, and one
university official was physically threatened because he spoke in favor
of the highway.

- Christians who were teaching the Bible belief that homosexuality is a
sin were physically attacked, and their materials were stolen and
destroyed.

- Anytime a tree is cut down, a big protest ensues.

- When the chair-throwing Bobby Knight was fired, the students rioted,
destroying property (including a statue in a public fountain), and
battling police.

- Two years later, we won the last regional basketball game at the NCAA.
As a result, rioters destroyed a lot of property and battled police.
Then they screamed about the extra police posted during the next game,
which we lost.

- Someone keeps smashing the windows at our local Starbucks.

- Someone keeps destroying lawn decorations.

- Someone keeps slashing tires on parked cars.

There are people in Bloomington who believe, if you are doing something
that is not "politically correct", that they have the right trespass, to
destroy your property, or to do other nasty things to you. Some of them
are elected officials. They are determined to get their way, or else!

And they want "tolerance" from the rest of us????

@ Exactly what do you define as corroborating evidence? A
@ video of lights in the sky? What does that prove? All it
@ proves is that there were lights in the sky.

Because techniques of videography exist, it doesn't even prove that.
I have two local videos which were faked using ground lights:

One of them shows a hovering UFO. Turning the black level control on
my TV showed me the pole holding up the sodium vapor light. Then I
visited the scene and found that light pole.

The other video was taken through a sheet of glass which was tilted to
reflect ground lights into the camera lens and make them move around.

@ Does it compute the actual size? Mexico city in 1997 supposedly
@ had multiple witnesses but this was a hoax! For that matter,
@ the 1991 videos of a UFO during an eclipse seem to be showing Venus
@ for the most part (interesting that all the astronomers in Mexico
@ city watching the eclipse did not see the UFO and neither did I
@ from Baja).
@
@ "By golly there's definitely something going on up there that
@ science needs to look at?"
@
@ Let's try multiple videos/photographs of the same object at
@ the same time from different locations that show something other
@ than a light in the sky or something at the limits of resolution
@ for the recording device. This would have to be supported by
@ eyewitness testimony all suggesting the same thing. There have been
@ multiple witness cases, but I have yet to see anybody do a real
@ bang-up job on investigating them. Nobody seems to be interested in
@ presenting flight paths, angular size, angular elevations, etc in
@ such reports of "mass" sightings. This would be the first thing I
@ would think of doing.

Oh, great. Now they will try to fake that too.

Of course, there is the problem of synchronizing the witnesses in time.
Two witnesses seeing the same object fly over simultaneously cannot
even provide triangulation information, unless there is some way to
get azimuth and elevation angles from both witnesses from precisely
the same moment. It's hard enough just to get correct angles, let
alone trying to synchronize the angles provided by two witnesses.

The Air Force repeatedly tried to do this in the 1950s with spaced
pairs of askanias (portable theodolites with clocks and clockwork
movie cameras). They NEVER got a fix by triangulation, because at
least one of the following events spoiled every attempt:

- One of the askanias was not properly calibrated to north.
- The wind-up clock in one of the askanias stopped, or was wrong.
- One of the askanias was out of film, or was not assembled.
- The movie camera in one of the askanias was not wound up.
- One of the askania operators was on break, or out of radio contact.
- One of the operators couldn't find the UFO in the sky.
- The operators found and tracked two different objects.
- The UFO was below the horizon of one askania.
- The UFO sighting was where the askanias weren't.


@ Instead we have the witnesses telling us how high it was and how
@ big it was. A proper investigation would ignore such estimates
@ and go for the angular sizes and elevations to compute the true
@ size and heights.

You need two synchronized witnesses to do this. One is not enough.

@ "As I say, it may be in the nature of the phenomenon not to
@ leave much in the way of solid evidence behind. This is true for
@ accepted phenomena such as ball lightning, for example."
@
@ If UFOs are something as transient as ball lightning or some form of
@ electromagnetic energy that is short-lived but this is not generally
@ the case. Examining the bluebook files and many of the reports I see
@ in databases, the phenomena is usually around 3-10 minutes in
duration.
@ Also, it is the popular theory that they are actual physical craft
@ that may be landing from time to time. These craft should leave
physical
@ evidence that would be convincing. However, even in the most promising

@ physical trace case, there is nothing to suggest that this was caused
by
@ something outside the earth. If so, such evidence should be presented
@ in a manner that is better than the MUFON journal/IUR. It should be
@ sent to the appropriate journal so experts can examine the data and
@ render their opinion. If the evidence was convincing, then you might
@ get your response that "by golly something is happening".

The problem is, we really don't have any test for aliens. Someone
thought
up one a few years ago, based upon the idea that materials foreign to
Earth would have isotope ratios different from the ratios found on
Earth.
Then I pointed out that chemical supply houses sell purified isotopes
for
use as markers, and that anyone could buy these, and mix up his own
batch
of material with any isotope ratio he wants.

Even alien DNA is out. With a DNA sequencer, anyone can make up any DNA
chain he wants.

From: Brett Holman <b.holman@physics.unimelb.edu.au>
Date: Fri, 6 Sep 2002 10:12:31 +1000
Subject: Re: [UFORL] The Birth of the 'Greys'

On Thu, Sep 05, 2002 at 01:11:10PM -0500, Robinson, Larry wrote:
> The problem is, we really don't have any test for aliens. Someone
> thought
> up one a few years ago, based upon the idea that materials foreign to
> Earth would have isotope ratios different from the ratios found on
> Earth.
> Then I pointed out that chemical supply houses sell purified isotopes
> for
> use as markers, and that anyone could buy these, and mix up his own
> batch
> of material with any isotope ratio he wants.
>
> Even alien DNA is out. With a DNA sequencer, anyone can make up any DNA
> chain he wants.

"Anyone"? Even if I had such a thing in front of me, I doubt I could
make up any DNA chain I wanted - because I don't know anything about the
subject. (Besides which, why do you think aliens would have DNA? They'd
probably have something which does the same thing, but evolution being
what it is, it's unlikely in the extreme to be identical to terrestrial DNA.)
I suspect it is technically somewhat more involved that you suggest. Ditto for
faking isotope ratios. I can't just manufacture an arbitrary object out
of arbitrary materials, adding in a few different isotopes to fool
investigators. The degree of technical knowledge and equipment
involved makes such a hoax extremely unlikely.

Science may not know what an alien will look like. But it will
know it when it sees it ...

Kevin wrote:

>For those of us who read history, we're bombarded with articles
>and books written years after an event in which the participants
>recall that event. We accept this testimony as accurate, rarely
>questioning the views of those who claimed to have been there.

Kevin,

This is such an excellent point.

>I have an article coming out in MHQ (The Quarterly Journal of
>Military History) about the claim that Davy Crockett surrendered
>at the Alamo. Most of this claim is based on a document that
>surfaced in 1956. It was the diary of one of Santa Anna's
>officers but is relevant to us because the forensic evidence

I recently watched a BBC TV documentary on the mythology of
'Custer's last stand'.

As you may now, aside from the archaeological evidence uncovered
in more recent years, amongst the earliest documented evidence
largely dismissed for a century were accounts from the victorious
Indians. These are now seen to be substantiated by the
archaeological discoveries.

As one writer comments:

"In the past, the recollections and accounts of those Indians,
who were the only survivors of the battle were ignored, if not
distorted, by a biased press. Even more unfortunately, a biased
historical establishment, which should have most vigorously
examined, analyzed, and presented all of the facts, dismissed
Indian accounts as unreliable".

There's obviously no substitute for factual evidence - can
anecdotal testimony ever be considered as unquestionably
trustworthy?
It's especially a huge problem within ufology, where frequently
what are deemed to be founding claims beyond any suspicion, turn
out to be not quite so dependable.

I suppose Glenn Dennis comes to mind, however, on this entire
issue, Roswell arguably merits a case study of its own!


Also highly relevant, particularly as it's regarded by many as
equally 'best evidence of alien visitation and the Government
cover-up', are the Rendlesham forest incidents.

Central to the UFO mystery was Staff-Sergeant Jim Penniston's
story of encountering a small, silent, triangular-shaped craft,
with enigmatic symbols, which he personally examined for some
twenty minutes before it zoomed off into the night sky.

There were apparently two other witnesses and one of them, Airman
1st Class John Burroughs, also went on record, confirming there
were, at least, strange lights', although he never observed a
structured object.

What could be more dependable and credible testimony to a craft
which Penniston avowed was not of this world.


Yet, when I discovered that copies of the witnesses' earliest
statements still existed and had been languishing within case
documents compiled by ufologists in the US, a different picture
emerged.

What had resulted in Penniston's public account becoming so
detached from the reality of events?

The explanation, it seems, was 'regressive hypnosis', during
which he essentially fantasised the story which became a
foundation of the forest UFO encounter.


>All this is relevant to the Hill case because the story as we
>have come to understand it was not given to us within days, but
>evolved over a period of years and was complicated by the
>nightmares of Betty and the use of hypnosis. And this means we
>must be very careful as we study events from the past.

If Penniston's hypnotised 'memories' were a proverbial 'flight of
fancy' and as he was apparently hypnotised not long after the
incident occurred, perhaps it's inherently indicative of the
overall context and that there are sufficient complexities
concerning witness recollections without compromising this
further using 'regressive hypnosis'.

Equally, if Larry Warren's recall of 'secret, alien underground
facilities', etc. at Bentwaters/Woodbridge are factual, then
'regressive hypnosis' - under which these claims surfaced - is an
invaluable investigative tool.

Conversely, if those claims are abject nonsense - same as
reported 'regressed abductee' tales about vats of body parts and
cattle mutes at Dulce underground base - how can any 'regressed
alien abduction' tale be remotely taken seriously?


In hindsight, one reason I had considered Zamora's Socorro
encounter to be a worthwhile historical research case is that the
evidence was so well documented, directly afterwards.


James Easton.
E-mail: voyager@ukonline.co.uk

Subject: Re: [UFORL] The Birth of the 'Greys'

Regarding:

>From: "Jim Speiser" <jimspeiser@yahoo.com>
>Date: Thu, 29 Aug 2002 09:39:55 -0700
>Subject: RE: [UFORL] The Birth of the 'Greys'

Jim wrote:

>I'm not downplaying any one particular cause of
>misidentifications. I'm sure that unfocused binoculars have
>caused quite a few problems in the past, as I'm sure Jupiter has
>been called a UFO many times in the past.
>
>It's the concurrence of all these various explanations that I'm
>questioning. It kinda reminds me of how Creation Scientists
>work. We have a jigsaw puzzle with many pieces missing. Those
>pieces we do have seem to form one picture; but the pieces can
>be rearranged and fit together extremely crudely to form a
>completely different picture. Of course in order to do that you
>have to hammer certain pieces into place.

Jim,

Perhaps an analogy between beliefs that, 'the animals went in two
by two...' and UFOs as proof of ET visitation, is entirely
appropriate.

In both instances, the onus is on believers to provide something
approaching tangible evidence.

And in both cases, if those beliefs are ever proven to be
factual, then the entire scientific and cohesive proof
accumulated during centuries and which has always indicated
otherwise must, unfathomably, especially in relation to the
fossil record, be mistaken.


What _doesn't_ require to be hammered into some comprehensible
form is that 'flying saucers' are borne of a blatantly specious
foundation.

Where are all those reports of 'bat-like' objects which Kenneth
Arnold first alerted the world to, rather than our subsequently
popularised and utterly misconstrued depiction of 'saucer-like'
craft?
There's no shortage of the latter... what became of the former?


"Their bald heads were disproportionately large for their puny
bodies. They had bulging, oversized craniums, a small jaw
structure, and an underdeveloped appearance to their features
that was almost infantile. Their thin-lipped mouths were narrow;
I never saw them open. Lying close to their heads on either side
were tiny crinkled lobes of ears. Their miniature rounded noses
had small oval nostrils.

The only facial feature that didn't appear underdeveloped were
those incredible eyes! Those glistening orbs had brown irises
twice the size of those of a normal human eye's, nearly an inch
in diameter! The iris was so large that even parts of the pupils
were hidden by the lids, giving the eyes a certain catlike
appearance".

It's from the tale of an 'alien abduction', on-board a 'flying
saucer'.

Not exactly plausible, some will conclude.

Although it's not Betty or Barney Hill's story, it does evidently
have some association.

The above, as you may recognise, is from Travis Walton's account:

http://www.traviswalton.com/aliens.html


The Hills' connection...

"Just two weeks prior to Walton's disappearance, NBC-TV aired a
two hour movie featuring the abduction tale of Betty and Barney
Hill. Rogers has acknowledged watching the first portion of the
movie, the portion that detailed the Hills' 'abduction'."

See:

http://www.debunker.com/texts/walton.html


'Regressive hypnosis...' there seem to be differing versions on
whether Walton's 'abduction' story only emerged afterwards.

What is understood to be the true context?

On his web site, Walton states:
"I did not recall any experiences under hypnosis that I could not
remember before. The hypnosis did help me verbalize my experience
in greater detail, without being overwhelmed by anxiety, but did
not help me regain any lost memories".

If this is so, why wasn't, unlike other 'abductees', his trauma
blocked from conscious memory?


The Hills' encounter reportedly occurred on September 19, 1961
and they were not 'regressed' until between January to June 1964.

During those intervening, say, two and a half years, from their
'abduction' by, certainly depicted 'Grey-like' entities and until
that was publicised, we should expect to find other examples of
the 'Greys' activities.

What exists from 19 September 1961 and before the Hills' story
was publicised?


James Easton.
