Once again, let me reiterate my position.

I believe that the residuum of high-strangeness, high-credibility
reports in and of itself constitutes evidence of the existence of
a phenomenon, for which the prosaic explanations thus far proposed
are lacking. I believe the explanations put forth thus far are
trite, over-used, and extremely generalized. "People see what
they want to see" may be good enough for Elvis sightings and
Marian visions, but not for UFO reports, which I consider to be
a couple of orders of magnitude more enigmatic, and therefore
more deserving of a closer look by science. I do NOT favor the
ETH, or any particular hypothesis at all. I just think these
reports should not be happening on such a widespread basis if
the only stimulus is misperception, with the occasional hoax.
>
> And in both cases, if those beliefs are ever proven to be
> factual, then the entire scientific and cohesive proof
> accumulated during centuries and which has always indicated
> otherwise must, unfathomably, especially in relation to the
> fossil record, be mistaken.

I know what you mean in terms of rewriting Evolution, but what
would NECESSARILY have to be re-written if UFOs turned out to
be extra-terrestrial, or...? Some discoveries go against known
science; others merely ADD to our knowledge. Is it not
conceivable that the answer to the UFO question could fall into
the latter category?

>
>
> What _doesn't_ require to be hammered into some comprehensible
> form is that 'flying saucers' are borne of a blatantly specious
> foundation.
>
> Where are all those reports of 'bat-like' objects which Kenneth

> craft?
>

This is one that I have pondered for decades. But recall that
while "flying saucers" started with Arnold, UFOs did not. So-called
"foo-fighters" were sighted before 1947.

>

> bodies. They had bulging, oversized craniums, a small jaw

I do not know Travis Walton well enough at all to comment on his
narrative. I do know Mike Rogers well enough to state fairly
emphatically that a hoax of this magnitude is simply not within
his personality inventory. It would serve absolutely no purpose;
and Mike Rogers is not the sort to arrange something like this
with no purpose. Further, how many people watched that particular
airing of "The UFO Incident," and how long would we they have to
wait after seeing it before they could have an abduction
experience that would not be ascribed to having seen that movie?


> On his web site, Walton states:
>
> "I did not recall any experiences under hypnosis that I could not

>

Unlike SOME other abductees. There are some that recall all the
details of their "experience" without any hypnosis at all. And..
we only have a few minutes out of five days total; perhaps the
most traumatic parts were in fact blocked from his conscious
recall.
Again, this is not necessarily to be construed as a defense of
Walton, it is just to point out that we are far too ignorant of
the situation to dismiss such stories based on the percipients'
differing reactions to their experiences.


>

Are you asking me if there are abduction accounts in between those
years? I'm not certain, but I think there are probably several in
the database that were recalled years after the fact, that fall
into that time period. I would suggest consulting with Hopkins
or Jacobs.

From: "Luis R. Gonzalez" <lrgm@arrakis.es>
Date: Fri, 6 Sep 2002 17:35:41 +0200
Subject: [UFORL] The Birth of the 'Greys'

As part of my project to document the birth of abductions. I have come
acroos a few references that I suspect are to backdated abductions (reported
several years later than occurence). Unfortunately, the author did not
include any reference. Can any of you point me to any original data?

Cases mentioned in "Physiological effects from abductions", John Schuessler,
MUFON UFO Journal #358 (February 1998), pp. 13-14.

Close Encounters followed by an abduction event

1) Woman abducted.- On Octiber 20, 1973, a woman was abducted from a spot
near her car and taken aboard a craft where beings conducted medical tests
on her, including blood tests, skin scrappings and a rectal exam. They
pressed needles into her arms and abdomen. Following the event she suffered
from depression, weight loss and sleep loss.

2) Blood taken in Sweden.- On March 23, 1974, a man was pulled from his car
near Lindholmen, Sweden, by a light beam from a UFO hovering overhead.
Inside he met four beings that caused pain in his cheek by taking blood. He
suffered a loss of time. After the event his wife cleaned the blood from his
face and found a hole in the skin just below his temple.

Abduction Events without a UFO sighting

1) Nebraska girl taken.- On October 7, 1955, a girl was abducted by a small
being from her bedroom in Nebraska. She was placed on a table of silver
metal where the beings took hair and blood samples. It was a painful event.

2) Pregnant woman abducted.- On January 17, 1970, a pregnant woman was
abducted from her home in Westbury, Long Island, NY. She was returned with a
mark on her abdomen like that from an amniocentesis test, marked with a spot
of blood on her gown. The spot on her abdomen was very cold to the touch.
She recalled the smell of ozone.

3) Georgia medical exam.- On December 17, 1971, a woman was abducted from
her home in Forsyth County, GA, and given a medical exam. She heard the
rushing sound of air and felt the coolness of the flooor. Following the
event, she had blisters on the skin, backaches, burns, insomnia, nightmares,
and her eyes were sensitive to light.

4) Idaho abduction.- On June 20, 1977, a woman awoke in her bedroom in Coeur
D'Alene, ID, feeling paralyzed and unable to speak or move. She saw a being
in the room. Suddenly, she was able to move and rushed into the front room
to find two hours had lapsed. She had a severe headache for the next two
days. Under hypnosis she found she had been abducted, had a warm light
placed on her back, was given an examination, and had observed a wheel-like
devide with medical instruments on it.

Any help to locate more information about these cases would be appreciated.

Yours,

Luis R. González Manso

From: Jim Giglio <jgiglio2@polaris.umuc.edu>
Date: Fri, 6 Sep 2002 19:22:18 -0400 (EDT)
Subject: Re: [UFORL] Disclosure Project

On Sat, 7 Sep 2002, Anthony Craig wrote:

> I would like to hear a few opinions on the Disclosure Project.
> Do they have any real evidence?

Here's something on one item of their evidence. You may recall
the May 9, 2001 PR event at the National Press Club. Some 20 or
so "witnesses" from inside the big bad conspiracies got up and
told their stories. One of them, a fellow named Mark McCandlish,
waved a photo around that supposedly showed a genuine UFO. I
almost dropped my teeth when I saw it; it's a well-known fake,
and has been known to be a fake for 34 years. It's the image
investigated by the Colorado project back in 1968
(www.ncas.org/condon/) and reported as Case 7. I leave it to the
reader to enjoy the story of how the faking was uncovered.

For some reason the image was not reproduced in the report. But
in 1995, Roy Craig, the primary investigator of the image, told
the story in his memoir of the project, and reproduced a
black-and-white version of one of the two original color slides.
I contacted Dr. Craig by e-mail and requested that he allow me to
borrow the image for scanning, and for eventual inclusion with
the on-line report. He generously assented, and the image is
currently stored at this URL:

       polaris.umuc.edu/~jgiglio2/major-y/

In pondering this little goof-up, consider that Steven Greer, the
head of the Disclosure Project, claims to be briefing people at
the highest levels of government on matters of absolutely vital
importance to the future of humanity; if he were taken seriously,
his assertions would have earth-shaking consequences in all
aspects of human existence. Given all that, you'd think he'd be a
bit more careful in vetting his "witnesses."

I have more, BTW; I'll dig around a bit and post it.

Date: Mon, 9 Sep 2002 12:39:05 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] The Birth of the 'Greys'


---- [o#o]-[o--o]-[o--o]-[o--o]-[o--o]-[o--o]-[o--o]-[]0000oo> ###

Larry Robinson S/AP/EIS         lrobins@indiana.edu

1025 E 7th St      Rm 112 I voted for gridlock.

-----Original Message-----
From: Jim Speiser [mailto:jimspeiser@yahoo.com]
Sent: Thursday, September 05, 2002 2:42 PMSubject: RE: [UFORL] The Birth of the
'Greys'

@ Larry:

@ Since when is science a "belief system"? I mean, outside of the
"belief"
@ (based on experience) that the scientific method generally works?

@ ==JJS==

@ "That evolution has occurred is a FACT, as demonstrable as the
heliocentric
@ theory of the solar system."

@ --Gould

I'm not from Missouri, but I've been there. So show me anyway.

We don't believe in the Geocentric theory of the Solar System. So why do
we
still say that the sun rises?

Science itself is not a "belief system", except for one little clause in
the
scientific method. That clause is the assumption that no action by any
deity
can change the outcome of an experiment. That assumption means that
science
can never conclude that a deity acted, even if that were actually the
case.

It also means that science can never be used to prove either the
existence or
nonexistence of God, or to decide any religious question. Any use of
science,
as long as it has this assumption, to prove the nonexistence of a deity,
is
the equivalent of using a premise to prove itself. That is an invalid
mode of
argument - faulty logic.

The belief system in the Evolution debate is in the many ASSUMPTIONS
made
by those who say that Evolution is a fact, including the assumption that
no
deity acted. Prove that these assumptions are false, and you prove
Evolution
as the origin of species to be false. Right now, we have no proof either
way.

Situational evolution through natural selection is a proven fact.

What is not proven is Evolution as the origin of all species, because
they
have not proven that NOTHING ELSE HAPPENED. They assume it. Random
chance is
the null hypothesis, and in order to prove the null hypothesis true, you
have to rule out ALL other possibilities - not just the ones the
scientists
happened to think of.

It's a situation similar to the bad argument that, because it wasn't a
bird,
and it wasn't a plane, it has to be Superman (an alien, remember?). In
order
to prove the presence of an alien by the process of elimination, you
would
have to prove that NOTHING else was possible except the alien. And that
"nothing else" includes a lot of things the UFO investigator didn't
think of.

So Evolution as the origin of species is not proven at all, except in
the
minds of those who believe that all of the following assumptions are
true:

- No deity acted to change the world.
- Nothing special happened - just random chance.
- True random chance actually exists (as opposed to pseudorandom events
which
appear to be stochastic only because we don't have all of the
information).
- The evidence found is being interpreted correctly.
- None of the evidence found is misleading.
- There is no other possible cause for the observed evidence.

And for the time scale used (only for those who argue that the time
scale
disproves the account presented in the Bible.):

- Time flow is a linear function.
- The gravitational constant is really a constant over time.
- The speed of light in a vacuum is a constant everywhere in space AND
time.
- The wavefronts from everything seen in space are real.
- The distributions over time of the isotopes used for dating are those
which have been assumed through curve extrapolation.
- Nothing happened to change the distributions over time of dating
isotopes.
- The deposition rates of strata are those assumed.
- Nothing happened to change the deposition rates of strata.
- Stars actually do what astrophysicists think they do.
- No actions by a deity occurred.

Like I said, these are assumptions. We have no real proof that they are
true.
We don't have any proof that they are false either. Evolution represents
the
theory with the highest correlation to the observed data. But
correlation does
not imply causality. Since we can't rule out other possible scenarios,
we
can't conclusively prove Evolution to be the origin of life.

You have to look at the whole scene, not just the picture the
Evolutionists
painted of it.

.

>As stated before, those investigating the case failed to do it right.
Their book is not very informative and I have yet to see anything with
better information available on the case. If I am reading this correctly,
the object was not even a boomerang but a circle of lights. Something
different than the other cases surrounding the Hudson Valley events. You
can't expect him to say it was a spaceship or something else on such
limitied flimsy evidence do you?

Of COURSE not!

>It was only a bunch of lights in a circle against a dark sky.
Which SHOULDN'T BE THERE.

>Nothing more and as a result, he could not draw anything conclusive about
it.

Absolutely, and he was correct not to. But then he dropped it like it was
beneath him or something, and probably went on to study some spot in a
nebula 8 billion light years away...

I'm NOT criticizing him for not coming forth and stating something specious
like, "it was therefore a spaceship." I'm simply saying that I feel we have
made our case to science, and science is saying, "OK, so we don't know what
they are. Now go away and leave us alone."

>>If it is left to us laypeople to fill in this vacuum, then science has no
one to blame but itself for the lack of scientific rigor and the subsequent
encroachment of superstition.

>Might I suggest that UFOlogy take some lessons from amateur astronomy.
There amateurs make meaningful contributions and assist scientific studies
by gathering much needed observational data on things like variable stars,
meteors, comets, etc. Many astronomers do it on their own with no funding
and many spend tens of thousands of dollars out of their own pocket
observing the night sky night after night. These are "laypeople" and they
do make a difference. Can UFOlogists state they doing similar on the same
scale?

Apples and oranges. Astronomy is perhaps the oldest science, ufology a
young proto-science (at its VERY best). It certainly would help if the
"professionals" would promulgate some form of protocol for study of the
problem, and then if (by some miracle) we conduct ourselves according to
said protocol and come up with something interesting, give our data the
thorough review it deserves.

In a previous post, you made a cursory list of data points you would like to
see in connection with a photographic case. In one sense that's very
helpful to us, as long as you are willing to stick to your word and consider
any case that meets those standards. But the problem is, we've been down
this road before. As I stated, Robert Sheaffer once told me that he would
seriously consider any case that involved "multiple independent photographs
of the same anomalous object." I consider the Hudson Valley case to fit
that particular criterion. But now, I am told we have to prove that the
photograph and the video are of the same object, AND provide all manner of
telemetry to go along with it - measurements which Larry Robinson implies
was next-to-impossible for the _USAF_ to obtain. The target has apparently
moved once again. My question: Assuming that the resources of armchair
Ufology are extremely limited, AT WHAT POINT DOES REAL SCIENCE TAKE
OVER?

@ Larry:

@ Since when is science a "belief system"? I mean, outside of the
"belief"
@ (based on experience) that the scientific method generally works?

@ ==JJS==

@ "That evolution has occurred is a FACT, as demonstrable as the
heliocentric
@ theory of the solar system."

@ --Gould

>I'm not from Missouri, but I've been there. So show me anyway.

By the way, I've been told that no one knows the origin of, or reason for,
Missouri being the "Show-Me State."

Please see:

http://www.talkorigins.org/origins/faqs-qa.html


>We don't believe in the Geocentric theory of the Solar System. So why do
we
still say that the sun rises?

You're kidding, I assume.

>Science itself is not a "belief system", except for one little clause in
the
scientific method. That clause is the assumption that no action by any
deity
can change the outcome of an experiment. That assumption means that
science
can never conclude that a deity acted, even if that were actually the
case.

I am not aware of this clause, at least not as you stated it. Perhaps you
mean something like this:
The universe may have both a natural and a supernatural component. Science
is equipped only to study the natural component, and so the interpretation
of any phenomenon should not reference the supernatural. This does not
obviate the possibility of a supernatural component, it merely acknowledges
that such a component is beyond direct observation, and therefore lies
outside the solution set for science. I see nothing wrong with this clause.


>The belief system in the Evolution debate is in the many ASSUMPTIONS
made
by those who say that Evolution is a fact, including the assumption that
no
deity acted. Prove that these assumptions are false, and you prove
Evolution
as the origin of species to be false. Right now, we have no proof either
way.

>Situational evolution through natural selection is a proven fact.

"Situational evolution"? I've not heard that term. Please explain. And,
please explain how it is a "proven fact," given that you do not accept the
assumption that no deities are involved.

What is not proven is Evolution as the origin of all species, because
they
have not proven that NOTHING ELSE HAPPENED. They assume it. Random
chance is
the null hypothesis, and in order to prove the null hypothesis true, you
have to rule out ALL other possibilities - not just the ones the
scientists
happened to think of.

I thought the null hypothesis was the one you didn't have to prove, only
disprove with a single counter example. (Forgive me if that's wrong, I'm no
scientist.)

>It's a situation similar to the bad argument that, because it wasn't a
bird,
and it wasn't a plane, it has to be Superman (an alien, remember?). In
order
to prove the presence of an alien by the process of elimination, you
would
have to prove that NOTHING else was possible except the alien. And that
"nothing else" includes a lot of things the UFO investigator didn't
think of.


>Like I said, these are assumptions. We have no real proof that they are
true.

No science, including kinesiology - whatever the hell that is - could
proceed without assumptions. Should we teach no science at all in school?


>We don't have any proof that they are false either. Evolution represents
the
theory with the highest correlation to the observed data. But
correlation does
not imply causality.

I beg to differ, it implies it, it just doesn't prove it.
In any case, that's as far as Science can ever go, is demonstrate
correlations and draw conclusions therefrom - and conclusions in Science are
ALWAYS tentative. This tentativity should not be a barrier to making
statements such as, "Evolution is by far the most likely cause of
biodiversity."

Subject: Re: [UFORL] The Birth of the 'Greys'

Mr. Budden strikes again!
I can not understand why he thinks that I believe un the ETH. Absolutely
wrong!
I hope his deductive skills are better when talking about EM pollution.

I have never believed in the ETH. I have always considered it a wrong
theory. I sincerely believe that abdcutions (and UFOS) are _only_ a
psychological phenomena, with
iatrogenic componets, and maybe, maybe, EM componets.

But Mr. Budden have to understand that he gives himself a bad methodological
image,
when he offers as an example of his theory a case he can not ascertain was
due to
EM allergy.

For the benefit of the readers, I enclose the review of his latest book
which appeared in EJUFOAS. I am still waiting for real data.

Luis R. González Manso

ELECTRIC UFOS por Albert Budden
Blandford, Londres 1998. ISBN: 0 7137 2730 6 (Tapa dura) 0 7137 2685 7
(Rústica)
Review by Luis R. González Manso. Abril 1999.

For several years, Albert Budden has championed (almost) alone a very
peculiar explanation for the UFO Phenomena (more precisely, about
abductions) which, turning down the ETH, tries also to avoid such a strong
scepticism as considering them hoaxes. His hypothesis: abductions will be
due to an allergic reaction by the witnesses to electromagnetic fields.

More precisely, he proposes that abductees, after suffering during their
formative years a "major electrical event" (lightning strike proximity,
major electrocution, etc.) become hypersensible to environmental
electromagnetic fields (natural or -specially- artificial: pylons, radio
transmitter, etc.) so as, if they live in an electromagnetic "hot spot"
where several field overlap, they can reach a threshold, a load phenomenon
that precipitates hallucinatory states, which are interpreted within an
alien cultural context.

The idea itself has considerable appeal (specially among sceptics, who would
not need to resort so much to hoaxes) and Budden has been able to answer
some of the simpler criticisms. For instance, those incidents happening in
rural areas or before the present time would be caused by natural
electromagnetic fields around faults, etc. Unfortunately, as it is usually
the case, maybe he tries to explain too much, when he applies the same
mechanism to "haunted houses" or "poltergeists", or when he says that the
witnesses themselves become electromagnetic broadcasters.

His methodology presents a different problem. When the investigator visits
the house of the witness with his electromagnetic detector, never fails to
find what he is looking for. When he interviews the witness following a
specially-designed questionnaire, answers are seldom negative. The failure
arises when nobody comments negative results with those same detectors in
the houses of their neighbours, or when the questionnaire does not contains
neutral questions or questions that should be answered in negative. Besides,
the author (whose wife is, precisely, one victim of such "electromagnetic
allergies" and he himself suffered a major electrical incident in his
infancy) resorts to dubious and non-proved Holistic Medicine techniques to
verify his hypothesis, enlists strange experiments based "on the secret
works of Nikola Tesla" to demonstrate the electromagnetic levitation of
non-ferrous materials (always outside the camera), or goes through all the
medical vademecun looking for an electromagnetic explanation for a symptom,
whose cause could be much more simpler.

All this leads him to suspect a terrible "cover-up" by the scientific
establishment in order to prevent the bankruptcy of the telecommunication
and energy industrial complex. Somewhere along this way a good idea full of
promises to explain part of this many-sided phenomena has slipped again. I
will recommend a careful lecture of this book in order to design experiments
which could help us to determine how much truth is in it.
.

Jim:

I doubt that ultralights are the cause of all of the Hudson Valley
sightings, but once people start looking for UFOs, they see them.
Stewart Air Force Base was going full blast back then with C5As
and lots of other stuff supporting Fort Drum New York, etc. This
pilot described to me how they began with dusk flying and after
they were reported as UFOs, started to try some deliberate hoaxing.

He said they first tried to coordinate the turning on and off spots
they carried with walkie talkies, but soon realized this was hard
to do. It turned out to just look better without this: the leader would
turn his light out first, then most everybody else, and then there
always was somebody who turned off the light last. This resulted
in a very neat saucer "zooming" away into space. He said if you
want to see a hovering UFO, you ought to see us in a great big
circle suddenly turning on our spots. Then he roared with
laughter.

They finally stopped because they feared they might be blamed for
traffic accidents because thousands were stopping during rush hour
to look at their hijinks. This lasted for several years.

I have personally seen such a formation here at Harrisburg and although
after looking at it from a distance in twilight I saw stars moving through
the formation so knew it was seperate planes, but couldn't hear
anything. Later after meeting the pilot he confirmed that there was a
ultra light flying club operating out of a small local field. I had also
investigated another such case a couple years before which had puzzled
me although I had concluded at the time that it possibly was geese
illuminated by streetlights. He confirmed that it probably was his club.

Some facts about ultra-light aircraft in the US:
1. They fly at less than 63 miles per hour. This is true airspeed, plus or
minus the wind speed. Sometimes they appear to be (and are almost)
"hovering".
2. The pilots and airplanes, many of which are homemade, are unlicensed,
although they must fly under FAA rules.
3. The planes are too small and fly too slowly to show up on radar displays.
4. Since they usually fly from and return to the same small strip, they
rarely, if ever, file flight plans, but fly under Visual Flight Rules.
5. They usually operate from small, sometimes isolated, rural grass strips,
and not from airports.
6. They have lights for twilight flight, but are not supposed to fly at
night.
7. Unless one is very close, or downwind, motor noises are often not heard.
When they are, they sound like a little buzzing lawn-mower motor, which is
about what they amount to

Clear skies,
Bob Young

@ Subject: RE: [UFORL] The Birth of the 'Greys'
@
@ >We don't believe in the Geocentric theory of the Solar
@ System. So why do we still say that the sun rises?
@
@ You're kidding, I assume.

Stimulating thought. This kind of argument was used to "prove" that the
Bible taught the geocentric theory.

@ >Science itself is not a "belief system", except for one
@ little clause in the scientific method. That clause is the
@ assumption that no action by any deity can change the outcome
@ of an experiment. That assumption means that science can never
@ conclude that a deity acted, even if that were actually the
@ case.
@
@ I am not aware of this clause, at least not as you stated it.
@ Perhaps you mean something like this:
@ The universe may have both a natural and a supernatural
@ component. Science is equipped only to study the natural
@ component, and so the interpretation of any phenomenon should
@ not reference the supernatural.

@ This does not obviate the possibility of a supernatural
@ component, it merely acknowledges that such a component is
@ beyond direct observation, and therefore lies outside the
@ solution set for science. I see nothing wrong with this clause.

There is nothing wrong with the clause itself. But it means that
science can never decide between an Evolutionary origin of life
and an origin of life orchestrated by a deity.

Meaning that neither theory has standing over the other.

@ >The belief system in the Evolution debate is in the many ASSUMPTIONS
@ made by those who say that Evolution is a fact, including the
@ assumption that no deity acted. Prove that these assumptions are
@ false, and you prove Evolution as the origin of species to be false.
@ Right now, we have no proof either way.
@
@ >Situational evolution through natural selection is a proven fact.
@
@ "Situational evolution"? I've not heard that term. Please
@ explain. And, please explain how it is a "proven fact," given that
@ you do not accept the assumption that no deities are involved.

Situational evolution is where the most adapted to a change in the
environment survive. I think that in the future, we may evolve an
opossum that does not stop in the road to get smashed by the first
car to come along.

@ >What is not proven is Evolution as the origin of all species, because
@ they have not proven that NOTHING ELSE HAPPENED. They assume it.
Random
@ chance is the null hypothesis, and in order to prove the null
@ hypothesis true, you have to rule out ALL other possibilities - not
@ just the ones the scientists happened to think of.

@ I thought the null hypothesis was the one you didn't have to
@ prove, only disprove with a single counter example. (Forgive me if
that's
@ wrong, I'm no scientist.)

The null hypothesis can never be proven, because it is usually random
chance. It must be disproved to prove something else. But the ONLY way
to
prove that the null hypothesis is the ONLY true possibility is to
DISPROVE
all other POSSIBLE theories.

That's the hard part.

Take aliens. Try to prove that space aliens do not exist. That is
exactly the same kind of null-hypothesis case as proving Evolution
to be true is. It requires an exhaustive search.

So the null hypothesis is assumed to be true until proven otherwise.
But that does not make it true.
@ No science, including kinesiology - whatever the hell that is - could
@ proceed without assumptions. Should we teach no science at
@ all in school?

The assumptions must be based on something tangible. The problem
with the assumptions used in Evolution is that there are assumptions
that depend upon assumptions which are based on assumptions of
other assumptions.

@ >We don't have any proof that they are false either.
@ Evolution represents the
@ theory with the highest correlation to the observed data. But
@ correlation does not imply causality.
@
@ I beg to differ, it implies it, it just doesn't prove it.

I am using "imply" in the logician's argument sense. Correlation
NEVER implies causality. It implies only that causality is not
impossible.

@ In any case, that's as far as Science can ever go, is demonstrate
@ correlations and draw conclusions therefrom - and conclusions
@ in Science are
@ ALWAYS tentative. This tentativity should not be a barrier to making
@ statements such as, "Evolution is by far the most likely cause of
@ biodiversity."

The above is the method of social science, not the method of physical
science.

Physical science can NEVER draw a conclusion from a correlation,
except that there "may be a causal connection".

This is the same mistake the environmentalists make all the time. They
find a correlation, and go on WITHOUT ANY PROOF to say that one causes
the other. Of course, this is because most environmental science
programs
are parts of social studies departments, not physical science
departments.

The physical scientist must demonstrate causal connections through
experiment, not speculation.

I remind people of the correlation between the disease rickets, and
being in certain families. For years, the scientists believed that
rickets was a hereditary disease. With the discovery of Vitamin D, it
was shown that poverty, not rickets, was inherited.

From: John Burtenshaw <jburtens@bournemouth.ac.uk>
Date: Thu, 12 Sep 2002 11:18:36 +0100
Subject: [UFORL] Gulliver's Travels

Hi All

I was reading Jonathan Swift's Gulliver's Travels the other day and this
passage struck me as the forerunner of modern UFO abduction stories.

I reproduce it complete with the old English spellings.

"I walked a while among the Rocks, the Sky was perfectly clear, and the Sun
so hot, that I was forced to turn my Face from it: When all of a Sudden it
became obscured, as I thought, in a Manner very different from what happens
by the Interposition of a Cloud. I turned back, and perceived a vast Opake
Body between me and the Sun, moving forwards towards the Island: It seemed
to be about two Miles high, and hid the Sun six or seven Minutes, but I did
not observe the Air to be much colder, or the Sky more darkned, than if I
had stood under the shade of a Mountain. As it approached nearer over the
Place where I was, it appeared to be a firm Substance, the Bottom flat,
smooth, and shining very bright from the Reflexion of the Sea below. I
stood upon a Height about two Hundred Yards from the Shoar, and saw this
vast Body descending almost to a Parallel with me, at less than an English
Mile Distance. I took out my Pocket-Perspective, and could plainly discover
Numbers of People moving up and down the Sides of it, which appeared to be
sloping, but what those People were doing, I was not able to distinguish."

Swift goes on to write about how many floors the "island" etc. The next
passage concerns Gulliver's "abduction"

"They made Signs for me to come down from the Rock, and go towards the
Shoar, which I accordingly did; and the flying Island being raised to a
convenient Height, the Verge directly over me, a Chain was let down from
the lowest Gallery, with a Seat fastned to the Bottom, to which I fixed my
self, and was drawn up by Pullies."

Once on board he tells of how the "island" was made to move using a giant
Lodestone.

"By means of this Load-stone, the Island is made to rise and fall, and move
from one Place to another. For, with respect to that Part of the Earth over
which the Monarch presides, the Stone is endued at one of its Sides with an
attractive Power, and at the other with a repulsive. Upon placing the
Magnet erect with its attracting End towards the Earth, the Island
descends; but when the repelling Extremity points downwards, the Island
mounts directly upwards. When the Position of the Stone is oblique, the
Motion of the Island is so too. For in this Magnet the Forces always act in
Lines parallel to its Direction."

Surely this is first mention of anti-gravity propulsion?
It makes interesting reading and does beg the question, "Is this the father
of UFO stories?"

Cheers

John

@ < How certain are we that the age of the earth is what the
@ scientists say it is, since this is also dependent on a
@ large number of assumptions.>>
@
@ I'm not sure, I've not read the literature on the age tests, but
@ I assume that error bars were given.

You assume? Hmmm. The concentration of a radioisotope use for
dating depends on two factors:

1. How long ago the isotope was incorporated into the specimen
under test.

2. The concentration of that isotope in the environment at the time
it was incorporated.

Scientists believe that the concentrations have not changed, so the
differences are due solely to elapsed time and half-lives. But a
low concentration of isotope in a specimen can either indicate that
the specimen formed so long ago, or that the specimen formed more
recently in an environment containing a lower concentration of
isotope.

But have concentrations changed? The truth is, we don't even know
that the concentration function is linear, let alone constant, since
we have absolutely no data on rates of isotope formation in the
time before Geiger counters and cyclotrons. We don't even know if
the concentrations of radioisotopes ran at a constant rate,
increased linearly over time, increased suddenly, or followed some
other function. The ASSUMPTION is that the availability of new atoms
of the dating isotopes was always the same. That assumption is in
turn based on an assumption that cosmic radiation reaching Earth was
always at the present levels. Which is based on more assumptions in
the current theories of astrophysics.

investigation.

- If you use Creationism, then you can't make the test because

they raised their eyebrows but began to wonder if the whole thing was faked.

"Chances are it would not have reached Hibbs."

I don't think so. Plenty of UFO films and photographs have reached
scientists/analysts through the years. Who was acting as the gatekeeper and
would Hibbs know if he was trying to be hoaxed or not? A scientist is not
going to pronounce something genuine. Again, the video was insufficient for
him to make some form of grand proclamation. It was just a video of a circle
of lights in the dark sky.

"No, I think it meets Sheaffer's criteria, but you've added to that."

It never met mine, which is what you asked.

"The video and the photo were not shot at the same time, but I still accept
them as valid, unless someone wants to demonstrate the possibility of
collusion."

Which video and which photo? There are many. Can you give us a date and
possibly something to work with? I doubt it meets the criteria I want. That
is something that can be verified. Two images taken from two different
locations with landmarks showing some form of structured object (not
formations of lights or singular lights). This is essentially what I want
to see. Again, look at my 4 September post:

"Let's try multiple videos/photographs of the same object at the same time
from different locations that show something other than a light in the sky or

something at the limits of resolution for the recording device. This would
have to be supported by eyewitness testimony all suggesting the same thing.
There have been multiple witness cases, but I have yet to see anybody do a
real bang-up job on investigating them. Nobody seems to be interested in
presenting flight paths, angular size, angular elevations, etc in such
reports of "mass" sightings. This would be the first thing I would think of
doing. Instead we have the witnesses telling us how high it was and how big
it was. A proper investigation would ignore such estimates and go for the
angular sizes and elevations to compute the true size and heights."
The photos and videos have to be done such that such computations can be
made. Anything less falls short simply because it is too easy for something
to be hoaxed in some manner.



"Your criteria sound reasonable, but may not be obtainable
due to the nature of the beast. I don't think such pictures exist of
ball lightning, for example."

Is ball lightning accepted as a fact? Anybody interested in trying to prove
its existence would take the effort to try and prove it. My criteria is
simple. Give me images where everyone can agree on computations of height,
speed, size,etc. I doubt that it would happen except in the unusual event of
some form of mass sighting of a structured object (like the Trents
photograph). Lights/groups of lights don't quite do it. They COULD (not
saying the are) be formations of aircraft with lights giving the impression
of something large. This is why I want something concrete. To actually do
this, I think UFOlogy needs to be proactive instead of waiting for this to
happen by chance. I have a few ideas but it would require the resources of
manpower, investment of some cash by those interested in establishing UFOs as
a genuine phenomena, and the leadership to organize it correctly. I doubt
this will happen simply because many UFOlogists don't want to dedicate the
effort.


"UFOs are too usually too transient for this kind of sophisticated
monitoring."

See what I mean? This is a self-defeating attitude. How do you know it
won't be possible if you don't try? Isn't this what UFOlogy wants or are
they willing to keep accepting ambiguous cases that may or may not be a
"True" UFO.

Tim Printy

Just to mention that the theory of evolution is entirely NON random. At
least I don't see anything random in the mechanism of natural selection.
Evolution has nothing to do with random chance. Yet the argument
"evolution=random chance" persists, especially in religiously colored
debates. Needless to say, it's an argument from ignorance.
Those who say this should read some basic biology...

<B>Look, up in the sky<BR>
<P ALIGN=CENTER><BR>
<P ALIGN=LEFT></FONT><FONT COLOR="#000000" style="BACKGROUND-
COLOR: #ffffff" SIZE=2 FAMILY="SANSSERIF" FACE="Arial"
LANG="0"></B>By Alexa Moses<BR>
September 14 2002<BR>
Icon<BR>
<BR>
<BR>
<BR>
One Saturday in October 1976, three men from Sydney drove down the South Coast
of NSW. For 21-year-old Nick Flaskas and Frank Zonaras, 20, it was a brief holiday
between university semesters. For Frank's younger brother Bill, it was a way to while
away an idle weekend. To get the approval of their parents, Flaskas and Zonaras had
turned their holiday into a quasi-scientific excursion: they were going to film an
eclipse of the sun.<BR>
<BR>
The scientific community were gathering in Bombala to see the eclipse, but when the
trio asked around, locals said they would get a better view at an isolated point in Ben
Boyd National Park.<BR>
<BR>
The group arrived at the point before 4pm, parked the car, and walked down to the
cliff, which faced the ocean. It was a clear afternoon, the ocean was smooth and the
location was so remote it was like, Flaskas says, "the other side of the moon".<BR>
<BR>
Turning their backs to the ocean, Zonaras and Flaskas began to set up their cameras:
Zonaras was using his new Super 8 video camera, and Flaskas was working the stills
camera. <BR>
<BR>
Bill was chucking stones off the cliff into the ocean. Suddenly, he called to the others
to turn around. Flaskas and Zonaras turned and saw the objects in the sky.<BR>
&nbsp; <BR>
<BR>
"There were two prominent objects and four smaller ones," Flaskas says.<BR>
<BR>
"The main object looked like a bell. Dome-shaped, a dark grey bell. And as we were
watching it, it looked like it was moving, first towards us and then away from us. It
was about 15 degrees above the horizon."<BR>
<BR>
The pair swung their cameras around to capture the objects on film.<BR>
<BR>
"Meanwhile the solar eclipse was starting so we thought, we'd better do the eclipse as
well or we'll get into trouble with our parents," Zonaras says. So they turned the
cameras around and quickly filmed the eclipse.<BR>
<BR>
When they looked oceanwards again, the mysterious objects had disappeared.<BR>
<BR>
More than 25 years later, the pair have created a Web site to tell of their experience.
Marketed for an American audience, <A
HREF="http://www.ufoearthcontact.com/">ufoearthcontact.com</A> features pay-
per-view of the footage that Zonaras took at Ben Boyd National Park. It costs
$US9.90 ($18.20) to view the film. The site also includes other case studies, an area
for visitors' UFO stories, and a guest book.<BR>
<BR>
The pair have appeared on ABC's Couchman show in 1991, and a television show
called The Extraordinary in 1994.<BR>
<BR>
Zonaras is now a Sydney accountant, and Flaskas the manager of a car yard. As they
discuss their experience, they interrupt, squabble over details and finish each other's
sentences like a well-worn comedy act.<BR>
<BR>
When asked if they believe in intelligent extra-terrestrial life, Flaskas says "of course"
but Zonaras just looks sheepish. Do they find it embarrassing to talk about? <BR>
<BR>
"No," Flaskas says, at the same time that Zonaras says "yes". They both laugh.<BR>
<BR>
"I had clients in New Zealand, and after this television show we were on was shown
in New Zealand they came back and sung that song at me," Zonaras says, singing the
theme from The Twilight Zone.<BR>
<BR>
"And you do our tax returns, they ask me?" he says.<BR>
<BR>
Zonaras originally wanted to forget about the sighting. After all, it was his footage
and he had a career in accounting to think about. <BR>
<BR>
Now, with the ability to stream video on the Internet, and a hefty dose of persuasion
from Flaskas, Zonaras agreed to get involved again. A healthy cash-flow opportunity
was waiting to be realised. <BR>
<BR>
Ufoearthcontact.com was created with the help of the director of Triode Internet, Paul
Black, who programmed the back end of the site. Video producer George Kolovos
designed the hub and worked on the streaming technology for video. <BR>
<BR>
However, so far the site hasn't been an other- worldly success. Traffic has been
humble since it launched in March, with around 35 unique visitors a day. It may also
reflect a common response to the story they have received from people since the event.
The vision of two grown men in suits claiming to have seen UFOs is somewhat hard
to swallow. Flaskas nods vigorously, having met with this reaction before.<BR>
<BR>
"But if you study any of the serious literature in all cultures in all civilisations, there
have been these sightings," Flaskas says.<BR>

Actually, there is a random element to evolutionary theory. This is when a
gene mutates, accidentally and by chance, and proves to give an advantage to
its owner. This mutated gene is then passed on because its owner survives.
This, as I understand it, is one of the basic concepts of evolution... or is
this outdated?

Steve

From: Robert Buljevic [mailto:skeptic@s1c.org]

Just to mention that the theory of evolution is entirely NON random. At
least I don't see anything random in the mechanism of natural selection.
Evolution has nothing to do with random chance. Yet the argument
"evolution=random chance" persists, especially in religiously colored
debates. Needless to say, it's an argument from ignorance.
Those who say this should read some basic biology...

From: "Jim Speiser" <jimspeiser@yahoo.com>
Date: Sun, 15 Sep 2002 13:39:20 -0700
Subject: RE: [UFORL] The Birth of the 'Greys'

The mutation is random; the selection for favorable mutations is non-random.
So while it's true that "there is a random element to evolutionary theory,"
it is false that evolution itself is a random process. The "break" in a
game of pool is somewhat random, but pool is not considered a game of
chance.

==JJS==

Yes, there is indeed. I think the issue is just that anti-evolutionists
assert that evolution is *nothing but* random chance, ignoring the
whole point of natural *selection* (as you note). Those mutations
which make an organism less likely to survive are swamped by those
which make it more likely to survive. The inputs are random, the outputs
are not - so evolution does not equal random chance. But then I'm
a godless liberal secular humanist, so I would say that, wouldn't I?

@ OK, your definition of a theory, then? And why we should

effect. It must provide predictions that are different from the
predictions of all other theories, such that experiment can decide
between the predictions. The predictions must not be vague. And the
alternative (null) hypothesis must provide precise predictions too,
or the theory is not testable.

@ OK, your definition of a theory, then? And why we should
@ accept it over the prevailing one?

A theory is a TESTABLE statement of the facts behind the observed
effect. It must provide predictions that are different from the
predictions of all other theories, such that experiment can decide
between the predictions. The predictions must not be vague. And the
alternative (null) hypothesis must provide precise predictions too,
or the theory is not testable.

From: Benjy Buckman [mailto:benjy@thebuckmans.com]
Sent: Saturday, September 14, 2002 5:28 AMSubject: Re:
[Young_Atheists_Freethinkers] Israel

Yes, that's me.
I can't say "evolution is taught" or "it's not taught," simply because
every school is different. In the very religious schools, it's generally
taught that evolution is wrong. In secular schools, evolution is taught
as science. In semi-religious schools (such as the one I'm in), it's
taught as science and students can decide if they accept it or not. The
biology books all have evolution, of course, and they all consider it
science; since there are no "religious biology" books, all the religious
schools can do is have their teachers say the books are wrong. Or they
can say that evolution doesn't contradict religion: that God directed
the evolutionary process, which [they say] could never have happened
randomly.
I'm not in biology anymore, but I was last year, and we learned
evolution, and we had an argument in class about it: the teacher, I and
some others said evolution is true, and some said it's not - in the end,
though, evolution was taught, because it's part of the state-run
curriculum.
So, summing up: any school that gets state funding has to teach
evolution. How they teach it, is up to them.

I would guess that the people who became success biologists do believe
evolution is true, and that those who believed otherwise chose other
fields.

  Benjy

From: "David Clarke" <cd292@crazydiamonds.fsnet.co.uk>
Date: Tue, 17 Sep 2002 10:28:43 +0100
Subject: Re: [UFORL] 1970 North Sea UFO incident

Greetings,

At 7.30 pm on 16 September 2002 viewers in the BBC TV
Yorkshire & Lincolnshire region (UK) saw a special investigation by
journalists from the 'Inside Out' team into "claims of an alien abduction
 in Yorkshire."

The programme hinged on the tragic loss of an RAF Lightning fighter
over the North Sea off Flamborough Head, Yorkshire, on the night of
8 September 1970, during an exercise that went tragically wrong. Its
pilot was a USAF Captain, Bill Schaffner, who was on exchange duties
with No 5 Squadron, RAF Binbrook, at the time.

The Lightning was recovered from the sea three months later but the
cockpit was empty and the body of Schaffner, a father of two, was never
found. This mystery led to speculation and rumour, not least because
the report of the RAF Board of inquiry into the tragic accident were not
released until recently

In 1992 the Grimsby Telegraph newspaper published a story claiming
Schaffner was scrambled to intercept a UFO which had been tracked
by the UK's radar early warning system in the Shetland Islands. Their
source for the information remained anonymous. His
claims, along with a bogus transcript of a conversation between
Schaffner and the RAF Ground Control, have been repeated
in a number of UFO books and on the world wide web, causing
distress to Schaffner's two sons who were interviewed on last night's
TV programme.

The full story of the BBC team's investigation into the story can
be found at:

http://www.bbc.co.uk/insideout/yorkslincs/prog_02/index.shtml

Follow the links to read a transcript of Captain Schaffner's final
conversation with the ground controllers, and see pictures from
the inquiry report, showing the aircraft's empty cockpit.

As the transcript makes clear, the 'UFO' shadowed by Schaffner
was in fact a RAF Shackleton, that was the target for the
TACEVAL exercise called without warning to test the squadron's
response to intruder aircraft.

The BBC team's investigations are confirmed by Squadron
Record Books from 1970 and 1971 released at the Public Record
Office (PRO) in 2001, summarised in 'Out of the Shadows'

Greetings,

At 7.30 pm on 16 September 2002 viewers in the BBC TV
Yorkshire & Lincolnshire region (UK) saw a special investigation by
journalists from the 'Inside Out' team into "claims of an alien abduction
 in Yorkshire."

The programme hinged on the tragic loss of an RAF Lightning fighter
over the North Sea off Flamborough Head, Yorkshire, on the night of
8 September 1970, during an exercise that went tragically wrong. Its
pilot was a USAF Captain, Bill Schaffner, who was on exchange duties
with No 5 Squadron, RAF Binbrook, at the time.

The Lightning was recovered from the sea three months later but the
cockpit was empty and the body of Schaffner, a father of two, was never
found. This mystery led to speculation and rumour, not least because
the report of the RAF Board of inquiry into the tragic accident were not
released until recently

In 1992 the Grimsby Telegraph newspaper published a story claiming
Schaffner was scrambled to intercept a UFO which had been tracked
by the UK's radar early warning system in the Shetland Islands. Their
source for the information remained anonymous. His
claims, along with a bogus transcript of a conversation between
Schaffner and the RAF Ground Control, have been repeated
in a number of UFO books and on the world wide web, causing
distress to Schaffner's two sons who were interviewed on last night's
TV programme.

The full story of the BBC team's investigation into the story can
be found at:

http://www.bbc.co.uk/insideout/yorkslincs/prog_02/index.shtml

Follow the links to read a transcript of Captain Schaffner's final
conversation with the ground controllers, and see pictures from
the inquiry report, showing the aircraft's empty cockpit.

As the transcript makes clear, the 'UFO' shadowed by Schaffner
was in fact a RAF Shackleton, that was the target for the
TACEVAL exercise called without warning to test the squadron's
response to intruder aircraft.

The BBC team's investigations are confirmed by Squadron
Record Books from 1970 and 1971 released at the Public Record
Office (PRO) in 2001, summarised in 'Out of the Shadows'
pgs 211-13.

John Burtenshaw asked:

>
> Can someone explain why the jet's canopy was closed with no pilot inside?
> The BBC story does not address this point.
>
> Having sat in the cockpit of a Lightning I can confirm that it is a very
> tight fit (I'm 5ft 8in tall), the canopy is powered so I'm assuming it was
> opened under its own power. lets try and put a sequence together here.
The
> pilot tries to eject but the seat fails. Somehow, after surviving a crash
> into the sea without loss of consciousness, he opens the canopy and gets
> out. Normally ground crew would shut the canopy, but the pilot, wet and
> cold, crawls high enough up the fuselage to the canopy release and locks
> the canopy shut then presumably swims off somewhere.
>
> Why did he not stay where he was using his life-jacket and SARBE (Search
> And Rescue Beacon Equipment) until the rescue chopper arrived?
>
> It just does not make sense to me.
>

Here is your answer, straight from the mouth of Group Captain
Barwood, who was involved in the RAF Board of Inquiry into
the circumstances of the accident:

[To set the context, when the Lightning was recovered on
the seabed at a depth of 190ft, the aircraft was almost
completely intact with the canopy closed. The cockpit was
empty but the seat was still inside, with the harness release
box undone and the harness still in position.}

Barwood: "When the aircraft was raised, it was extablished
that the seat firing mechanism had been initiated, but that the
cockpit canopy jettison mechanism had failed to fire. The
cockpit area was completely undamaged, but the visor
attachment track on the pilot's flying helmet had contacted
the instrument panel. This probably had no effect on the
pilot. He had accidentally flown into, or onto, the sea and
the very large belly fuel tank with which the aircraft was
fitted acted as a boat hull to take most of the impact load
[During salvage the ventral tank and the belly of the aircraft
were found to be ripped open and there was under-tail
damage].
"The pilot had attempted to eject, but the canopy mechanism
would not fire as the firing mechanism had been incorrectly
assembled. (The breech firing mechanism of the cockpit
canopy jettison system had been clamped in a vice,
partially flattening the threads, so that when assembled,
it was not screwed completely home, so that the firing
plunger did not contact the percussion cap with sufficient
energy to fire it). He then opened his cockpit canopy
manually using the ordinary post-flight opening mechanism,
which is hydraulically operated. He still could not eject as
the inderdictor wire had not armed his seat firing mechanism.
He undid his combined harness quick release box and
climbed out of the cockpit. His dinghy lanyard was
still connected and as he separated from the cockpit this
extended - fully. At full extension it would check his upward
movement, so he released it.

"The pilot's body was never recovered. The cockpit
canopy hydraulic pressure system slowly decayed so
that the canopy closed, trapping the extended dinghy
lanyard line. We did find some broken visor
transparency on the cockpit floor. This would have
broken when the pilots Mk. 3 helmet had hit the
coaming beneath the in-flight refuelling panel and it is
possible that a sharp edge cut his life preserver. We
shall never know."

Bear in mind the above information was available
in 1997 when aviation historian Martin Bowman
published his book on the English Electric Lightning
(Crowood Press, Wiltshire).

It is also consistent with the official line taken by the
MOD in response to inquiries about the incident
since at least 1992. There is nothing to suggest there
was ever a 'cover-up' - this was simply a tragic
accident.

Dave Clarke

www.flyingsaucery.com

>fitted acted as a boat hull to take most of the impact load
>[During salvage the ventral tank and the belly of the aircraft
>were found to be ripped open and there was under-tail
>damage].
>
>"The pilot had attempted to eject, but the canopy mechanism
>would not fire as the firing mechanism had been incorrectly
>assembled. (The breech firing mechanism of the cockpit
>canopy jettison system had been clamped in a vice,
>partially flattening the threads, so that when assembled,
>it was not screwed completely home, so that the firing
>plunger did not contact the percussion cap with sufficient
>energy to fire it). He then opened his cockpit canopy
>manually using the ordinary post-flight opening mechanism,
>which is hydraulically operated. He still could not eject as
>the inderdictor wire had not armed his seat firing mechanism.
>He undid his combined harness quick release box and
>climbed out of the cockpit. His dinghy lanyard was
>still connected and as he separated from the cockpit this
>extended - fully. At full extension it would check his upward
>movement, so he released it.
>
>"The pilot's body was never recovered. The cockpit
>canopy hydraulic pressure system slowly decayed so
>that the canopy closed, trapping the extended dinghy
>lanyard line. We did find some broken visor
>transparency on the cockpit floor. This would have
>broken when the pilots Mk. 3 helmet had hit the
>coaming beneath the in-flight refuelling panel and it is
>possible that a sharp edge cut his life preserver. We
>shall never know."
>
>Bear in mind the above information was available
>in 1997 when aviation historian Martin Bowman
>published his book on the English Electric Lightning
>(Crowood Press, Wiltshire).
>
>It is also consistent with the official line taken by the
>MOD in response to inquiries about the incident
>since at least 1992. There is nothing to suggest there
>was ever a 'cover-up' - this was simply a tragic
>accident.
>

From: "Keith J Matthews" <kmatthews@lunet.ac.uk>
Date: Sun, 22 Sep 2002 21:39:46 +0100
Subject: Re: RE: [UFORL] The Birth of the 'Greys'

Larry

You are apparently not denying evolution. The term for what you dispute is
abiogenesis, which has nothing to do with evolutionary theory.

And while we're on the subject, 'evolution' in itself is not a theory; the
'theory' part that fundamentalists get upset about is the 'theory of
evolution by natural selection'. The theory is a means of modelling a
phenomenon in an attempt to explain it. No scientist would claim that the
theory of evolution by natural selection is the only possible explanation,
but they could not deny the fact of evolution. I use the word 'fact' because
there is a geological stratigraphic sequence containing fossils that show
change through time; that change is identical across the world, in broad
terms; it is easy to document, from this geological sequence, small changes
in individual plant and animal types that eventually lead to the development
of new species and genera. The common complaint of fundamentalists that
no-one has ever observed evolutionary change because of the putative
time-scales involved is irrelevant; astronomers are competent to deal with
phenomena that they can never observe in the present; archaeologists are
happy about dealing with long-lost societies; particle physicists are able
to examine entities so small they cannot be seen. There is a huge body of
fossil evidence for biologists to use as a basis for examining the history
of life. More than that, geneticists are able to model changes through time
to assess when species diverged (and it's gratifying to note that although
hominid palaeontologists originally pooh-poohed the very remote date of 7 to
11 million years ago at which the geneticists claimed that the human and
chimpanzee lines diverged, there are recent fossil discoveries of creatures
that clearly belong on the human side of the divide that are over six
million years old).

You ask:

>Look at Evolution. What kind of test can I devise to determine the
>truth? All I have is the writings of others, plus some circumstantial
>evidence. I can't do any experiments

Yes you can. You find a geological sequence of fossiliferous rocks. If you
want to falsify evolutionary theory, you find fossils of creatures that are
in the wrong sequence according to evolutionary theory. People have been
looking at these rocks for over two hundred years and there is not yet a
single example of fossils occurring in the 'wrong' order.

I'm a bit unclear about why you thing that the concept of evolution is
something that governments imposed on us. I was always under the impression
that it was something that naturalists formulated in the first half of the
nineteenth century. Or am I missing some global conspiracy?
It's interesting looking at this debate from the other side of the Atlantic,
because it doesn't really exist here. The terms that are bandied about, such
as 'evolutionist' and 'liberal' have a very quaint ring to them. No
biologist that I have ever met would call themselves an 'evolutionist', as
it's a term that smacks of religious belief. No matter what fundamentalists
(and, it has to be said, certain postmodernist philosophers) say, science is
not a religion as it proceeds to describe existence from an assumption of
ignorance, whereas religions proceed from an assumption of revealed
knowledge that is immutable. Using terms that characterise people in
pseudo-religious terms may be acceptable to a fundamentalist audience, but
it's a gross caricature of reality.

As for 'liberal'... You use it in a pejorative sense, which is surely
bizarre (if very American). My understanding of the philosophy of
liberalism is pretty close to the image you have of the immediate
post-revolutionary constitution of the USA; something that promotes the
rights of the individual as opposed to the coercive power of the state. I
fail to see your problem with it.

Keith Matthews
http://www.kmatthews.org.uk

Subject: [UFORL] SETI "Impressed" by NASA/'Crop Circle' Cover-up?

CROP CIRCLES AND THE MOD - Our World Exclusive article by Nick
Pope is essential reading for those in the Crop Circle community.

THE MOON LANDINGS: NASA'S PROOF! - Take a look at the solitary
image NASA has put forward which it says is evidence that they
landed men on the Moon. You won't believe it!

Some might say it's all patently ludicrous and the latter, in
reverence to those who have given their lives to space
exploration, is markedly lamentable.

Still, cue contemporary 'ufology', courtesy of 'UFO Magazine'
[UK]:

http://www.ufomag.co.uk/Sept02.htm#top

They continue:

THE MOON LANDINGS: NASA'S PROOF! - Take a look at the solitary
image NASA has put forward which it says is evidence that they
landed men on the Moon. You won't believe it!

This is part of a special section examining a veritable feast of
lunar tales; from stolen moon rocks to the Hubble Space Telescope
[HST] and its ability to take close-up images of the lunar
surface. Using NASA's own claims and statistics (plus information
issued by an astronomer working out of a University in Northern
England) we reveal a massive 100% factual contradiction. No more
excuses NASA. Point the HST at the Apollo landing sites and
settle this particular conspiracy of 'did we, or didn't we?' to
rest once and for all!
[END]


Allegedly, even the foremost 'SETI Institute' are comfortable
with these perpetual, some might conclude more than an insult to
intelligence and shameful, allegations.

"A few days ago, on Monday, 12 August, I made my second visit in
as many days to the National Space Centre in Leicester. Here I
met and interviewed Seth Shostak of the SETI Institute. The full
story will feature in our October issue, but I wish to place on
public record my thanks to officials at the Centre for extending
their kind invitation. Throughout our near two-hour-long
interview, Seth was happy to answer every question I put to him
and was very forthcoming in his comments. I was much the better
informed at the end of the interview, and I know that all who
eventually digest what he had to say will share that view.

UFO Magazine have struck up an excellent working relationship
with leading officials at the Centre who have been impressed by
the professional and objective approach we bring to the subject".


Perhaps somewhat ... astounding... to hear that the 'SETI
Institute' are reportedly impressed by "a professional and
objective approach" which proclaims the entire foundation of
space research is utterly corrupt and hides evidence of contact
by demonstrably mythical 'flying saucers', who evidently are
responsible for the 'crop circles' that bemuse so few...


On behalf of our 'UFO Research List' [UFORL], I have invited the
'National Space Centre' in Leicester, Seth Shostak and the 'SETI

Oh, really? How about launching a satellite, or going to the Moon?

How about trigonometrically measuring the relative sizes of the sun,
earth, and moon about 300 years before Christ - and accurately measuring
the size and shape of the earth through observed behavior of the sun?

I would call those experiments.

There is a difference between observing a system in operation, and
inferring things from the way they got piled up in the ground years
ago (when nobody was looking).

An experiment would be to predict what the planet would do next.

How can you predict how strata would be arranged, except by using the
same strata found elsewhere? That uses the system to define itself.

Also, how do you date the strata, when the dating methods depend on the
assumptions made about the deposition rates of the strata, and the
assumptions made about the strata depend on the assumptions made about
the dating methods?

From: Brett Holman <b.holman@physics.unimelb.edu.au>
Date: Wed, 25 Sep 2002 15:01:20 +1000
Subject: Re: RE: [UFORL] The Birth of the 'Greys'

On Tue, Sep 24, 2002 at 03:18:18PM -0500, Robinson, Larry wrote:
> Oh, really? How about launching a satellite, or going to the Moon?
>
> How about trigonometrically measuring the relative sizes of the sun,
> earth, and moon about 300 years before Christ - and accurately measuring
> the size and shape of the earth through observed behavior of the sun?
>
> I would call those experiments.

Indeed - so would I. I was employing sarcasm - sorry if it wasn't
heavy enough! :)

> There is a difference between observing a system in operation, and
> inferring things from the way they got piled up in the ground years
> ago (when nobody was looking).
>
> An experiment would be to predict what the planet would do next.

But compared to *what*? *You* were the one who said there needed to
be a control for it to be an experiment (as in "I don't call looking at
strata an "experiment", because there is no control group.") Where is the
control group here? Do we have a universe without gravity to compare it to?
Or perhaps an Earth not in a solar system? Maybe there's a Ptolemaic solar
system somewhere around here we can test it against ... The concept
of a control is of limited value in observational and historical
sciences like astrophysics and geology - we only have one Earth, one
universe, one history. Yet remarkable progress is still possible.

> How can you predict how strata would be arranged, except by using the
> same strata found elsewhere? That uses the system to define itself.

Well ... at a pinch ... I'd say you'd have forms morphologically
closest to today's near the surface, with increasing (and radical) divergences
the further down the strata you go. That prediction comes out of
the theory, not other strata - even if we had only one vertical set of
strata to look at, we could still (rather weakly) test the theory.

> Also, how do you date the strata, when the dating methods depend on the
> assumptions made about the deposition rates of the strata, and the
> assumptions made about the strata depend on the assumptions made about
> the dating methods?

Do the dating methods depend *only* on the assumptions made about the
deposition rates of the strata, and do the assumptions made about the strata
depend *only* on the assumptions made about the dating methods? No,
of course not. They depend on lots of other things and results from
other areas of science. If they depended only on each other, then
yes, it would be circular. But they don't, and so that gives us
a handle on solving it.

Subject: Re: RE: [UFORL] The Birth of the 'Greys'

I don't know;

I would call these things observations not experiments. Observing nature and
deriving conclusions based observations is a valid way of doing science.
Experimenting, I.E. altering some aspect of a set of conditions and
observing the results is another perfectly valid method.

Both methods require that the results or the observations must be duplicated
in order to ascertain an established fact. For example, if I say "a hammer
will tend to fall towards a known gravity source", I am stating a fact which
can be easily duplicated. If I say, sometimes a hammer will fall away from a
know gravity source, I might be speaking the truth however no one has ever
observed this happening spontaneously.

If I say, "persons from another solar system are abducting and experimenting
on millions of Earth people" I am not speaking a fact but a belief. I cannot
prove that people are being abducted whether I believe in this or not. There
has never been any outside observation of this phenomena as of yet. No one
outside of the persons who claim to have been abducted can testify that this
phenomena is an established fact. All we have are suppositions and beliefs,
not science.

Unfortunately, believing in something gets one closer to religion but not
necessarily closer to the truth.

G.P.

From: "Guy Pettingill" <guy_pettingill@arlof.eckerd.edu>
Date: Thu, 26 Sep 2002 10:49:21 -0400
Subject: Re: [UFORL] The Birth of the 'Greys'

However; we have an abundance of evidence that one *can* sail off of the
ends of the world. This was an absurd concept 100 years ago but, it is a
meaningful reality today.

I believe that one can apply scientific principles to something even as
absurd as the *fact* that people claim to have been abducted by
extraterrestrial beings in spacecraft. Only by applying rigorous standards
to reporting, responsible follow-ups, careful analyses and conclusions
*based on the evidence* not on a particular world view or belief system will
ultimately reveal the answer to this puzzle. When the answer is reviled it
may very well not be what people on both sides of the issue expect. One has
to accept this as a consequence of the scientific process.

Analyses of beliefs and especially religions belief is a worthy subject in
it's own right but, once again it is important to maintain objectivity
regarding this subject or one might find oneself prostelitizing rather than
analyzing.

G.P.

@ But compared to *what*? *You* were the one who said there needed to
@ be a control for it to be an experiment (as in "I don't call
@ looking at
@ strata an "experiment", because there is no control group.")
@ Where is the
@ control group here? Do we have a universe without gravity to
@ compare it to?
@ Or perhaps an Earth not in a solar system? Maybe there's a
@ Ptolemaic solar
@ system somewhere around here we can test it against ... The concept
@ of a control is of limited value in observational and historical
@ sciences like astrophysics and geology - we only have one Earth, one
@ universe, one history. Yet remarkable progress is still possible.

The test is to compare the predictions of a geocentric system to
those of a heliocentric system. One test is to look for stellar
parallax. It would be absent in the geocentric system.

@ > How can you predict how strata would be arranged, except by
@ using the
@ > same strata found elsewhere? That uses the system to define itself.
@
@ Well ... at a pinch ... I'd say you'd have forms morphologically
@ closest to today's near the surface, with increasing (and
@ radical) divergences
@ the further down the strata you go. That prediction comes out of
@ the theory, not other strata - even if we had only one vertical set of
@ strata to look at, we could still (rather weakly) test the theory.

Yes, but compared to which predictions made by what other theory??? You
need something to test the theory against, either a control group, or
another theory that makes different predictions. And they cannot be
vague predictions for either theory.

@ Do the dating methods depend *only* on the assumptions made about the
@ deposition rates of the strata, and do the assumptions made
@ about the strata
@ depend *only* on the assumptions made about the dating methods? No,
@ of course not. They depend on lots of other things and results from
@ other areas of science. If they depended only on each other, then
@ yes, it would be circular. But they don't, and so that gives us
@ a handle on solving it.

It becomes a circular argument, because the strata are dated only by
assumed deposition rates, and radioisotope dating.

But WHERE do we get the values for these?

On long half-life elements, the half-life is calculated from the
observed ratios of the element and its products AS FOUND on the earth.
They figure this out by counting strata from the surface in supposedly
undisturbed areas (assuming, say, that each layer is a year). It's more
accurate than the value they get from calculating the probability of
the decay of any one atom. But THEN they use the half-life they
calculated to determine the ages of strata.

But this is based upon the assumption that nothing happened to change
the abundance of the source isotopes some time in the geological past,
and that the ratios observed today are solely due to radioactive decay.
What if the amounts of radioisotopes either increased gradually over
time, or went through shifts in concentration? It changes the whole
time scale.

It's also based on the assumption that their assumption of the rate of
deposition of material in strata is correct. If the strata were
deposited at different rates (say several layers a year, corresponding
to weather patterns), it throws off the whole calculation.

@ Of course they don't! No geologist pretends that deposition rates of

@ anything else. And it's not just one test of date, it's a whole suite
@ of techniques that depend on the measurable decay rates of materials
@ that still exist. To make the ludicrous claims that creationists do,
@ that the rates have been "slowing down" since the moment of creation
@ 6006 years ago, betrays a complete ignorance of the mechanics of
@ radioactive decay.

@ Keith Matthews

You mean 6005 years ago. There is no year 0 in the calendar, because it
was based on Roman numerals, which could not represent 0. The year 1 BC
immediately precedes the year 1 AD.

Actually, that would be the time of the fall of man, not the creation.
Before Adam and Eve ate the fruit of knowledge, they wouldn't have
known about time.

But there IS another possibility, rather than the slowing down of
radioactive decay: The concentrations of these isotopes in the surface
environment (which the strata were made from) could have been LOWER in
the past (when the strata were deposited), and then increased in the
environment over time to the levels found today. This makes the strata
appear to be older than they are.
How could the concentrations increase over time? Increased solar or
cosmic
radiation, accumulation of material created by solar or cosmic radiation
(if the creation rate is greater than the decay rate), volcanic activity
bringing up materials from deep in the earth, and meteoric deposition
are
just a few possibilities that come to mind.
