From: Brett Holman <b.holman@physics.unimelb.edu.au>
Date: Fri, 27 Sep 2002 14:38:03 +1000
Subject: Re: RE: [UFORL] The Birth of the 'Greys'

On Thu, Sep 26, 2002 at 11:03:37AM -0500, Robinson, Larry wrote:
> @ -----Original Message-----
> @ From: Brett Holman [mailto:b.holman@physics.unimelb.edu.au]
> @ Sent: Wednesday, September 25, 2002 12:01 AM
> @ To: UFORL@yahoogroups.com
> @ Subject: Re: RE: [UFORL] The Birth of the 'Greys'
>@
> @ But compared to *what*? *You* were the one who said there needed to
> @ be a control for it to be an experiment (as in "I don't call
> @ looking at
> @ strata an "experiment", because there is no control group.")
> @ Where is the
> @ control group here? Do we have a universe without gravity to
> @ compare it to?
> @ Or perhaps an Earth not in a solar system? Maybe there's a
> @ Ptolemaic solar
> @ system somewhere around here we can test it against ... The concept
> @ of a control is of limited value in observational and historical
> @ sciences like astrophysics and geology - we only have one Earth, one
> @ universe, one history. Yet remarkable progress is still possible.
>
> The test is to compare the predictions of a geocentric system to
> those of a heliocentric system. One test is to look for stellar
> parallax. It would be absent in the geocentric system.

Yes - but this is not a control group (which is the main
point in your post that I objected to); it's an alternate hypothesis.
In observational sciences like astronomy and geology, we compare the
predictions of each hypothesis to what we observe. Heliocentrism (loosely defined,
of course) and evolution win; geocentrism and creationism do not. There are no
control groups.

> @ Well ... at a pinch ... I'd say you'd have forms morphologically
> @ closest to today's near the surface, with increasing (and
> @ radical) divergences
> @ the further down the strata you go. That prediction comes out of
> @ the theory, not other strata - even if we had only one vertical set of
> @ strata to look at, we could still (rather weakly) test the theory.
>
> Yes, but compared to which predictions made by what other theory??? You
> need something to test the theory against, either a control group, or
> another theory that makes different predictions. And they cannot be
> vague predictions for either theory.

What do you mean "what other theory???" Don't you have an alternate
theory? If so, we can compare how well evolution performs against that.
If not, what exactly is your problem with evolution? We can only go with
the best explanation on offer. I don't know why you seem to think evolution
is somehow untestable.

And they are not vague predictions; evolution, at least, makes quite specific
predictions.

> It becomes a circular argument, because the strata are dated only by
> assumed deposition rates, and radioisotope dating.
>
> But WHERE do we get the values for these?
>
> On long half-life elements, the half-life is calculated from the
> observed ratios of the element and its products AS FOUND on the earth.
> They figure this out by counting strata from the surface in supposedly
> undisturbed areas (assuming, say, that each layer is a year). It's more
> accurate than the value they get from calculating the probability of
> the decay of any one atom. But THEN they use the half-life they
> calculated to determine the ages of strata.

This is completely wrong. Half-lives are measured in a lab - even for
isotopes with half-lives of millions of years. I don't know where you get
this idea from. The measurement has nothing to do with geology at all, it's pure
*physics*; I can explain further if you want. So, no, this is not circular at all.

> But this is based upon the assumption that nothing happened to change
> the abundance of the source isotopes some time in the geological past,
> and that the ratios observed today are solely due to radioactive decay.
> What if the amounts of radioisotopes either increased gradually over
> time, or went through shifts in concentration? It changes the whole
> time scale.

"What ifs" don't count - evidence does. Do you have any evidence for
this happening?

For a start, there are multiple decay chains we can use (eg Ar-Ar, K-Ar,
Rb-Sr, and so on). These are independent dating mechanisms, and
they tend to agree. Different isotopes have different decay rates, so for
this to occur by chance, across many different decay chains - which is what
would have to happen if, as you suggest, the isotope concentrations
increased over time - is unlikely *in the extreme*. In fact, the amount
of change in isotope concentration for *each* chain would have to vary
by place and by stratum in just such as way as they all give consistent
ages - ie consistent across strata, locales and decay chains. This is
ludicrously unlikely.

See also

<http://www.talkorigins.org/faqs/faq-age-of-earth.html>
<http://www.talkorigins.org/faqs/faq-meritt/age.html>

> It's also based on the assumption that their assumption of the rate of
> deposition of material in strata is correct. If the strata were
> deposited at different rates (say several layers a year, corresponding
> to weather patterns), it throws off the whole calculation.

How many layers per year do you think would need to be laid down
to create a rock with, say, 4 million layers? (The standard
geological interpretation of this is that the Green River formation was
laid down over 2 million years, with 2 seasonal layers added per year.)

<http://www.cs.colorado.edu/~lindsay/creation/varves.html>

From: TPrinty@aol.com
Date: Thu, 3 Oct 2002 18:42:57 EDT
Subject: [UFORL] Rudiaks accusations on Professor Moore's writings/integrity

List,

In md-september, David Rudiak produced his scathing rebuttal on the NYU
flight #4 hypothesis for the Foster ranch debris part of the Roswell
incident. In addition to David's rebuttal about certain facts, he then
decided that not only was Professor Moore mistaken but he was a hoaxer/liar
as well. He stated that Moore deliberately alterred data on several key
issues.

Having long been a proponnent of the NYU hypothesis, I was taken aback by
several of the accusations and went about looking at Rudiak's claims. After
all, to state that Moore was mistaken is one thing but to state he was
deliberately falsifying and alterring data was another. After examining
Rudiak's work and looking at the facts, I found most of these claims of
falsifying data are due to an overzealous personal attack on Moore. They are
not what Rudiak claims and, in several cases, Rudiak was wrong or may have
done some alterring of data himself. One can even say that Rudiak has acted
hypocritically in his writings.

I found several problems shortly after Rudiak posted his piece for all to
view and immediately began to write a rebuttal on the work for my own web
page. I held back for a week or two because of several reasons.

1) I was curious if Professor Moore or any of his supporters/close contacts
might present some response. The word that I received was that this was
apparently not going to happen.

2) To see if anybody else would notice some of the errors that Rudiak made
in his computations. To date, I have seen nobody notice them or, at least,
publicly announce them.

3) To see if anybody was going to suggest to Rudiak that he may be going
over the top in his accusatons. In fact, there were a few posts on UFO
Updates that seemed to support his attack.

4) I just wanted to try and get the facts, as best as I can determine them,
correct. This was not easy since many of the issues are open to
interpretation contrary to what Rudiak has written.

Since none of items 1-3 have occurred, I am now publishing my rebuttal on
the web at http://members.aol.com/tprinty2/rudiak.html. This is for all to
examine and I hope to encourage some hopefully "friendly" debate on the items
in question.

You may see Bruce Hutchinson posting a similar post on the Updates list. He
was helpful in correcting my less than perfect grammar and adding a few items
to the page. However, all the basic work is mine and any mistakes are mine.
Bruce was just a sounding board on ideas.

I am perfectly willing to discuss necessary corrections when obvious errors
are noted in this piece. However, I would hope that not only there be a
critical look at what I have written but also a critical look at Rudiak's
work, which seems to have not happened to date (other than this piece). I
prefer for this discussion not to degenerate into a rather rude and senseless
exercise.

Anyone wanting specific information that I used that is not on the website
can email me and I will gladly give them a copy.

Tim Printy

color=#0000ff><FONT
 size=2>&lt;<SPAN
 class=420155503-
12102002>&nbsp;&lt;&nbsp;</SPAN></FONT></FONT></FONT><BR>The
 polygraph has always been a controversial topic, and much of the public -- and
 many introductory textbooks in psychology courses -- treat the matter with
 considerable skepticism. However, the more strident criticisms of the
 polygraph were spurred by inadequate earlier techniques, long since soundly
 rejected by academic scrutiny. Contemporary studies have found moderate but
 significant validity in the most common of modern techniques, the "Control
 Question Test" (CQT).&nbsp; </DIV>
 <P>A recent article in the Journal of Credibility Assessment and Witness
 Psychology reviews the empirical and review literature concerning CQT, and
 concludes that, "when the ecologically valid laboratory studies and the high
 quality field studies are considered, both indicate high validity for the
 CQT." <A href="http://anw.com/fire/GPriceReport.htm#1">[1]</A>&nbsp; </P>
 <P>The Fifth Circuit of the U.S. Court of Appeals, in its decision in the U.S.
 vs. Posado in 1995, overturning "per se" exclusion of polygraph evidence, gave
 the following overview of the state of the evidence for polygraph:&nbsp; </P>
 <BLOCKQUOTE>
  <P>"There can be no doubt that tremendous advances have been made in
  polygraph instrumentation and technique in the years since Frye. The test at
  issue in Frye measured only changes in the subject's systolic blood pressure
  in response to test questions. ... Modern instrumentation detects changes in
  the subject's blood pressure, pulse, thoracic and abdominal respiration, and
  galvanic skin response. Current research indicates that, when given under
  controlled conditions, the polygraph technique accurately predicts truth or
  deception between seventy and ninety percent of the time. Remaining
   controversy about test accuracy is almost unanimously attributed to
   variations in the integrity of the testing environment and the
   qualifications of the examiner. ... Further, there is good indication that
   polygraph technique and the requirements for professional polygraphists are
   becoming progressively more standardized. In addition, polygraph technique
   has been and continues to be subjected to extensive study and publication.
   Finally, polygraph is now so widely used by employers and government
   agencies alike."&nbsp;</P></BLOCKQUOTE>
 <P>And according to another court opinion:&nbsp; </P>
 <BLOCKQUOTE>
   <P>"The predominant format employed in the field of polygraphy is the
   'control question' technique ... There is no dispute in this case that the
   'probable lie' version of the control question technique, when properly
   employed, is a highly accurate method for detecting deception and possesses
   the type of scientific validity that satisfies the reliability prong of Rule
   702. Through numerous field and laboratory studies, researchers have
   determined that polygraph examinations using this technique produce results
   that have an accuracy rate of approximately ninety percent. ...&nbsp; </P>
   <P>"The most thorough treatment of polygraph admissibility issues can be
   found in two district court opinions from Arizona and New Mexico [Galbreth
   and Crumby] ... both courts found that polygraph theory and technique had
   been tested by the scientific method and repeatedly validated in field and
   laboratory studies, subjected to stringent peer review and extensive
   publication, shown to have a remarkably low error rate when properly applied
   by a skilled polygrapher, enjoyed substantial acceptance within the
   scientific community, and was widely used within government and industry."
   <A
href="http://anw.com/fire/GPriceReport.htm#2">[2]</A>&nbsp;</P></BLOCKQUO
TE>
 <P>Significant, and probably appropriate, obstacles remain before polygraph
 evidence finds a widespread and well-defined place in the courtroom, most
 notably with respect to the required standardization of examiner training, and
 in the ratification of techniques that are demonstrated proof against any
 physical and mental "countermeasures" that may be attempted by fraudulent
 claimants. However, a picture of significant validity and progress
 emerges.&nbsp;&nbsp;<SPAN class=420155503-12102002><FONT face=Arial
 color=#0000ff size=2>&nbsp;</FONT></SPAN></P>
 <P><SPAN class=420155503-12102002><FONT face=Arial color=#0000ff
 size=2>&gt;&gt;</FONT></SPAN></P>

From: Vicente-Juan Ballester Olmos <ballesterolmos@yahoo.es>
Date: Sat, 12 Oct 2002 12:04:01 +0200 (CEST)
Subject: [UFORL] FOTOCAT Project News

FOTOCAT (acronym in Spanish for Catalog of Photographs) is an in-progress
project from the Anomaly Foundation <http:/www.anomalia.org>, a
not-for-profit organization set up in Spain in 1997 mainly to fund UFO
research, publish journals and books, and preserve from extintion
endangered UFO records.
Started initially with the objective to organize our 35-year photographic
UFO/IFO archives, when it acquired significant proportions it naturally
developed into a worldwide catalog with the purpose to integrate all UFO
reports published in the mainstream literature where photography, film or
video had been taken.
FOTOCAT has now 2,500 entries and it is rapidly expanding. We plan to
release it through the Foundation´s web site for public knowledge and
usage when its size its considered to be acceptably representative of the
"UFO photograph phenomenon" at world scale. At this stage, there are still
some regional or yearly weaknesses.

LATE NEWS!
FOTOCAT accepts and looks for material donations in order to become a
comprehensive tally of this specific segment of UFO phenomenology. One of
our efforts centers in the acquisition of photographic records from
various sources. It is with satisfaction that we can report here that a
collection of 500 slides from the well-known ufologist from Argentina, Mr
Guillermo Roncoroni (unfortunately deceased) were donated to the Anomaly
Foundation thanks to the good services of his Argentinian colleagues and
noted researchers Mr Alejandro Agostinelli and Mr Roberto E Banchs. This
set splendidly documents such UFO cases in Latinamerica.

Very recently, Mr Philip Klass has generously donated his personal
collection of 300 slides to our Project, and we have to thank the
assistance provided by Mr Milton Hourcade. In this set we may find
extraordinary photographic coverage of outstanding UFO events like
Delphos, South Hill, or Socorro, as well as many other excellent
documents.

Finally, a noted figure in the UFO field in the United States, who has
collected an impressive amount of photographic material, has decided to
include the Anomaly Foundation in his Last Will as future beneficiary of
his UFO photo assets.

We request researchers from all corners of the world to submit us copy of
any list of UFO/IFO photocases produced or to exchange regional catalogs
with us. We will gladly submit what we have for a given country for
correction and improvement.

Thanks for your time and best regards,
Vicente-Juan Ballester Olmos
Research Director, Anomaly Foundation

46080 Valencia

Additional evidence why a helicopter was not likely to have been
the object Zamora witnessed can be found in Ray Stanford's book,
'Socorro Saucer'.

Stanford writes:

"Zamora reported that as the craft rose vertically and then moved
away, he observed an estimated four-foot-long elliptical opening
on the bottom of the object, out of which the flame issued".

He further explains [the asterisks denotes Stanford's emphasis]:

"Zamora felt a distinct heat on his body coming from the craft's
exhaust, but *there was not nearly so much heat as there should
have been if this were a rocket's exhaust of equal size and
brilliance*.

The sound made up for it, however, Zamora thought later.

Something else, though, made the 'flame', streaming downward only
fifteen paces from Zamora, seem unusual.
He told me, 'That roaring flame. It looked like it should'a
bounced [deflected] off the ground, *but it didn't*.

In fact, *it was more like some fiery Excalibur, actually
penetrating into the rocks and the earth*, instead of deflecting
off to the side as a gaseous rocket exhaust would have done'."

Stanford adds, "I was puzzled about this as I stood at the
landing site that afternoon...".


Stanford also documents the following:

"[State Patrolman] Jordan said that what most impressed him at
the landing site was the way the 'flame' had evidently 'sliced' a
large greasewood bush, located almost centrally in the landing
gear quadrangle, without leaving any signs of strong
*turbulence*, as the exhaust of a powerful rocket thrust unit or
even the whirling of helicopter blades would have done.

'They'll never explain that thing Lonnie saw as any 'pogo' [VTOL
aircraft], helicopter, or anything I know about,' Jordan said
firmly. 'The flame from that damn thing just sliced that
greasewood bush in half, *just burned it off clean, like a blade
of fire had cut right through it*'."


Stanford then reports his later conversation in a restaurant with
two women, who "lived on the south side of Socorro".

They claimed to have heard two 'roars' in the sky, with
approximately a minute between, just before six o'clock on 24
April.

In response to Stanford's question, "Couldn't you have heard a
jet, or something from White Sands?", he was reportedly informed
by one of the witnesses, "No... it was nothing like that. We hear
jets all the time. This thing sounded different, and it wasn't
like anything we ever hear from over on the range. And it wasn't
a helicopter, either".


Captain Richard Holder was the "up-range commander at White Sands
Stallion Site". On the evening of 24 April, 1964, he had been
contacted by local FBI agent J. Arthur Byrnes, Jr, who informed
Holder of Zamora's report.

Holder interviewed Zamora and Ray Stanford writes of Holder,
"...we have good reason to believe his statement to the press on
Saturday, 25 April, the day after the incident. He said, 'I was
contacted on the evening of 24 April by local authorities to
determine whether White Sands missile range or Holloman Air Force
Base had anything which might produce the conditions described.
*Neither White Sands missile range nor Holloman had an object
that would compare to the object described. And there was no
known firing mission in progress at the time of the occurrence
that would produce the conditions reported*'."


In personal correspondence, which I will not directly quote
without permission, Ray Stanford - who vehemently still believes
the object was potentially/definitely of ET origin - does
emphasise Zamora's bewilderment why the object on departure did
not disturb _at all_ the abundant ravine sand, as a helicopter
obviously should have.

Why didn't a 'rocket', either?

It's a question I've asked before and which remains devoid of any
'not a hot-air balloon' rationalisation.

Where is any challenge?


Incidentally, re the possibility that Zamora may simply have
encountered a then entirely uncommon hot-air balloon... although
the involvement and influence of those early, circa 1964, hot-air
balloon pioneers, Ed Yost, Don Piccard, Tracy Barnes and Mark
Semich are well documented, what about Jimmie Craig?

Never heard of him?

You won't find any mention on the Internet.

Jimmie Craig was an associate of Ed Yost - who effectively
invented the hot-air balloon in October 1960.

Craig was also the 'U.S National Hot-air Balloon Champion' in
1964 and 1965, when it was still a nascent sport with relatively
few participants, certainly during 1964.


That aside, for now, in summary and bearing in mind fundamental
inconsistencies previously highlighted, are there any arguments
why we can not, surely, dismiss outright Dave Thomas'
commendable, proposed 'helicopter/Lunar Surveyor' explanation?


James:

<div><font size="+1">UFO encounter: Car's rear window &quot;sucked
out&quot;</font><font size="-1" color="#000000"><br>
<br>
</font><a
href="http://the.standard.net.au/news/saturday/story6.html"><font
size="-1"
color="#000000">http://the.standard.net.au/news/saturday/story6.html</font
></a><font size="-1" color="#000000"><br>
<br>
Saturday, October 19, 2002<br>
Report: KRISTA HAMBLIN.<br>
Picture: DAMIAN WHITE<br>
© Copyright 2002 The Standard - a member of The Fairfax Publishing
Group<br>
<br>
</font><font color="#000000"><i>Sue Sharples looks through the hole
where her windscreen used to<br>
be before it was sucked out by what she says was a UFO.</i><font
size="-1"><br>
<br>
PURNIM grandmother Sue Sharples can't explain the metallic object<br>
she saw in the sky yesterday.<br>
<br>
She also has no idea where the rear windscreen of the vehicle she<br>
was driving has gone.<br>
<br>
Mrs Sharples said yesterday she was driving with her husband along<br>
Mortlake Road on the northern side of Warrnambool when the couple<br>
noticed a shiny object above the vehicle.<br>
<br>
Their baby grandson was in a capsule in the back seat.<br>
<br>
Mrs Sharples said that after a few fleeting glances, they watched
the<br>
rear windscreen disappear upwards after it seemed to have been
sucked<br>
from the car.<br>
<br>
THE BACK WINDOW.<br>
</font></font><a
href="http://the.standard.net.au/images/saturday/19sue.jpg"><font
size="-1"
color="#000000">http://the.standard.net.au/images/saturday/19sue.jpg</font
></a><font size="-1" color="#000000"><br>
<br>
She admits their story is &quot;absolutely unbelievable&quot; but that
the proof lies<br>
with the vehicle's missing window.<br>
<br>
&quot;There is not a scratch on the car. Nothing,&quot; she said.<br>
<br>
Two searches of the area failed to locate the missing window.<br>
<br>
The couple's son-in-law phoned police in case someone had been
hurt<br>
by the projectile.<br>
<br>
Experts from Windscreens O'Brien can't explain how the window could
have<br>
disappeared.<br>
<br>
After inspecting the car, a spokesman said the window could not have
been<br>
kicked out and there was no sign it had been cut free.<br>
<br>
The seal was still attached and there were no glass splinters, he
said.<br>
<br>
The windscreen was fitted to the 1994 Toyota earlier in the year.<br>
<br>
&quot;How can you say what something is when you have never seen
one<br>
before?&quot; she said. &quot;It's just absolutely amazing.&quot;<br>
<br>
-end-<br>
<br>
FOLLOW UP.<br>
<br>
The family has been interviewed and the investigation by Phenomena<br>
Research Australia (PRA) is still in progress. PRA reported in a<br>
Press Release that &quot;the case is very complex, but like the
police<br>
we have no reason to dispute the statements on the witnesses. The<br>
have given Statutory Declarations and Police Statements.&quot; Dr
Barnett,<br>
Deputy Director of PRA said.<br>
<br>
The car will be examined and checked for samples, but it looks
clean,<br>
so I expect little from that area. When we find the real window I
will<br>
get it over to the examination lab for a good check&quot;.
Barnnet.<br>
<br>
ANOTHER FOLLOW UP.<br>
<br>
</font><font size="+1" color="#000000">&quot;Was a person abducted
that night, by a UFO?&quot;</font><font size="-1" color="#000000"><br>
Monday, October 21, 2002<br>
<br>
Dr Barnett went on to report &quot;We also have an abduction that on
the same night<br>
that we have under investigation, in that case the person is still
missing.<br>
The abduction that was related to the police and our investigators
involves<br>
a flying object that chased the missing person. The witnesses who
reported<br>
the story, have given a description of the object and that is in the
early stages<br>
of the investigation.&quot; he said.<br>
<br>
As of this morning [21st] the car and the missing person have not been
located.<br>
The police can do little at present as there is no indication of a
crime. They can not<br>
do very much in any official capacity unless some crime or belief that
the person<br>
is at harm, the facts are people can do what they want and if they
want to hid or<br>
run away then thats not a police matter, unless they are under age.&quot;
He said.<br>
<br>
The Director of PRA Mr John Auchettl said in the release, &quot;It is
early days on this<br>
case and it will take a bit of leg work to get to the bottom of this
mystery, but like<br>
the other 'lost indow' case, I have at present, no reason to question
the statements<br>
by the witnesses, but I need to get hold of the lost person, and so
would the police.&quot;</font></div>

From: "Luis R. Gonzalez" <lrgm@arrakis.es>
Date: Fri, 25 Oct 2002 21:07:00 +0200
Subject: Re: [UFORL] Best Evidence

In August Greg Sandow wrote:

>Another example, from a book by a hypnotherapist named Michael Nash. Nash
had a patient >suffering from anxiety because of consciously recalled
abduction memory. Nash, who apparently >had never heard of the abduction
phenomenon, assured the patient that the memories couldn't >possibly be of
real events. He hypnotized the patient, and was astonished to find more
abduction >details emerge, even though he'd told the patient that none of it
really happened. The patient, who >believed that the events were in fact
real, eventually got over the anxiety, and warmly thanked >Nash -- who,
utterly astonished, concluded that it was possible to relieve anxiety even
while the >patient still believed in the fantasies (as Nash saw it) that
were associated with it.

At last, I have been able to locate a copy of the article in question:

"Memory Distortion And Sexual Trauma: The Problem of False Negatives and
False Positives"
Michael R. Nash
International Journal of Clinical and Experimental Hypnosis, Vol. XLII, nº
4, October 1994, 346-362.

The details are substantially right, except for a revealing difference.

The patient did NOT recalled consciously any abduction... at least, at
first.

Let me quote:

"A 31-year-old single, White male patient consulted me reporting recent
multiple flashbacks of a previously unremembered traumatic incident that
occurred when he was 17 years old (...)

"What he had always remembered was that on a hot summer day he and a male
friend had taken a trip to a particularly scenic and isolated part of the
Rocky mountains, only a few miles from home. He and his friend both remember
walking along a path together about twilight. Then they came upon something
very odd. It was a kind of brightly glowing caterpillar on the path. They
both ran up to the caterpillar for a closer look. Suddenly there was a
bright flash of light which startled them both; they ran in fear. Then there
was another flash of light; they continued running. The odd thing was that
when they returned home they discovered that it was 11:30 at night. They had
lost approximately 2 hours of time. The patient reported that this
occurrence was the sort of scary story he and his friend would relate at
appropiate times to friends around a campfire. It had always puzzled him,
but in a fanciful and not distressing way. Three months before he consulted
me, he picked up one of the popular books about UFO abductions, and thus the
problems began. He read 60 pages and was so terrified that he threw the book
away. He contacted the author of the book who happened to be conducting a
workshop in a neighboring state. In short, the patient and his friend
visited the author; they were both hypnotized by him at different times that
weekend. Whereas my patient's friend reported only vague, generic memories
of being abducted, my patient had an extraordinary hypnotic experience
filled with vivid details of the aliens....

Try another example...

Luis R. González Manso

Glen wrote:

>As odd as it sounds, the situation with missing people is a
>strange one - you see, unless the police feel that there are
>no "suspicious circumstances" or "serious concerns for the
>safety and welfare" etc... police will not give it all the
>resources the case may need.


Glen,

Point appreciated.

To recap, the claim is:

>"Was a person abducted that night, by a UFO?"
>Monday, October 21, 2002
>
>Dr Barnett went on to report "We also have an abduction that
>on the same night that we have under investigation, in that
>case the person is still missing.
>
>The abduction that was related to the police and our
>investigators involves a flying object that chased the
>missing person. The witnesses who reported the story, have
>given a description of the object and that is in the early
>stages of the investigation." he said.
>
>As of this morning [21st] the car and the missing person have
>not been located. The police can do little at present as
>there is no indication of a crime....


I asked, "How can there feasibly be, 'no indication of a
crime'"...

The witnesses allegedly reported, "a flying object that chased
the missing person".
The key phrase here is 'chased'.

If, say, someone was driving home and never arrived, then
that's indeed primarily a missing person.

If, however, it's reported that they were observably being
chased by another vehicle, is there "no indication of a
crime"?

I dare say it depends on the interpretation of 'indication'.


If someone went to the police and reported that their wife had
never arrived home from work - still, as above, statedly
missing next morning - and they had been informed her car was
seen to be followed/pursued/chased by another, would the
police take no action whatsoever?

Would they furthermore disregard that, "The witnesses who
reported the story, have given a description of the
vehicle[object]" which was noted to be following her car?

Does it not qualify as "suspicious circumstances" and/or
"serious concerns for the safety and welfare"...?


Answers to the other questions I raised would be interesting.


Presumably, the supposed witnesses must have personally known
the missing person and their family, otherwise they wouldn't
know that person was still missing next morning.


Essentially, the obvious point is that, if proclaiming, "We
also have an abduction [by aliens] that [sic] on the same
night..." it does actually require some meaningful evidence.

Even if the chase vehicle was from outer space, it's still a
'missing person', at most.

And a missing car.

Unless, as queried, Dr Barnett had significant evidence,
before publicising the extraordinary allegation, that both
were kidnapped by ETs...


James.

No! Not that same old "biased Condon Report" propaganda again.

Every couple of years, the "UFOs are real" camp comes up with the
same untenable argument: "Scientists always assume that 'UFOs
do not exist', and that's why we don't have proof."

There are a couple of things wrong with their arguments:

1. UFOs exist only until we find out what they are. Once we find
out, it's no longer a UFO, but an IFO -- even if it turns out to be
an alien spaceship.

2. When dealing with a question of whether something exists, it is
impossible to prove that it does not exist without an exhaustive
search. An exhaustive search of the entire universe (or even our
galaxy) is out of the question with the current instrumentation we
have. So we MUST assume that space aliens do not exist until we have
tangible proof that they do. If we assume otherwise, than the
question can never be answered.

Sturrock's book lists the entire report and this may be the quote you are interested
in:<BR>
<BR>
"The panel also reviewed some of the conclusions advanced in 1968 by Dr. Edward U.
Condon, director of the Colorado Project. He asserted that "nothing has come from
the study of UFOs in the past 21 years that has added to scientific knowledge," and
that "further extensive study of UFOs probably cannot be justified in the expectation
that science will be advanced thereby." While agreeing with the first conclusion and
its extension to the present, the panel considers that there always exists the possibility
that investigation of an unexplained phenomenon may lead to an advance in scientific
knowledge."<BR>
<BR>
Page 122 The UFO Enigma Peter Sturrock<BR>
<BR>
However, Condon himself wrote something similar in his summary.&nbsp; For some
reason this is often overlooked in writings about the Condon study.&nbsp; Condon
wrote:<BR>
<BR>
"Earlier we said that we do not think study of UFO reports is likely to be a fruitful
direction of scientific advance; now we have just said that persons with good ideas for
specific studies in this field should be supported. This is no contradiction. Although
we conclude after nearly two years of intensive study, that we do not see any fruitful
lines of advance from the study of UFO reports, we believe that any scientist with
adequate training and credentials who does come up with a clearly defined, specific
proposal for study should be supported."<BR>
<BR>
Condon Report<BR>

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>

Subject: RE: [UFORL] Classic Cases

This is an interesting list. Some of the cases are solved or probably
solved, but others are baffling:

5/1/52, 5/14/52 - These are on my puzzling cases list

8/13/60 - This one has all the characteristics of a fire balloon

4/24/64 - The most likely explanation is an early manned hot air
balloon.

9/3/65 - This case has two internal inconsistencies:

- 1. The testimony of the order they arrived at towns does not agree
with
the order of the towns on a Texas road map.

- 2. The UFO was bright enough to read by, yet it threw a shadow from
the
moon.

3/14-20/66 - Most of the sightings have fire-balloon characteristics.

10/18/73 - Possibly a meteor combined with an optical illusion, but no
proof of this.

9/1/74 - An interesting single-witness case -- except that he had with
him the means to make the crop circles.

10-11/75 - The SAC base events are now known to have been a secret test
of stealth technology.

9/19/76 - Possibly a clandestine spy mission.

1/1/78 - Same time as Valentich case. Possibly (but only possibly) a
stunt to advertise, or to win a tabloid prize.

3/4/88 - The parent object has fire-balloon characteristics. But the
description of the secondary objects tend to disprove that, unless they
were birds or insects.

5/25/95 - This seems puzzling, unless it is similar to the 3/13/97
Phoenix
case.

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Wed, 6 Nov 2002 10:00:08 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Looking for ULO

At first, this sounds like another RADAR calibration device. These are
dropped from airplanes over rural areas, to reflect calibrated amounts of
RADAR waves. This is then used to calibrate RADAR receivers on the
ground and in other planes.

But the "book" jogs my memory. I have a photo of it! It was a crude prank
made by some college students. The object was left for others to find,
but only the pranksters themselves said the object had fallen.

By the way, I distinguish between "prank" and "hoax" in the following way:

- A PRANK is a fake UFO (such as a fire balloon), or fake traces
supposedly made by a UFO (or a sledgehammer), provided by the prankster
for others to see and report.

- A HOAX is a fabricated report of a UFO event that never happened. It
can include "evidence" (such as the pad prints left by a power company arm
lift truck) which the hoaxter reports as being left by a UFO.

Some cases can be a combination of hoax and prank.

the camera lens. Most of his

solved it in 1994 while fixing my Collaro.


#3: 05/07/52 Barra Da Tijuca Brazil (Ed Keffel)

The proof that this is a montage is in photo #5. The light comes from
the bottom
of the object. This is impossible if the photographer is standing on the

#4: 03/03/67 Picacho Peak, Las Cruces NM (?)

This was a clear rubber suction cup stuck to the car window the picture
was taken
through. The photographer did not notice it when the photo was taken.


#5: The "Mutes".

11/29/74 Meeker Co. MN (?) Mutilated pig; cult, power sag put out yard
light.
12/L3/74 MN, TX, OK, CA (many) Mutilated livestock; cult, drugs found in
bodies.
05/L5/75 CO, TX, OK, CA, WY (many) Mutilated livestock; Helicopter cult,
arrests made
09/L4/75 WI, IA, (many) Mutilated livestock; Helicopter cult; Cult
imitators
09/L4/75 WI, IA, (many) Mutilated livestock; Insurance scam
10/**/77 Colorado Springs CO (many) Mutilated livestock; Helicopter cult
10/**/78 Logan Co. CO (Tex Graves, many) Mutilated livestock; Helicopter
cult
07/**/79 Walsenberg CO (C E Potts) Mutilated livestock; Cult

One or more satanic cults were stealing farmers' cattle for ritual
sacrifices. One cult
even had a helicopter, with lights on it arranged to look like a flying
saucer. In
addition, some farmers were caught in an insurance scam where they
presented cattle
which died naturally (not covered) as mutilated by aliens (believe it or
not, covered).

The case was solved in 1975 when arrests were made by a sheriff in
Colorado.

These cults have since migrated to other countries to escape US law
enforcement.

Cases where the identification was unusual:

07/17/56 Natal South Africa (Elizabeth Klarer)

I have one of these. It is a "Spin-O-Reno" toy. This is a plastic plate
about 10 inches
in diameter, with a raised center and a deep rim on the bottom, designed
so kids can
easily do the "plate spinning on a stick trick" normally done in
circuses.


03/04/62 Sheffield England (Alex Birch)

I wanted this mobile of rockets and saucers (printed on cardboard) as a
kid. A friend
down the street had one. Print the photo light, and you can see the
cartoon drawings
on the objects.


08/02/65 Tulsa OK (Alan Smith)

The flashbulb didn't go off! All that showed up was the color wheel used
to illuminate
an aluminum Christmas tree. The next frame on the roll is the same shot
with the flash
going off properly (and the wheel has rotated).


10/21/65 St George MN (Arthur Strauch)

Again, the flash didn't go off! It's a night-light plugged into a wall
socket. Look
at it through a blue filter and you can see the shape of the bulb.


08/08/65 C53 Beaver Co PA (James Lucci)

How did these shots fool so many people? It's a handheld small plate lit
by a
flashlight. The "exhaust" is the hand and arm.


S/NN/66 Provo UT (air) This is Condon Report case # 7

I used to have the same plastic top from a cookie jar. The jar was clear
plastic,
in the shape of Santa Claus, and was sold full of butter cookies. This
was his hat.
There were other photos in between the two photos of the object.

In a message dated 11/7/2002 3:40:10 PM Eastern Standard Time,
lrobins@indiana.edu writes:

<< MY 5 BEST CASES. All are multiple witness sightings:

<snip>

#2: 07/14/52 Newport News VA (air: Nash, Fortenberry) 6 red circles came
toward plane from front, passed underneath it; Then objects reversed course
and sped away in front of the plane, joined by 2 more >>

Hi, Larry:

I think that the Nash, Fortenberry sighting can be explained by a fragmenting
bolide meteor. The witnesses thought that the lights were below them, but
didn't see them below the horizon. Instantaneous change of direction was
as the meteor fragments burned out and seemed to zoom away. The last
two were noticed as they burned out, after the pilots changed seats.
They thought these last two were joining the others, but the pilots just
assumed they had passed under their wing.

The giveway is that the ufos seemed to reverse direction in order, from
front (first fragment) to back, but then blinked out randomly (by size of
meteor fragment). Other witnesses saw the lights in the distance,
in a line.

Clear skies,
Bob Young

From: YoungBob2@aol.com
Date: Thu, 7 Nov 2002 23:46:06 EST
Subject: [UFORL] Best and Worst

Regarding the Loring AFB incidents, part of the "Northern Tier
SAC" sightings:

I have a friend who has been a lifelong astronomy enthusiast who
was a member of the airbase security unit at Loring at the time.
He told me that other guards would report UFOs which were
astronomical objects, and even auroral rays would be reported as
UFOs behind the trees. He told me it was really wild, that
other guys were reporting "everything" as UFOs. In his opinion,
and he was out there at night on patrol, was that nothing out of
the ordinary (beyond aircraft and sky objects) happened.

In fact, he said that it did just the opposite for him, it destroyed
his notions about UFOs for good.

Philip J. Klass has proposed that astronomical objects (one
light and no radar contact, for example) and flights by a
civilian helicopter taking survey pictures provide good
explanations. See the details of his investigation in: 'UFOs:
The Public Deceived', Prometheus Books, 1983, pp. 89,
92-97,105.)

Clear skies,
Bob Young

Bentwaters and the UFO-on-the-side were more interesting cases to me.

She really saw it! That UFO-on-the-side saucer was a hot-air balloon
kit sold by Edmund Scientific. It came with that lettering. I still
have the catalog (found it in the attic the other day).

Bentwaters was a really intriguing set of natural phenomena and
coincidences. It took a lot of patience and thought to work all of
it out.

I have always thought that the Turkey Springs case was either an
attempt to provide an excuse for failing to complete the contract on
time, or an attempt to win the National Enquirer prize.

I will have to look (and it will be several weeks, because I have
to do a lot of cleaning for an appraiser who is coming). But I think
the stealth explanation of the SAC case is in one of the following
books:

Peter Brookesmith: UFO - The Complete Sightings
Peter Brookesmith: UFO - The Government Files
The UFO Encyclopedia

I have my reservations on the Hudson Valley case, because the one
photo I have is a photo of part of a carnival ride, with electric
bulbs of different colors arranged in a partial ellipse.

Hi Bob, list,

Compare this with a comment I found in a UK Civil Aviation Authority
Commercial Air Transport Airmiss report (7/94) concerning a 'UFO'
sighting by a Bell Air pilot flying over the North Sea:

"An RAF Fylingdales [space tracking station]
spokesman said it is well known that the human eye's perception of such
occurrences is notoriously innacurate, due to the immense speeds and
distances involved. What may appear to be only metres away is in
reality probably several hundred miles distant. In a subsequent conversation
the pilot, who was amazed and intrigued by the explanation, said that
the whole incident took place in less than a second - but even so he had
the distinct, though inexplicable, feeling that the object had definite
shape and form."

The pilot had reported to ATC seeing "an object seen to
fall almost vertically downwards in front and to the right of the aircraft,
emitting large sparks and possibly flames. He estimated the distance
at about 300m. It was travelling extremely fast, making it difficult
to identify or assess the size, but the pilot remarks that it appeared to
be 3 to 6 ft long and regular in shape, giving the impression of
being a man-made object."

The 'object' in this case was identified as being part of Soviet Soyuz
space vehicle burning up on re-entry.

There were no Soyuz spacecraft in 1952, but just as likely that
Nash-Fortenberry saw a piece of 'natural', as opposed to man-made
space junk, as Bob has suggested.

Best,
Dave Clarke

From: "rotsky" <rotsky@wanadoo.fr>
Date: Fri, 8 Nov 2002 22:14:25 +0100
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Best and Worst

I see that Fortean Times has covered that alleged UFO chase by a couple of
F-16s, which was discussed here recently. In a way, this is an example of
how a story can gain currency because of too little analysis or information
at the beginning.

The FT story (presumably because of space restrictions) doesn't go into any
of the possible explanations that were offered here. As it stands, it's a
story that is likely to get repeated & passed on, and in doing so will gain
credibility as an 'unexplained'. Technically, of course, it *is* unexplained
as there is no conclusive proof of any of the several potential mundane
explanations being the true one. Naturally, in the process of being passed
on, this tale will not carry with it those potential explanations.

It's important to consider these stories in context. And the context here is
that, since the attacks of 9/11, there has been a heightened state of
security in the US, with the security services being a little touchy. Those
in the aviation world are aware that:
1) there are many new areas of restricted airspace in the US;
2) many of these are temporary (eg, over Dubya's house, when he's at home),
so...
3) there are lots of pilots having trouble keeping track of these areas and
equally having trouble keeping out of them, because the airspace is so
complex in some places, so that...
4) there are multiple incursions into these areas every day, resulting in
the scrambling of military jets to intercept, but...
5) often the infringing aircraft bumbles out of the area again and either
the jets are recalled without making contact or they look but simply can't
find the offending aircraft (this has happened *a lot* - the aircraft may
have landed or dropped off the radar screens for one reason or another).

Of course, eventually, this context will be forgotten and the unexplained
*mystery* will gain credibility...

a+
Steve

From: "James Easton" <voyager@ukonline.co.uk>
Date: Sat, 9 Nov 2002 04:36:34 -0000
Subject: Re: [UFORL] The Best and Worst of UFOlogy

If all UFO sightings have a prosaic explanation, I dare say
it's arguable that cases which seem to best support the ET
hypothesis [ETH] are conversely 'worst' cases, i.e., the most
deceptive.

In terms of offering tangible evidence, five prominent cases
might be:

1. Kenneth Arnold's sighting.
2. Roswell.
3. The Billy Meier flying saucer portfolio.
4. The Trent photographs.
5. Ed Walter's flying saucer portfolio.


Arnold's is significant not only as the effective genesis of
flying saucers; he did note the distance seemingly covered by
those nine unidentified aerial objects in a measured time and
could subsequently calculate their airspeed.

That was the initial reason his story was picked up by an
excited media - the USAAF had no known aircraft capable of an
apparent 1,200 m.p.h.

Arnold's evidence seemed trustworthy; the fact these were
described as "somewhat bat-shaped" and tail-less objects only
added to the mystery.

If it _was_ reliable [evidence otherwise re 'Arnold's peak'
previously highlighted], then his sighting remains puzzling
and an indication of intelligently controlled aerial craft
with no contemporary, earthly counterparts.


Roswell may be long resolved, however, only days after
Arnold's report, the USAAF did announce they had recovered a
'flying disk', even though the earliest newspaper descriptions
were clearly of a flimsy, kite-like object.

To many, the perceived Roswell cover-up remains a foundation
of belief and it has of course spawned a succession of bogus
documents which are themselves advocated to be tangible ETH
proof.

_CLOSE ENCOUNTER ON INTERSTATE 84_

By: Philip J. Imbrogno

In the past, the state of Connecticut has always been an
area of few UFO reports, however this is no longer true.
Since 1985 the counties of Fairfield and Litchfield and
Hartford has seen a dramatic rise in the number of UFO
reports. This UFO is described as being a semi circle or
boomerang with multi-colored lights. Even more incredible
the size of this UFO has been reported to be the length
of a football field! This UFO that has been seen recently
in Connecticut is without a doubt the Hudson valley UFO
which is described in my book NIGHT SIEGE THE HUDSON
VALLEY UFO SIGHTINGS (Ballantine Books 1987).

For some reason unknown to this researcher the giant
boomerang UFO has shifted its activities from New York to
Nearby Connecticut. The most recent sightings took place
on May 26 of this year around interstate 84 one of the
most heavily traveled highways in the northeast.
Between 9;30 and 10;15 PM more than 200 people phoned
local and state police to report a huge object with
bright lights flying low over the highway near the towns
of Newtown and Southbury in Connecticut. Those witnesses
that called state police in Southbury were told that it
was nothing more than a group of Ultralight aircraft from
Candlewood airport flying in close formation and hanging
colored lanterns from the bottom of the plane. The police
also told witnesses that the aircraft were painted black
so that all that can be seen is the lights. Many of the
witnesses to the phenomenon found it very hard to believe
the official explanation.

[...]

Another witnesses was Mr. Randy Etting a commercial
airline pilot with over thirty years of experience. Mr.
Etting said that the idea of the ultralight theory "is
the prattling of idiots" Mr. Etting observed the lights
from his home in Newtown Connecticut at about 9:45 pm. He
said that there were at least eight lights of different
colors flying very close together and without a sound. As
the object passed his home he observed it in a pair of
7X35 binoculars. Mr. Etting told me that the UFO was one
object and he saw some type of heat waves coming from the
object which distorted the area around the lights.

Mr. Etting watched the object with neighbors and his son
for over ten minutes as it slowly drifted to the north
west. All the witnesses agree that the UFO was one solid
object and round in appearance.

The Etting party was observing the UFO while it was
passing close to I-84. At this time over a dozen cars
pulled over to view the UFO as it passed overhead.

[...]

_Photographic Proof_

This UFO was so bright and large that it was only a
matter of time before someone would come forward with a
photograph. To our surprise we were contacted by a person
of high standing in the Southbury area who took a picture
of the object as it moved very slowly over I-84 at about
9:30 PM. The photographer wishes to remain anonymous
since his position is very sensitive. He is a very highly
trained college educated man who fears that the publicity
surrounding the photograph could hurt his career. He gave
us full rights to the photograph and his sighting account
providing we do not use his real name. We will refer to
him as David.

David was on I-84 on official business when he saw the
lights. The lights were in the northwest and heading
east. As he watched, the object tilted and all the lights
got much brighter. He was pulled off the road at the time
and had his camera ready. The UFO was about 45 degrees
above the horizon. Due to traffic he had time to take
only one picture. His camera was a 35mm with a 50mm lens
at 1.8, the film type was Kodacolor asa 400 and the
exposure was 1/60th of a second, or 1/125. He was not
sure of the setting, but feels it was 1/60th of a second.
The object then moved toward the east without a sound.
During an interview with this researcher, David told me
that the he was sure there was a solid object behind the
lights. He also said that when the object turned it
looked like the lights on the sides were pulling out from
the main mass, but he realized that this effect was due
to the object changing position from his point of view.

_What about the Photo_:

Several photo-analysis experts are now looking at the
photograph. Our initial study showed that the image is
without a doubt hanging in the sky above the ground. Also
the photograph was looked at by Dr. Willy Smith a
scientist and UFO researcher of some repute. Dr. Smith's
initial calculations show the object to be anywhere from
650-1600 across!

We believe that this photograph is one of the best night-
time UFO pictures taken in the past twenty years. There
were quite a few witnesses to the sighting over a twenty-
five mile radius, all reporting the same thing. A close
examination of the original negative shows that the
lights are reflecting off of some type of structure in
the central part of the object .Also the lights are in a
perfect half circle. There is no doubt that what ever the
UFO photograph represents it is one solid object. We hope
to get more data on the photograph and the sightings in
the weeks to come. I have taken an add in the local

What about the theory that the UFO is nothing more than

My list of baffling cases are as follows:
I have drawn only from those instances where I
have personally interviewed the witnesses, and located related
documents at the PRO:

1. 16 January 1947. North Sea. 'Unidentified aircraft' tracked on
GCI radar at 38,000 feet over Dutch coast at speeds between
400-1000mph. Pursued by RAF Mosquito which obtained AI
contact during a chase which lasted 1 hour, ending above the
Norfolk coast. Listed as 'unidentified' by Air Ministry when details
were passed to Project Sign in July 1947. Summary described
how 'aircraft' took "efficient controlled evasive action."

2. August and September 1950. Disc-shaped UFO reported
in daylight above RAE Farnborough by RAF test pilots,
investigated by the MoD's Flying Saucer Working Party.

3. 21 October 1952. Gloucestershire, UK. Three 'flying saucers'
sighted visually at 30,000 feet by the pilot and navigator of an RAF
Meteor jet. Visual contact and radar confirmation by GCI and
Air Traffic Control. QRA squadron scrambled but failed to
make contact. See 'Out of the Shadows', pg 98-100.

4. May 1957. North Sea. UFO tracked on
GCI radar, RAF Bawdsey. Two USAF F-84D Sabres scrambled
from Manston to intercept. One aircraft obtained AI lock on
target at 32,000 feet "the blip was burning a hole in the radar
with its incredible intensity"...pilot ordered to shoot down target
with missile but UFO broke lock and disappeared at speed.

These are the four cases that remain 'baffling' to an old cynic
like me.

Dave Clarke

From: "James Easton" <voyager@ukonline.co.uk>
Date: Sun, 10 Nov 2002 02:33:32 -0000
Subject: Re: [UFORL] The Best and Worst of UFOlogy

Regarding:

>From: "Jim Speiser" <jimspeiser@yahoo.com>
>Date: Sat, 9 Nov 2002 00:52:34 -0700
>Subject: RE: [UFORL] The BEst and Worst of UFOlogy

Jim wrote:

>The object depicted on the MUFON link is indeed the
>photo I was provided by Phil Imbrogno. Beyond being
>elliptical and multi-colored on a black background, I
>don't see any reason to suspect that this photo is in
>any way related to the Nashville photo.

Jim,

When the 'Nashville' photographs surfaced again, featured
on:

http://www.rense.com/submissions/3ufosday.html
http://www.nationalufocenter.com/features/bethune.htm

...I highlighted that they were apparently of a
disco/lighting rig, which had been featured in a magazine
- see:

http://www.ufoworld.co.uk/ftp/nashvlle.jpg
http://www.ufoworld.co.uk/ftp/nashcomp.jpg


On:

http://www.nationalufocenter.com/features/bethune.htm

...the photograph at top of page doesn't appear amongst
those on the Rense site and what seems to be another from
the collection can be found at the bottom of the
following page:

http://www.filersfiles-ufo.com/


I first saw some of these photographs in the May/June
1995 issue of 'UFO Magazine' [UK]. The story was that
they had been taken by a retired US Naval Commander who
insisted on remaining anonymous due to his military
background. He reportedly claimed there were around 80
photographs in total.

Some copies had been given to Tony Dodd from 'UFO
Magazine' when he was in the U.S. and although they were
proclaimed to be genuine, on 11th January 1998, during an
IRC chat, Graham Birdsall, the magazine's editor,
acknowledged:

Dave_UFO:
Wendelle Stevens made a big play of the Nashville,
Tennessee UFO which you have featured. It now appears
that these photograph's were nothing more than disco
lights and dry ice in some sort of night club. Has
Wendelle Stevens made any further comments on this?

Graham:
No, he hasn't. But you are correct, the Nashville UFO
pics do appear to have been a classic set of disco
lights. People who are in the business of hoaxing take
great delight in fooling the UFO community, so we have to
be constantly on our guard. It's frustrating, and time
wasting, but Wendelle's in his eighties now and I feel
for the guy.
[END]


It was only on seeing these photographs again that I
realised they were similar to another photograph I had
come across since 1995. I located a bookmarked, on-line
copy and it turned out to be the Waterbury picture, at:

http://www.geocities.com/Area51/Zone/9047/870526.htm

As an exercise, I first compared this with an extract
from one of the Nashville photos:

http://www.ufoworld.co.uk/ftp/saucers.jpg

In order to do so, it was apparently necessary to both
flip and 'mirror' the Nashville images, i.e.:

http://www.ufoworld.co.uk/ftp/upended.jpg

Any evident correlations were then noted:

http://www.ufoworld.co.uk/ftp/saucers2.jpg
http://www.ufoworld.co.uk/ftp/saucers3.jpg
Could the Waterbury photograph also have come from that
collection, taken when the rig was simply displaying a
circle of lights.

The possibility seemed more likely when I discovered that
it perhaps wasn't even necessary to flip and mirror the
Nashville image for comparison - the Waterbury photograph
on MUFON CT's web site may itself be a reverse print.

It's my understanding it should in fact look like this:

http://www.angelfire.com/de/xphiles1013/waterbury2.jpg

That's how it is published in two books I'm aware of.


It's open to anyone how they judge the overall evidence.

One other point though; if you look at the supposed
Nashville UFO photographs, you will find that one of the
various lighting effects available is a sequence of large
red lights, interspersed with smaller pale-blue lights -
for example:

http://www.rense.com/submissions/ship2.html

Is it merely further coincidence that smaller, pale-blue
lights can be seen in the Waterbury photograph [they're
much clearer in book prints].

I would have to say it's also disconcerting that the
origins of our Waterbury photograph are anonymous.


Incidentally, for those who haven't seen it, there's an
interesting letter re the Hudson Valley sightings from
Robert R. Young, in Magonia Monthly Supplement, October
1999:

http://www.magonia.demon.co.uk/arc/00/ms20.html

Anthony,

Many of these cases have been researched in detail and
have an evident/proven, prosaic explanation.

We can come back to that; there are however some which
ostensibly seem to inexplicable and yet, rarely receive
attention.

I would suggest one of these is the Lake Erie, March 4,
1988 incident:

http://www.fufor.com/case880304.htm

This is not only, as you highlight, a multiple witness
event, it's one which was, importantly, documented by the
US Coast Guard at the time.

That FUFOR summary contains some anomalies and an error
at the outset. It's reported:

"Sheila and Henry Baker were driving home with their
three children about 8:35 p.m."

It was apparently at 8:35 p.m. when these witnesses
called the Coast Guard [according to the Coast Guard
documentation] and any initial sighting must have
occurred some time before.
There's a reasonably well-known case investigator's
report online at:

http://chabin.laurent.free.fr/triangul.txt

This cites the Baker's first observation occurred at
around 6:30 p.m., which would indicate it was some two
hours before the Coast Guard were contacted.

However, it's not straightforward as Sheila Baker
apparently first telephoned the Eastlake police, then
Lost Nation Airport in Willoughby, then Fairport Harbor
Coast Guard, then [possibly] Wright-Patterson Air Force
Base, then the Coast Guard, again, several times...

That evidence and much more, doesn't appear to be
contained within most/any other online copies of Richard
P. Dell'Aquila and Dale Wedge's investigative account -
it looks to be from:

"Uploaded with permission of Christopher Evans of the
'Cleveland Plain Dealer' on an article entitled 'Space
Case - The Night The Coast Guard Got Buzzed', dated July
12, 1988".

See also:

http://www.angelfire.com/ms/area51stuff2/eastlake.html


Striking to read that Mrs Baker had allegedly shut her
kids in a closet, "pulled down all the window blinds,
turned off the lights and locked the bedroom door",
because of a perceived 'UFO threat'.

We can but surmise how much of Christopher Evans later
article is maybe 'journalistic license'.

Factual anomalies are different accounts of when the
Baker's visited the beach for a closer look and that they
were both on the beach and had also returned in fright to
the house at specific points.

That aside, the Coast Guard 'teletype', reportedly,
confirms [this capitalised text may 'wrap around']:

THIS UNIT SENT 2 CREWMEMBERS TO INVESTIGATE. BEFORE THEY
ARRIVED O/S, WE RCVD 2 MORE CALLS RPTNG THAT THE OBJECT
HAD APPARENTLY DISPERSED 3-5 SMALLER FLYING OBJECTS THAT
WERE ZIPPING AROUND RATHER QUICKLY. THESE OBJECTS HAD
RED, GREEN, WHITE AND YELLOW LIGHTS ON THEM THAT STROBED
INTERMITTENTLY. THEY ALSO HAD THE ABILITY TO STOP AND
HOVER IN MID FLIGHT.

WHEN MOBILE 02 GOT O/S, THEY RPTD THE SAME ACTIVITY. THEY
WATCHED THE OBJECTS FOR APPROX. 1 HOUR BEFORE RPTNG THAT
THE LARGE OBJECT WAS ALMOST ON THE ICE. THEY RPTD THAT
THE ICE WAS CRACKING AND MOVING ABNORMAL AMOUNTS AS THE
OBJECT CAME CLOSER TO IT. THE ICE WAS RUMBLING AND THE
OBJECT LIT MULTI-COLOR LIGHTS AT EACH END AS IT
APPARENTLY LANDED.

THE LIGHTS ON IT WENT OUT MOMENTARILY AND THEN CAME ON
AGAIN. THEY WENT OUT AGAIN AND THE RUMBLING STOPPED AND
THE ICE STOPPED MOVING. THE SMALLER OBJECTS BEGAN
HOVERING IN THE AREA WHERE THE LARGE OBJECT LANDED AND
AFTER A FEW MINUTES THEY BEGAN FLYING AROUND AGAIN.

MOBILE 02 RPTD THAT THEY APPEARED TO BE SCOUTING THE
AREA. MOBILE 02 RPTD THAT 1 OBJECT WAS MOVING TOWARD
THEM AT A HIGH SPEED AND LOW TO THE ICE. MOBILE 02
BACKED DOWN THE HILL THEY HAD BEEN ON AND WHEN THEY WENT
BACK TO THE HILL, THE OBJECT WAS GONE. THEY RPTD THAT
THE OBJECTS COULD NOT BE SEEN IF THEY TURNED OFF THERE
LIGHTS. ONE OF THE SMALL OBJECTS TURNED ON A SPOTLIGHT
WHERE THE LARGE OBJECT HAD BEEN BUT MOBILE 02 COULD NOT
SEE ANYTHING, AND THEN THE OBJECT SEEMED TO DISAPPEAR.

ANOTHER OBJECT APPROACHED MOBILE 02 APPROX. 500 YDS.
OFFSHORE ABOUT 20 FT. ABOVE THE ICE, AND IT BEGAN MOVING
CLOSER AS MOBILE 02 BEGAN FLASHING ITS HEADLIGHTS, THEN
IT MOVED OFF TO THE WEST.

THE CREWMEMBERS WERE UNABLE TO IDENTIFY ANY OF THE
OBJECTS USING BINOCULARS AND AFTER CONTACTING LOCAL
POLICE AND AIRPORTS, THIS UNIT WAS UNABLE TO IDENTIFY THE
OBJECTS, AND RECALLED MOBILE 02.
[END]


Incorporating time which had elapsed before the patrol
arrived and that they seemingly, "WATCHED THE OBJECTS FOR
APPROX. 1 HOUR BEFORE RPTNG" what was further activity.

It must have been about a two hour show...

Any suggested explanations from list members?
It's claimed:

"S. and H. stood watch through the night. In the morning
all that remained were scattered chunks of broken ice.
But that evening, the triangles returned.

Sheila called the Coast Guard. This time they sent three
people. But they arrived too late and the triangles were
gone. To reassure the B's, they called Lost Nation
Airport and talked to Elizabeth Mele in the control tower
who told them the two bright lights in the sky were Venus
and Jupiter, and the flashing lights were gases in the
atmosphere".

This seems quite specific; "and talked to Elizabeth Mele
in the control tower".

Is there any other known evidence that Mrs Baker reported
the 'triangles' had come back?


Christopher Evans' article states, "Four years later,
she's still confused".

Four years later?

She's not the only one who's confused.

Contrary to aforementioned online sources, I surmise that
FUFOR's reference is correct in dating the article to
July 12, 1992.

A speculative online search has discovered the following:

The News-Herald
Monday, March 7, 1988

SKY-GAZERS MISTAKE PLANETS FOR UFOS

Visitors from another planet have nothing to do with the
UFOs which were reported along the lake shore Friday and
Saturday nights. But, according to the Coast Guard, the
planets Jupiter and Venus are involved.

When the US Coast Guard at Fairport Harbor received
reports Friday night [that would be the 4th and tie-in -
James] of UFOs in the sky, it checked with area airports
to learn what their radar indicated.

"We thought it might be someone in trouble setting off
flares," said Petty Officer John Knaub. "So we
investigated ourselves."

Coast Guard members saw the lights over the lake about
1/4 mile east of the mouth of the Chagrin River. "But
Lost Nation Airport advised us that we were seeing the
planets Jupiter and Venus, which are lined up together in
the sky. Apparently the gases in the atmosphere created
the appearance of smaller objects around them."

The UFO reports rolled in again Saturday night, when the
sky remained clear and was dominated by a full moon.

Knaub said the phenomena is visible around 9PM, as sky
gazers look west along the lake from Fairport Harbor.
[END]


'Petty Officer John Knaub' is identified in Christopher
Evans 1992 article:

"Mobile Unit 2 was a 1984 blue Chevy Suburban and the two
guys in it were gung-ho. Seaman James Powers and Petty
Officer John Knaub said they could see the lights from
Fairport Harbor".


How could Knaub, only three days later, reportedly
support the premise he had spent over an hour being
bemused by stars and 'atmospheric gases'.

To recap:

WHEN MOBILE 02 GOT O/S, THEY RPTD THE SAME ACTIVITY. THEY
WATCHED THE OBJECTS FOR APPROX. 1 HOUR BEFORE RPTNG THAT
THE LARGE OBJECT WAS ALMOST ON THE ICE. THEY RPTD THAT

P 060150Z MAR 88

SUBJ: INCIDENT REPORT: UNIDENTIFIED FLYING OBJECTS

1. UNIDENTIFIABLE FLYING OBJECTS 1/4 MILE EAST OF CEI

REQUEST INCIDENT CLOSED THIS UNIT. BT TOR-03:06:02:00

From: "Bill Chalker" <bill_c@bigpond.com>

Subject: Re: [UFORL] Re: So who was the first to view the RAAF UFO files?

Thank you James for the opportunity to reply to"Glen Hough's" misguided
message:
http://groups.yahoo.com/group/UFORL/message/1274

My previous message:
http://groups.yahoo.com/group/UFORL/message/1218
still stands as pretty much all I want to comment about "Hough's" messages.

But there are certain important points that need to be addressed more fully.
Again I'll try to make it clearer.

My book "The OZ Files" (1996), "UFOs Sub Rosa" (1996) (see:
http://www.theozfiles.com/ufos_subrosa.html and
http://www.project1947.com/forum/bcoz1.htm ) and other more recent materials
are not the first time I'm reviewed or examined RAAF materials. I have
listed a range of my publications at:
http://www.theozfiles.com/selected_bibliography.html
of which the following are pertinent to the issue:
"The RAAF Investigation of UFOs", MUFON UFO Journal, No. 143, January, 1980,
pgs. 3-6. This article first appeared in the ACOS Bulletin, No.20, August,
1979, and in UFOs over Australia, ACUFOS, 1985.
"UFOs and the RAAF - the Inside Story", UFORAN, Vol.3, Nos. 2,3 and 4,
March-April, May-June, and July-August, 1982. This article appeared in
abridged form in the MUFON UFO Journal, Nos. 175 (Sept. 1982) and 176 (Oct.
1982).
"Yes, There is a UFO Cover-up", OMEGA-Science Digest, Nov/Dec,1983. 1982:
"UFOs: Australia's Secret Documents Revealed", OMEGA-Science Digest,
Sept.-Oct. 1982. This article appeared in the APRO Bulletin, Vol.30, No.10
(Oct.'82) & Vol.30, No.11 (Dec.'82) as Australian A.F. UFO Report files.
"UFO Sloring (UFO Coverup)", produced by SUFOI/Kim Moller Hansen, from a
selection of my RAAF research papers, 1985 (in Danish).
"The North West Cape Incident: UFOs and nuclear alert in Australia", IUR,
Jan/Feb, 1986, Vol.11, No.1.
"The UFO Connection - Startling Implications for NW Cape and Australia's
security", OMEGA-Science Digest, March/April, 1985. This article along with
Addendum (letter) appeared in FSR, Vol.31, No.5, July, 1986.
"Working with the Government", in Spencer/Evans "Phenomenon", Futura,1988, a
nd Avon, 1989.

Late in 1982 my summary report: STUDY OF OFFICIAL AUSTRALIAN
GOVERNMENT
INVOLVEMENT IN UFO CONTROVERSY A PROGRESS REPORT was
published in various
places. A copy of that report is on the net:
http://ufocasebook.com/ausgov.txt
My point here that my research work was undertaken back in 1982 and beyond,
and published extensively.

If others did similar research then or earlier - great. But what do we know
about it?

"Hough" claims:
>I have it on good authority that he has been told on numerous
>occasions that his claim was wrong, and yet he continued to pretend
>and disseminate this wrong data.

I have certainly not been told by "good authority" that my "claim" is wrong.
By "good authority" I suspect "Hough" is trying to invoke "bower bird" type
individuals, who seem more intent on sitting on info rather than sharing it.
When they "sit on it" and don't share it I guess we will never know if
their "claims" have substance, unless they can be verified independently.
"Hough" is so hung up on so called "claims" he seems to really have missed
the point. In this field of research I believe it is important to share
research and information. I did that back in 1982 with the material I found
then, based on a lot of hard work on my part and the cooperation of the
Department of Defence.

There have been people who have made proclaimations or statements about
getting access to files and being aware of this and that. But unless those
statements are backed up by accessible data etc it is difficult to give them
much credence, particularly when one's own detail enquiries based on direct
file examinations fail to confirm such statements. But of course the "bower
birds" will crow that I've been looking in the wrong place or I've not been
digging deep enough or I'm totally on the wrong track. These sorts of
suggestions would be largely baseless or hollow if they are not backed up by
substance. The usual retort has been that they won't share that kind of
information and they will release their alleged information when it suits
them. Thats fine but don't expect me to then except their claims as factual
when nothing has been presented to validate them. "Hough's logic" seems to
be that those that have done that undocumented or unrevealed research don't
need to substantiate their activities. I guess he is right. There is no
obligation to do so other than the principle of sharing information and
assisting research, with the broader aim of widening our base of knowledge
on UFOs that is available to public researchers and the general public.
I've experienced the difficulties of verification with Defence, but at least
there it was often possible to verify a chain of evidence that certain
things were done.

Here is a brief extract from a 1982 "progress" report I circulated back
then. It was published in a number of places at the time:
____________________________________________________________
During 1982, I was able to:

a. Examine the majority of the extent UFO files held by the Royal
   Australian Air Force (RAAF).
b. Examine the entirety of the extent UFO files held by the Dept. of
   Aviation.

c. Initiate discussions with a defence scientist privy to the
   official files and the inner working of governmental policies and
   approaches to the UFO subject.

d. Initiate enquiries with other Australian agencies and individuals
   re UFO file holdings.

e. Undertake enquiries with overseas government departments re UFO
   file holdings (in particular, the Ministries of Defence in the
   U.K. and the USAF re Project Blue Book, the latter, in relation
   to Australian cases).

f. Undertake discussions with the Department of Aviation/Bureau of
   Air Safety investigation on the Valentich affair, and

g. publish some of the results of my enquiries.
_____________________________________________________________
This progress report was as accurate as my knowledge and understanding at
the time could make it. One can pick holes as much as they like if they are
so inclined but no one else was publishing the results of that kind of
detailed research to a wider public research audience at the time or before
other than myself. If others did so they didn't share their research with
the wider research community like I did. If others did similar research they
choose not to reveal it to a wider audience. It seems "Hough" is one of
those types who doesn't feel that it is worthwhile to share information and
research around and seems totally preoccupied with misguided and stupid
attacks on someone who believes that that sort of research should be widely
published and disemminated.

I am against what I refer to above as "bower bird" research where for
whatever reasons people do research but sit on it and do not share that
information. If such people can overcome their own reasons for that sort of
mentality then maybe we might actually learn some interesting things. Maybe
somebody did do earlier extensive research of the RAAF files etc. It would
be great if someone who has any information of that nature could actually
make it available to a wider audience. It may change our understanding of
the knowledge we have about official files in Australia.

To conclude, while it might be interesting to determine who was the first to
view the RAAF UFO files, and dissect the detail of "claims" and
"counterclaims", I think it is much more inportant to make the results of
such "viewings" and research available to the wider research community and
the general public. I did that back in 1982-84 and since then. At the time I
understood I was the first to do that and I still believe I was. Anyway
that is secondary to the achievement of making a lot of information
available to a wider audience so that those so inclined to do further
research etc can do so.

If this stupid debate has any positive outcome I hope it will be to entice
out those who claim to have done earlier research based on direct "viewings"
of the RAAF files and that they will finally after all these years, from the
70s or earlier, they might reveal what they found out to a wider research
audience and the general public.

Regards to the list,
To "Hough" - get a life,

Bill Chalker

P.S. It is dissapointing that in airing "Hough's" message that his earlier
rants were aired yet again. For those inclined to get into those again I
trust you will at least do your homework and look at the full discussion on
these points (particularly my responses to them in the UFORL file archive),

Hi Bob ---

The possibility of Soviet 'intruders' is certainly a possibility in terms of
cases 1 and 4, but there are problems -- for example:
>
> 1. 16 January 1947. North Sea. 'Unidentified aircraft' tracked on
> GCI radar at 38,000 feet over Dutch coast at speeds between
> 400-1000mph. Pursued by RAF Mosquito which obtained AI
> contact during a chase which lasted 1 hour, ending above the
> Norfolk coast. Listed as 'unidentified' by Air Ministry when details
> were passed to Project Sign in July 1947. Summary described
> how 'aircraft' took "efficient controlled evasive action."

Did the Soviets have aircraft with this level of performance (altitude,
speed, range, manoeuvrability, etc) as early as Jan 1947, and
furthermore would a Russians have run such a risk? This was
not a 'recce', as the 'unidentified aircraft' crossed the coast and
penetrated deep within UK territory. What's more, this was repeated
again the following night, triggering a second air defence alert.

If the Soviets were capable of such incursions early in 1947, I'd
like to know more! Ditto for 1957 (the latter case is weaker as
we have only the testimony of the USAF Sabre pilot, the
documentation - if any existed - has disappeared).

>
> 3. 21 October 1952. Gloucestershire, UK. Three 'flying saucers'
> sighted visually at 30,000 feet by the pilot and navigator of an RAF
> Meteor jet. Visual contact and radar confirmation by GCI and
> Air Traffic Control. QRA squadron scrambled but failed to
> make contact. See 'Out of the Shadows', pg 98-100.

Russian or US (Bell X experimental a/c) were top of the list of
possibilities when the Air Ministry looked at this one, but were
apparently ruled out quickly. This was a two-witness visual, with
two correlated ground radar tracks. The three 'saucers' were
in echelon formation, one canted slightly, and disappeared in
the blink of an eye. The only possibility considered were some
kind of meteorological phenomena, lenticular clouds etc (time was
daylight, midday)...but how likely is this at 30,000 feet? And how
does this explain the radar tie-in?

I'm all ears!

best,

Dave Clarke

ww.flyingsaucery.com
