Jim,

I wondered if the 'Nashville' photographs were perhaps of
a concert light show, taken from within the audience.

However, a notable point is their high-quality and
relative lack of hand-held camera-shake; wouldn't a
tripod have been necessary for the 'bright lights against
a dark background', lengthy exposure?

That's not likely in either a concert or disco,
suggesting the photographs may have been stage-managed
and taken to demonstrate the lighting-rig's capabilities.

They might also have been separately stage-managed with
the realisation it would make a convincing UFO hoax. Yet,
if so, why didn't those photographs first appear until
the mid-1990s [if anyone knows differently, please say
so].

There's also a possibility that even if the Waterbury
photograph is one of the same rig, the other photographs
could have been taken, perhaps by someone else, years
later.


>Perhaps I should attempt to contact Imbrogno.

It would be interesting to know exactly when he was first
given that photograph.

In an article [date unknown] entitled, 'Close Encounter
on Interstate 84', which has been transcribed and is
online - see:

http://ebe.allwebco.com/Sections/UFOs/Archive/interstate8
4.shtml

...Imbrogno writes:

"This UFO that has been seen recently in Connecticut is
without a doubt the Hudson valley UFO which is described
in my book NIGHT SIEGE THE HUDSON VALLEY UFO SIGHTINGS
(Ballantine Books 1987).

[...]

_Photographic Proof_

This UFO was so bright and large that it was only a
matter of time before someone would come forward with a
photograph. To our surprise we were contacted by a person
of high standing in the Southbury area who took a picture
of the object as it moved very slowly over I-84 at about
9:30 PM. The photographer wishes to remain anonymous
since his position is very sensitive. He is a very highly
trained college educated man who fears that the publicity
surrounding the photograph could hurt his career. He gave
us full rights to the photograph and his sighting account
providing we do not use his real name. We will refer to
him as David.

David was on I-84 on Official business when he saw the
lights. The lights were in the northwest and heading
east. As he watched, the object tilted and all the lights
got much brighter. He was pulled off the road at the time
and had his camera ready. The UFO was about 45 degrees
above the horizon. Due to traffic he had time to take
only one picture. His camera was a 35mm with a 50mm lens
at 1.8, the film type was Kodacolor asa 400 and the
exposure was 1/60th of a second, or 1/125. He was not
sure of the setting, but feels it was 1/60th of a
second".
[END OF EXTRACT]


If Dave had already pulled off the road and had his
camera ready, why only take one photograph, given this
unique and exceptional opportunity?

He's allegedly using quality equipment and presumably
experienced [did he always, conveniently, have ASA 400
low-light, 'night-time photography' print film loaded?].

So why only take one shot, knowing that even with 'fast
film', hand-held attempts at night photography are
characteristically blurred - several 'once in a lifetime'
shots, in the hope of at least one worthwhile photograph,
would only have taken a few seconds.

Surely, any practised photographer would have focused,
literally, on obtaining this and it would have been
instinctive.

What was the issue with 'traffic', if he was parked off-
road?


Nevertheless, significantly, Imbrogno adds:

"A close examination of the original negative shows that
the lights are reflecting off of some type of structure
in the central part of the object. Also the lights are in
a perfect half circle".

As we can see from the 'Nashville' photographs, that
would be consistent with a 'saucer-shaped' object, not
merely a 'boomerang' as implied.

What, however, happened to that crucial, stated original
negative - is it still available?

If so, can it be confirmed whether the discernable
'structure' is similar to our 'Nashville UFO'?


Perhaps it's also coincidental that the Waterbury
photograph is claimed to date from May 26, 1988 [MUFON CT
date it as 1987 - elsewhere it's 1988] and I understand
the lighting rig [I've checked this and it is apparently
for a disco and included smoke effects] was featured in a
contemporary article.

This, however, needs to be verified and I'm attempting to
do so.


>As to the "ultralights" explanation, I recall that many

Are you at least satisfied that the ultralight hoaxes did

I know I-84 very well. It's a busy, multilane highway. When you stop for
any reason, and park "off the road," you pull over onto a narrow
shoulder, with traffic -- including huge trucks -- roaring right by you,
only a few feet away. Some people get badly spooked by this. My wife,
for instance -- she absolutely won't stop on highways like this. I can
well imagine the discomfort "Dave" might have felt.

We should also appreciate that some people are also spooked when they
see what they think are UFOs. Add this to the trucks roaring by, and I
can well imagine Dave wanting to get away as soon as possible. As for
the camera, he might have been carrying it with him for all sorts of
reasons, loaded with low-light film. For instance, I've driven often
enough with musical equipment, including microphones and a portable DAT
recorder, not to mention a laptop computer. Not because I expect to use
all this en route, but because I'm taking it, let's say, from my New
York apartment to my country house. Doesn't strike me as at all
suspicious that Dave would have had this camera with him.

Greg Sandow

There was sort of "double trouble" here - two different questions being
answered by each aircraft mission - from 1943 to around 1958. They were
still learning about anomalous propagation then. They did not yet know
what caused false echoes on a RADAR screen, or how to tell the false
echoes from the real ones. They called them "weather", "angels", and
"UCTs" (Uncorrelated targets). A UCT is simply any target on RADAR which
the operator cannot match with a known flight.

Every time they got a UCT, they sent up a plane. In addition to
reporting
real objects (such as aircraft), they also collected data on what they
DID find at the site if no aircraft was present. Eventually, they
learned
a lot about RADAR propagation, and how the following effects caused
sightings. The result is that most aircraft are required to have active
transponders now. The following causes of RADAR anomalies were
discovered
over this period:

1. Multiple Reflections - The RADAR beam bounces off of more than one
object
before returning to the RADAR set. The false target is displayed in the
direction of the first of the objects the beam strikes, and at a
distance
corresponding to the total path length the reflected beam took. Often,
the
second reflector is an efficient reflector, such as a flat plane (e.g. a

surface on a building) or a corner reflector (e.g. the inside of a dump
truck or an open-top rail car).

Multiple-reflection targets can be identified because they almost always
exhibit at least one of the following behaviors:

a. Always keep the same compass bearing from the RADAR set, approaching
directly toward the set and receding directly away from the set.

b. Always have the same compass bearing from the set as a known plane,
and
always are farther from the set than the plane.
c. Appear only on the far side of a highway or railroad near the set.

d. Give the same transponder information as a known plane on the
display.
In this case, the closest duplicate code is with the real plane.

2. Anomalous Propagation - Atmospheric conditions, mostly temperature
and
humidity gradients, bend the RADAR beam so it strikes the ground, or
targets
(buildings and vehicles) on the ground, and then returns to the set by
the
same path. RADAR sets with height finders report these targets to be
much
higher than they really are. As atmospheric conditions change, or as
vehicles
move, the targets appear to move.

Anomalous propagation can usually be identified by the appearance of one
or
more of these behaviors:

a. A LOT of UCTs appear at one time.

b. No transponder signal accompanies the UCT.

c. Erratic flight paths, hovering, impossible maneuvering, or extremely
high
speeds.

d. Stationary blips appear on RADAR using MTI (Moving Target Indicator),
which
is supposed to eliminate stationary blips.

3. Second-trip Echo - This happens when an object beyond the normal
range of
the RADAR set returns an echo. The travel time is so long that the RADAR
set
has already sent out the next set of pulses pulse before the echo
returns. So
the RADAR set displays the target much closer than it really is. It
should
really be called a "second pulse return". The usual causes of this are
anomalous propagation, which bends the beam gradually (so it can strike
objects
beyond the horizon), and astronomical objects. I know of several cases
where
the moon was the offending object.
Second-trip echoes can be identified by one or more of the following
behaviors:

a. Flight paths that curve first toward, then away from, the RADAR set.

b. Flying in a curved path toward the RADAR set, then staying for a long
period
in the dead zone directly over the set, then leaving in a curved path to
join
its original trajectory before it turned toward the set.

c. Lower speeds when closer to the RADAR set.

d. Some of them may hover for very long periods. These are reflections
from
fixed objects or the moon.

e. The ones caused by ionized meteor trails have very high speeds.

f. The transponder codes are either absent, or are garbled (The echo
comes
back with the answer to the wrong question - the question sent out in
the
previous set of pulses).

4. Internal electronic problems within the RADAR set - This happens when
some
part of the RADAR set fails, interacts with other items in the
environment of
the equipment (such as a vacuum cleaner vibrating the floor), or is
adjusted
improperly by the operator. The following is a list of this kind of
failure:

- Noisy electronics

- Improperly adjusted gate (sets the threshold of strength of the
weakest blip
allowed to appear on the screen).

- Mechanical vibrations disturbing the mercury delay line.

- Secondary reflections within the delay line.

- Missing tube or circuit board shields.

- Damaged cables.

5. It is also possible for someone to build a device that fools RADAR
sets
into displaying false targets.

- It could have been an exercise in interception, with the pilots not
being told it was a drill.

- It may be that the visual targets and the RADAR targets were not the
same things.

visual system, and relative motions due to the jet's own actions,
combined to produce an optical illusion.

From: "rotsky" <rotsky@wanadoo.fr>
Date: Tue, 12 Nov 2002 23:32:04 +0100
Subject: RE: [UFORL] The Best and Worst of UFOlogy

Excellent information, Larry. Just want to pick up one small point, which is
relevant because it can play a role in today's radar 'sightings'.

It's incorrect to say most aircraft are required to carry active
transponders, though the authorities are certainly trying to move that way.

Transponders are required to enter certain types of airspace -- Class A and
B in Europe and I think it's the same in the US. Also, if you want to
transition military, restricted or other special-use type airspace you will
also need a transponder. In most cases, you will need a Mode C transponder,
which returns the aircraft's height as well as 2D location to the radar.

However, outside those kinds of airspace, a transponder is optional. And
this includes a lot more airspace and airports than you might think. Pilots
flying VFR can opt to squawk a VFR conspicuity code (7000 in most places -
it was 1200 in the US, don't know if that's changed in line with the rest of
the world). However, radar operators have the option to filter out VFR
squawks -- and frequently do -- because they clutter the radar screen so
much.

Transponders work with secondary surveillance radar, not primary returns, so
often the only way a small plane shows up on radar is if it chooses to
squawk. Turn off the transponder (or switch to VFR) and you can disappear
off radar. Now, if I was a private pilot who'd blundered into the prohibited
zone over Camp David (the Secret Service is trying to increase this to a 30
mile radius, by the way) I'd be awfully tempted to turn off my transponder!

a+
Steve

accidents, highways were backing up as thousands of
commuters were stopping to watch them".

...then where are any of these incidents duly exposed as
such?
Instead, we seem to have numerous, comparable
observations of 'UFOs' and definitely no ultralight
hoaxes at all.



James.

_One giant hoax for mankind_

Nasa has missed a good opportunity in cancelling the book
planned to give a rebuttal of the Moon hoaxers, argues
BBC News Online David Whitehouse.

[...]

What always puzzles me about conspiracy advocates is
their lack of critical thinking and how they parade their
deficiencies as virtues.

It is as if the question is all important and the answer
irrelevant; as if the need to believe the conspiracy
overwhelms the evidence.

As for the evidence that the Moon landings were a hoax -
there is none. Or at least, none that stands up to
anything more than trivial investigation.

The fact is every single shred of so-called evidence put
forward by the Moon hoax theorists is either obviously
stupid - a result of their own ignorance of basic science
- or has a straightforward explanation.

[...]

_They are not alone_

The Moon hoaxers are not the only ones. There are also
the UFO conspiracies, the flat-Earth conspiracies and
those who actually believe that crop circles are made by
some non-human force/alien/entity.

So are they all true? Are there alien bodies held in a
deep freeze in Area 51 in the US? Does the US Government
really have a crashed UFO it picked up at Roswell in
1947? Are crop circles made by aliens who, given their
diverse descriptions, appear to be having a convention on
our small planet?

[...]

Perhaps those who believe these crazy ideas think that
the world would be a more interesting place if the X-
Files were true? Perhaps they fervently believe they are
on a righteous crusade to uncover the "truth".

[...]

From: "Greg Sandow" <greg@gregsandow.com>
Date: Sun, 17 Nov 2002 17:24:43 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] RE: UFO skeptics debunked

> > And of course there's one part of the discussion that you don't
> > mention. Namely, that in many eyes the leading UFO skeptics
> have been
> > notably debunked. Why on earth, then, should anyone be required to
> > take them seriously?
>>
> > Greg Sandow
>>
>
> Could you provide some more details on this? Who, where and how?
>
> Anthony

Very reasonable question. I wish there were a detailed study of the
leading published UFO skeptics, comparable (on the believing side) to
Philip Klass's two books on UFOs, or Terry Matheson's "Alien Abductions:
Creating A Modern Phenomenon," a skeptical close reading of the
abduction literature.

Of course, there are detailed debunkings of particular skeptical
analyzes -- see, for instance, Jennie Zeidman's study of the Ohio
helicopter incident, which debunks Klass's alleged solution, or Brad
Sparks's study of the RB-47 case, which likewise debunks Klass. And also
Sparks's comments on IFO cases, and why they don't have the significance
skeptics think they do. (This was posted to UFO UpDates not long ago,
and ought to be in their archives, though maybe it's hard to find,
because Sparks himself didn't post it.)

The best source for critques of the skeptics would be many entries in
Jerry Clark's UFO Encyclopedia, in which Jerry comments on some of the
skeptics' work. Probably you can find these by looking up the skeptics'
names in the index, especially Klass and Menzel. The stuff on Menzel is
especially telling -- how even skeptics in the Air Force thought he was
a pest, because his solutions of many cases were so unreasonable. And
how he distorted details of a sighting he himself had, to make it easier
to solve.

Beyond all this would be something I'd dearly love to see -- a study,
not of individual skeptics' analysis, but of skepticism as an
intellectual movement. Marcello Truzzi has written some brief comments
on this; I don't know where they were published, but I might be able to
find them if anyone's curious to read them. Marcello is a sociologist at
the University of Michigan, who was one of the founders of CSICOP but
then broke with them in part because he thought they were too rigid. I
have some fairly simple thoughts in an unpublished essay of my own
called "Who's Afraid of UFOs?" It's on my UFO website,
www.gregsandow.com/ufo. (My professional site, for my work in music, is
www.gregsandow.com, if anyone's interested.)

I have some general comments to make, but first a disclaimer: I'm not
saying that skeptics have no value (on the contrary, they're crucially
important for the study of UFOs). And I'm not saying they haven't solved
some UFO cases (though they, as a group, are pretty stingy about giving
ufologists credit for cases they've solved). Nor am I saying that
ufologists don't also have faults, or that some skeptics don't do
thorough, responsible work. But organized skepticism does, I think, have
some notable problems, which I'll outline by looking at the four leading
published UFO skeptics of the past generation, Menzel, Klass, Oberg, and
Sheaffer.

Oberg is the easiest to deal with, because (at least as far as I know)
he hasn't written much about ufos, though he's made many statements in
the media and online. His book on the subject is "UFOs and Outer Space
Mysteries," and it's a pretty lightweight read. Mostly it debunks things
that are easily demolished -- the claim, for instance, of a man named
George Leonard that analysis of NASA photos reveals alien artifacts on
the moon. After many pages of such things, serious ufology is dispensed
with in one final, very perfunctory chapter. The narrative strategy here
-- if I may borrow a term from literary studies, and especially from
Matheson's abduction book -- is first to make the whole subject seem
like nonsense by studying things that really are nonsensical. Then the
impression that it's all nonsense substitutes, in the final chapter, for
any real analysis. Not exactly a responsible way to proceed, but that's
what he does.

And I must say that the one time I talked to Oberg, he did something
similar. I was interviewing him for a magazine article (which never was
published, as things turned out). He didn't know me at all. But when I
mentioned some evidence suggesting that the Roswell crash might have
been alien, he changed the subject quickly. The evidence -- which I'm
not claiming proves anything definitively -- was the tape of a phone
interview Kevin Randle did, with one of the alleged witnesses, the
commander of the military police on the Roswell air force base. This
man's reaction to Kevin's questions certainly suggested that something
truly extraordinary went on. When I told Oberg about this, he shifted
direction angrily, and started denouncing Kevin for allegedly taping the
interview illegally. He never commented, not one word, on what the MP
commander actually said. (And he was wrong about the illegal taping. In
the US, the legality of taping phone conversations is complex, depending
on laws which vary from state to state. You can't make any judgment
about the legality of any call unless you know the law in the states
both parties were in when they talked.)

Klass and Menzel, it seems to me, simply make things up. The classic
Menzel example is his solution of the Father Gill case. This, for those
who might not know it, involved an Anglican missionary in New Guinea,
who said he saw a UFO (a fairly classic flying disc) hovering for some
20 minutes at very low altitude. He said that beings on the craft waved
at him. A group of New Guineans signed statements saying they'd seen all
this, too. Menzel decided that Gill must have been astigmatic, and that
he wasn't wearing his glasses. This, Menzel said, made the stars appear
oval-shaped to him. As for the waving aliens, these, Menzel said, were
just Gill's eyelashes, moving in front of his eyes when he blinked! The
New Guineans, for their part, were simply in awe of the "Great White
Father," and would sign anything he asked them to.

Now, the trouble with all this is, first, that Father Gill wasn't
astigmatic, and didn't wear glasses. Seconldy, the New Guineans weren't
at all in awe of any white man. In fact, their feelings went the other
way; they generally resented the presence of Gill and other
missionaries. So Menzel is completely wrong, but what's really notable
is that he didn't bother to investigate. He simply published his theory,
without making any move to check the facts. His little essay on this, in
fact, is utterly loony, so much so that it's worth tracking down and
reading, in "UFOS: A Scientific Debate," a collection of papers edited
by Carl Sagan and Thornton Page.

The really delicious part is when Menzel goes on and on about how he
tried out many lenses to approximate the effect of astigmatism in his
own eyes, to see if the stars really would look like ovals. Lots of time
for that, none at all to check the most basic facts of the case. His
final sentence is notable, too. It's something to the effect of, "This
theory may seem unlikely, but it's more likely than the presence of an
actual alien spaceship over New Guinea." In other words, "There can't be
any UFOs, so just about any theory I make up will serve to explain any
sighting."

Klass made up his solution to the Socorro case. He decided it was a
hoax, ultimately done by the mayor of Socorro, who wanted to bring
tourists to his town -- and profit from it personally, since (if I
remember this correctly) he himself owned the land where the UFO
allegedly landed. There was no evidence at all for this. And since the
mayor never made any effort to hype the event to attract tourists,
there's at least circumstantial evidence that Klass's theory isn't true.


Klass also made up part of his explanation of the Travis Walton
abduction. Walton was part of a crew working on a forestry project for
the federal government. Klass decided they were going to be late in
finishing this work, feared penalties for their lateness, and made up
the UFO event as an excuse for not getting the job done. Again, there
was no evidence at all for this, and Walton, understandably exasperated,
has circulated a letter from the official he was doing the job for,
stating that there hadn't been any problems. I'm not aware that Klass
has ever retracted his claim, though. He certainly didn't make any
inquiries before publishing his theory. (I'm not saying he didn't
investigate the case. He did a lot of work on it. He just didn't inquire
about this particular point -- a curious omission, given how much work
he did in other areas.)

I interviewed Klass for several hours (for the same article for which I
talked to Oberg), and learned a lot about how he thinks. Or, at times,
doesn't think. He's often said that abductees are little nobodies, or
words to that effect, who tell their stories in order to get on TV. I
told him that this wasn't true of most of the abductees I've met; more
than anything else, they wanted privacy, as far as I could judge. So I
asked Klass if he knew any abductees. "Only the ones I've appeared with
on TV," he said, showing with one stroke that his theory was based on a
highly selective sample, to say the least. Most remarkably, he seemed
not to know what he'd just revealed. I could add that his book on
abductions is based on practically no research -- he didn't talk to
abductees or abduction researchers.

At another point, we discussed a famous 1948 sighting by two commercial
airline pilots, who saw what they thought was a huge craft with windows
pass by their plane. Klass believes this was a meteor, which is a
reasonable explanation. In his book "UFOs Explained," however, he
doesn't just say the pilots could have seen a meteor, or that he thinks
they saw one. He says they "incontrovertibly" (or some word like that)
saw a meteor. I asked him why he was so certain, given that no large
meteor was known to have passed through the atmosphere at that time. His
answer was difficult to get; he kept changing the subject. But when the
answer came, it was remarkable: "Since there are no unknown structured
craft in our atmosphere, a meteor was what the pilots saw." (Or words to
that effect.) In other words, since he knows there aren't any UFOs, this
couldn't have been one. But of course this is one of the cases Klass
uses in his book to show that there aren't any UFOs, so he's engaging in
circular reasoning.

Intellectually, Klass is really a weird duck. We got in a long argument
when I wrote about our conversation in an article about UFOs for The
Village Voice, a leading weekly in New York. First he denied we'd ever
met. I convinced him that we had(by showing him a page he'd signed, and
conveniently dated, in one of his books, and by describing his study,
his wife, and his dog). Then, in a remarkably addled fashion, he
complimented me on my powers of observation, and then said that my
recollections of facts aren't reliable! He didn't seem aware that he'd
contradicted himself.

His reason for this judgment, he said, was that I'm a music critic, and
that music critics only write their opinions. This, of course, isn't
even close to true, since I do other kinds of journalism, and in any
case there are lots of facts a critic has to get straight in a music
review. To demonstrate this (and also because the whole exchange was so
weird that I wanted to see where it would go), I sent him copies of some
of my writing. He replied by taking issue with some of my musical
judgments! I'd said, in one review, that the first violins of the New
York Philharmonic weren't very strong (something, I might add, that was
known to everybody in the music business). Klass, suddenly a music
expert, told me this couldn't possibly be true, because if it was, the
music director would have fired them. The words "contract" and
"musicians' union" apparently aren't in his vocabulary. The spectacle of
a man persevering in a pointless attack, even when he's far out of his
depth, was absolutely breathtaking. Unfortunately, he's sometimes
conducted his UFO theorizing in much the same way.

Sheaffer, finally, made up one part of his critique of the Hill case. He
thinks (speaking now only of the Hills' sighting, and not of their
abduction) that the Hills saw Jupiter, and thought it was a UFO. To
establish this, he uses Betty Hill's drawing of things she saw in the
sky, the moon, Jupiter, and the supposed UFO. Sheaffer believes she
actually saw the moon, Jupiter, and Saturn, but to make that plausible
he has to assume that Hill made a large mistake in her drawing, and that
in fact the three objects weren't where she said they were.

All this suggests, to me, a fairly simple agenda -- a determination to
solve UFO cases, which exists before these skeptics actually study any
of the evidence. They have, in other words, a preconception that UFOs
aren't real, and then sometimes twist their analyses to make that seem
true.

But this now enters the larger area of skeptics' intellectual culture.
This would be a fascinating study. Skeptics, for instance, tend to
assume that alien visits are impossible, because interstellar distances
are so vast. Klass says this in so many words. (As do many SETI
scientists.) I even once saw someone -- Martin Gardner? -- estimate the
probability of alien visits, in an issue of The Skeptical Inquirer. It
was something like .000000001.

How do they know this? Paul Davies -- a very serious Australian
physicist, and hardly a UFO believer -- notes in his book Are We Alone?
that if you believe faster-than-light travel is impossible, you're
making an assumption that's usually never mentioned. That assumption is
that we've already advanced far enough in science to know beyond doubt
some basic laws of the universe. Now, Davies is willing to make that
assumption, but I believe (to judge from an e-mail exchange I had with
him) that he understands the assumption is somewhat arbitrary. We really
can't know, at this stage, what science will show us in the future.

And in fact I've seen two notable scientists lose their intellectual
footing when they try to show that interstellar travel won't work. One
of those is Frank Drake, the noted SETI pioneer (and inventer of the
Drake Equation, which purports to show at least a ballpark estimate of
how many civilizations there are in our galaxy). He argues, in his book
"Is Anyone Out There?" that interstellar travel, even slower than light,
would take too much power to be practical. He then considers an
objection from a colleague, who says that the abilities of a
civilization to generate power increase exponentially over time. Drake's
answer is that even if there were enough energy to fly to other stars,
cosmic rays would burn the travelers up! Just like UFO skeptics, he's
making this up. There's no evidence at all for his view, or at least not
for his certainly. He's just emotionally committed to the idea that
interstellar travel is impossible, and will argue for it, no matter how
unreasonable he's got to be.

Sagan gets into similar trouble in his book "The Cosmic Connection,"
when he makes a curious argument against any idea that UFOs could be
alien. He makes complex calculations, based on the number of
civilizations in the galaxy, the amount of time it would take them to
travel to us, and the ways they might decide what planets to visit. He
then concludes that, if even one percent of UFOs sightings represent
genuine alien craft, the number of visitors is too large to be possible.
In order to send out enough probes to reach us that many times, alien
civilizations would have to use more metal than exists in the entire
galaxy! Very ingenious, but it rests on a silly assumption -- that every
sighting is of a separate spaceship, indvidually arrived at the end of a
long voyage. Why can't people be seeing the same craft over and over? Or
why can't there be one large "mothership" sending out smaller scout
craft? These objections are so elementary that I have to assume Sagan's
emotions overwhelmed his thinking. He, too, I'd guess, so badly wants to
prove UFOs aren't real that he'll resort to anything to make his point.

The ufologist (and science historian) Michael Swords makes a nice point.
He notes that SETI astronomers believe that there are many civilizations
in the universe, and that interstellar travel is impossible. A smaller
group of astronomers who support the idea of colonizing space make
opposite assumptions -- that interstellar travel is indeed possible, and
that there isn't any intellligent life anywhere else. If these positions
are scientifically respectable, Swords asks, why aren't there scientists
who believe that there's abundant life elsewhere _and_ that interstellar
travel is possible? The answer ought to be obvious: If you believed
that, you'd have to believe we might be visited.

This is one take on skeptics' intellectual culture. I might also ask why
these leading published skeptics don't criticize each other -- don't, in
print, say that some published explanation of a case is inadequate. (I'm
not saying that no skeptics do this. We can see on this list that some
do. I'm asking why the most famous ones haven't done it.)

I might also ask why psychosocial theorists seem largely ignorant of
social science -- and why, generally, skeptics make huge social science
assumptions (about, for instance, the influence of the media on UFO and
abduction accounts) without noticing they're doing it, and certainly
without proposing protocols by which their theories might be proved.
(Social scientists have their methods, just like physical scientists,
but UFO skeptics don't seem to know this.)
But this e-mail is far too long, and I'll stop here. Comments welcome.
I'll try to find time to address them.

Greg Sandow

< Sheaffer, finally, made up one part of his critique of the Hill case. He

abduction) that the Hills saw Jupiter, and thought it was a UFO. To
establish this, he uses Betty Hill's drawing of things she saw in the

Greg, when you make the claim that somebody has made something
up, you should at least read the relevant section of his book a couple
of times to make sure you know what you're talking about. In other
words, that you haven't just got a preconception about what skeptics
are thinking and, in your haste, twist your analysis to make that seem
true.

Robert Sheaffer, in his book, The UFO Verdict - Examining the
Evidence (Prometheus Books, 1981) pp. 34-36, cites the Hills' actual
words under regressive hypnosis, from John Fuller's book, The
Interrupted Journal, Chapter 7. Sheaffer wrote (page 34) that, "Betty
reported seeing a 'star' or planet below the moon. On the following
page he wrote that she described a second planet looking "like a star,
a bigger star, up over this one,".
Her complete quote is about seeing, "a star down below the moon, on
the lower left side of the moon. And then right after we left Lancaster,
I noticed that there was a star, a bigger star up over this one."
It was this second brighter object which she thought was a UFO.

Sheaffer noted (p. 35) that this exactly matches the configuration
of the moon, Saturn and brighter Jupiter.

I have checked these objects in a planetarium program, Cartes du
Ciel, and see that at 11 PM they would have been visible less than
15 degrees high in the South West, out Betty's side window, as
seen travelling South on Route 3 through the White Mountains
(I assumed a location near Woodstock, N.H. at 44 deg N,
71 deg 45' W).

Object         Azimuth      Altitude

Moon         226 deg        13 deg
Jupiter (UFO?) 224 deg       11.5 deg
Saturn       228 deg        9 deg

If the original stimuli for this incident can be attributed to these
astronomical objects, it suggests a Psycho-Social cause.

You say that, "To establish this, he uses Betty Hill's drawing of
things she saw in the sky." He made no such claim, using her
own recorded words as transcribed in the Fuller book.

In your obvious hasty skimming of his chapter, you must have
this confused with his comments about the alien star map that
Betty said she had seen while in the UFO. This had nothing at
all to do with the initial UFO sighting.

About how many books poor Phil has written -- sorry. I had a brain
glitch, of the kind that once made me misstate the name of one of the
senators from Ohio in an article, even after I'd interviewed him. It
happens.

What's really silly is that I've read four of Phil's books, even the
first one, in which he put forth the theory that UFOs are plasmas. When
I said two books, I was thinking of UFO's Explained and UFOs: The Public
Deceived, which I think of as Phil's two serious volumes, the ones we
really have to pay attention to. The others -- apart from the Roswell
book, which I haven't read -- are flawed even by skeptics' standards.
The abudction book is a real disaster -- as I said, no real research
went into it. The first book, UFOs Identified (which I was lucky enough
to find a few years ago in a used bookstore) is his most open-minded
writing, but unfortunately the ideas in it have been pretty thoroughly
discredited.

As for Robert Sheaffer's view of the Hill case, I've done more than read
his book. I've been with Robert when he made a detailed presentation of
his views, seen them debated, and heard him agree, explicitly, to
exactly what I said in my post. Unfortunately I'm not free at this
moment say when and how that happened, since it's all part of a book
project that hasn't yet been made public. But I guarantee you it
happened.

Robert gave a paper on the Hill case. In the course of it, he showed his
sketch of what he thinks Betty Hill saw. Another ufologist, a name I'm
sure most of us know, pointed out that Betty's drawing of what she saw
differed from Robert's version. We all compared the two sketches, which
were projected on a screen -- Betty's sketch of what she said she saw,
and Robert's sketch of what he thinks she really did see. They were
notably different. Robert then said (and these are his exact words)::
"If Betty's statements are taken as literal truth, then my hypothesis
cannot be correct." He added that he doesn't think Betty's statements
are correct, because of her later record of reporting constant UFO
sightings, which seem hard to believe. My point stands, though. As part
of his debunking of the Hill case, Robert chooses to believe that Betty
Hill did not in fact see three objects in the sky where she said she saw
them.

I like Robert, by the way. We bonded about opera -- he's a very fine
amateur tenor, who's sung roles in many opera productions.

Oh, and Bob -- if you think my view of skeptics is "half-baked," why
don't you go into the oven, turn up the heat, and tell us what's wrong
with it?
Greg Sandow

Duke of Mendoza's compliments to all:

>Subject: Re: [UFORL] RE: UFO skeptics debunked

<snip>

>No wonder your attempted debunking of the skeptics is half-baked.

Indeed. "Skeptics make things up," we are told by Prof Sandblow.
If I had a shilling for every fiction skeptics had created and a
shilling for every fiction credulous ufologists had invented,
swallowed, promoted, and failed properly to investigate, I think
the soi-disant "UFO research community" would provide the better
return. Even if you took a proportional view of this, I think
you would still end up richer -- that is, pro rata, there is, I wager,
more bullshit, bad logic and misinformation lying around in the average
credulous publication than you will find in the average skeptical
one. Of course skeptics can be sloppy and biased. Yes, Menzel was
grossly out of order over Father Gill: but then Klass and Kottmeyer
have publicly disagreed over what actually happened (another little
myth disposed of) and each has paid close attention to the "facts"
(the anecdote) as recorded.

I find it interesting that Menzel, who has been dead for rather
a long time, still causes seismic quaverings in the souls of
people such as the Cardinal of Canby and Prof Sandpit, who are
presumably alive within certain definitions of the term.

Another piece of half bakery: the laws of science may not be laws
one day! Bollocks, actually. Newtonian physics and quantum mechanics
do *not* contradict each other, despite popular perceptions to the
contrary. They complement one another. Thus there is no reason to
suppose that FTL travel of large masses will ever be possible.
There are dozens of reasons to conclude that intelligent life is
extremely rare. Thus to say

>In other words, since ... there aren't any UFOs, this
>couldn't have been one.
is not unreasonable *provided that* you translate "UFO" as
"ET craft". (Of course there are UFOs -- the only real question,
as Allen Hynek so pithily put it, is "Unknown to whom?")

>But of course this is one of
>the cases Klass uses in his book to show that there
>aren't any UFOs, so he's engaging in circular reasoning.

Er, no. He is saying: there is no good reason (you may argue,
of course, as to the basis of his reasoning) to suppose there
are any ET craft in our skies, and this is an example of a
meteor that was (for various reasons) taken to be one, but
wasn't. I defy anyone to find words to the effect of "ergo
there are no ET craft" in Klass's analysis. Ergo there is no
circular reasoning. Klass's position, not unlike my own, is
if it isn't an ET craft (an option so remote as to be
negligible in interpreting the data), then what was it? This
doesn't mean his solution to any given case is correct. It
may be a stab in the dark (Menzel did a lot of stabbing in
the dark, and Bruce Maccabee complains that skeptics deploy
what all scientists do, alternative hypotheses within the
limits of current knowledge... and this is wicked?)

Finally, Prof Groggow complains that psychosocialist ufologists
seem not to know about sociological research protocols. Mmm.
I can't speak for anyone else, but a long time ago I became
familiar with academic sociological research techniques when
I was trying to get a handle on the appeal of popular music
(sociologists will stop at nothing in their quest for wisdom)
and then, a few years later, became involved in real market
research. Let it be known that anyone seriously interested
in improving the sales of Persil would regard most academic
sociological research as useless. You would be as well off
flying by the seat of your pants, if you are lucky enough to
have either one. It has to be said (and said, and said) that
there isn't actually a "psychosocial school" of ufologists,
but there is a bunch of people with not much credulity left
about anything, who like to say to one another: "Well, how
does this sound? Any mileage in that?", and who mostly get
the answer, "Mmm. Interesting. Yeah. Could be. Why not...
Well come to think of it, I'll tell you why not, when I
get around to it."

Quite the weirdest thing about Grunge Sindoom's analysis
of "skepticism" is that it takes four Americans as paradigmatic
of the species. Perhaps this is that paradox, American
parochialism, busy at work. De troot am, man, that
ufological skepticism has many more faces than those
plastered across the fronts of a few CSICOP heads, and
most (that I am aware of) would agree that there are UFOs
out there. What they reasonably doubt is that they are ET.

best wishes
Pissinginthewind D. Micturator
"Cape Horn, Save Me Soon!"

From: "DukeMendoza@onetel.net.uk" <Horseman@onetel.net.uk>
Date: Tue, 19 Nov 02 00:18:45 +0100

Ducal compliments as ever but while I'm about it---

>Subject: RE: [UFORL] RE: UFO skeptics debunked
>Sent:    18/11/20 20:33
>Received: 18/11/02 23:42
>From:     Greg Sandow, greg@gregsandow.com

>The abudction book is a real disaster -- as I said, no real research
>went into it.

Actually, rather a lot of research went into it, particularly
into the limitations of hypnosis as a research "tool". Klass's
argument would not have been forwarded, nor would it have been
retarded, by talking to abductees or abductologists. That wasn't
the drift of the book, but that in itself doesn't lessen what
value it has. I have to say I cannot imagine how any discussion of
"abductions" with victims or investigators would, by itself,
contribute to any assessment of the veridicality of the reported
experiences. You need to look a long way out from and around
abduction and UFO culture to reach even tentative conclusions
about that.

>The first book, UFOs Identified (which I was lucky enough
>to find a few years ago in a used bookstore) is his most open-minded
>writing, but unfortunately the ideas in it have been pretty thoroughly
>discredited.

Here Klass suffers from Steuart Campbell Syndrome. Campbell wrote
an interesting book, which may be true in parts, about 10 years
ago, that purported to explain every classic UFO sighting as one
kind of mirage or another. The error is not in the particulars:
it is in assuming that one explanation dissolves all UFOs into
IFOs according to a particular king's writ. Klass made the same
mistake in characterizing abductees as "little nobodies who want to
be on TV". That may, or may not, have been true of those "abductees"
he met in TV studios, but it doesn't justify the generalization.
That does not mean that absolutely no one fits the generalization.
One of my best abductee friends is permanently dying to be on TV,
actually, and an astringent view of him might well conclude that he
is an economic failure and general little nobody. Be that as it may,
Klass's greatest errors are to assume that (a) abductees have only
one stimulus [desire for fame] (b) that they are in control of their
own interests. If you wonder what I mean by the latter, think of
Linda Napolitano. This brings us back to the question of whether
credulous ufologists or skeptics are, by and large, the more
honest (intellectually or otherwise) parties when it comes to
assessing the truth or significance of any particular UFO-related

-------

Bob,

Fundamentally, Greg Sandow is arguing that no witness of any event, UFO or
otherwise, ever makes the slightest error or misperception in later
recounting it. Therefore, if there is even a minor discrepancy between what
was *reported*, and the proposed prosaic explanation, then the prosaic
explanation is excluded. It follows from Greg's line of argument that
eyewitness accounts, such as Mrs. Hill's, are not merely reliable, but
little short of *infallible*. (This, of course, flies in the face of
everything that is known about the inaccuracy and malleability of human
perception and memory.)

Similarly, people are arguing that since Jimmy Carter said that his UFO was
30 degrees up, and Venus was only 25 degrees up, Carter's UFO couldn't
possibly have been Venus. Same argument, same fallacy.

In both cases, the UFOlogists are ignoring an important skeptical argument:
If Betty Hill was seeing a real UFO, then there would have been *3* starlike
objects near the moon: Jupiter, Saturn, and the UFO. But she reported seeing
only two. Similarly, Carter did not say that he saw two bright objects
towards the west - Venus and his UFO - he saw only one.

Most works by people who come up with a single theory that explains all
UFO cases are "discredited". In fact, it is the heterogeneity of the UFO
problem that makes it harder to solve. There can't be a single theory
that explains all UFO sightings, because they have such a variety of
causes.

I have identified several causes which lend the strangeness to cases
which are misidentifications of conventional objects:

1. The number one cause of misidentification is trying to use human
vision beyond its capabilities. When an object is seen against the sky,
the observer has NO WAY to find out its distance, size, speed, or
altitude, unless special circumstances reveal one of the values (which
then makes the other three easy to find). Those circumstances are:

a. The observer recognizes the object, and thus knows its true size.
This is how pilots can find the distance, speed, and altitude of other
airplanes.

NOTE: If the observer makes an initial wrong guess of the object's
identity, it will lock him in on WRONG values for the 4 variables.

b. The object is within 30 feet of a witness with two good eyes.

c. The object passes directly in front of AND behind objects at known
distances.

d. The object lands at a known location. But if the object appeared
to touch down, but did not, the note above applies.

e. The object casts a shadow in a known location from a known light
source.

f. The object is a light source, which illuminates other objects and
casts shadows.

g. The object is within 250 feet, and is close enough to another
object at a known distance to be in the same primary visual field of
an observer with two good eyes. Then visual parallax can give a rough
indication of relative distance compared to the known object.

NOTE: The sky can NEVER be used for visual parallax. Attempting to
use it for visual parallax causes the "moon illusion", where the moon
seems to change size depending on where it is in the sky.

***

Actually, from the descriptions given in "UFOs Identified" and the dates
and locations of many of the sightings quoted, I think most of his
"plasma balls" were fire balloons. There was a big upsurge in fire
balloon cases in 1965 and 1966, mostly due to an article on how to make
them that was published in one of those "science project" tabloids. I
read the article myself in early 1965, but as a teenager, I didn't have
enough money at the time to buy the magazine.

My case files contain over 100 known fire balloon cases (where the
pranksters admitted their pranks) in those two years. A large number of
releases were concentrated in three areas where pranksters admitted
sending up many fire balloons over spans of weeks. The areas were:

1. Within a 50 mile radius of Manchester New Hampshire (including
Exeter).

2. The Los Angeles California area.

3. The Seattle-Tacoma (Puget Sound) Washington area.

saw nighttime ad-planes (See Hendry's "UFO Investigator's Handbook"

John Fuller "investigated" the possibility of an ad-plane, by calling
the one company he knew about that had such a plane. But he never
checked to see how many other ad companies in the area also had such
planes, or whether an out-of-state company could have been using one.

I still remember the first ad-plane I saw - in the same year - October
12, 1961. At first, I thought it was a space ship too (at age 10). So
did commentator and UFO book author Frank Edwards. In 1996, I found
out that he had been looking at the very same object I was looking at.

theater I was at, so I could read the sign when it got closer (the
intended purpose of the flight). But the plane didn't fly over the
downtown area of Indianapolis (where Edwards was), so he saw it only
in an edge-on aspect. So we went to "Autorama" at the Fairgrounds to
see the "personal car of the future" (as advertized on the plane),
while Edwards started researching his UFO book "Flying Saucers -
Serious Business".

> Actually, rather a lot of research went into it, particularly

> argument would not have been forwarded, nor would it have been

That last sentence is certainly true. And of course Klass had a lot to
say about hypnosis in his book. When I covered the same ground in my
private research, though, I found that he'd done a remarkably
superficial job in looking at the subject. Though to be fair, I'd have
to check some dates -- the date his book was published, and the date of
some of the papers I looked at. Maybe his book came out before some of
the interesting stuff I found out about. Anyhow, the debate about
hypnosis, and its power (or lack of same) to uncover memory is more
complex than Klass makes it out to be. Most astonishingly, by the way,
he wildly misconstrues the paper on hypnosis he's most anxious for
everyone to read. This is by Martin Orne, a well-known forensic
psychologist. Klass writes as if Orne says hypnosis is of no use at all
in police investigations, but in fact Orne says no such thing. This
amazed me, I have to say. I looked up Orne's paper precisely because
Phil said it was important. I didn't have any idea of checking up on
Phil. I wanted to read the most powerful evidence for his point of view.
So imagine my surprise when I found Orne saying that police departments
should, in fact, use hypnosis in their investigations. Orne did say (and
this was the part of the paper Phil seemed to respond to) that police
should be careful to corroborate any information they got from hypnosis,
and that testimony soley derived from hypnosis should never be
admissable in court. But he doesn't at all say that police should never
use hypnosis as one of many investigative tools.

As for this:

>I have to say I cannot imagine how any discussion of
> "abductions" with victims or investigators would, by itself,
> contribute to any assessment of the veridicality of the reported
> experiences.

Peter, that's just silly. First you have to know what the reported
experiences are. And, also, how the abductees and investigators claim to
know about these experiences. These things you find out to some extent
in the abduction literature, but -- at least in my experience -- you
learn a lot more if you actually talk to the people involved.

That's especially true if you're going to criticize the use of hypnosis
in abduction research, as many skeptics have. In fact, many skeptics --
Klass, for instance, and also, in a paper published in a psychology
journal, a team of psychologists headed by the late Nicolas Spanos (I'm
spelling his first name from memory; hope I have it right) -- talk as if
all abduction stories come out only thorugh hypnosis. But this is
precisely what you learn is _not_ true, if you take the trouble to
actually learn about the subject before you write your critiques of it.
Abductees come to abduction researchers with memories of _something_.
That's why they think they're abductees. Well, that used to be true. Now
the subject is so well known that some people assume they're abductees
on the basis of nothing but feelings. But when I spent a while talking
to many of the abductees who work with Budd Hopkins, and also -- most
crucially -- reading the letters they sent him before they'd met with
him -- it became very clear to me that these people had all kinds of
memories before they were ever hypnotized. And this, as has been often
enough remarked, is one fact about the abduction phenomenon that
skeptics routinely ignore.

This doesn't mean that abductions have to be real, by the way. Only that
you need to know what the starting point is before you can judge the
effect of hypnosis.


>Be that as it may,
> Klass's greatest errors are to assume that (a) abductees have only
> one stimulus [desire for fame] (b) that they are in control of their
> own interests. If you wonder what I mean by the latter, think of
> Linda Napolitano.

How well do you know Linda? Her involvement with Budd, his book, and the
public discussion of her case had all kinds of consequences she didn't
expect. But to anyone who knows her as well as I do, the idea that
anyone (like Budd) manipulated her is pretty laughable.

Most abductees I've known have very powerfully controlled their own
interests. That's one reason you don't know them, or even know about
them. One of their greatest interests is privacy, and that they've
thoroughly maintained.

To be fair, Peter, you did a certain amount of investigation for your
own abduction book. But not enough.

I wish I had Betty's sketch of what she says she saw, and Robert's
sketch of what he thinks she saw. I could (the list permitting) attach
them to this e-mail, and then everyone could see what I saw. Betty and
Robert agree on the number of bright objects in the sky at that moment.
Betty thinks they were Jupiter, the moon, and the supposed UFO. Robert
thinks they were Jupiter, the moon, and Saturn. Or at least this is what
he said, with no ambiguity, in the discussion I talked about. But as it
happens, Saturn couldn't have been any of the three objects Betty drew,
if her sketch was accurate. That's because it was in another location in
the New Hampshire sky that night. (Robert did careful research about
this.) Robert therefore, to make his theory work, assumes that Betty's
sketch is wrong. Rather notably wrong, I might add.

There's another issue in all this, by the way. Betty says these three
objects stood out in the sky because they were all very bright. Robert
says that Saturn, too, is bright, and that Betty would necessarily have
included it in her sketch. That's another reason why he believes she
drew the moon, Jupiter, and Saturn. But this leads to arguments about
exactly how bright Saturn is. At the discussion I mentioned, this
certainly came up, and another participant took strong issue with
Robert's opinion. It's not easy to resolve a subjective impression of
brightness, but here we might use one of the social science protocols
I've mentioned. That is, instead of letting discussion fall into a
volley of "It is!" It isn't!" one puts together a panel of neutral
judges, to go out on an appropriate night and make their own independent
ratings of how comparatively bright Jupiter and Saturn are.

Greg Sandow

Thus when mankind is presented with a totally bizarre,
shocking, traumatic event (the Boomerang?), a mental
circuit cuts out. Instead of a challenge for action,
there is a dead battery. This is, of course, well known
in individual cases of amnesia in, for example, "shell
shock":

into play? If so, might it be possible that collectively

policemen, media people, the FAA etc.?

in history.... and the Boomerang is its most recent and
spectacular example... when the breaking point of the
collective mind occurs, it must openly disregard patent
evidence of the senses: it can no longer encompass them
within their normal borders.

indifferent to the evidence, because their minds couldn't
bring themselves to accept that such a Holocaust could
possibly be, despite ample evidence. It was also a

indifference.

of what happens when the collective mind wilfully
disregards evidence, when "it can't take it".

phenomenon. [In] thousands of instances and over many

From: "David Clarke" <cd292@crazydiamonds.fsnet.co.uk>
Date: Fri, 29 Nov 2002 17:38:40 -0000
Subject: [UFORL] Re: Rendlesham file released under FOIA

The Times (London)
Friday, 20 November 2002

www.times.co.uk

HOW UFO FEVER TAXED MEN FROM THE MINISTRY

A report of alien sightings prompted floods of letters to the
MoD, reports Alan Hamilton. New laws have made these
public, explains Frances Gibb.

While British and American defence chiefs were supposed to
be keeping a watchful eye on the Soviet threat in Europe during
the 1980s, they were spending an undue amount of energy
dealing with little green men.

The so-called Rendlesham File, now available for public inspection,
is a fat catalogue of increasingly despairing correspondence
between the Ministry of Defence and members of the public
after the sighting of unexplained lights in Rendlesham Forest,
near the RAF base at Woodbridge, Suffolk, in December 1980.

The story was given wing by its detailed disclosure in the News
of the World in 1983.

Soon after the alleged incident, reported by the USAF deputy
base commander at nearby Bentwaters, the MoD drew up an
internal memo: "No evidence was found of any threat to the defence
of the United Kingdom, and no further investigations were carried
out.

"No further information has come to light which alters our view
that the sightings of these lights was of no defence significance."

Nothing was picked up on radar that night, officials added, and
they concluded that the airmen had confused the lights with the
beam of Orford Ness lighthouse, distorted by trees, or a natural
fireball.

But the Ministry and the RAF were bombarded with inquiries from
the public.Officials suggested that besieged officers at Bentwaters
should take the line that "there was no question of any contact
with alien beings."

They should also dismiss rumours that the UFO story was a
cover-up for the crash of an aircraft carrying nuclear material.
Still the letters poured in. Two years later an increasingly short-
tempered MoD was writing to one correspondent demanding a
full investigation: "There is no organisation in MoD appointed
soleyl for the purpose of studying reports of such objects, and
no staff are employed on the subject full-time."

It added: "We have to recognise that there are many strange
things to be seen in the sky, but we believe there are adequate
explanations for them."

Things got worse as forged letters purporting to come from MoD
officials began to circulate. One, apparently on Ministry notepaper,
claimed that a craft of unknown origin and "crewed by several
entities" had landed near Bentwaters.

The entities, it went on, were about one and a half metres tall
and wore nylon-coated pressure suits but no helmets. They had
claw-like hands with three digits and an opposable thumb. One
self-styled researcher into "cosmic conspiracy", having seen the
letter, wrote to the MoD requesting further information on the
craft which had landed for several hours to carry out repairs,
during which time the USAF base commander had conversed
with its crew.

An MoD official replied tersely: "I am afraid that it is a forgery...
I have no idea where it came from or why it was written and
can only conclude that it was intended by someone as a joke."

MPs forwarded letters from worried constituents convinced of a
cover-up. One passed on by David Alton, MP, said in part: "There
is clear evidence that British airspace and territory were intruded
upon by an unidentified vehicle on two occasions in late
December 1980, and that no authority was able to prevent this."

Some correspondents continued to harry MoD until officials were
driven to reply: "I suggest that there is little point in continuing
this correspondence."

The final letter in the fiel is dated July 1992, in which an MoD
official writes to the RAF liaison officer at Bentwaters asking if
the original USAF report of the sightings was genuine, "as a
number of hoaxes have been circulating for years."

Squadron Leader P. Rooney at Bentwaters had the last word:
"I have no records on this subject and the file to which you
refer has long been destroyed."

WHAT AIRMEN FOUND IN THE WOODS
A GRAPHIC description of the "unusual lights" that were suspected
of being a UFO is described in the Rendlesham file.

The lights were spotted by two USAF security police patrolmen,
according to a report dated January 1981 headed "unexplained
lights," written by Lieutenant Colonel Charles Halt, deputy base
commander at RAF Bentwaters in Suffolk.

He states: "Thinking an aircraft might have crashed or been
forced down, they called for permission to go outside the gates
and investigate.

"The individuals reported seeing a strange glowing object in the
forest. The object was described as being metallic in appearance
and triangular in shape, approximately two to three metres across
the base and approximately two metres high. It illuminated the
entire forest with a white light.

"The object itself had a pulsing red light on top and a bank of blue
lights underneath. The object was hovering or on legs. The
object was hovering or on legs. As the patrolmen approached the
object, it manoeuvred through the trees and disappeared. At this
time, the animals on a nearby farm went into a frenzy. The object
was briefly sighted approximately an hour later near the back gate."

The report goes on to describe the depressions found in the ground
and in a tree the next day. "Later in the night, a red sun-light light
was seen through the trees. It moved about and pulsed. At one
point it appeared to throw off glowing particles and then broke into
five separate white objects and then disappeared.

"Immediately thereafter, three star-like objects were noticed in the
sky, two objects to the north and one to the south, all of which
were about ten degrees off the horizon."

The MoD made further inquiries. No unidentified flying object had
been seen on radar at the times in question nor was there any
evidence of anything having intruded into British airspace.

One theory, it concluded, was that what was seen was the beam of
Orford Ness lighthouse, with distortions caused by its being seen
through trees. But "in the absence of any hard evidence" the MoD
remains open-minded about these sightings.

PUBLIC'S RIGHT TO KNOW EXTENDED

DETAILS about UFO sightings, clinical trials, accident investigations
and Whitehall meetings will be released to the public under plans
to open up government.
Public access to information from government bodies is to be
extended by the scrapping and amending of up to 100 pieces of
legislation, the Lord Chancellor's Department announced yesterday.

The changes are being made under the Freedom of Information Act
which is being phased in over the next three years.

@It's Cortile. And no, I don't think there are any others that fit that
@strict definition. There are, however,

@1) The Travis Walton case, in which 6 men witnessed Travis get zapped
@by a beam from a "UFO", and he later disappeared, and reappeared 5
@days later, claiming to have been abducted;

There are several possibilities to this case, including:

- An "excuse" for being behind in a contract termination date.
- An attempt to win the National Enquirer prize.
- A prank played on the other workers, that got out of hand when the
press and the government became involved (revealing the prank might
mean serving time in jail).

Note that the description of the UFO and the beam could easily be
satisfied by a fire balloon, an adjustable focus flashlight, and some
dust or fog.

@2) A case in Maine, I think, where several men camping out were
@abducted simultaneously (Allagash River?)

I have an account of this case. It is one of the typical cases where
nobody thought there was an abduction, until hypnosis was used to
"recover missing time". It then became a case of whether or not the
hypnotist accidentally edited the memories of the witnesses.

@3) The Maureen Puddy case, in which a woman was "abducted" in front
@of two researchers; at least she "experienced" an abduction, but
@they saw nothing.
This is sort of a "negative evidence" case, since the others did not
witness the abduction. But there are still three possibilities, however
remote:

- Post-hypnotic suggestion from an earlier (possibly party) hypnosis.
- Mental illness.
- Aliens who can manipulate either time or thoughts (can't conclusively
rule it out).

@If there are others, I have not heard of them, which is why I think
@they make such a big deal out of the Linda Cortile case and these
others.

From: "James Easton" <voyager@jeaston.com>
Date: Tue, 3 Dec 2002 07:29:04 -0000
Subject: Re: [UFORL] The Rendlesham file

Regarding:

>From: "Dave" <dave4us@yahoo.com>
>Date: Sat, 30 Nov 2002 07:26:18 -0000
>Subject: [UFORL] The Rendlesham file

Dave asked:

>how and where can i read..the O F F I C A L
>file????.....

Dave,

A recommended starting point is:

http://www.flyingsaucery.com/


Although the Ministry of Defence's [MoD's] file clarifies
crucial issues about their perception and investigation
of Halt's memo, one conspicuous puzzle seemingly remains.

In 'Skycrash', Jenny Randles [Brenda Butler and Dot
Street] published an assertion how Jenny, via author Paul
Begg, had been advised that an acquaintance of Paul's -
given the pseudonym of David Potts - was a radar operator
at RAF Watton. Although Potts wasn't directly involved, a
colleague told Potts that on 27 December, 1980 an
'uncorrelated target'[UCT] had been briefly tracked on
radar, heading inland from the coast and was lost in the
vicinity of Rendlesham forest.

A 'couple of days later', some 'intelligence officers'
from the USAF had asked to look at radar tapes of the
incident and told an astonishing story that the UCT might
have been a UFO which had crash-landed in Rendlesham
forest [and more].

In an addendum within 'Skycrash', Jenny highlights that
during June 1984, after an extensive search, she found
the original notes recorded from her first telephone
conversation with David Potts [not Paul Begg] in
February, 1981, which confirmed [the book's italics
undernoted]:

"Potts definitely gave the date as 27 December, but added
that the radar tapes of this night, _and several others_,
were removed. He further claimed that RAF Bentwaters had
called Watton and _asked_ for radar information of a
visual sighting on that night _as it was happening_.

Furthermore, he recounted how the Intelligence Officers
had informed that the Base Commander and several officers
had been called out into the forest from a party on base
which they were attending. This was in response to the
original discovery of the landed UFO. They took with them
a battery-operated portable tape recorder and made a
transcript of ensuing events as they unfolded".


The claim that, "RAF Bentwaters had called Watton and
asked for radar information of a visual sighting on that
night as it was happening", would equate with subsequent
documentation from Watton of Lt. Col. Halt's enquiry
during the early hours of 28 December.

At that time, Halt and team he had assembled to
investigate a report the 'UFO was back', were observing
what seemed to be unusual, star-like, lights in the sky.


According to the MoD's record's, after Halt's memo -
dated 13 January, 1981 - was received, they did ask if
Watton could shed any light on proclaimed events.

What the MoD did not, apparently, pursue, was
interviewing Halt, or anyone stationed at the twin RAF
Bentwaters/RAF Woodbridge complex.


How then, was Jenny able to be made aware during
February, 1981, that Watton had been contacted by
MoD/USAF personnel and they:

"...recounted how the Intelligence Officers had informed
that the Base Commander and several officers had been
called out into the forest from a party on base which
they were attending".

[...]

"They took with them a battery-operated portable tape
recorder and made a transcript of ensuing events as they
unfolded".

Both aspects are confirmed factual and central to events
on said night. Halt, a (one of several) Deputy Base
Commander - not the Base Commander - had duly been called
away from an officer's belated Christmas party, did
assemble a select group of officers to accompany him and
recorded on a microcassette what he deemed were key
incidents during his 'real time' investigation.

Evidently, either :

- MoD officials visited Watton in response to Halt's memo
and although the MoD had not been in contact with base
personnel, they somehow knew, "that the Base Commander
and several officers had been called out into the forest
from a party on base which they were attending... They
took with them a battery-operated portable tape recorder
and made a transcript of ensuing events as they
unfolded"...

That's not tenable - the MoD must have had further,
undocumented, contact to be aware Halt aborted
'attendance' at his Christmas party, gathered a team,
made the recording, et al...

or...

It was USAF personnel who 'accompanied' the MoD's
enquiries and presumably mentioned, perhaps by that time
on-base rumours, of a 'Base Commander'/interrupted
Christmas party/tape recording, etc...

...?


James.

From: "David Clarke" <cd292@crazydiamonds.fsnet.co.uk>
Date: Tue, 3 Dec 2002 09:23:27 -0000
Subject: [UFORL] Re: MOD blocked release of Rendlesham file - Ombudsman

BBC News Online, 3 December 2002

www.bbc.co.uk

UFO CASE 'BLOCKED' BY MOD

Details of one of Britain's most famous UFO scares
was among information repeatedly suppressed by
government defence chiefs, according to a Westminster
watchdog. Parliamentary Ombudsman Ann Abraham
said the Ministry of Defence (MoD) broke open
government rules three times in recent months over
cases including the Rendlesham Forest UFO scare.

Complaints about the MoD's refusal to list countries
prioritised for arms sales or reveal details of an armed
services survey were also up-held.

Former defence minister Peter Kilfoyle said the examples
outlined in the report on the Ombudsman's work between
May and October were symptomatic of a "culture of secrecy"
in the MoD.

"It is one of those departments that have always opposed
freedom of information and are not very attuned to what is
required in a modern, open and accountable government,"
 he said.

"Other departments and Whitehall as a whole have a
problem with openness but the MoD is on of the more
incorrigible cases of government by secrecy," he said.

Details of the alleged sighting at a Norfolk RAF base
more than 20 years ago were released last week after
the Ombudsman ruled the MoD were wrongly suppressing
them.

The "Rendlesham File" concerns a sighting of a "glowing"
triangular object by US Air Force police in Rendlesham Forest,
near RAF Woodbridge in Suffolk.

The documents have only previously been made available
to around 20 people who used the American Freedom of
Information Act to gain access to them.

In the early hours of 27 December, 1980, a number of
US Air Force men witnessed the object hover in the darkness,
transmitting blue pulsating lights and sending nearby farm
animals into a "frenzy".

While the actual documents had not been released, the details
were widely known, the Ombudsman said in her report.

"Given their age and the fact that these documents contained
no information not already in the public domain, the Ombudsman
saw no reason why they could not be disclosed," the report said.

The Ombudsman also partially upheld complaints against the
Cabinet Office, DVLA, Driving Standards Agency and the
Department for Work and Pensions, the report revealed.

Restrictions on the MoD's "Rendlesham File" were dropped as
part of an opening-up of the inner workings of Whitehall.

Ministers are attempting to lift the official veil of secrecy by
repealing or amending a raft of legislation banning access to
information.

Government departments will now be required to release
information on the internal workings of Whitehall, including
minutes of meetings of top civil servants.

Ministers say they will repeal or amend up to 100 items of
legislation which are currently prohibited from disclosure.

***
For the full text of the Ombudsman's judgement go to:

www.ombudsman.org.uk/pca/

click 'What's New' and then 'Parliamentary Commissioner
for Administration - Access to Official Information -
Investigations Completed May-October 2002.

Ministry of Defence - Case A29/02 - Refusal to release
information relating to the Rendlesham Forest UFO
incident can be found on pgs 9-11 of the file in pdf
format.

"Mr E" who made the complaint is of course Eric Morris
of the British UFO Studies Centre.

Date: Tue, 3 Dec 2002 13:32:47 +0100
Subject: [UFORL] Roswell

You may be interested to know that in the last issue of the British "The
Skeptic" (Vol. 15 nº 3), David Hambling proposes an intriguing answer to the
Roswell's alien corpses.

He mentions Nick Cook's book "Zero Point" where he presented a secret 1947
memorandum by Lt General Twining, listing six traits for the flying discs
sighted in UFO encounters:

1. metallic or light reflecting
2. no trail
3. circular or elliptical
4. formation flying
5. no associated sound
6. level speed above 300 knots

Twining states that "it is within the present US knowledge... to construct a
piloted aircraft which has the general description of the object above which
would be capable of an approximate range of 7.000 miles at subsonic speeds".

David Humbling writes:

"The (reconnaissance) balloons (sent over Russia) match the description in
the 1947 memo very closely. They were circular, appeared metallic, flew
silently leaving no trail and flew in formation. Their level speed was not
quite 300 knots, thought in the jetstream they could shift a respectable 250
mph.

However, the biggest clue is the fact that the man in charge of the balloon
spying program was one general Nathan Twining -the same Twining who wrote
the original memo.

(...) One notably discrepancy is that the memorandum talks about "manned
craft", whereas the balloon programmes we know about were unmanned (...) If
a manned balloon lost pressure at high altitude, the unfortunate crew would
rapidly die from the lack of oxigen. Their bodies would be freeze-dried by
the effects of extreme cold and very low pressure. How these shrunken,
frozen mummies would appear is anyone's guess (...) Any fatalities would
probably have led to the termination of a secret manned balloon program...

Fascinating. Not for a moment do I believe this is the explanation for the
alleged Roswell aliens (I am satisfied those are only rumours and hoaxes)
but the possibility of a high altitude manned balloon project should be
considered.

Luis R. González Manso
