Hi,

This is indeed a point I have pondered since the MoD report on Rendlesham
was first obtained by Andy and Dave last year.

As I have mentioned before there were too many consistencies between the
story as related to Paul Begg and myself by Potts during late Jan/early Feb
1981 for it not to be based on Potts actual attendance at the visit by the
intelligence staff as he claimed. For, recall, he was not claiming to have
witnessed the UFO tracking but 'was' saying that he was there when the radar
tapes were taken for study. So his account in that regard is first hand.

The party aspect was one area of clear overlap - ie the relating of an
feature of the case unknown through any other source that early. So was the
tape recording. This was the earliest reference to its existence by anyone.
But there were other features, too, including the nature of the alleged EM
effects.

Indeed - if you subtract the wild story about aliens and the base commander
chatting to them - the version as relayed by Potts is remarkably close to
the version on record today from witnesses. More consistent with the facts
as we eventually came to understand them many years later than virtually any
of the stories fed to us at that time by sources who were actually on
Bentwaters. Presumably because the rumours about what happened grew and grew
with each retelling and so wannabe airmen fed UFOlogists various distorted
tales.

Incidentally, Potts was absolutely adamant (as I have always reported) that
USAF intelligence personnel were in the party that was involved with taking
the radar evidence for study. It was this fact that caused him to be the
most intrigued because Watton was a joint civil/military base (Potts himself
was not RAF) and had no US association in the way that Bentwaters did.
Consequently approaches to them were made via the British government and it
was not usual practice to be handing over MoD property to Americans, which
is the impression Potts says he was given about what was going on that day.

This is not entirely in line with what Andy and Dave have discovered from
the then base commander at Watton about what happened . There does not seem
to be any official indication of USAF intelligence involvement. So why was
Potts so adamant about this allegation?

Were USAF intelligence staff from Bentwaters unofficially present on the
day? Was it merely a courtesy to let them tag along? Or was there some kind
of interaction between the MoD defence intelligence staff and USAF
intelligence from that early date - which does not seem to be recorded in
the Rendlesham file?

This is one of several reasons why the file seems incomplete - in the sense
that there are some good circumstantial indications of activity by somebody
from the UK and US government prior to the lowkey investigations that we are
told were commenced after the receipt of the Halt memo.

Halt himself told me he regarded this memo almost as a sop to be sent to the
MoD air staff for their files. That is one reason it underplays the case
(something that bothered me enough to ask him about).

Think about it. If you are wanting to inform Whitehall for the very first
time of a UFO encounter that you (as a man hoping to rise up the ranks ) are
directly endorsing to those who have a say in your future - do you withhold
the fact that you have:

1) Tape recorded the events as they happened

2) Collected soil samples and plaster casts of the indentations (some of
which Halt still has)

3) Had a base photographer there to document everything.

In other words, do you file with the people you are seeking to impress
merely an anecdotal account essentially asking them to trust to your word -
when instead you had what amounts to analysable physical evidence that
potentially turns this case into a lot more than a LITS story.

To me all this just doesnt hold together. Halt implied to me that he would
have made this data available to the MoD if they had come back expresssing
interest. It was a sort of test after the attitude of the British police
that had not sat with the USAF. But the MoD clearly knew of some (or all?)
of it anyway because the file reveals their very early awareness of the Halt
tape which is not mentioned by his memo. So they found this out by some
other route, we must assume that means Moreland.

So, we need to ascertain what else they learned about the hard evidence that
is not in the file. Not to mention why they didnt pursue it. There does not
seem any indication in the file that they even asked Moreland to pop along
to Halts office, get a copy of the tape, send them a report on it, or
whatever. Surely (unless you have already decided that the case is a
collosal waste of time - which the file covering the period Jan - April l981
does not suggest) then it seems bizarre that such vital evidence is known to
be sitting on a British base but it creates not a flicker of interest in
Whitehall.

I would have thought that any alert investigator is not going to form an
opinion on what may or may not have occurred minus any analysis of such
critical things like a live tape record, samples, plaster casts and site
photographs.

So why this discrepancy? Is it because they 'had' heard the tape, or at
least had a report on it to suggest the associated evidence was not worth
much in terms of evaluation? If so, where is that report to convey the
reasoning and when was it filed? And why is it not with the records if these
are comprehensive accounts of the MoD study of the case?

Similarly, if you are the MoD following up this case, as they did to the
extent of making enquiries regarding radar and radiation levels, would you
not at least ask the USAF what the status was of the physical evidence that
had been secured. Because, even though this other evidence is not mentioned
in the Halt memo its existence is obvious from first hearing of the Halt
tape which clearly describes it being collected. And the MoD clearly were
aware of the Halt tape, as the file reveals. So one assumes they knew of the
other evidence too, at least in that indirect manner.

There is an inconsistency here that puzzles me.

Especially as there are those reports, which I heard first hand from
forestery workers, villagers and farmers circa l983, that around New Years
Day l981 (two weeks before the Halt memo was at Whitehall) some people with
British accents and smart suits were wandering around the forest and asking
questions of locals seemingly about the matter.

Its been absurdly suggested that these relate to simply Brenda Butler and
Dot Street asking questions. But that is rubbish. They were there weeks
before Brenda and Dot went out there. And they were told similar things by
witnesses on their first visit as I was two years later.

 I asked questions of locals both in the presence of B & D and on my own and
nobody ever suggested that the visitors were UFOlogists or these two women.
The visitors were widely assumed to be from some scientific body or
government agency. Possibly even from Bawdsey. But there was no question
that someone British knew about the case in sufficient detail to be digging
around the forest days after the events and long before the MoD file
suggests that should be possible.

So I am not yet satisfied we fully understand the genesis of government
interest in this case, regardless of the file.

I dont think these people were reporters, BTW, since the way in which the
case reached the media is well established and offers absolutely no hint of
prior knowledge by either local or national sources. Besides which it seems
hard to believe that any media source that knew of the case and went to such
trouble to ask questions so early would never have revealed that aspect
after the case became so celebrated. Its an angle you would expect them to
play up. So it seems unlikely these New Year visitors were reporters.
Therefore, who were they?

To me there remains a disquieting sense that there are as yet unrevealed
aspects to the MoD investigation of this case (possibly at a level other
than the air staff) that would make sense of what we know supposedsly
occurred post the events in comparison with what the file tells us.

None of which is to say anything specific about an explanation. I am less
interested these days in what caused the RF case (as I suspect this will be
debated until Doomsday) than I am in how the MoD reacted to it, as an
illustration of how they would react to any real UFO incident if one were
ever hypothetically to occur. For me the MoD response as publicly reported
is sadly lacking and I live in hope that it merely looks so inept because we
are missing half the pieces of the jigsaw.

But knowing the British government hope and expectation have a habit of
being confounded!

Best wishes,

Jenny Randles

Larry:

Here it is:

FOREST SERVICE CONTRACTING OFFICER FOR THE TURKEY SPRINGS,
ARIZONA, CONTRACT
OF 1975, MAURICE MARCHBANKS, HAS AGREED TO ANSWER THE
FOLLOWING QUESTIONS
FOR THE RECORD:

1. Is it necessary for a contractor to provide an "act of God" excuse to a
contracting officer before the Forest Service can proceed with a termination
of that contract for default?
Answer: NO

2. Is it necessary for a contractor to provide any excuse to a contracting
officer before the Forest Service can proceed with a termination of that
contract for default?
Answer: NO

3. Assuming that Rogers did want out of his Turkey Springs contract, via
termination for default, is it true that Rogers could have easily
accomplished this at any time by simply walking off the job and not coming
back?
Answer: YES

4. Was it your normal course of action, after a contract had been defaulted,
that the Forest Service would readvertise that contract for new bids and
that the original contractor would only receive his 10 percent retention
money if the new low bid was equal to or lower than the original bid price,
and only then would the original contractor receive that money after the
entire process was complete (a process not uncommon to last four months or
more) and only then after the additional time needed for the check to be
processed
and sent?
Answer: YES
5. Would you consider it to be "dishonest" or "deception" if a contractor of
yours had other working contracts, other than the one held with you, even if
you were not personally aware of those other jobs?
Answer: NO

6. Is it true that [PJK] called and talked to you upwards of ten times
during the year of 1976 and that you grew quite weary of his persistent
hectoring?
Answer: YES

7. Is it your honest appraisal of the real situation on the Turkey Springs
contract that Rogers had nothing to gain by a UFO story as far as his
contract was concerned?

Answer: YES
signed Maurice Marchbanks, February 6, 1993

Hi James -- I may be able to sort out this puzzle for you..

> How then, was Jenny able to be made aware during
> February, 1981, that Watton had been contacted by
> MoD/USAF personnel and they:
>
> "...recounted how the Intelligence Officers had informed
> that the Base Commander and several officers had been
> called out into the forest from a party on base which
> they were attending".
>

The sequence of events is this: Halt gives his report to
Don Moreland, the RAF Liaison officer at Bentwaters, after
the Christmas break. Moreland sends this off to DS8 at
Whitehall, expecting MoD to follow it up [ie visit to interview
Halt].

Instead, as we know from the MoD file, they do nothing
except circulate Halt's memo (with the wrong dates) around
various defence intelligence branches and radar stations.

The two main radar stations - Eastern Radar (Watton) and
SOC Neatishead, say they did not detect anything on the
(wrong) nights in question or their films were faulty. But
evidently, some verbal (or telecon) report had been made
by RAF Watton. Halt had, if you recall, called them directly
in the early hours of 28 December whilst in Rendlesham
forest and asked them to check if anything was visible on
radar.

The CO at Watton was Squadron Leader Derek Coumbe.
I interviewed him last summer, and he confirmed he recalled
the call from the USAF security police at Bentwaters as the
event was taking place. He asked his duty controller to scan
the radars but said *nothing* was visible (this is confirmed
in his memo to DS8, which forms part of the file).

Furthermore Coumbe admitted that as a result of the interest
shown in the incident, *he personally* ordered all radar
tapes, both from 28 December and surrounding days, to be
impounded. He said that shortly afterwards (ie end of January
1981), a joint USAF/RAF team from MATO (Military Air
Traffic Organisation - based at Uxbridge, Middlesex) arrived
at Watton and removed the radar tapes for examination. At
least one of them (possibly that of 29 December) was
faulty.

This visit *must* in context be the source of the rumour
heard by David Potts in Feb 1981 and later passed onto
Paul Begg and Jenny Randles. It suggests to me that the
subject could not have been treated as "above top secret"
if the USAF/RAF team were prepared to discuss the event
so openly with a civilian ATC operator. The story about
the base commander communicating with aliens may well
have been a joke, taken seriously by Potts and later by
UFOlogists, with the results we have seen.

We don't of course know the results of the examination of
the radar tapes. But the Rendlesham file contains memos
dated 1983 by Sqn Ldr Jack Badcock of RAF (Ops) GE2,
who was the senior officer charged with the investigation of
all unidentified flying objects tracked by radar.

His conclusion, dated 21 March 1983 to MoD reads:
"Neatishead...had nothing unusual to report, and nothing more
substantive has come to light. I have received no evidence that
any radar [ie Watton] reported unusual tracks."

That seems to be the top and bottom of it. The radar tapes for
Watton and Neatishead were impounded and examined,
as a result of Halt's memo. It seems they were examined for
the whole of the period concerned, and nothing unusual was
seen.

As a result, the MoD decided there was no point in taking
Halt's report further - ie by interviewing him and the other
witnesses, because there was no radar corroboration of
his story. i.e. "no defence signficance."

It might seem odd to us, but that is the MoD attitude. They
see it thus - all they get by interviews is 'witness testimony'
that is ambiguous without hard evidence (ie radar tracking)
to back it up.

Therefore:

> Evidently, either :
>
> - MoD officials visited Watton in response to Halt's memo
> and although the MoD had not been in contact with base
> personnel, they somehow knew, "that the Base Commander
> and several officers had been called out into the forest
> from a party on base which they were attending... They
> took with them a battery-operated portable tape recorder
> and made a transcript of ensuing events as they
> unfolded"...
>
> That's not tenable - the MoD must have had further,
> undocumented, contact to be aware Halt aborted
> 'attendance' at his Christmas party, gathered a team,
> made the recording, et al...
>
> or...
>
> It was USAF personnel who 'accompanied' the MoD's
> enquiries and presumably mentioned, perhaps by that time
> on-base rumours, of a 'Base Commander'/interrupted
> Christmas party/tape recording, etc...
>

It seems that a combination of both of the above options is
what actually happened. All we have are the memos, but
evidently there was much telephone communication ongoing
between Bentwaters, DS8, the radar stations and MATO,
which would explain the 'missing links.'

I hope this is clear!

Best,

Dave Clarke

www.flyingsaucery.com

Compliments of the Duke of Mendoza:

Some of you will have seen on another list my
comparison of ufological discourse with the game
"Mornington Crescent", which has both no rules
and many rules, and all the rules that may or may
not exist are capable of being made up on the
spur of the moment. The analogy may (or may not
-- I am thinking of hiring Colin Bennett as a
consultant ambiguist on this one) be valid, but I
do detect the flavour of Mornington Crescent in
the notion that one can't judge the abduction
phenomenon (witnessed or otherwise) entirely from
the published literature. Rather, one has to talk
to abductees to discover the true picture...

Consider:

Two men play poker. At the showdown, one has aces
backed with eights. The other has a straight flush.
The player with the dead man's hand refuses to
accept he has lost because among the remaining
un-dealt cards in the pack, he says, is a royal
flush that would have come his way if the game had
but gone on long enough.

Consider:

A scientist publishes a paper in which he claims
to have invented an anti-gravity drive. No other
scientist can replicate his results; several
criticize the design of the equipment, and many
others comprehensively trounce his theory. His
response: "O, but we solved all these problems
years ago and have a working anti-gravity drive.
We just didn't publish the results this time.
And if you don't believe what we're saying, you
won't be allowed to look at the raw data either."

If information isn't in the public domain it's
effectively worthless. So a critic of abduction
claims who bases his criticisms on the public face
of the alleged phenomenon is doing no more than a
fair and reasonable job -- dealing with checkable
stuff. If in the process he severely misrepresents
that, then of course he must expect criticism in
return. But he can't reasonably be castigated for
not dealing with information which is by definition
esoteric and may well be denied him.

Not long ago a citizen of Minnesota entertained the
masses on UFO UpDates by maintaining there were many
documented witnesses to the Trindade Island sighting
of c.1958. He managed to name a few, but couldn't
justify the claim that either 48 or 100+ persons
had witnessed the UFO (in fact he avoided addressing
that issue, despite many, many reminders); and in
any case statements are actually available from
only one or two people, one of whom took the famous
photographs. In effect the other witnesses are
non-existent, since we have nothing with which to
judge the quality or nature of their witnessing(s).
Claims of "witnessed" abductions have exactly the
same non-status as the Trindade case. Nonetheless
those who guard the canons of ufological wisdom
insist that the Trindade case "stands". Look ma,
no feet.

In the wondrous Linda Napolitano case, we also
*actually* have but one witness. No one has produced
the "agents" Richard and Dan, and the "Third Man"
has denied any involvement. Cf Trindade.

You don't win a game of Mornington Crescent by changing
trains at places like Oxford Circus or King's Cross,
and you don't justify ufological wisdom by following
the usual rules of evidence, logic, or proof. You just
toss out a few things and run with what the faithful
pick up. Nothing spectacular has happened in the last
decade in the field, and even among its early promoters
Roswell is beginning to creak. So to keep the peasants
in their pews and the tithes coming into the temple, we
are about due another biggie of the order of Gulf Breeze.
I wonder what it will be.

best wishes
Pimms D. Martini
Parsons Green

OK, what IS adequate? I can't think of anything except Hollywodd special
effects, or fireworks, that could produce such an effect. All real
energy
weapons are INVISIBLE between the "gun" and the target, unless there is
dust, fog, or smoke present. Something has to scatter parts of the beam
away from their intended path, or the beam COULD NOT BE SEEN by any
observers who are off-axis. Energy does not just change course for no
reason. The only thing I can think of which produces such an effect
without
a scattering medium is fireworks.

@and I don't know WHERE you got the "dust or fog" since none was
reported.

See above. Beams are not visible unless such materials are present - or
unless the beams are added by production crews as SPECIAL EFFECTS. And
those appear only on film or video, not on the set.

Often, powerful searchlights on rotating platforms are used to advertise
special events here. But if there are no clouds, and if the air is quite
clean, the searchlight beam is not visible at all. Other times, it
appears as a traveling spot on clouds, with no beam seen coming up from
the ground. But usually there is enough moisture, smoke, or dust in the
air to render the beam visible as a shaft coming up from the ground.

Look at the Bush's Beans ad, where the man turns on a security system,
rather than trusting the dog. In reality, those LASER beams could not be
seen, unless smoke, fog, or dust scattered part of the beam into the
eyes
of the observer. They were added as special effects after the footage
was
shot.

I can't see the beam of my LASER pointer except where it strikes
something
- unless smoke, fog, or dust is present in the air. All I see is a
little
dot on the blackboard, not a line stretching from the LASER to the
blackboard.

When you see sunbeams, you are seeing light scattered from droplets of
water in the air. Without them, the sunbeams vanish.

We have to think in terms of real physics, not what we see on TV. A Star
Trek phaser (assuming we could make one) could not be visible either,
without something to scatter some energy aside, or something becoming
incandescent due to an incredible amount of energy.

@Alas, in your future postings, I shall be forced to regard you as "The
@Boy Who Cried Fire-Balloon."

I don't just label things as fire balloons without many indication that
one might be present. I look for the characteristics of fire balloons
(and equally, all other prosaic possibilities) when I look at any
description of a reported UFO. In order for me to suggest a fire
balloon,
there must be a preponderance of fire balloon characteristics, with NO
characteristics present that refute a fire balloon.

The descriptions by the men in the truck meet that criterion.

Of course, I have to reject ALL distances, sizes, speeds, or altitudes
reported by eyewitnesses, unless something other than typical human
visual
estimates of these values provides the values. The human eye does not
have
the capability to provide these values for any unknown object which is
seen
against the sky and is farther away than 30 feet.
Characteristics of fire balloons:

- One light, or a cluster of lights, seen against the night sky
- Usually looks a lot bigger than it is
- Usually orange* or white, but can be any color (colored wax, straws,
bag)
- Can change color (advertising printed on bag)
- Sometimes appears as a lighted horizontal disk* (suit bag not visible)
- Framework can appear around the lights
- Can hover*
- Can do steady or wobbly* motion (depends on construction and wind
motion)
- Can do the classic "swinging pendulum" or "falling leaf" effect*
- Can do an oscillating coin effect*
- Can "turn on a dime"*
- Can appear to travel at fantastic speeds (distance grossly
overestimated)
- Can take a straight, or erratic* flight path (depends on wind motion)
- Can fire "missiles" at the ground (candle falls)
- Can emit sparks or shoot projectiles (fireworks attached)
- Can land, and then take off
- Can set fires (which is why fire balloons are illegal in most places)
- Can suddenly disappear*
- Some can disappear and reappear (relighting trick candles)
- Can suddenly appear to rush directly away from the witness*
- Can explode (firecracker attached)

In fact, the effects marked by an asterisk are the classic effects that
are reported again and again as the strange effects of UFOs, and that
make
many people believe that UFOs are intelligently controlled.

I also have too many friends who have confessed to me that they launched
some when they were kids.

Now, were there any effects reported by the witnesses in that truck that
are NOT on the above list?

******

In 1993, policemen in a helicopter near Louisville KY reported that a
fire
balloon was "larger than their helicopter" and that it made "ramming
attacks
at them". The whole effect was caused by the human visual system's total
inability to find out the size, distance, altitude, or speed of an
unknown
object in the air if it is farther away than 30 feet.

They overestimated the size, thinking of an airplane. This then threw
off
their distance, speed and altitude estimates, because pilots normally
use
the KNOWN size of a given type of airplane to estimate the other values
from the angular size and velocity they witness. The ramming attacks
were
caused by the overestimated size, combined with the helicopter's own
motion. The fire balloon was nearly stationary during the entire
incident,
as testified to by the witnesses on the ground.

From: "Greg Sandow" <greg@gregsandow.com>
Date: Tue, 3 Dec 2002 23:55:37 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Re: Abduction eyewitnesses

> Some of you will have seen on another list my
> comparison of ufological discourse with the game
> "Mornington Crescent", which has both no rules
> and many rules, and all the rules that may or may
> not exist are capable of being made up on the
> spur of the moment. The analogy may (or may not
> -- I am thinking of hiring Colin Bennett as a
> consultant ambiguist on this one) be valid, but I
> do detect the flavour of Mornington Crescent in
> the notion that one can't judge the abduction
> phenomenon (witnessed or otherwise) entirely from
> the published literature. Rather, one has to talk
> to abductees to discover the true picture...

Feh. Peter, you -- an experienced journalist -- should know better than
this.

Some subjects are well documented in published writing. Others aren't.
If you were writing about contemporary classical music, and wanted to
say something about the early days of the European avant-garde --
Boulez, Stockhausen, and their colleagues -- you could read the
published literature. It's perfectly adequate.

But if you wanted to say anything substantial about the early days of
the American minimalist composers -- Steve Reich and Philip Glass --
.you'd have to talk to them and to people who worked with them. The
published literature isn't good enough, even though these composers are
now very famous.

Abductions fall somewhere in the middle. Yes, a lot has been written.
But suppose you wanted to evaluate one fairly simple theory -- that the
standard abduction scenario is suggested to abductees by abduction
researchers, most likely during hypnosis. This isn't an unreasonable
idea. It's been proposed many times. And given the vagaries of hypnosis,
it seems perfectly possible..

How, then, would you decide whether or not it might be true? What data
would you need? Well, if you want to know what influence researchers
have on abductees, you'll have to know what abductees begin with -- what
they think before they ever meet a researcher. How many of them claim to
remember the events in the standard scenario? How many remember none of
it? How many remember some part of it, but not all, and fill in the rest
with hypnosis? Most crucially, I think you'd want to know how many
abductees fall into each category.

You won't find this information in the published literature. The closest
you'll get is a much-repeated claim that 25% of abductees remember their
abductions without hypnosis. But what does this actually mean? Does it
mean that 25% of abductees remember everything consciously, and never
have any memories amplified by hypnosis, or that 25% simply remember
_something_? I've never seen this written about in any detail. To get
any idea of where abductees start, what they think they remember before
they talk to any investigator, you'll simply have to talk to the people
involved. The literature, on this question (though not necessarily on
others), isn't good enough.

And there's an extra complication here. By now, just about everyone
knows at least the outlines of the standard scenario. So it might not be
hard for investigators to encourage abductees to believe it. To really
understand where the scenario comes from, I think you have to learn what
happened in the early days of abduction research. You have to find out
exactly how the scenario first emerged, in interviews and/or hypnosis
sessions conducted in the early '70s. There wasn't nearly as much media
contamination then. Besides, people like Budd Hopkins and David Jacobs
say that they themselves didn't know the scenario. They say they learned
it from abductees. Is this true? To answer this question, you need a lot
of data about what actually went on in those early days of abduction
research -- and you'll find only the vaguest beginnings of it in the
published literature.

Greg Sandow

>so openly with a civilian ATC operator.

Hi,

I agree, Dave, to a point. But this was no 'rumour'. Potts was claiming to
have actually been there and heard first hand the justification offered by
the USAF intelligence staff present at this visit to Watton. They reported
the reason they claimed to need the radar data. To see if it correlated
with a UFO incident reported from base personnel.

They then documented that sighting in detail, many facets of which match the
story as we now have it. So if this was a rumour it was a mostly accurate
one. And surely the MoD / USAF intelligence do not routinely act on rumours.
They presumably went there fully briefed.

>The story about
>the base commander communicating with aliens may well
>have been a joke, taken seriously by Potts and later by
>UFOlogists, with the results we have seen.


Well, I can see how you might think this. But I dont believe it holds up.
Certainly, I can envisage said USAF chaps saying something like 'we want
this material to check alongside a reported case where several of our
officers claim that such and such and such and such occurred' (long
account - mostly accurate - of the sighting follows) and 'oh, by the way'
(big grin) 'the base commander went out there and chatted to little aliens
floating beneath the UFO'.

Meant as a joke, Potts fails to see this and reports it along with the true
facts. Its just about credible I guess.

However, the big problem is that you date this radar visit (from talking to
the commander) to post the Halt memo - ie late on in January. That means it
was more or less immediately prior to Potts talking to Begg - which was
around the third week in January. But by that date the aliens chatting with
the base commander storyline was already out.

It was provided to Brenda Butler by Steve Roberts in the first few days of
January (around the 5th or 6th was the best I could document it when
studying Brenda's notes about two years later). It was certainly prior to
the Halt memo, let alone the Watton radar visit if that did occur as late as
you suggest that it did .

So, unless we have the timing completely out - in which case the radar data
visit occurred before the Halt memo got to Whitehall - there was no joke
told to Potts that he took seriously before UFOlogy later did the same
thing. He was the second to be told this jest.

As for UFOlogy being fooled - thats not emtirely fair as I never took this
story seriously. Indeed it was so absurd it was the main reason I always
suspected a set up - ie deliberate disinformation fed out to both Potts and
the UFO community in order (one might logically assume) to try to discredit
the existence of any sort of incident should we choose to talk about it. As,
of course, base public affairs knew very well that we would.

This was a case known by too many people for the lid to have been kept on
indefinitely. USAF intelligence had to know that it was going to come out
and my bet is they used this story as a contingency plan to dump on the
credibility of the case as and when it did so.

You will see that clearly from my early writings on the matter. My
suspicions of an intelligence set up are the reason I started thinking along
the nuclear mishap route. I just could not buy that some dubious USAF guy
(whom I am virtually certain was not involved in the case but whom Halt iden
tified to me as a base public affairs intelligence officer) would blab in a
pub to a local ghost hunter in the same month as a USAF intelligence officer
visiting Watton should (seemingly with sufficiently straight face to be
believed by a radar operator) recount the same looney tunes saga. Moreover
that they are not at all discouraged from similarly blabbing in a pub to a
writer or repeating it to a UFOlogist days later. This smells fishy.

(Dont forget - as it may be important - that neither person initially told
this story was a UFOlogist - Paul Begg was unfamiliar with UFOs, which is
why he came to me - his forte was mysterious vanishings and the like - and
Brenda was not a UFOlogist either but a local ghost hunter and folk tale
enthusiast - the reason she took it to Dot Street, a BUFORA member...So, if
this was a tactic to feed out a yarn it may have been deliberate that it
went to two people unaware of how credible/incredible this story was in UFO
terms)

Note also that both these men (Roberts and Potts) went to great lengths to
avoid any kind of public personal outing. I had to promise Potts
strenuously not to identify him. Roberts would never even talk to me when I
was working on Sky Crash (let alone go public or talk to others) and I have
no independent evidence that he even exists - but for the fact that his
story to Brenda kick started the whole thing from their point of view.

There is something not quite right with this picture isnt there? And the
connection here is an utterly absurd story (that no other witness bar Larry
Warren) has ever remotely suggested to be true. In fact the likes of Halt
and Burroughs have laughed it out of court as much as they do the lighthouse
theory and do so by using cogent arguments. Burroughs told me that if Gordon
Williams had been out there then it would have changed everything. They are
adamant this story is total rubbish.

Yet both versions of it surfaced independently within a couple of weeks of
each other in Jan l981 via different sources offered to people who seem
likely to talk in public about a case otherwise not talked about officially.
And both trace back to USAF intelligence. (Indeed it is even possible
Roberts was the same person who was at Watton that day).

You characterise this as a joke that UFOlogists fell for and, whilst it is
possible it was a joke, I deny that UFOlogists fell for it - since I never
did and was one of the only ones to see both these versions come together
that Jan/Feb. Brenda too had at least some suspicions borne out of Roberts'
rather less than straight behaviour.

Recall also that Roberts further implies (to my thinking at least) that he
was an intelligence officer by his securing of the NASA/USAF memo we report
in Sky Crash. The one that at the time was unreleased even by FOI in
America. The one that was low key but a darned good way to try to put
UFOlogists on his side and create the impression he was bona fide and
therefore should be believed even if he is alleging total drivel about
aliens, base commanders and sign language.

The release by him of that memo is an unforgotten (but IMO) vital clue in
this case.

To me (and to Halt BTW) this was further evidence that Roberts was playing a
game and was acting in an intelligence role.

I think it is at least a credible argument that there is a reason beyond a
simple joke in all of this - that maybe these intelligence sources seem to
have wanted the crazy version of this case (the totally discredited 'aliens
chat to base commander' line) to be fed out alongside the less dramatic
truth and spread from the start of this case so as to make it impossible to
tell sufficiently early what was truth and what was not truth.

It does not matter now. If this was an intelligence tactic it was directed
at the needs of the cold war nuclear missile toting era of the early l980s.
So it only had to work short term.

If it was not a tactic to try to discredit the case by allowing UFOlogists
to over egg the pudding then why did it happen twice? If it was not to try
to deflect attention onto aliens and away from any genuine probe into a more
terrestrial incident (as I have long suspected) then what was it?

After all this tactic matches rather well the long term policy used by
intelligence services regarding MIB. I know Dave and I probably strongly
disagree over this but I genuinely think (see my Men in Black book) that at
some points during the history of UFOlogy witnesses have been visited by
intelligence agents who have quite deliberately acted up to the fantasy
model of a man in black in order to allow the witness to discredit
themselves - and thereby their case - in the eyes of sober members of the
public.

All these poor witnesses have to do is tell the truth about what happened to
them and because that truth is an absurd nonsense tacked onto the reality of
their initial sighting then their whole case is destroyed in the eyes of
many people.

After all, if you claim that something is on your roof then most people will
probably go take a look. If you claim that this something it is a pink
elephant dancing ballet in a tutu, most people will think you are nuts and
simply walk away. I suspect that similar thinking has been applied by
intelligence agencies at times should there be a danger of a story getting
out that they would rather not too many people dig into at the time.

After all, at the very least, we know that there was huge fuss over the
placing of US nuclear missiles at UK bases in the early 80s and that it
seems that Bentwaters (covertly) had such weapons. Something obviously
occurred in Dec l980 and regardless of what it was there was possibly real
risk of hard digging into the nature of these events uncovering the nuclear
weapons angle. If so then many a question might be asked at a very awkward
time about whether it was right to ship in more missiles to any places where
things like this were going on.

Possibly somebody calculated that some version of this story would
inevitably emerge as so many people were involved in it that silence simply
could not be secured. But the best way to prevent any sober investigation
into its true nature was to feed it out yourself in a sufficiently ludicrous
way that only UFOlogists would be interested.

I had an argument with Ralph Noyes over this and he said you would never
draw attention to an event by bringing up newsworthy UFOs. That seems
credible on the face of it. But the point is that here all those involved
perceived this event in UFO terms already so if it came out it would be in
the form of a UFO story. You could not alter that.

Regardless of whether you believed this was a bunch of trained airmen going
loopy over a lighthouse (ergo - can they be trusted to look after nuclear
missiles?) - or it was a genuine UFO (ergo - are our weapons safe from UFOs
at such a place?) - or the sightings were caused by something terrestrial
and nefarious (ergo - we would much rather folk think it was a UFO than a
secret test we dont want them to know about) - the course seems self
defined. But it makes sense to create a UFO story with built in absurdity to
ensure that not too many people took this case seriously.

And they didnt. Not even in UFOlogy. Dave, despite what you say about
UFOlogists falling for this story, in reality UFOlogy took a heck of a lot
of convincing that there was even a case. If you actually look at the UFO
records between l981 and l983 (pre NOTW splash) you will see that this was a
story regarded as so cracked that not even most UFOlogists bought it before
the Halt memo was revealed to them at the BUFORA conference in August l983.

Thats another important element to this case. As is the aside in the
Moreland/MoD memo in the Rendlesham file where it is quite rightly argued
that UFOlogists will not be sufficiently interested in my nuclear mishap
theory to pursue the case. They would only pursue it if they thought it was
an alien UFO.

Regardless of what lies behind this case ponder what that tells you about
government thinking on UFOs. That in order to get UFOlogists to take on this
case (which may be the point of the info leaks to Brenda and to Potts) it
had to be alien UFO orientated to get anyone to sit up. Now, whilst the
actual witnesses were telling a UFO story its an interestingly low key one.
A sort of UAP with electrical effects but not really anything that stands
out as being alien or a spaceship.

It seems improbable that in the early days the witnesses as we now know them
can be thought responsible for a story getting out anything like the version
of 'aliens chat to base commander hovering under a domed disk spaceship'.
Its nothing like the truth and these witnesses are flat out opposed to it.

Yet it originated somewhere and, by accident or design, offers the absurdity
level and ETH features that the real story lacked but the powers that be
probably thought UFOlogy would need in order to turn this case into
something wild and unbelievable. They might have feared that a true version
would be low key enough to get people asking questions because it might have
something at its heart...but, I mean, aliens chatting to a base commander
(whom simple checks can prove was not there) whilst repairing a striken
Roswell like spaceship - only bozos are going to do more than smile and move
on.

This is a tactic intelligence agencies have used outside of UFOlogy and its
a brilliant one if a witness chances to see something sensitive and the
powers that be cannot realistically shut them up. So they encourage them to
talk but give them a little something extra unbelievable to talk about in
addition to the reality of what they saw - something that in effect destroys
their case.

I see pretty good signs here that something like that went on in the early
days of the Bentwaters case. Since it is pretty obvious that there was no
alien contact at all (and certainly none like that fed out to Brenda via
Steve Roberts or at Watton) the question is why did this sort of muddying
activity occur?

So, yes, this could all be the 'joke that got out of hand' syndrome, since I
know it happens sometimes with witnesses. But the fact that the same joke
was fed out twice in addition to telling a story that otherwise is basically
true (merely open to debate as to what caused the events that took place)
ought to give anyone cause to wonder if it was not more than a simple jest.

Especially given the apparent origin of this 'joke' which seems to point to
USAF intelligence.

Like I said something is not right here and it is probably hoped that we all
just conclude it was likely a joke and move on after 21 years.

But just because a story is absurd and untrue (as this one pretty obviously
is) does not necessarily mean that it was merely told for amusement.

Best wishes,

Jenny Randles

Subject: RE: [UFORL] The Rendlesham file

We need to remember that Reagan had just been elected President of the
US, and Iran was close to releasing the hostages. So there was plenty
going on in the intelligence world around then.

I don't know where (other than it was a website) I read this, but
someone
postulated a spy-satellite film drop occurred in Rendlesham Forest due
to
a malfunction in the recovery device of the film capsule.

Remember that a film capsule must re-enter the atmosphere, and thus, it
looked like a small Apollo capsule.

That triangular shape would fit this.

The UFO story would then be a cover for collecting the capsule.

@ of 'aliens chat to base commander hovering under a domed disk
@ spaceship'.
@ Its nothing like the truth and these witnesses are flat out
@ opposed to it.
@
@ Yet it originated somewhere and, by accident or design,
@ offers the absurdity
@ level and ETH features that the real story lacked but the
@ powers that be
@ probably thought UFOlogy would need in order to turn this case into
@ something wild and unbelievable. They might have feared that
@ a true version
@ would be low key enough to get people asking questions
@ because it might have
@ something at its heart...but, I mean, aliens chatting to a
@ base commander
@ (whom simple checks can prove was not there) whilst repairing
@ a striken
@ Roswell like spaceship - only bozos are going to do more than
@ smile and move
@ on.
@
@ This is a tactic intelligence agencies have used outside of
@ UFOlogy and its
@ a brilliant one if a witness chances to see something
@ sensitive and the
@ powers that be cannot realistically shut them up. So they
@ encourage them to
@ talk but give them a little something extra unbelievable to
@ talk about in
@ addition to the reality of what they saw - something that in
@ effect destroys
@ their case.
@
@ I see pretty good signs here that something like that went on
@ in the early
@ days of the Bentwaters case. Since it is pretty obvious that
@ there was no
@ alien contact at all (and certainly none like that fed out to
@ Brenda via
@ Steve Roberts or at Watton) the question is why did this sort
@ of muddying
@ activity occur?
@
@ So, yes, this could all be the 'joke that got out of hand'
@ syndrome, since I
@ know it happens sometimes with witnesses. But the fact that
@ the same joke
@ was fed out twice in addition to telling a story that
@ otherwise is basically
@ true (merely open to debate as to what caused the events that
@ took place)
@ ought to give anyone cause to wonder if it was not more than
@ a simple jest.
@
@ Especially given the apparent origin of this 'joke' which
@ seems to point to
@ USAF intelligence.
@
@ Like I said something is not right here and it is probably
@ hoped that we all
@ just conclude it was likely a joke and move on after 21 years.
@
@ But just because a story is absurd and untrue (as this one
@ pretty obviously
@ is) does not necessarily mean that it was merely told for amusement.
@
@ Best wishes,
@
@ Jenny Randles

Rendlesham Forest: December 1980<br><br>

Did the Americans drop a satellite on Suffolk?<br><br>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbs
p;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Rendlesham Forest, 27/28 December 1980<br><br>
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------<br>
Introduction<br><br>
The Rendlesham Forest event, on or around the night of Saturday to
Sunday,<br>
27/28 December 1980, is one of the most famous 'UFO' incidents in
Britain. More<br>
than fifty witnesses, both military and civilian, have come forward to
give<br>
their impressions of what happened, and the case prompted the disclosure
of one<br>
of the few official defence documents relating to a UFO sighting.
Explanations<br>
of the event range from crashing alien spaceships to wild drug parties,
and<br>
from distant lighthouses to bizarre secret military
experiments.<br><br>
Put simply, the theory I am presenting here suggests that the men of the
67th<br>
Aerospace Rescue and Recovery squadron, based in Rendlesham Forest, were
just<br>
doing their job. It is known that a spy satellite was orbiting at that
date,<br>
and it is known that the 67th was one of the units assigned to collect
the film<br>
capsules dropped from the satellite. Here I am putting these two
facts<br>
together.<br><br>
The Theory<br><br>
While the mother satellite carries on in its orbit the capsule begins
re-entry<br>
over the North Sea, heading SSW. Some Lockheed HC-130 Hercules aircraft
and a<br>
group of HH-53C helicopters of the 67th ARRS are on station over the
Dogger<br>
Bank, waiting to retrieve the falling capsule, either from mid-air
(by<br>
Hercules) or from the sea (by helicopter). But the parachutes on the
capsule<br>
fail to open. Whereas the parachutes would have slowed down the
satellite<br>
substantially, changing its trajectory, the capsule still continues along
its<br>
original descent path, flying fast and high above the waiting (and
now<br>
redundant) aircraft.<br><br>
The possibility of a parachute failure had already been explored by Big
Bird's<br>
controllers, and re-entry for film capsules had been calculated in such a
way<br>
that if everything went wrong, and the capsule did become a free-falling
rock,<br>
it would still land at a site where the recovery team can collect it. In
this<br>
case the back-up recovery site is RAF Woodbridge itself. Only a few
minutes<br>
after the 67th learn of the parachute failure, the capsule, recovery
lights<br>
blazing, flies over Lowestoft (getting noticed on radar in the process)
and<br>
crashes into Rendlesham Forest at the end of the airfield's runway.
The<br>
emergency base crew start rushing about in the forest to find the thing,
and a<br>
cover story is put into immediate effect.<br><br>
Neither the USAF nor the MOD want people to know that they've been
aiming<br>
satellites into Suffolk, yet many civilians (and military personnel at
the base<br>
not privy to the secret Big Bird recoveries, too) are bound to have
seen<br>
something come crashing in, and have noticed the base burst into a flurry
of<br>
activity. The cover story spreads deliberate misinformation about the
incident,<br>
claiming that a 'UFO' has landed. Any other story (eg. a meteor or a
plane<br>
crash) would need some sort of hard evidence the 67th would later have to
show<br>
investigators, but a 'UFO' story is implausible enough to discredit
witnesses.<br>
The bare bones of the story are: saucer with lights, jeep engines
failing, cows<br>
going crazy in the fields etc. Deliberate confusion is spread about the
date<br>
and the specific location of the incident. Depressions are dug in the
ground,<br>
and shown later to the police. The radar tape is taken. Engineers come in
to<br>
repair the damage done to the runway lights by the capsule's crash.
Base<br>
personnel not in on the truth hear the rumours and organise their
own<br>
'sky-watching' parties in the next few nights. Senior base personnel
similarly<br>
unaware of the 67th's activities insist that Colonel Halt sends a memo to
the<br>
MOD, which he does. The MOD refer researchers to UFO stories, both now
and in<br>
1983 when the incident blows up in public again. Halt is later promoted.
Over<br>
time the whole thing becomes a mass of claim and counter-claim.<br><br>
Discussion of the theory looks critically at the basis of the theory, and
the<br>
Appendices (The 67th ARRS, Big Bird, Satellite Recoveries, RAF Woodbridge
and<br>
Bentwaters, A Soviet Satellite crash?) contain supporting
information.<br><br>
I would like to thank Richard Kidd and Michael Akeroyd for comments
and<br>
suggestions.<br><br>
Alan Akeroyd<br><br>
August 1996<br>

==============<br>

Discussion<br>
Discussion of the theory<br>
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------<br><br>
So, is the theory likely?<br><br>
Although the 67th ARRS is recognised as a satellite capsule recovery
squadron,<br>
few people seem to have considered that the incident might be based on
the unit<br>
trying to recover a satellite. The 67th was a specialist space capsule
and<br>
aircrew retrieval unit, it was one of the very few in the whole of
Europe<br>
specialised for such a purpose, and it was so important that it did not
even<br>
report to the USAFE like the vast majority of American squadrons here,
but<br>
reported directly to the DoD in Washington (see The 67th ARRS). And
the<br>
Rendlesham Forest event involves something 'crashing out of the sky'
right at<br>
the end of the 67th's runway. Out of all the places where this object
could<br>
have landed, it did so on the very runway of a satellite retrieval
squadron.<br><br>
Some UFO commentators have noticed this, but the reasoning used to
account for<br>
this appears less plausible. Jenny Randles suggests that the Americans
could<br>
have successfully stolen a Soviet satellite from orbit and somehow guided
it<br>
down into the forest, but this is unlikely for several reasons (see
Soviet<br>
satellite crash). More outlandish theories are that visiting aliens
crashed<br>
there because they found a satellite retrieval base intrinsically
interesting<br>
to visit; or that RAF Woodbridge was sufficiently secure to arrange a
meeting<br>
between earth representatives and space alien envoys.<br><br>
But these all seem to get way from the point a bit.... The 67th was in
Suffolk<br>
to recover American satellites. That was its job. At the very least we
should<br>
consider the possibility that the 67th was trying to do just that in
December<br>
1980.<br><br>
Did it go up, or down?<br><br>
The witnesses into two groups: civilian and military. Overall there were
at<br>
least fifty witnesses in some form or another, which is why Rendlesham
Forest<br>
has become the most famous and best-attested 'UFO' case in Britain. But
they do<br>
not all come out with the same story.<br><br>
The military witnesses reported saucers, aliens, strange lights, jeep
engines<br>
failing, cows going berserk, radioactive marks on the ground and on tree
trunks<br>
etc. They saw an alien spacecraft carefully and quietly ease itself
through the<br>
forest before finding an open field, and soaring back up into the sky
again.<br><br>
The civilian witnesses restrict their account to seeing something come
down - a<br>
light crashing in from over Lowestoft, falling into the forest. And then
they<br>
saw the airbase burst into frantic activity. But no one seems to have
seen the<br>
object go back up. For this, all we have to go on is the word of people
who<br>
would have an interest in keeping the real reason secret.<br><br>
Would the Americans really have done this?<br><br>
A great deal rests on whther the US military could have been capable of
staging<br>
such an operation, and on how accurate is the science of pin-pointing
satellite<br>
re-entry. Could anyone predict so precisely where a satellite would fall?
The<br>
answer in this case is probably yes. The Americans knew exactly the orbit
the<br>
craft was in, because they had put it there. They knew exactly when to
fire the<br>
de-orbit engine on the film capsule, and exactly how fast it was going.
They<br>
had gained much experience in plotting both manned and unmanned
spacecraft<br>
re-entry trajectories. If anything, the back-up recovery site would be
more<br>
precisely known than the primary mid-air one, as for the back-up there
would be<br>
no chance of the parachute-borne capsule being blown by high winds. The
film<br>
capsule wasn't coming in from far, either - only 170-ish kilometres. And
they<br>
had given themselves plenty of room for error at Rendlesham, as they
could be<br>
out by a good few miles and still crash the thing into uninhabited forest
or<br>
farmland.<br><br>
But would they have done so? The Americans could organise a film capsule
drop<br>
into the North Sea, granted; that does not really affect anyone. But what
this<br>
theory demands is that they chose as their back-up recovery site an area
in<br>
civilian Suffolk.<br><br>
Clearly this was an dangerous and stupid thing to do, and it could well
have<br>
been fatal if it had gone wrong. If they did do this then it is no
surprise<br>
that they tried to cover the whole thing up. Dropping a large, heavy lump
of<br>
metal at 27,000 km/h into a suburb of Ipswich would be an scandal, if
true. Why<br>
would the Americans think that the recovery of a film capsule was worth
the<br>
risk?<br><br>
Perhaps they never really believed that the parachutes would fail. They
never<br>
failed on any of the Mercury, Gemini and Apollo missions, after all.
These were<br>
good, strong, US-built parachutes; so the question of placing the
back-up<br>
recovery site never seriously arose. They believed, firstly, that they
could<br>
indeed target a satellite so accurately that it would land on the very
runway<br>
of the airfield itself; and secondly, that this belief would never be put
to<br>
the test. But on 27/28 December the parachutes did fail. Fortunately
for<br>
everyone, the first belief was true, and the capsule stayed on course.
But<br>
perhaps it scared them, and they never planned a recovery this way
again.<br><br>
More research<br><br>
It should be easy to prove this theory wrong. The most important aspect
to<br>
research is to discover precisely when Big Bird 16 dropped its film
capsules. I<br>
have yet not been able to find this out, but of course that's not to say
the<br>
information is not around somewhere. If Big Bird did not do a drop on or
around<br>
the 27/28 December 1980 then there is no way a film capsule can account
for the<br>
event. (If BB 16 did drop one, however, then the theory becomes a great
deal<br>
stronger.)<br><br>
Appendix 1: The 67th ARRS<br>
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------<br><br>
Night Owls<br><br>
The 67th Aerospace Rescue and Recovery Squadron arrived at RAF Woodbridge
in<br>
December 1969, having transferred from Moron AFB in Spain. The 67th was
not<br>
strictly part of the United States Air Force in Europe (USAFE), but
was<br>
directly answerable to the Department of Defense in Washington. The
67th<br>
specialised in rescue and night-time operations, including the delivery
and<br>
retrieval of Special Forces personnel in foreign territory in
clandestine<br>
operations, and was one of the few units to be equipped with<br>
spacecraft-recovery Hercules HC-130 aircraft.<br><br>
The Aerospace Rescue and Recovery Service merged with Special Operations
Forces<br>
in 1983; the rescue service split off again in 1990, but the 67th (now
renamed<br>
the 67th Special Operations Squadron) formed part of the new AFSOC group.
Air<br>
Force Special Operations Command's brief includes &quot;unconventional
warfare,<br>
special reconnaissance, psychological operations, personnel
recovery,<br>
county-terrorism, counter-narcotics&quot; (Chinnery 1994).<br><br>
Today the 67th SOS is part of the 352nd Special Operations Group based at
RAF<br>
Mildenhall, and flies HC-130 N/Ps. The squadron took part in the Gulf
War,<br>
operating out of Incirlik Air Base in Turkey. It's nickname is
&quot;Night Owls&quot;.<br><br>
Aircraft<br><br>
In mid-1979, just before the Rendlesham Forest UFO incident, the 67th
operated<br>
the following aircraft:<br><br>
one&nbsp; x Lockheed Hercules HC-130 H<br><br>
four x Lockheed Hercules HC-130 N<br><br>
one&nbsp; x Lockheed Hercules HC-130 P<br><br>
nine x Sikorsky HH-53 C &quot;Super Jolly Green Giant&quot;<br><br>
The HC-130 H is an extended-range version of the basic Hercules, having a
range<br>
of 3602 km (2238 miles), used for recovering personnel, equipment etc.
Since<br>
1964, 43 HC-130 Hs were built, most going to the US Coastguard; but eight
were<br>
delivered to the USAF, of which at least four were adapted specifically
for<br>
mid-air recovery of space capsules.<br><br>
The HC-130 N &quot;Combat Shadow&quot; is a USAF search and rescue
version of the HC-130<br>
H, used explicitly for aircrew or space capsule recovery, and having
advanced<br>
direction finding equipment and helicopter refuelling capabilities.
Combat<br>
Shadows were used during the Gulf War for refuelling. Chinnery sums up
the<br>
HC-130 P/N variants as &quot;initially modified to conduct search and
rescue<br>
missions, provide a command and control platform, air-refuel helicopters
and<br>
carry supplemental fuel for extending range or for air refuelling... the
HC-130<br>
flies clandestine single- or multi-ship missions, usually in low
visibility or<br>
darkness, intruding into politically sensitive or hostile territory to
provide<br>
air refuelling for special operations helicopters&quot;
(p.270).<br><br>
The HC-130 P is another Hercules variant, again designed for
refuelling<br>
helicopters in mid-air, and for recovering parachute-borne payloads.
Twenty<br>
were built for the USAF. modified from HC-130 Hs by including refuelling
drogue<br>
pods. According to the 1979-80 edition of Jane's (p.376), a typical<br>
helicopter-refuelling mission would involve the HC-130 P taking off with
33,385<br>
kg (73,600 lb) of fuel on board, meeting up with the helicopters at a
range of<br>
about 925 km (575 miles), transferring 22,000 kg (48,500 lb) of fuel, and
then<br>
returning home.<br><br>
The HH-53 C is a night operation rescue and retrieval helicopter,
developed<br>
purely for the ARRS, with forward-looking IR radar, refuelling boom
and<br>
on-board IBM computer.<br><br>
So the picture we build up of the 67th in 1980 is one of an
specialised<br>
night-operations squadron, based in Suffolk, flying mid-air space
capsule<br>
retrieval missions. The HH-53 C helicopters would fly out to the Dogger
Bank<br>
area, to pick up the capsule floating in the North Sea should the
circling<br>
Hercules aircraft miss it on its way down. Most of the helicopters' fuel
is<br>
used up flying north, but the HC-130s double up as refuelling bases for
the<br>
copters, so that's not a worry. (A Hercules itself can quite easily
stay<br>
airborne for eight hours, running off two engines.)<br><br>
Appendix 2: Big Bird<br>
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------<br><br>
The Satellite<br><br>
Big Bird was a 'low altitude surveillance platform' (LASP), the main US
spysat<br>
during the 1970s. The core of the Lockheed-built satellite was a
large<br>
Cassegrain telescope with a 2.4 m (8 ft) focal length. Behind the
telescope<br>
itself were two cameras: a KH7 Eastman Kodak one for photographing large
areas,<br>
and a Perkin-Elmer high resolution camera for detail (0.3 m resolution
from 160<br>
miles up, allegedly). Big Bird was basically a cylinder about 15.2 m long
and<br>
3.05 m in diameter, and weighed about 8,165 kg. Power came from two large
solar<br>
arrays, and a fat battery for darkside work; a 6 m extendable antenna
allowed<br>
it to communicate with its controllers. Big Bird was manoeuverable too:
it<br>
carried a restartable liquid propellant engine, which was periodically
refired<br>
to keep the thing in orbit.<br><br>
Big Bird could also carry another satellite as piggy-back, usually an
ELINT<br>
electronic warfare one which would be sent into a higher orbit of its
own.<br>
Carrying another satellite would bump Big Bird's weight up to at least
11,000<br>
kg or so.<br><br>
The first Big Bird was launched on 15 June 1971 from Point Arguello
at<br>
Vandenberg AFB. The last one was launched in 1984.<br><br>
Big Bird 16<br><br>
This one was launched from Vandenberg AFB on top of a Titan 3D rocket at
10.48<br>
am local time (18.48 GMT) on Wednesday 18 June 1980. The satellite went
into a<br>
96.46% orbit (as determined by the Royal Aeronautical Establishment the
day<br>
after its launch), which is a polar one typical of spy satellites;
the<br>
satellite orbits the poles while the Earth slowly revolves beneath it,
allowing<br>
the satellite coverage over the whole of the Earth's surface. The orbit
was<br>
also extremely low - only 265 km up at its highest altitude - again
typical of<br>
spysats, as the lower the camera the better the pictures. Such a low
orbit<br>
necessitated a fast orbit speed (Big Bird 16 circled the Earth every
88.87<br>
minutes), and had the effect of substantially limiting the satellite's
life, as<br>
at that altitude it was only a matter of time before the drag of the
atmosphere<br>
sucked it back towards Earth. Even with a booster engine on board Big
Birds<br>
could only stay up for about six months or so.<br><br>
Like all satellites, Big Bird 16's orbit was elliptical, although only
slightly<br>
so in Big Bird's case, its orbital eccentricity being 0.007,
essentially<br>
circular. However, Big Bird 16 definitely did have a lowest point of
approach<br>
to Earth (169 km at its lowest, rather than 265 km at its highest) and it
would<br>
make sense to collect a dropped film capsule on its low pass rather than
a<br>
higher one. This lowest point is known as the 'argument of perigee'; for
Big<br>
Bird 16 it was 145%, which translates as a latitude of 35% north, with
the<br>
satellite on its southward pass.<br><br>
Big Bird 16 was &quot;de-orbited&quot; on 6 March 1981 after 261 days in
orbit. Instead<br>
of allowing it to re-enter the atmosphere, with the possibility that
would<br>
bring of bits of Big Bird falling to the ground anywhere the Soviets
might pick<br>
them up, the USAF controllers detonated an on-board explosive.<br><br>
Note on designation<br><br>
The launch on 18 June 1980 is generally recognised to be that of the
sixteenth<br>
Big Bird. Jane's however designates it as Big Bird 15, not recognising a
1977<br>
launch as being a Big Bird one.<br><br>
The international designation for Big Bird 16's launch is 1980-52 A,
which is<br>
how it is identified in the Royal Aeronautical Establishment's satellite
orbit<br>
tables.<br><br>
The film capsules<br><br>
Big Bird 16 carried six recoverable film capsules, each with its own
de-orbit<br>
engine. Over the course of its six month life, BB 16 dropped all of
these, and<br>
the core of this theory is that such a film capsule was dropped on the
night of<br>
27/28 December 1980. The precise structure of a film pod is still
classified,<br>
as far as I am aware, but it is still possible to reason out what it
would have<br>
been like. A film capsule would have contained:<br><br>
1 a solid fuel de-orbit engine. Solid fuel allows a design with as few
moving<br>
parts as possible. The engine ejected before the capsule re-entered the
Earth's<br>
atmosphere.<br><br>
2 drogue and main parachutes and cords, which would have taken up most of
the<br>
bulk of the capsule. When (if) the capsule lands in the sea, explosive
bolts<br>
would fire to eject the parachutes and so prevent the capsule from
being<br>
dragged underwater by current.<br><br>
3 a barometric pressure gauge, to begin parachute deployment at the
right<br>
altitude, and to eject the parachute again if necessary before hitting
the<br>
water.<br><br>
4 a telemetry beacon, keeping in radio contact with the ground
crew.<br><br>
5 possibly a more basic radio beacon too, sending out simple pulses, so
the<br>
capsule can be located if the telemetry link is broken, and to guide
the<br>
aircraft in to its general position at night.<br><br>
6 a massively powerful light, so that the aircrew can home in on the
capsule<br>
during a night pick-up, and for the helicopters to locate it in the sea
if the<br>
Hercules fail.<br><br>
7 a battery to run all of this equipment.<br><br>
8 a solidly-built heat shield, which would also eject should the capsule
hit<br>
water.<br><br>
9 possibly some sort of self-righting equipment (balloons or floats) if
it hits<br>
water.<br><br>
10 and, of course, the exposed film itself.<br><br>
All of this is based on what is known about other American capsule
recoveries,<br>
such as Discovery, the space shuttle solid fuel rocket boosters or the
Apollo<br>
missions (see Satellite Recoveries). It's clear that the term 'film
capsule'<br>
applies to a fairly large and expensive piece of kit.<br><br>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbs
p;
(See BIG_BIRD.GIF for a Map of the situation)<br><br>
Appendix 3: Satellite Recoveries<br>
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------<br><br>
The vast majority of satellites which re-enter the earth's atmosphere
burn up,<br>
of course. However, ground controllers occasionally want to recover them
for<br>
reasons of cost, military security, or for the simple fact that humans
are on<br>
board; and for these reasons satellite recovery has become an important
part of<br>
space technology.<br><br>
Discoverer<br><br>
Discoverer 2 (1959) was the first recoverable space capsule launched,
but<br>
errors caused by ground control meant that it crashed into ice near<br>
Spitzbergen. This was only the first of many such failures. Discoverer
13<br>
almost made it: circling U2 spyplanes and radar aircraft tracked it on
its way<br>
down through the atmosphere, but the mid-air retrieval failed, and it
landed in<br>
the sea. On 18 August 1960 Discoverer 14 was launched, and was
later<br>
successfully snatched in mid-air by a C-119 skimming across the top of
its<br>
parachute and catching the capsule by a line stretched from the cargo
door.<br>
(The pilot was awarded the DFC for this, and the capsule was put on
display in<br>
a museum.)<br><br>
The USAF was eager to perfect this technique at night, and over the
course of<br>
time the Americans put brilliant strobe-lights and telemetry packages
on<br>
Discoverers.<br><br>
However the overall success rate was not improving, and the adverse
comment<br>
attracted by continuing failures led the military to classify all its
satellite<br>
launches from 1961 onwards.<br><br>
Originally the capsules were collected by ship if the mid-air pick-ups
failed.<br>
The last three ships were retired in 1974, and helicopters have been used
since<br>
then.<br><br>
Space shuttle rocket boosters<br><br>
Few civilian space objects are designed to be retrieved, but one example
is the<br>
pair of rocket boosters which help the shuttle for the first few seconds
of its<br>
launch. (It was an O-ring failure on one of these boosters which caused
the<br>
Challenger explosion in 1986). Once ejected from the ascending shuttle,
the<br>
boosters reach 4650 km/h before being slowed by atmospheric drag. A
barometric<br>
switch deploys the pilot parachute at an altitude of 4,694 m, and then
the<br>
drogue follows; the main parachutes come on at 2,012 m, slowing the
booster's<br>
fall to about 376 km/m (about 233 mph). They only fully inflate at 670 m
and<br>
the vehicle decelerates to 111 km/h (69 mph) before hitting the water.
On<br>
splashdown an impact switch separates the parachutes so that the booster
is not<br>
dragged underwater. The space shuttle boosters are of course far too
large for<br>
a mid-air recovery to be contemplated.<br><br>
Soviet recoveries<br><br>
Russian Cosmos satellites of the early 1980s were often low altitude
spysats<br>
like Big Bird, although of a much simpler design (see Soviet satellites),
and<br>
they too were expected to re-enter and be recovered. The Soviets,
however,<br>
relied on land recovery. C1227, for instance, re-entered at the same time
as<br>
the Rendlesham Forest incident, landing by parachute in Kazakhstan on
28<br>
December 1980, and emitting a &quot;two-tone&quot; recovery beacon so
that the Russian<br>
military could find it (ie. alternately transmitting a brief signal on
two<br>
separate frequencies). More advanced satellites sent telemetry. Most
Russian<br>
military satellites, however, were detonated at the end of their missions
so<br>
none of it could be recovered by the West.<br><br>
In October 1976 a Soyuz manned capsule accidentally landed in Lake
Tengiz. &quot;The<br>
main parachute dragged the capsule over the water for some time.
Some<br>
electrical connectors corroded in the salty water of Lake Tengiz and
the<br>
reserve parachute was deployed due to an electrical short. This
reserve<br>
parachute became filled with water and sunk to the bottom of the lake.
Had the<br>
lake not been shallow the reserve parachute may have pulled the capsule
below<br>
the water...&quot; (Haeseler 1995). The two cosmonauts were eventually
rescued after<br>
11 hours in the airtight capsule.<br><br>
<br>
Appendix 4:&nbsp; RAF Woodbridge and Bentwaters<br>
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------<br><br>
Woodbridge<br><br>
RAF Woodbridge opened in 1943, as one of three airfields set up to
accept<br>
damaged or fuel-short bombers returning from raids over Germany, and
were<br>
therefore fitted with long, heavy-duty runways. Woodbridge was chosen as
the<br>
site for one of these as it was &quot;nearly fog free and had no
obstructions for<br>
miles&quot; (Bowyer 1979), although more than a million trees had to be
cleared from<br>
Rendlesham Forest to take the new base.<br><br>
After the end of the War it was used for experimental work: Lancasters
based<br>
there dropped 'Grand Slam' bombs on Orford Ness, and the Blind
Landing<br>
Experiment Unit was located there. The RAF abandoned Woodbridge in March
1948.<br><br>
On 5 June 1952 the USAF took it over for the home of the 79th
Fighter-Bomber<br>
Squadron, flying first F-84s, then F-100s. In 1958 the 81st Tactical
Fighter<br>
Wing moved in and upgraded the runway to take F-101 Voodoos, Phantoms
(from<br>
1966) and F-4Ds (from 1969). At the end of 1969 the 79th Tactical
Fighter<br>
Squadron (as the 79th was now known) moved to Upper Heyford, and the 67th
ARRS<br>
flew in from Moron AFB in Spain.<br><br>
Bentwaters<br><br>
RAF Bentwaters, only a few miles from Woodbridge and essentially part of
the<br>
same complex, opened in 1944 and was transferred to the USAF in July
1950,<br>
becoming the first base in Europe to receive F-86 Sabres. Phantoms turned
up in<br>
1965 and F-4Ds by 1973; by the autumn of 1978 it was the main European
base for<br>
A-10s. Bentwaters at the time of the Rendlesham Forest incident was
occupied by<br>
the 81st Tactical Fighter Wing's 91st and 92nd Squadrons.<br><br>
Appendix 5: A Soviet Satellite Crash?<br>
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------<br><br>
The possibility of the Americans stealing a Russian satellite has already
been<br>
suggested as an explanation for Rendlesham Forest. Jenny Randles
speculates<br>
that the USAF could have 'guided down' a Soviet satellite from its
orbit,<br>
perhaps one with a 'nuclear engine', which would be enough of a secret
for the<br>
Americans to concoct a UFO cover story. The fact that a Russian satellite
did<br>
re-enter on the night of 27/28 December 1980 seems to support this.
However, I<br>
think enough is known about the Russian satellites at the time to rule
this<br>
out.<br><br>
There were only two Russian satellites in orbit at the time which could
be<br>
serious contenders, C1227 and C749.<br><br>
Cosmos 1227<br><br>
C1227 was a third generation photo reconnaissance spysat, designed to
take high<br>
resolution photographs of a single area, and was essentially a<br>
spherical-cylindrical shape, weighing about 5,900 kg or so. It was
launched<br>
from Plesetsk in NE USSR on an A-2 launcher on Tuesday 16 December 1980,
at<br>
3.15 pm local time (12.15 GMT), and was put into a standard low-level
polar<br>
spysat orbit, like Big Bird.<br><br>
C1227 had a much shorter life span, however. Like all third generation
Russian<br>
spysats, it was designed to stay up for only 13-14 days or so. (For this
reason<br>
the USSR needed to launch dozens of satellites to offer permanent
coverage - 34<br>
were launched in 1980 alone.) Once in a 350 x 420 km orbit it only
needed<br>
eleven days in which to cover the whole of the earth's surface in 2%
wide<br>
strips. C1227 lasted 11.8 days, in fact; it re-entered at 7.00 GMT on
Sunday 28<br>
December, and landed in Kazakhstan.<br><br>
Are the Americans likely to have tried to capture it?<br><br>
No. A cheap expendable capsule like C1227 would not have been worth the
bother.<br>
It certainly would not have had a 'nuclear engine', as the Russians would
not<br>
have needed to go to the trouble of putting one on board if they knew it
would<br>
be coming back down in eleven days or so. Third generation spysats did
not even<br>
have solar arrays, as they could happily run off a battery for the short
time<br>
they were in orbit. Nuclear fuels are used only rarely in satellites,
and<br>
certainly not for anything which even has a slim chance of coming back
into the<br>
earth's atmosphere.<br><br>
Moreover, if we are to believe that the US did successfully capture a
satellite<br>
from its orbit, then we would expect the Soviets to freeze their
launch<br>
programme until they figured out a way of combating this threat. But the
Cosmos<br>
launches carry on as normal after C1227, implying that nothing odd had
happened<br>
at all. And, despite all the revelations of the USSR's space launches
which<br>
have emerged since 1989, nothing has appeared about a 'stolen'
satellite.<br><br>
Finally, a 7.00 GMT re-entry time is a bit late for an event supposed to
have<br>
occurred around midnight.<br><br>
Cosmos 749 C-1 upper stage<br><br>
C749, on the other hand, was a much better piece of kit. This was a small
ELINT<br>
(electronic intelligence) satellite, only weighing 2,200 kg or so, and
had been<br>
launched on top of a C-1 booster from Plesetsk years previously, on 4
July<br>
1975. C749's orbit was higher and lasted longer: 1,911 days, according to
the<br>
RAE satellite tables. On the other hand, C749 was not heat-shielded, and
would<br>
have burnt up in the upper atmosphere had it not already been detonated
by its<br>
ground controllers on 26 September 1980.<br><br>
The important thing about C749, from the Rendlesham Forest point of view,
was<br>
its upper stage booster, the part of the C-1 rocket which had put it into
its<br>
final orbit. Instead of falling back into the atmosphere as intended, the
upper<br>
stage went into orbit on its own, even being given an international
satellite<br>
designation number (1975-62 B). The lifetime of the upper stage lasted
2,001.84<br>
days, only decaying on 25 December 1980.<br><br>
It is this decay which has caused much speculation. The RAE tables
comment that<br>
it was &quot;observed over Sussex, England&quot;, and Jenny Randles in
Sky Crash states<br>
that its break-up was seen over the Thames estuary. Randles wonders
whether US<br>
helicopters picked it up from the sea, then accidentally dropped it over
the<br>
forest, causing all the panic.<br><br>
But it must be stressed that the 25th December re-entry was not of a
satellite,<br>
only a charred piece of upper stage rocket, barely a cylinder of metal,
surely<br>
not worth the effort. And there is no suggestion of the 67th guiding the
thing<br>
back; the upper stage was free-falling.<br><br>
Could anyone steal a satellite from its orbit, anyway?<br><br>
How likely is it that the Americans had the technology in 1980 to 'steal'
a<br>
foreign, orbiting satellite, and to guide it back to earth? Admittedly
they<br>
knew precisely what was up there, and what orbits satellites were in, as
in<br>
1980 the 'Spacetrack' system at NORAD headquarters in the Cheyenne
Mountains<br>
was working well, making thousands of satellite observations a day,
logging<br>
decay and predicting re-entry. And both sides collected each other's
space<br>
debris whenever possible - hence the necessity of blowing up redundant
military<br>
satellites while still in orbit.<br><br>
But nothing has turned up to suggest that either side could bring a force
to<br>
bear on a satellite in its orbit (or a re-entering capsule) to actively
force<br>
it down. The efforts made by the US to develop Star Wars technology as a
way of<br>
destroying satellites while still in orbit suggests that no such
system<br>
existed. And even if the US military did have such a system, would they
have<br>
aimed the incoming satellite at Suffolk? (Of course, they could have
aimed it<br>
at the North Sea, and it hit Rendlesham Forest as its back-up, but then
we are<br>
back to the Big Bird theory anyway.)<br><br>
There remains the possibility that a Russian satellite crashed onto the
end of<br>
the runway at RAF Woodbridge by accident, but this coincidence - that
a<br>
satellite should by chance fall into the hands of the only satellite
retrieval<br>
unit for thousands of miles - just beggars belief.<br><br>
