From: "Greg Sandow" <greg@gregsandow.com>
Date: Wed, 11 Dec 2002 15:34:59 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Re: Abduction eyewitnesses

Just so we all understand what's going on here....

> Let's take this back a bit to where we started.
> Greg maintains Klass's book on abductions is a
> disaster, in part at least because Klass didn't
> step outside his N Street apartment and talk to
> alleged abductees. I maintain Klass did a good
> job on abductions simply by addressing the then
> available literature (a rather smaller body of
> work than it is now).
>
> If, as an experienced journalist, I am confronted
> by a collection of preposterous claims published
> in (let's say) half a dozen or so texts, I have a
> choice: either (a) to entertain my readers with the
> loopiness I find in those pages, or (b) to ask
> myself why all this is going on and go out and do
> some field work. Klass chose the former course;
> within certain admitted limits (time, money) I
> took the second route in my own book on abductions.
> Klass was not obliged to go any further than he
> did

Translation: First you decide -- before doing any research -- that
something is nonsense. Then you can write about it without doing serious
work.

It's a nice gig, if your conscience allows it.

>. That I did was more the product of an
> incurably nosey temperament than any sense of
> obligation

Further explication of the charming principle I translated above. If you
feel "nosey," then by all means investigate. If not, sit back in your
armchair, and pontificate.

>Klass took the internal contradictions
> of abduction lore and hung them out to dry. Some
> of those contradictions were perhaps news to the
> abductologists he lampooned -- all the problems
> with hypnosis, for example. The problems remain in
> the texts he discussed, and no concessions have
> been made by abductologists, over the issues Klass
> raised, in their later productions. Another way of
> putting this would be to say: Well, gosh, yes, we
> could all be being molested nightly by aliens,
> but these clowns don't know how to make their own
> case. Klass exposed the disastrousness of the
> abductologists' own approach. His objections, and
> the respectability of his "journalistic" approach,
> stand regardless of any purported reality to the
> abduction phenomenon (zero as it may be).

This is comical. Peter talks as if he thought Klass's book was Terry
Mathieson's. Matheson, a literary theorist, set out explicitly to treat
abduction narratives as "texts." He then examined their narrative
strategies (a good literary theory term), and their internal
contradictions. He's good at it, too. That makes his book one of the
more valuable screeds by a UFO skeptic. He set clear limits, and kept
within them.

Phil did nothing of the sort. He set out to write a book about the
abduction phenomenon itself. He didn't say that he limited himself to
what's in the books. He conveyed the impression (but then doesn't he
always?) that he speaks with the voice of authority. Oh, for just a
speck of Mathieson's modesty! Certainly in person he didn't set any
limits on his purview. He never told me, "Look, all I know is what I
read." He made global statements.

So Peter -- who has now become an amusing literary theorist in his own
right -- has deconstructed Phil's text, and rebuilt it as something it
never was. All because, as he knows in his heart, he has no serious
answer for what I've been saying.

> >a much-repeated claim that 25% of abductees remember their
> abductions
> >without hypnosis. But what does this actually mean? Does it
> mean that
> >25% of abductees remember everything consciously, and never have any
> >memories amplified by hypnosis, or that 25% simply remember
> >_something_? I've never seen this written about in any detail.
>
> Take another look at Kevin Randle's book. That's
> pretty detailed, on this claim, though I will concede
> that I'd like to see a whole lot more work done on it.

But not detailed, anywhere in the book, on the scope, methods, or even
much of the data involved with the study it reports.


> And yes, you would have to interview a lot of abductees.
> However, the claim wasn't abroad when Klass wrote his
> book and, I have to say again, he was under no particular
> obligation to explore it *even had it been*. Maybe
> Unca Phil's book is the way it is because, like the rest
> of us who write books, he did actually want to finish
> it one day and see it in print. As an experienced
> journalist, Prof Bandboy ought to know the significance
> of a deadline.

Translation: If you're on deadline, you're allowed to do sloppy work.

That's not a good rule to follow in the professional journalistic world.
If Phil had followed it in his paying work for Aviation Week, they'd
have fired him. On deadlines for a daily newspaper and a weekly
magazine, I've talked to more primary sources for single article than
Klass may have done for his entire book. And it was easy to do. I picked
up the phone, and made a dozen calls between 9 AM and lunch. Phil
couldn't manage that?

Bottom line, no matter how wildly Peter may rave: When the true facts
are easy to find, there's no excuse for writing things that aren't
correct.

Greg Sandow

From: "Robert McLean" <robert.mclean2@virgin.net>
Date: Mon, 16 Dec 2002 23:31:51 -0000
Subject: Re: [UFORL] Rendlesham

Rob

Do you have a copy of Georgina Bruni's book? If so, have a look at the photo
taken from East Gate by Adrian Bustinza. Trees on both sides of the East
Gate access had road had recently been logged. Visible in the photo is a
line of mature trees on the other side of the main acess road, about 400 m
to the East of East Gate - this is the access road that comes in from the
direction of Bentwaters, and leads down to the Forestry Commission offices.

Logging was underway behind that stand of trees. There was already a large
open space behind those trees, at least 400 m deep, with no ground cover. By
late February 1981 they had finished logging to the eastern boundary of the
forest. At some point (I do not know when) those trees in Bustinza's photo
were also logged.

It is possible that the line of trees adjacent the road no longer extended
very deep. I have worked out that the old East Gate shack was within a
narrow strip (roughly 60 m wide in the north-south direction) from which a
direct view of the lighthouse would be had if there were a direct line of
sight to the eastern edge of the forest (ie about 1 km east). This can be
shown by plotting elevations vs distance on graph paper. This is quite a
coincidence, when you consider how big the forest and the Woodbridge base
are. They just happened to see a flashing light through those trees near
ground level while standing within this narrow strip where the lighthouse
could have been directly visible. When Burroughs says in his statement "We
went down east gate road and took a right at the stop sign and drove down
about 10 to 20 yards to where there is a road that goes into the forest. At
the road I could see a white light shining onto the trees" the road he
refers to was just a narrow track (they dumped stumps along this track after
logging - still there today) not to be confused with Road 12, and directly
in the middle of the narrow band in which there could have been a line of
sight to the lighthouse.

The other factors were the bright meteor just before 3 am. I have the
British Astronomical Association Meteor Section newsletter which references
this. Just two observers reported the meteor, but there is no information
regarding where the observers were or what part of the sky the meteor
crossed. I am in the process of finding out if this information exists. (I
know Ian Ridpath said it entered the atmosphere over Woodbridge, but I have
not found any basis for this.)

Jupiter and Saturn were also very close in the sky, about 1 degree apart,
and rising in the east in the early hours of the morning - a possible source
of the steady "blue" lights.

Best regards
Robert McLean

Squadron [ARRS] and they have refuted any connection.
There were statedly no helicopters from the 67th ARRS in
operation during our late December 1980 'UFO' incidents.

Indeed, Halt commented on this during one of those
pivotal 1997 'on-line' interviews with Salley Rayl:

RAYL: ...What type of aircraft were at the base at that
time and were there any in the air at that time?

[...]

HALT: There were approximately 120 to 125 A-10s. There
were I'm trying to think, about 12, 14 C-130s, several H-
3s it was in a rescue squadron, plus the A-10 squadrons.
The A-10 squadrons were done for the holidays. Not
flying, doing any night flying. The rescue squadron was
done. In fact, the rescue commander at that time, a good
personal friend of mine, really chastised me for not
calling him immediately, cause he said I could have
gotten a chopper in the air within an hour or two. I kind
of don't believe that because, you know, you'd have
trouble finding a crew and get one free-flighted, but
there was no aircraft activity. In fact, the tower at
Woodbridge was down.

RAYL: Well, it was Christmas time, too.

HALT: Yeah. It was Christmas time. In fact, the tower at
Bentwaters was manned only for an emergency. In other
words, there was a standby crew up there, but it was not
active.

RAYL: So, there were no jets, helicopters or any other
aircraft, American aircraft, that were scrambled at that
time.

HALT: There were none that were scrambled from
Bentwaters, and I knew of nothing in the air at that
time.
[END]


It was pointed out to myself by Chuck Dalldorf:

I was an aircraft maintenance technician with the 81st
TFW working on A-10A and prior to that F-4D's during my
tour which lasted from December 1977 through July 1981.
I had also been assigned several times to the 67th ARRS
on temporary duty to work on both the HC-130N/P's and the
HH-53's as well.

[...]

There were no alerts anytime during the week between
Christmas, 1980 and New Years Day 1981 at RAF Bentwaters
or RAF Woodbridge. No alerts for the 81st Tactical
Fighter Wing (A-10A) or for the 67th ARRS (HC-130 and HH-
53).

As a matter of fact, traditionally we had always been
able to get a few extra, non-leave days off over the
holiday week, at least in aircraft maintenance. We would
split the time off between the married people who
generally wanted the period including Christmas off to be
with family, and then the single GI's who generally
wanted the period including New Years off. I don't have
a 1980 calendar available, however, depending on when
Christmas Day and New Years Day fell, it would have been
something like this:

Let's say Christmas Day and New Years Day fell on a
Saturday. People who wanted to be off for Christmas would
start their unofficial vacation on Friday morning and be
off with no obligation through to the following Wednesday
morning (coming back to work that day). People opting
for New Years would then take Wednesday through to the
following Monday off (coming back to work that Monday
morning). While you were off, you were not on call and
had no obligations. Unless the base was called on alert,
then all deals were off and everyone reports.

There was a trip that I helped run with my landlord, Joe
Haninia of Woodbridge Town who ran a travel service for
the base called Big Ben Travel. The trip went from RAF
Bentwaters to Edinburgh to celebrate Hogmanay in
Scotland. We left the base and were not recalled. There
were 28 people on the trip from both the 81st TFW and the
67th ARRS.

The week I worked I was at the RAF Woodbridge shop and it
was a very quiet week. Some delayed maintenance (there
were few if any flying hours going on). It was a good
time to take care of paperwork, make sure there was
training going on, etc. I was an E-5, Staff Sgt. at the
time.
[END]

Hi James,

Thanks for a refreshing, non-conspiratorial post on the Rendlesham
incident. You have dealt with each 'theory' and explained quite
cogently why none stand up to critical scrutiny.

It seems to me that people are desperate to salvage something from
the story, almost as a reaction to the amount of effort and verbiage
that has been invested in it over the years. It's a reaction well
known in the sociology of cult belief -- that disconfirmation of a
strongly held belief can actually lead to it being strengthened. It's
a similar reaction to the Government denying a rumour -- all it
does is strengthen the conviction of the conspiratorial-minded that
 the story is true.

What Rendlesham amounts to is a group of US airmen seeing
strange lights in the forest. Actually, people have been reporting
strange lights in the Suffolk countryside for centuries (check out
local folklore). This one got lots of attention because these were
'military types' therefore there must be some form of conspiracy
behind it (crashed saucer, nefarious experiments, recovery of
satellites, blah di blah).

I think this says more about UFOlogy and conspiracy theory than
it says about what actually happened -- which seems to be what
many of the 'witnesses' are saying, if you read behind the lines.

Rob

The lighthouse is very bright on a dark night when you have a direct view of
it.

The trees at the eastern edge of the forest were planted in straight rows
running east-west. PC Dave King described to me the view he had of the
lighthouse through the trees, due east of East Gate. He remembers seeing the
lighthouse flash while looking down long rows of the trees. However, it
seems he was taken to a portion of the forest different from that where
Burroughs, Penniston and Cabansag had their experience, and this could
explain why he never met up with anyone else after having been taken out
there by the airmen.

Col Halt says on the Halt Tape that the branches that seemed to have been
broken were small branches about an inch or less in diameter, about "15 to
20 feet up".

The Corsican Pines at the supposed location, due east of East Gate near the
eastern edge of the forest, were 60 years old. Such trees are about 70 feet
tall, and when growing closly in the forest plantation do not have any
branches other than the odd broken, rotten stub at such a low height. Live
branches are more like 40 to 60 feet up. The stand of trees Halt was in was
therefore much younger.

If you have a good look at Gulyas's photos of the landing site in You Can't
Tell the people, you'll see:

- that the trees are not planted in rows
- that the trees appear to be a lot shorter than 60 year old Corsican Pines
- that some trees are quite close together - not thinned out and managed

I believe the location Halt investigated was about 500 m south east of the
generally accepted location. This is small privately owned patch of pine
trees, which has never been well managed. There is no direct view of the
lighthouse there (which is why it took so long for Halt's party to spot the
flashing light), but it is close (within 100 m) to the paved road that runs
through Capel Green. BCP were probably startled by vehicle lights coming
through the trees, when they didn't know there was a nearby road.

If I am right, then Col Halt's party initially spotted the faint flashing
glow in the sky from the Shipwash lightship, and followed this into the
field south of Oak Wood. The field initialy slopes uphill, and as they got
to the crest, the flashing would have got brighter, until they got a direct
view of the lightship. At that point they were surprised by the light from
Orfordness coming through the south east corner of Oak Wood. This is
supported by the Halt Tape, because there comes a point when they spot a
second light "at 11 o'clock" (actually 15 degrees apart). The "throwing off
sparks" arrises because the lighthouse and lightship appear to be somewhat
synchronised:

Shipwash cycle was: flash/ 2.5 s interval/ flash/ 2.5 s interval/ flash/ 15
s gap [repeat]

Orfordness is: flash/ 5 s interval/ flash

So flashes of one would have appeared to have been correlated with flashes
of the other - no wonder they were confused!

The relevant extract of the Halt Tape is:

----------------------

HALT: It's coming this way. It is definitely coming this way.



<BREAK>



VOICE: Pieces are shooting . . .



HALT: Pieces of it are shooting off.



ENGLUND: At 11 o-clock.



HALT: There is no doubt about it. This is weird!



<BREAK>




BALL: Look to the left.
VOICE: Yeah, definitely...



BALL: Look to the left.



BALL: Two. Two lights.



HALT: (Whispering) Go ahead.



BALL: One light to the right . . .



HALT: (Whispering) Hey.



BALL: . . .and one light to the left.



HALT: (Whispering) Keep the flashlights off.



HALT: There's something very, very strange.



<BREAK>



HALT: Check the headset out, and see if it gets any stronger. OK, give us,
give us your...



VOICE 2: Make a notation that this is on a beta reading too.
HALT: It's on a beta reading?


----------------

After losing sight of Orfordness lighthouse and Shipwash lightship, Halt
spotted Shipwash again in the "second farmer's field" at 115 degrees
magnetic:

HALT: At two forty-four [2:44 am], we're at the far side of the farmer's . .
. the second farmer's field and made sighting again about 110 degrees. This
looks like it's clear off to the coast. It's right on the horizon. Moves
about a bit and flashes from time to time. Still steady or red in color.


By this point, he must have realised it was manmade light.

So Halt is truthful in saying that he saw the "lighthouse" to the right of
the UFO (ie Orfordness), and that the "lighthouse" was visible "the whole
time".

From: "Jenny Randles" <nufon@currantbun.com>
Date: Thu, 19 Dec 2002 14:54:59 -0000
Subject: Re: [UFORL] Rendlesham

Hi,

It seems a little patronising to read suggestions that because of the
sociology of conspiracy theory, or whatever, it is evident that some of us
(presumably myself included) are desperate to want to believe that something
strange occurred in Rendlesham Forest. IOW that we do so for reasons
unconnected with the evidence itself and because we have a need to
perpetuate mystery.

Humans certainly do prefer mystery to explanations but my view of most
serious UFOlogists is that they are driven by the evidence and would not
deny that just to cling on to some myth. I agree that many people
peripherally interested in UFOlogy might not really look for solutions
to spoil the fun because it is the thrill of the unknown that creates their
interest.
But serious UFOlogists are characterised by a quest for answers and usually
go where the evidence trail leads - at least they do in my experience.

The truth is that I dont know what happened in Rendlesham Forest and dont
have a motivation
for it to be either strange or ultimately simple. It has certainly
unravelled
towards being more mundane than profound and continues to unwind as each new
fact emerges. But the truth remains contradictory and uncertain with some
areas of
legitimate doubt over interpretation.

I will accept whatever the collective facts ultimately decree - if indeed
they ever allow for more than reasoned guesswork - which is often how UFO
cases end up. But doing that, I feel, is an objective approach and I find it
a little odd that if you are unwilling to say now that this case is a dead
duck that this somehow implies that you are under the influence of nefarious
sociological forces . Rather - I would suggest - you are
just being cautious about the nature of a confusing case where
nobody has anything other than a personal take on what might have happened.

Of course, it is evident that there are elements of misperception and human
psychology involved in this case as there are with every sighting. This has
helped it to become clarified by the passage of time. But such personal
elements apply equally well from a skeptical perspective, I suspect.

However, my remaining concerns over the evidence here and my reasons for not
simply yet accepting that it was all a collection of well resolved and in of
themselves non strange elements have nothing to do with my being involved in
this case since l981 or needing to preserve it in amber in some way. If I
was logically satisfied that it was totally resolved then I would be
delighted to say so.

Thats true, for example, with the Peter Day movie film case (see 'The UFOs
that Never Were') - which I spent many years investigating, gradually
piecing together the evidence and being led inexorably toward the conclusion
that
this case is solved. And that is despite the fact that I came to like the
primary witness, that he profoundly disagrees (as do some of the others) and
that to accept this case as closed has put me in conflict with these people.
Peter Day in particular seemed to think that I had betrayed him by accepting
a prosaic explanation. But it is how the facts panned out and I could not
simply hold onto any stranger opinion (eg that the UFO was some kind of
UAP - possibly ball lightning - as I once had thought possible) because the
evidence did
not honestly allow for that IMO.

And, indeed, the word opinion is the key. We all make honest value
judgements of the evidence and ought to respect the thinking of others when
they do the same - even if in doing so they oppose our own assessment.

I have had more than a little flak from UFOlogists and witnesses over my
persusion that the Jan l995 British Airways sighting over Derbyshire is not
a major case but (like the Chiles-Whitted case which it so closely
resembles) a misperception of a bolide. I reach that conclusion because it
is where the weight of evidence seems to take you. But it is just
in my opinion once again. I well know that others disagree and thats fair
enough. They may be right. I may be wrong. I just do not happen to think
that they
are. But I certainly doubt that they evaluate the case differently from me
out of some sort of sociological motive that thereby devalues their opinion.
They simply read the evidence in a different manner, because UFO evidence is
wont to be open to various possible interpretations.

If I was sure that Rendlesham was now completely resolved I would have no
hesitation in saying so. However, the evidence points towards parts of it
being clearly resolved and other parts having at present what we might term
a possible
resolution. There remain issues that leave me feeling ghe need to keep an
open mind
- for instance, the reports of the apparent
electrostatic field seemingly described by Burroughs and Pennistone. These
seem
difficult to ascribe merely to stress - especially given their comoarison
with other close encojnter cases - although, I agree, it is not
impossible to do so.

But in the least that is one legitimate reason to hesitate before saying
this case is done and dusted. Although it certainly 'has' had a coat of
Pledge applied!
It may be that the evidence will, as with these other cases, ultimately lead
one to accept that Rendlesham is fully resolved - in the same way as I
think Roswell probably will prove to have been. And I certainly very much
doubt that Rendlesham involves anything particularly bizarre come what may
and certainly
not alien in origin. But right now there are sufficient reasons to at least
suspect that there could be more to the evidence than we know. And that
hestitation
is because of the facts of the case not some inner need to retain mystery.

Debate, such as on this list, is healthy and proper. But why can we not
accept that until a case is resolved to the satisfaction of any sane and
objective UFOlogist that there
will necessarily be a range of opinions - all potentially valid - as to what
might have happened? Is it really necessary to infer that if someone
disagrees with our own conclusion that they have
psychological or sociological motives ? Can they not simply have
interpreted the facts
in a different way?


Best wishes,

Jenny Randles

Jenny writes that:

So it's OK to say exactly what I had said as long as:

a) we don't use social science terminology (sociology, rumour, etc) and

b) we don't apply this rule to "serious UFOlogists" who are elevated above
those lesser mortals who are only "peripherally interested in UFOlogy".

Why is it "patronising" to suggest that it is only human nature to want to
believe something strange happened in Rendlesham forest?

And equally that 'UFOlogists' however detached they claim to be can and do
perpetuate ambiguity and mystery, often without realising they are
doing so.

This is hardly 'sociology of conspiracy theory', but common sense and
has been remarked upon many times by commentators who are outside of
the UFOlogical goldfish bowl and hence more likely to be objective.

I must confess I had to stifle a laugh when I read Jenny's claim that
"serious UFOlogists are characterised by a quest for answers and
usually go where the evidence trail leads."

Has Jenny read Jim Moseley's 'Confessions of a Grave-Robbing UFOlogist"
and taken note of his definition of 'serious UFOlogists' ?

Anyhow, I digress.
My post corrected innacurate statements (for example the claimed lack of
USAF officers in the MATO team which 'confiscated' the
radar tapes) based upon a mis-reading of material that has been published.
It is from mis-readings and misinterpretations such as this that
'serious UFOlogists' construct mountains out of molehills.

Jenny makes much of the 'mysterious visitors to Rendlesham forest' in
late December 1980 who are inferred to be British MoD people, but cannot
provide us with anything more solid that anecdotal evidence from
"farmers, foresters etc."

That is what I meant by perpetuating mystery, and I have yet to see anything
more definite from Jenny to make me change my mind.

However our opinions may differ on the nature of what happened, I agree
that something 'strange' certainly did happen in Rendlesham forest,
December 1980!

But human nature - and the will to believe - is often the *strangest*
phenomenon of all.

>
> Debate, such as on this list, is healthy and proper. But why can we not
> accept that until a case is resolved to the satisfaction of any sane and
> objective UFOlogist that there
> will necessarily be a range of opinions - all potentially valid - as to
what
> might have happened? Is it really necessary to infer that if someone

> psychological or sociological motives ? Can they not simply have

> in a different way?

How many cases are ever "resolved to the satisfaction of any sane
and objective UFOlogist" ?

Who defines or decides who is a serious UFOlogist and who isn't?
Based upon what criteria?

After all there are still "serious UFOlogits" (I
take it we are using Jim Moseley's definition) who believe that Thomas
Mantell died at the hands of an 'alien' UFO.

As for opinions, of course everyone has the right to hold and express
opinions -- but it is simply nonsense to claim, as Jenny does, that *all*
opinions are "potentially valid", especially where these are based
upon defective and anecdotal information from second, third and
fourth hand sources.
To the contrary, I would point to that old journalistic maxim, which has
served me well:

"Opinions are free, but facts are sacred."


With best wishes,

Dave Clarke

Dear Linda,

Regarding the purported Ministry of Defence [MoD]
document publicised at:

http://www.earthfiles.com

under the heading...

"December 9, 2002 - Update on British Rendlesham UFO
Incident from a U.S. Air Force Eyewitness. Click report

This document was known to be a hoax over 15 years ago
and is highlighted in 'Skycrash', by Jenny Randles,
Brenda Butler and Dot Street.

Therein, Jenny wrote:

"This anonymous memo was sent, as a photocopy to the
research team in early 1994, obviously as an indented
'real' leaked document [if it was a genuine 'leak', then
hardly likely to masquerade as something released under
the US FOIA with blanked-out segments - James].

We have investigated it... and our conclusion is that it
is a deliberate fake by certain parties, whose identities
are strongly suspected by us.

There are a number of valid reasons for believing that
this is a hoax.

For one thing, the MoD letter-head is of a style not used
on public letters until late 1983.

[...]

On 19 June, 1984, after several attempts, Andrew
Mathewson, new head of DS8 at the MoD, wrote to Harry
Harris, calling the memo 'very interesting' but adding 'I
have to say it is a forgery and probably intended as a
joke'.

This hoax has clearly been planned to test us, or more
likely, to impugn our credibility should we fall for the
trick. We call their bluff".
[END OF EXTRACT]


It's a pity that so many years afterwards, someone has
still fallen for it.


At the time this bogus photocopy was sent to Jenny and
Co., there was still considerable confusion about the
dating of any 'UFO' incidents and no surprise that we now
understand said memo ridiculously dates an 'acknowledged
alien spaceship landing' as occurring two nights later
than factual misconstrued events it professes were
'covered-up'.

"Not long after midnight on December 26, Sgt. Penniston
was asked to investigate odd lights seen moving in the
Rendlesham forest between Bentwaters and Woodbridge.
Joining him was USAF Airman First Class John Burroughs
and several other security and military personnel".

As Penniston should confirm, aside from Burroughs, the
only other person directly involved was Airman Ed
Cabansag - not 'several others'.


It was John Burroughs who alerted myself to the
'earthfiles' allegations.


Penniston reportedly claims:

"The patrolman who was with me was John Burroughs. He has
worked the law enforcement side. In fact, he had worked
directly for Bud Stefans, but he was one of the guys who
went out there with me.

Q: SO, IS HE THE ONLY ONE WITH YOU?

Well, immediately next to me at 10 feet, yes. We, of
course, we had another one back about 100 meters and
there were others back at a logging road. Of course,
there were several people at the East Gate. And all of
this was observed from Bentwaters, too".
[END]
It's long been established that SSgt Bud Steffans [sic] -
who was on patrol with Burroughs remained back at 'east
gate'. There were never 'several people'.

How could there be?

It was Burroughs and Steffan's patrol - checking out an
isolated post - which first reported 'unfamiliar lights',
seemingly within Rendlesham forest.

Penniston and Cabansag responded to the report and
consequently Burroughs, Cabansag and Penniston [BC&P]
received permission to investigate further, leaving
Steffans back at east agate.


There were never 'others' back at the logging road which
BC&P followed into the forest - it was only MSgt
Chandler, who subsequently arrived after hearing the
radio communications.

For verification, see Penniston's previous - quite
different - claims and further, factual, background, at:

http://www.rendlesham.com/

The huge discrepancies with Penniston's seemingly ever
elaborate story are evidenced therein.


Meanwhile, Burroughs still maintains, as he always has,
that they never encountered anything more enigmatic than
'unusual lights'.

He also acknowledges that the three man patrol ultimately
travelled for some two miles before realising one source
of lights they had pursued was a coastal lighthouse.

As for Penniston's infinitely more convoluted tale,
Burroughs concludes that 'Jim' has been "heavily
influenced" by subsequent 'hypnotic regression'.

As I'm not championing a classic 'ET landing and
nefarious secret government cover up' assertion, I have
no dilemma concerning such widely divergent witness
testimony.

However, I certainly wouldn't promote such claims until I
had resolved the manifest contradictions.


The inherent explanation will perhaps be self-evident to

From: "David Clarke" <cd292@crazydiamonds.fsnet.co.uk>
Date: Sun, 22 Dec 2002 16:13:59 -0000
Subject: Re: [UFORL] Rendlesham

Tim Printy wrote:

>I do believe there was a somewhat negative (and perhaps - omigoodness -
"skeptical")
>response about David and Andy's work (Correct me if I am wrong but I think
Jenny is
>also involved) concerning the 1956 radar visual case at Lakenheath by
several prominent
>UFOlogists.

Yes, the 'serious UFOlogists' who populate UFO Updates were most concerned
that someone was looking hard and deep at one of the 'holy cows', as
Lakenheath-
Bentwaters had become.

Since the testimony of the key USAF ATC witness, Forrest Perkins, came to
light
in 1968 via the Condon report, very little follow-up investigation had been
done
on this 'classic' case. The exception was Jenny's seminal work in tracing
the
key RAF radar controller, Freddie Wimbledon, and two of the Venom
night-fighter
crews, who were involved in the 'interception' part. Over the past two
years,
with a lot of luck and help from many different sources, we have been able
to
piece together what really happened - a story which is radically different
to what
has become part of the UFOlogical legend.

I've spent the best part of two years working almost exclusively on the
Lakenheath-
Bentwaters case, and related UK radar-visual incidents from the 1940s and
50s
and have to say that big question marks remain. The RAF destroyed the
majority
of their files on all these incidents in 1961, so the true sequence of
events may
never be known. But I suspect that a number of these early cases were a) the
by-products of experimentation with Electronic Counter Measures (or 'radar
spoofing'); c) natural phenomena mis-interpreted within the context of
evolving
radar technology and d) a few 'unknowns' too.

>I think there is a tie-in on how hard it is to convince "UFOlogists" that a
case is
> solved to their satisfaction to the level of notority this case has
received over the years.
>The 1956 radar case was a favorite of McDonald's so it can not be
discredited can it?

Witness the reaction of the true believers when it became known that new
evidence
had been uncovered during the re-investigation. The assumption made by Jerry
Clark and others that we had decided beforehand that the case would be
debunked
whatever the cost. In actual fact, if you read our (now very out of date)
summary
in 'Out of the Shadows' we did actually end up suspecting something unusual
did in fact happen, but that lack of data meant the case is never likely to
be
resolved.

>Isn't this one case where the Condon report suggested a "True UFO" existed?

That was Gordon Thayer's conclusion in 1968 in his report to the Condon
study.
It was good enough for McDonald, and that was good enough for Clark, and
so it goes on.
But the facts are that the case was passed to the Condon team in Feb 1968,
just months before the team were due to report, so they were unable to fully
investigate at the time. All they had were the 12-year-old memories of the
USAF ATC man at Lakenheath, plus the highly confusing teletypes from
sent by the people Lakenheath to BlueBook in 1956.
These two sources were *all* Thayer had to make his 'true UFO' conclusion:
he never made inquiries with the RAF or British MOD, who played a major
role in the incident. If he had done this in 1968 we might know a whole lot
more
about the case.
As it is, all we have to go on is a mishmash of contradictory accounts, hazy
memories and missing evidence. Rather like a huge jigsaw puzzle with all the
key pieces of the jigsaw absent.
This is the sort of palimpsest out of which 'classic UFO cases' are born.

>Based on this type of response to this case, the Mantell case, and many
others,
>I don't think it matters who solves this type of "classic" case (skeptic,
debunker,
>UFOlogist). There will always be those that state, "but this does not
explain the
>statements made by this witness".

I agree -- and the Lakenheath-Bentwaters case is a classic example. We know
that spurious responses on radar can appear as a result of a) atmospheric
phenomena and b) man-made spoofing. The UFOlogists will argue, as they
have done with the Washington DC wave, that radar operators could not
possibly have been deceived because of their 'familiarity' with these
phenomena.
Therefore estimates of speed, manoeuvrability, etc are accepted as facts
because they are made by people who we rely upon to guide our aircraft
safely around the skies. This is a familiar argument, but does not stand up
to
scrutiny.

>Perhaps I can sum this up in one simple
>statement that I think applies to most (if not all) UFO cases:
>"The longer a case becomes a "classic" or the greater the amount of
publicity
>it receives, the less likely it will be accepted by UFOlogists as solved no
matter
>what evidence is presented."

Which is precisely my point: 'UFOlogists', even serious ones, are just as
likely
to be influenced by the will to believe as anyone else. It's human nature.

Best,

Dave Clarke

"Did not notice any object at top, did not note if top of

behind the hill".

The low sun was reportedly a factor and Zamora also
noted, "Was still driving car and could not pay too much
attention to the flame".
It seems that Zamora suddenly became aware of the
descending flame and because he had to concentrate on
driving, "could not pay too much attention" to whatever
the source object was.


>c1/ When L.Z enter with his car on the gravel road, he

>can see _at high_ distance when he saw the two

If it was a hot-air balloon, those 'legs' would be the
struts supporting a platform/basket.

Strictly, Zamora did not claim to have seen "two legs",
only "what appeared to be two legs of some type from the
object to the ground".


>c2/ L.Zamora saw 2 entities but don't saw the basket.
>It's only possible if the envelope is N.E side and the
>basket S.W (masked at his view by the envelope). Is it
>logic if the wind and the balloon go to S.W ?

There wasn't necessarily a basket, possibly only a basic
platform. For example, see the contemporary, early, 1963
platform on display at the 'Musee des Balloons', Chateau
de Balleroy:

http://www.balloonlife.com/publications/balloon_life/9512
/history.htm

Zamora also confirmed that when he first viewed the
landed object from distance, it was only for a couple of
seconds and again, he didn't, "pay much attention":

"Had stopped about only a couple seconds".

"The only time I saw these two persons was when I had
stopped, for possibly two seconds or so, to glance at the
object".

"When I first saw the object (when I thought it might be
a car) I saw what appeared to be two legs of some type
from the object to the ground. At the time, I didn't pay
much attention to what it was--I thought it was an
accident--I saw the two persons. I didn't pay any
attention to the two "legs?" The two "legs" were at the
bottom of the object, slanted outwards to the ground. The
object might have been about three and a half feet from
the ground at that time. I just glanced at it".


In the book 'Socorro Saucer', author Ray Stanford, who
interviewed Zamora in the days directly afterwards, notes
that even when Zamora was later at his closest to the
object, he couldn't see all of it as the bottom was
obscured by a tall greasewood bush.

Stanford is offering an explanation why Zamora briefly
observed, "what appeared to be two legs of some type",
yet those believed 'landing marks' required four legs to
be consistent.


>d/ Are the soil traces conform with a basket which bump
>into ground ?

As I previously revealed - see:

http://www.ufoworld.co.uk/v18.txt

[BEGIN]
If it was a hot air balloon, then any landing would not
have been a 'touchdown' and the balloon's platform is
likely to have dragged along the ground, even for a short
distance.

At this time, it seems that an extremely basic,
rectangular wooden or metal platform with 'railings' was
gradually being superseded by the more familiar wicker
basket.

The 'official' case investigator was Dr J. Allen Hynek,
former Chairman of the Astronomy Department at
Northwestern University and who became a consultant for
the US Air Force's 'Project Blue Book'.

In a private memo dated 20 May, 1964, Hynek wrote that,
contrary to the landing marks being 'impressions', they
were in fact, "4 rectangular scrapings as if a
rectangular object had scraped along digging into the
ground" and that "the gouging was done away from the
center in every case".

There is a photograph, published in several books, which
shows one of the 'imprints' and the rocks which had been
placed around to protect this presumed 'trace evidence'.
As one of Richard Hall's colleagues further commented:
"It shows several small rocks protruding _in situ_ from
the crater as if they belonged there but now are exposed
-- so they could not simply have been accidentally kicked
in by investigators from the surrounding soil outside of
the landing print. These small rocks have obviously _not_
been pressed down into the bowl shape of the crater by
any 'great weight'. A 'great weight' would have pushed
the small rocks down into the soil so that their tops
would have been flush or almost flush with the contour of
the crater, and they most likely would have been crushed
or broken -- but they are not pushed down or broken. The
imprints look like they have been dug or gouged out
exactly as Hynek said, _not_ pressed down by a massive
object".

Once again, the facts are somewhat different from those
published in UFO lore.
[END OF EXTRACT]


>Precisly, has somebody a proof that a basket with

>can make this 4 imprints concordant with the mesurement

>basket ?

I haven't measured pine needles but using an AN/PDR-27 with the beta window open
usually gave some deflection on many sources such as rocks. Also, the number of
"clicks" reported by the operator don't seem to agree with his readings.&nbsp; If I
recall correctly it was a few hundreds clicks per minute that signified 0.1 mrem (this
value may be off by this is what I remember from my navy days).&nbsp; The 0.07
value should have been a lot more than a few clicks described on the tape.&nbsp;
Also, the meter movement can be affected by the operator.&nbsp; The bearings on the
meter needle were very good and just waiving the meter around would cause
deflections.&nbsp; The unit came equipped with a strap to minimize this efffect.
Considering the values described (only 7 minor units on the lowest scale which is
about a 7/50th of full scale), it is not impossible that the individuals were causing
some of the deflection while they were using it.&nbsp;

From: Vicente-Juan Ballester Olmos <ballesterolmos@yahoo.es>
Date: Tue, 31 Dec 2002 00:44:03 +0100 (CET)
Subject: [UFORL] FOTOCAT News December 2002

PROJECT FOTOCAT NEWS, December 2002

FOTOCAT is a catalog of UFO photo events which presently contains 2800
records. Managed by Vicente-Juan Ballester Olmos and owned by Fundación
Anomalía, a bilingual News report appears in
<www.anomalia.org@fotocat1.htm>, and a preliminary content report (in
Spanish) can be found in <www.anomalia.org@infofotocat.pdf>.

We continue receiving various forms of cooperation from specialists
located in many parts of the world. For example:

* Mexico is a country which has produced lots of UFO imagery. The critical
researcher Luis Ruiz Noguez, much experienced in processing photographic
cases, is assisting us by reviewing the Mexican section of FOTOCAT and
sending new cases. This help is proving to be invaluable.

* Famous US writer Ronald Story has been kind enough to donate a copy of
the CD Rom version of his huge UFO Encyclopedia, which includes a vast
number of images of unidentified flying objects.

* Thanks to Patrick Ferryn, from the serious Belgian UFO association
SOBEPS, we have received 10 years of old issues of its excellent journal
Inforespace, to complete our collection.

* Ole Henningsen, an ufologist from the Danish group SUFOI, has helped by
reviewing cases reported in Denmark.

FOTOCAT in the media
A Letter to the Editor describing the project has been published in the
Winter 2002 issue of the CUFOS International UFO Reporter as well as in
the January 2003 issue of Fortean Times (Great Britain).

Also, an interview by C. Riffo to this compiler has been released (in
Spanish) in the Terra portal:

<http://www.terra.cl/ovnis/index.cfm?id_reg=215500&pagina=entrevistas&categoria
=entrevistas>

Cases Per Country
FOTOCAT has been tallied by country, and we present the distribution of
cases for those countries contributing over 1 % of the total (28):
USA:           795 cases (almost 30% of the grand total are US cases!)
Spain:         376 cases (it represents the higher sample ever collected)
Australia:     142 cases
Argentina:     123 cases
Italy:         119 cases
France:     119 cases
Great Britain: 119 cases
Japan:         113 cases
Mexico:             112 cases
Chile:         95 cases
Poland:             67 cases
Sweden:             66 cases
Space:      55 cases (astronaut cases or footage from spacecraft)
Canada:             52 cases
Brazil:        47 cases
Switzerland: 34 cases (the effect of Billy Meier)
Germany:       32 cases
Russia:     28 cases

There are regions of the globe with a good coverage, while there are
others still poorly documented in this catalog. The process of extracting
cases from mainstream UFO journals like MUFON UFO Journal, Flying Saucer
Review, Lumières Dans La Nuit and many others will balance the equation.
We also expect that the contributions from colleagues will generate a
representative census of cases worldwide, larger than any other produced
before. When it is posted in the internet for free access, we hope it will
be a useful piece of information for students of this elusive phenomena.

Help Needed
Readers and investigators are requested to contribute lists of local cases
to FOTOCAT by writing to <fotocat@anomalia.org>. Other ways to participate
in this program are by reviewing the case lists we will produce for
specific countries on demand, with the purpose to correct dates or
location names, add the names of photographers, informing about potential
explanations, and sending information on cases unknown to us.

Vicente-Juan Ballester Olmos
Research Director, Anomaly Foundation (not-for-profit organization)
<www.anomalia.org>

There's one further aspect we can highlight which

In 'Left at East Gate', within the transcript of Halt's

see a 'UFO' himself.

Halt then describes a subsequent, reported sighting from
Senior Airman Palmer, stationed at 'east gate' and how,
alas, by the time both Halt and Williams arrived, there
was no 'UFO', per se...


Warren mentions to Halt that this was an incident
involving his colleague and friend, Steve La Plume.

Steve has been a welcome contributor to previous list
discussions and in an update, new to the list, recalls:

I know that there has been much broo ha ha over the
Christmas incident of 1980 but little has been said about
the sighting that Senior Airmen Palmer and myself had a
few weeks later.

A few things to point out is that when we saw this thing
it was like a plane or a satellite in the sky. Very far
off and basically just moving up and down kind of zig
zagging in the southern sky. It head out toward the
North Sea and we lost it behind the forest.

The thing I remember most was that once Palmer confirmed
with the tower that the only thing up were a few choppers
and a C-130, we decided to call it in because we had been
instructed to report anything like that.

Well man the shit hit the fan for Palmer and me. As soon
as he called it in the phone rang in the shack at the
East gate. Lt. Englund was there and told me to report -
which I did. He then told me to stay put and keep an eye
out. I relayed this to Palmer.

Col. Halt, the Bentwaters Deputy Base Commander showed up
- also present was a high ranking officer whom I thought
may have been his equivalent on Woodbridge with his wife
and son. No lie! I remember the Nikon camera around the
kid's neck. But mostly I remember his wife being all
excited and saying "Oh boy, maybe we get to see one" or
something very close to that.

Lt. Englund finally showed up and told me not to be
nervous but that Col. [sic - James] Williams would be
here in a minute and would ask me to report and I was to
say all safe and secure. He also informed me that the
Col was just voted a General by Congress a few days
earlier. I had just turned eighteen. (no pressure Steve
just stay calm).

After reporting they all jumped in an official Air Force
Blue with yellow lettered station wagon and headed out
toward the forest. I was baffled as to why since the
thing was miles in the sky and just went over in that
general direction. I did not protest I just let them go
and screwed around with the starlight scope we were given
to "keep an eye on things".

About an hour later they came back and went their
separate ways. Of course they posted me on the gate for
the rest of the night instead of riding around with
Palmer (who was LE [Law Enforcement - James] not
Security). My security clearance had not come in yet and
I was usually stuck giving latrine or lunch breaks to the
Lee's. Otherwise, I was at the Bentwaters or Woodbridge
front gate or stuck out at East Gate looking for East End
Charlie - the WWII German pilot ghost.
[END]

I thought this might be of interest - I noticed it on a
web site for former base Security Police personnel:

[BEGIN]
As I write this, I am looking at two 3X5 inch index
cards.. part of a larger group of index cards which
comprised my diary while at RAFs Woodbridge & Bentwaters.
Now read verbatim what I wrote back in June 1980 onto
these two 3X5 cards.. clearly, a half a year before the
now famous December 1980 incidents:

"15 June 80 - Interesting nite - it's our 2nd mid and
Wagner & Campbell have A-2. They sighted a UFO at five
different occasions that nite. Described as a red globe
20ft. in diameter. It hovered at times over aircraft
pads/structures. Labrucherie also sighted the UFO; he had
A-1. At one time they said the UFO glided over the trees
to a meadow where it suddenly disappeared into a white
flash (pooof!) and then nothing; except two deer which
they say were not there previously. I believe this story
to be authentic."

A-2 was the area security patrol & A-1 was the entry
control post to the Alpha aircraft parking area at RAF
Bentwaters. The word "mid" references our midnight shift.

Ken Kern.
[END]


Extraordinary; multiple observations [although a second-
hand account] of one or more, suspicious, unidentified
aerial lights in a what should be a secure area and
they're reconciled as 'UFOs'.

If "our 2nd mid", sounds like they might have been young,
inexperienced Airmen, only recently arrived on base.

Can we perhaps presume these incidents [especially the
materialising deer] were not reported!
